I absolutely loved the original Killing Floor. And there is a base for an extremely great game here.  The optimization is extremely good and gun play is fun. The main problem here is an extreme lack of content. The game is still missing a sharpshooter class, and the official map pool is tiny. And most perks only have 3-5 guns with usually only 2 viable towards the end of the match. Content updates have been few and far between, expect to wait up to 3 month for a small amount of content. For example our last update that gave us any real content was on 3/24/16 it was two gun, one map, vs mode, and some bug and balance fixes. The last major patch before that was on 12/3/15 and added a new boss, two maps, a perk, new character, and micro transactions. The game has been in Early Access for around a year and very little has been added in terms of content. At the current rate of development it will take another year or two to have enough content that I would consider this game as a full release. I would recommend that you wait another year before considering this game because you’ll have a way better experience and hopefully more content. I’ll update this review when I feel this game is ready to be recommended.

My main complaint is the batmobile. The controls are a bit odd to me,  and the game forces you to use it alot, when I prefer gliding around the city.

I play my games on a laptop, which uses an i7 4th gen processor that runs @ 2.60GHz and an Nvidia Geforce GTX 960m 2GB, alond with 16 gigs of ram. Now I'm just going to say this: A 2 GB graphics card will NOT run your game at anything above low setting, at 720p.  That being said, If you have a 2GB graphics card, but NEED high, 1080p, 60FPS gameplay, stay away. However if you dont mind making a few sacrifices, get the game.  Its worth it.

This game is a lot like Chibi Robo. It's cute, amounts to something, and provides fun when there's something to do.  But there's no end-game after the final boss except to finish achievements.  And by finishing achievements I mean finishing the achievements you can. Sadly this game has a lot of content that remains inaccessible after you finish the area.  For example, there are a few friends and such, like Clyde, that if you do not approach them incredibly early they remain barred for the rest of the game.  Likewise, there may be chinpokomon and even items that you miss should you move too quickly through areas.  This renders a somewhat nervewracking dungeon crawling experience if you're trying to achieve everything.
I give this game an 8/10.  It makes no big flaws (though glitches and bugs can potentially ruin your game if you don't have a previous checkpoint) but at the same time offers nothing worth sixty dollars (I highly suggest waiting for a sale).  Combat, graphics, equipment, etc. are all at acceptable levels, but nothing exceeds expectations.  Conversely, it relies way too much on its South Park-esque charm to make up for not having any uniquely interesting aspects.  As such while I would recommend this game, it would only be to South Park fans who will be reduced to giggling children when they see their favorite references.  Let's hope that more interesting DLC or updates come out for the game.  Personally, I would enjoy a time machine that would allow you to play past boss fights and visit previous areas, but would settle for anything at all that gives me something to do besides hitting parking meters until I can get my Hasselhoff Rhinoplasty.

Killling floor is certainly a rising star, a diamond in the rough, a game that clearly has potential, as evident by the fact that the core game runs flawlessly for the most part, looks amazing and operates smoothly. But alas, due to the recent actions overtaken by the developer of the game, TWI, this potential is all but wasted.
First of all, ill elaborate a bit more on what makes Killing floor 2 a good game in principal. The graphical upgrade over its predecassor is clearly visible, and much welcomed. The new gore system, along with the persistent blood mechanic is also a nice and fitting addition to the game. Weapon handling is moreover, heavily improved, with loads of new animations, and weapon features. All of these make for a solid base, in which KF2 could build so much on, and become a truly amazing game.
As for the actions that completely undermine the current and future success of the game, they seemingly have no end, but ill try and sum them up.
Firstly comes Balance. One of the very reasons TWI decided to go the EA route with KF2, was that they wanted to balance out the game, before they released it. However, since release, the game has become progressively even more and more unbalanced. This in it of itself due to a plethora of reasons. First of all the Devs seem to be of the mindset, that if something is overperforming in contrast to something else, the "OP" weapon is to be brought down, to match the underperformance of the other equipment. This would make sence in a PvP game, were you go against each others equipment, but when this principle is used on a PvE game, the result is that in the end, you end up with everyone on the human side having equaly underperfoming equipment, that is useless against the normal, but in contrast overperforming equipment of the AI. This has resulted in many classes and weapons having been rendered useless, and only but a few last pieces of equipment and classes, remain META and useful. Secondly, the artificial enhancement of the difficulty of the AI, also plays a part in the inbalance. Namely, absurd systems, as AI teleporting magicly on the map, or magicly raging for no reason, when the AI numbers are diminished play a huge part in making the game unnesseserily hard. In this way they also force the player to stay on the move, thus taking away any prospect of playing defensively, a strategy option that brings much needed life to PvE games. Lastly, contrary to what the developer has promised, community and player feedback is listened to rarely if at all. They ignore issues brought up by the community, or even suggestions based on data, and instead only change stuff that are easy to change, or that they themselves agree with. Overall, they seem like they are more interested in making a game they themselves would like to play, and not something the community and the players would.
The second nail in the coffin, so to speak, was the poor handling and introduction of the completely consumer unfriendly Microtransaction system. With the system at hand, anyone interested in interacting with cosmetics in the game, be it because they like fassion gaming, role playing, completioning or because they would like to support the developer, are bound to get ripped of, That is because currently, theres only 2 ways to acquire cosmetics. 1) spend away money at RNG keys and crates, in hopes of getting what you want. 2) paying the arbitrarily set ludicrous prices in the steam market. (There is also the "option" to get cosmetics by crafting low tier drops into them, but based on calculations done by many, expecting to acquire anything of value from this, will require you to play for an absurd amount of time. Therefore this isnt really an option). In both cases, you should expect to pay upwards of 10 dollars, just for a few cosmetics, and god forbid you go for, again arbitrarily, "precious" or "master crafted" items, as these will cost you the price of the game itself severalfold. As if this wasnt enough, this horrid system, often found in F2P games, is put in a 25 euro game, about 7 months into EA, almost without any notice.
The third major hinderance to the success of the game, is the development plan and time scedule. First of all, the game has surpased the developers own estimation, and the end is nowhere near. By the time it is finished, if at all that is, it will surely be half a year late, if not more. And while the game is already way past its deadline, the developer is still messing around with modes and ideas, no one asked for, like PvP modes, while also retracting on key features promised to be in the game (like crawlers walking on ceiling and walls). The update scedule is also severly lacking. They release an update every 4-6 months, by which time everyone has left, because they have played the same thing over and over, and when they come back they play the new things over and over for the next week then get bored again. This vicious cycle results in players loosing interest, even when new content is released.
The last but not least flaw that has to do more with the developer, but also with the game is transparecy. EA is supposed to be a platform, in which developer and player are in close relation, having constant discussion over the game. This can only happen when the developer informs the consumers over their plans, shows that they take into consideration their ideas, and implement the best of them, and give heads up on the progress they are making on a weekly or monthly basis. None of the above are achieved, ironicly so, since the developer even wants to claim they are "doing EA right".
In conclusion, there is no doubt, that given proper care, and management, this game can really shine, and thrive. However, if the current corse is sustained by the developers, its future is bleak at best, non existant at worst. Radical changes ought to be undertaken, in order for the aformentioned core problems that infest the game to be solved, and right now, no will for reparation is epxressed by the developers. Thus I can not recommend the game, especially in its EA fase. Its surely a game you should keep tabs on, in case the developers get their act together, but for now, its only good for just that.

I don't review a whole lot of games but I have to throw out a positive review to curb all the hate lately.  I will acknowledge the fact that development for this game has been slower than the creators anticipated, but the updates that we have received have been of high quality.  It's going to get finished, just slower than expected.  Tripwire has apologized to their community, citing internal issues that have slowed things down.
I will also acknowledge the fact that adding in microtransactions before the game is finished was a mistake.  Worse yet, Tripwire has yet to respond to the communities overwhelming criticism of this issue.  It in no way has any impact on the gameplay, and adds an extra layer of loot crafting/discovery that I find to be kind of fun, but the gaming community is just so SICK of microtransactions that spending any amount of development time on this has turned off a lot of the fans.  Especially before finishing with all the promised perks, maps, and zeds.
People are also complaining about the PVP mode because they never said anything about it when early access started.  I have no problem with this.  If they want their game to compete with the classics like Left 4 Dead, I understand why they wanted to add it in.  Plus, it adds a whole new way to play the game.  And something like PVP absolutely needs to be tested and balanced over and over, and early access is a good place for that.
BUT, these issues aside, this game is incredibly fun, and practically feels like a finished product.  You'll get dozens of hours of fun in with your friends, and in the end, doesn't that make it worth the buying price?  Look at how many hours all the negative reviewers have played.  Don't tell me they didn't find this game fun at all.  I am very satisfied with the $30 I paid, and knowing there will be more features added to the game in the future will keep me coming back.  Plus, mods.  I think I've downloaded and played 30 different modded maps.
On a side note, I knew exactly what I was doing when I bought an early access game.  I knew full well the developer had no contractual obligation to consider my opinions or even finish the game.  I took the risk, because I really wanted to play this game.  You, as well, need to consider those risks.  Early access is not new, so none of us should be surprised if this game ends up stuck in development limbo for eternity. (I'm pretty sure that won't happen though)

The game also has a STACK of lore for you - each item has its own flavour text, and there are logs for all of the monsters you can kill as well. I've thoroughly enjoyed my time with this game, and if you like a challenge, you will too.

This game is well worth the price.  First of all, the gameplay is fantasitc.  The game is set up to get more diffficult as time goes on, as about every 5 minutes the difficulty will increase, which increases spawn rates.  The starting difficulty is Very Easy, but don't be fooled, as even the weakest enemies will still do a sizable chunk of damage.  To survive, you have to keep moving and fighting, or risk being overwhelmed.  However, more enemies means more things to kill for cash, which is used to open chests and purchase items. There are two types of items in the game that you can get through a variety of means such as opening chests, killing bosses, and using shrines..  The first are the common passive items that give bonuses  buffs or simple mechanics (such as 14% reduced damage taken, or causing dead enemies to drop pieces of meat that restore your health).  The other items are active items which are used once then go on a cooldown before you can use them again.  They can be anything from a barrage of missiles, a gateway to teleport you between two locations, and many more.  As for the combat, each class has 4 skills, which vary greatly between each class, but are organized broadly to make learning each class intuitive.  The first skill is your primary weapon and main method of dealing damage.  The second skill is usually a crowd control option with either a big AoE or piercing.  The third skill is a defensive tool used to block or avoid damage, and get out of tough spots.  Finally, the fourth skill are special attacks/abilities that deal a variety of effects, with the fourth usually being the strongest and is upgraded with a specific item.  Each of the skills (aside from the first) have a cooldown that varies in length for each one, with no two classes having the same cooldowns.  There are ten classes (9 of which have to be unlocked), each with their own strenghts and weaknesses.  The First Class, the Commando is one of the most well rounded, and has excellent mobility and damage, making him a great choice even after having unlocked other classes.  As for the monsters, there is a good variety between the monsters, with each of them feeling unique and dangerous, ranging in size from relatively large to holy hell that mountain is trying to kill me!  You are the smallest thing on screen making you realize exactly how much peril you are in.
As for graphics, they are great.  The looks good, and unless you have a strong distaste for pixels.  There isn't anything wrong with them.  Stages are well designed, each feeling vastly different from the last.  Both foregrounds and backgrounds are well detailed, and pleasing to the eye, yet grim at the same time.  Each stage has two different settings that the game will randomly choose between, which add to the replayability.  The soundtrak is probably the most amazing thing about this game, and I highly recommend that you listen to it.  It is spectacular.

I'm not really considered a die-hard fan of KF considering I've only casually played the first one for about 2 years on and off. I thoroughly enjoyed that game though so I had to try this one out. This game exceeded my expectations because I thought it was just going to be a visually superior copy of KF1 with same everything else. Not quite.
Although weapons and characters are not as plentiful as the first game (yet), the current selection still offers a lot of enjoyment considering how much special attention the audio and animation get. But not to say that the textures, lighting, physics, gore, etc are also really amazing. The best aspects of this game are probably the weapons, gore, and bullet time that makes it seem like your Neo minus the stunts.
Throughout an entire game, no matter how many zeds you kill, there blood splatter will remain on the map and eventually lead to large blood soaked areas. It's a really cool thing because I have yet to see another game that does this.
The weapons are loud, detailed, and just plain fun to use. It's hard to describe in detail but just keep in mind a lot of work went into them. The fact that there's to two end-match bosses now are really cool because you didn't get that option in the previous game. You won't know who you're going to fight until it's time to fight it.
Bullet time is cool as hell. Things slow down for a few seconds allowing you to react and make a few extra carefully placed shots. The zeds are a whole lot creepier too. Lively animation and sounds completes the immersion in this game, especially for Scrakes and Fleshpounds. First time I heard the stomping of the Scrake as he was pointing at me was insanely intimidating.
As for bad there really isn't anything major at all. I have a few gripes. The characters now have dialogue with unique voices but limited lines. Most of what they say is just stupid and cheesy too. Things like "If I weren't killing zeds, I'd make a snowman". The randomness in characters was fitting in the first game because it felt more like a casual arcade-style survival shooter. In this it makes me feel uncomfortable as if there should be some consistency. Here you got some samuri guy, a gangster, generic military guy from first game, Mr. Foster, a punk girl, etc. This line-up would have felt better in KF1 but this no longer feel like the type of game that would work in. Idk maybe it's just me.
Other things is the workshop. Tripwire decided to go the CS:GO approach and let people buy keys to unlock cases or USB drives that can be achieved from in-game. Only purpose of these is to unlock random accessories to be used by your character. All of which is optional of course but IMO it all looks ugly and not something I would ever use. So to me receiving these cases and USB drives are completely useless and only good for getting a nickel in the community market. This seems to be the topic of a lot of controversly lately and I don't think it constitutes a negative review at all. That and PVP which I have yet to try, because co-op is amazing enough I don't really want to try anything else.
So maybe the devs jumped the gun buy implementing microtransactions in Early Access before releasing more maps and weapons. Just ignore it and carry on. But people are going crazy and are just looking for another negative review to agree on so they can feel better about their opinion on the insigificant crap. Which is why you all gave me a thumbs down for a "helpful review". Personally I feel like the game is going uphill from when it was first released and everyone needs to chill. Come back and complain when you invest in a Early Access game where the developer disappears forever and there's no way to get your money back.
Another thing people seem to complain about is forum cencorship. I don't visit the forums so I can't speak on this. But your review is supposed to reflect the game itself for the most part. Not what goes in the the forums. If things are going downhill in there, make a note of it in your review but don't let it determine your overall recommendation for this game. I feel the vast amount of negative reviews is unjustifiable all because Tripwire decided to implement PVP and Versus early and started policing their forums. Relax.
Anyways, so for the most part yeah there's a lot of the same things carried over from the first game to this, but they built upon everything so much that it doesn't even feel remotely familiar. It's an amazing game worth every cent to me. Let the developers do their thing and just enjoy their game in the eman time.

I absolutely loved the original Killing Floor. And there is a base for an extremely great game here.  The optimization is extremely good and gun play is fun. The main problem here is an extreme lack of content. The game is still missing a sharpshooter class, and the official map pool is tiny. And most perks only have 3-5 guns with usually only 2 viable towards the end of the match. Content updates have been few and far between, expect to wait up to 3 month for a small amount of content. For example our last update that gave us any real content was on 3/24/16 it was two gun, one map, vs mode, and some bug and balance fixes. The last major patch before that was on 12/3/15 and added a new boss, two maps, a perk, new character, and micro transactions. The game has been in Early Access for around a year and very little has been added in terms of content. At the current rate of development it will take another year or two to have enough content that I would consider this game as a full release. I would recommend that you wait another year before considering this game because you’ll have a way better experience and hopefully more content. I’ll update this review when I feel this game is ready to be recommended.

This is the best purchase ive ever made where i knew almost nothing about the game beforehand and its the only rougelike if been able to enjoy since Binding of Isaac, which ill be comparing this to a lot.
Risk of Rain is like you combined the gameplay systems of dota 2 and put them in a side scrolling shoot'em up, a formula that works suprisingly well and makes for some great gameplay. The real reason i love this game aside from the good gameplay is that it feels fair and balanced so i dont feel like im getting ♥♥♥♥ed over by rng (Binding of Isaac, Spelunky, Rouge Legacy, etc.) every item feels like it is useful and there are no items that feel like a guarenteed win, like getting epic fetus in Binding of Isaac. The levels are prebuilt and not randomly made so it doesnt feel like im getting ♥♥♥♥ed over by the level layout, though it doesnt matter so much in RoR as in other rougelikes ive mentioned, items and enemies are randomized so the rng is still there its just not as offensive as it is in something like BoI. What also makes it great is the multiple classes that you can play as that all play radically different and actually change the way you play and your playstyle rather than just new moves and such that hardly change the game at all, the ways to unlock them are for the most part interesting except for some like the huntress who is completely dependent on getting lucky with drops to unlock. the art direction is top notch and for once im not upset that an indie game uses NES type graphics like its going out of style because RoR actually makes it look interesting. Enemy and Boss designs are good for the most part, the final boss in particular is fantastic and i really did not see an amazing final boss fight from this game. Not a lot of negative things i can say other than the sound and music isnt too great, the platforming needs improvement, and some characters are much less viable than others. tldr game is great, if you like rougelike gameplay and hate the rng ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t it comes with try it out (EDIT: Sound and music are finei just hadnt listened to it enough, game is a bit buggy and will chug frame rate if there's too much on the screen but thats to be expected)

I bought this game at launch, and I jumped through all the hoops and hurdles and .ini tweaks to get it to run and look nice. It still ran pretty bad. I held off on reviewing it until the patches were released, and there's been a bit of improvement to how the game performs. At 1440p with everything on max(I have a GTX Titan X and i7-5920k), I'd get around 40-50 frames pre-patch. Post-patch, I hover around 80-90, which is good for my high refresh rate panel.
Anyway, this review isn't about tech stuff, and you should really research before you buy if it'll run well on your rig. This game is a good conclusion to the Rocksteady trilogy of Arkham games. A lot of ends were tied up pretty nicely, the improvements in combat are much appreciated, and the colorful Gotham City is a sight to behold. Finally, a fully realized Gotham City! Sure it's pretty fun the first.... ten times you use the tank, but It's too much. A handful of the boss fights are basically tank fights. Blah.
Let's cut to the chase. Yeah, Warner Bros really screwed the pooch with the PC release, but I'm reviewing the game as a game in its optimal performace. You're well within your right to say "F that, I won't support this game!", and I wouldn't object. This game is mired in controversy, but at its core, it's a fun game. We just have to clean all the mess the publishers smeared all over it first.

Not recommended in its current state. There's always hope this could become a great game, but let's consider the reality of that from experience of what has been and recent news:
As of May 2016 , the game has been in development for quite some time already. It seems like every time they release a patch, new problems arise. The updates are few and far between as well. Most recently, the updates have come a bit faster. Should be mentioned though, that was after a really long period where nothing happened. In other words, a lot of hasty "catch up" work has been done. With mixed results. The game is still largely incomplete, that has to be said.
It just can't hold a candle to what KF1 was, so old fans look elsewhere. You will be disappointed. It may be visually appealing, but lacks the soul of the original. KF2 could still be reviewed as a stand alone, online shooter. Which is the stance I have taken for most of this review.
With 200+ hours of game time, unsure if I will keep playing this. Once you progress in level, the idea is to move up to a higher difficulty for more of a challenge. Usually people play on Normal until level 5 or so, then Hard for level 10 or thereabouts, Suicidal is for a class level of about 15 and finally Hell on Earth (HoE) is for levels 20-25. Some will complain if you join HoE with anything less than the maximum, level 25. Beware. The same goes for the other difficulties, above Normal. People have a difference in opinion of what the minimum level to play a difficulty setting is, just as people differ in how well they can play. Note: This all may change, if they alter the game mechanics or tweak the balance. Just know that when you reach HoE as it sits now, there really aren't that many players out there. Filling up a team can be difficult then, so this game sort of has an "expiration date" when you have progressed. Heck, sometimes even finding 1-2 others to play with can be nearly impossible. Kinda like a story driven, puzzle game gets "done" in the way there is a conclusion to be reached, this one just stops dead in it's tracks after a while. Only KF2 is not supposed to be that... It's supposed to be an endlessly replayable shooter. No matter if you maxed out on levels. Well, they failed big time in that regard. You can play solo, but the fun is playing with others. This was designed as a cooperative experience, like KF1 which they based it on. Not sure who asked for PVP, but they added that recently. They should have finished up the other parts instead.
Fact of the matter is, there are too many arguments that arise. Not just about levels, but on how the game is supposed to be played. Quite a few of my friends who played this from the start, have now quit KF2 and moved on to other, better and more complete games. I am considering the same. Tripwire said they would have a more strict anti-troll and anti-harassment policy for KF2. I have not seen much of that. You pretty much have the option here of finding good people trough a lot of testing times with ragers, haters and just plain immature people. Some sore loser dies, they call a vote kick on some random person to blame. This easily means you, and especially the medic class gets a lot of undeserved hate. Even if the survivors really did all they could to help, lots of haters just refuse to accept failure. Some kids swear and are offensive. You just ask them to stop, they gang up on you and call a votekick. Someone's friend wants to join, you were in the game from the start but you're not on the "list". Guess what, votekick to ditch you so that some late joiner can take your place. After a lot of that and more variations of the same category, if you are lucky, you find enough of the good kind to make up a team. If you are all online simultaneously, and all of you can actually sit through one of these matches. That takes a lot of planning, which gets ever increasingly more difficult to do, seeing as so many players stop gaming KF2. If you don't have a full team of 6 players you know and trust, best get ready for vote kick battles between cliques of friend groups who want control of the server.
There are less problems on the lower difficulty settings. So if you are looking for a game to play just for a bit, then go for it. Consider the price, if you think it's worth it for a 1-200 hours of gaming. That's where most of the positive reviews are coming from, those who have played it just a bit. So many happy reviewers who have 50 hours. When everything is new and exciting, it's easy to rave about something then. See this review as one for how KF2 held up to the test of time. Yes, it's still in early development. After 1+ year. Just saying these days new, big games are being developed and released frequently. That in itself, may be an omnious sign of where KF2 is headed.
So, there we have it. Hoping for an improvement, really. But where this game is at the moment, stay clear. If possible, I will update this review or write a new one should the situation improve. *Fingers crossed*

Sid Meier's Civilization V is a strategy game that allows you to play as a certain civilization as a notable leader in human history. This allows you to build your new civilization up from the ground as a small camp to a world superpower by researching technologies, inspiring other civilizations with culture, becoming the leader of the world, building up the strongest military, and/or ruling the world through your religion.
The game looks very appealing, veiwing the whole world like you are looking down on a game board because it goes by hexes (Spaces that allow a unit/resource/city to occupy). The world looks very colorful as it includes different types of terrain such as oceans, desserts, grasslands, and even arctic regions. The game also includes a choice between different generated fields or "Game Boards" such as different sized continents or a Pangea like continent. You can choose between many different civilizations in history from the United States, to England, to Germany, to Portugal, to the Zulu tribe and different Native American tribes. You can even customize the options even further by determining the number of civilizations and city-states and can determine which type of victories there are within the game. These include Domination, Science, Diplomatic, and Cultural. The Steam Workshop allows you to customize the game even more.
I think this game is very entertaining because you can build up many cities to your own customizations especially if you include your own mods. However this game can be very long and can be stretched out from hours to weeks for a single game, depending on how long you play. I still love this game regardless!

Risk of Rain is a "Rouge Lite" platformer developed by two college students under the name Hopoo Games. In the game you control one of twelve total characters, marooned on a strange and unknown planet, each with their own abilities, stats and uses. You traverse the multiple levels attempting to get back to the ship you crashed on the planet with, facing enemies and bosses of increasing strength and gathering the lost cargo of the ship to make you more powerful along the way.
This is a 2D action platformer, where, as previously stated, you attempt to get to the final level and escape the planet you were marooned on. As you play, you unlock more characters and items in a similar way to The Binding of Isaac where as you play and make progress, you gain new items and characters. The characters are all different and have different abilities across the board. The default character, The Commando, have a high fire rate and deals moderate damage, but high knockback, making him a good crowd control character. On another end The Sniper has an ability that guarantees critical hits on stronger enemies, making him much better for bosses or singular targets.
The goal of each level is to reach a teleporter to, you guessed it, teleport to the next level after fighting a 90 second long wave of enemies and killing all the enemies before you can progress. There's a unique difficulty mechanic in this game, it becomes more difficult the longer you play, what I mean by that the seconds that you spend in each level increases the difficulty, adding a sort of risk reward system when you have to decide if you should farm the level more or check for items that you missed,
Overall, Risk of Rain is a high quality game that I'd recommend to people who are looking for a challenge or a good game to play with friends, did I mention this was Co-Op? Yeah, it is. Risk of Rain gets a 9/10 from me.

It's no secret that Arkham Knight was nothing short of dumpster fire when it first launched on the PC. Months later after subsequent patching and fixes, does the game run any better? Well, yes, but not by much. The game still suffers from stuttering under certain settings and unless you have high-end hardware, this isn't going to be very playable for you. It's a shame considering the game looks exceptionally great, with detailed character models, lighting, and rain effects that surpass what was capable of its predecessors. Similarly, the sound in Arkham Knight is excellent, especially given the roar of the Batmobile, the sound of gunfire, the patter of Batman's cape as you glide through the wind, and the voice acting as well is superb, with Mark Hamill delivering one hell of a final performance as The Joker. The music is intense, brooding, and atmospheric (as it should be), as Nick Arundel and David Buckley return to compose for the Arkham series. Overall, in every department except for system performance, Arkham Knight delivers.
You're the Goddamn Batman. After years of plotting, the supervillain Scarecrow unleashes a widespread attack on all of Gotham City. Millions of Gotham citizens are deported as the police and Batman prepare to do battle with an army of supervillains. However, they must also confront a mysterious new villain-- the Arkham Knight, a militia commander with a connection to Batman's past, if they are to take back Gotham once and for all.
The much hyped concluding story to the Arkham Trilogy is the one that ultimately falls the flatest in the whole series. It's definitely got it's moments, and some very clever plot points (such as Batman having visions of Joker) make for some really out of the box encounters, but none of it makes up for the remainder of the story. It goes from one meaningless conversation with Alfred to one meaningless encounter with drones again and again until some kind of plot twist occurs that doesn't have the impact it should. At the very end, I found myself describing the story for Arkham Knight wtih two words I thought I'd never say about an Arkham game: boring and forgettable.
Arkham Knight finally gives you a fully-realized Gotham City, littered with detail and complexity unlike any city you've explored in any video game. Much of the city is fully destructable, which may make for fun Batmobile rampages, but doesn't help the fact that the city feels lifeless and empty. Having civillians on the streets and people walking about would have certainly made this less so. Arkham Knight features the most side content in any Arkham game yet, but sadly its arrangment of side content has devolved into an Ubisoft open world style of activities. Each activity repeats itself a certain number of times before you've completed all of that activity. Rarely do these activities feature the type of meaningful engagements found in the side content of previous Arkham games, and as a result, end up feeling repetitive and pointless. Thankfully there is some fun stuff to do, such as milita checkpoints and riddler trophies, but the rest feels like a wasted opportunity.
Arkham Origins, a spinoff of the Arkham series that was fairly successful, proved how well-realized and fun the gameplay forumla for the Arkham series can be after multiple games. In Arkham Knight, nearly every aspect of the pre-exisiting gameplay has been improved; the free-flow combat is faster and features more moves and abilities to take down an even wider range of enemy types; stealth encounters feature more challenging enemy types and more ways to take down enemies; gliding is faster and more maneuverable than before; there are several new and different gadgets than previously featured; and the level design is just about as great as it was before, albeit lacking ample puzzle variety that would require you to use all of your gadgets more often. For the most part, all of these gameplay elements feel pretty solid.
However, there is one new feature in Arkham Knight that hurts the focus on these great gameplay elements and ultimately brings down the game: the Batmobile. While the induction of Batman's greatest gadget seems like a brilliant idea on paper, the execution in-game is kinda iffy. It's very fun to drive around in and tear through the streets of Gotham, though gliding remains to be a more effective method of traversal (and its more fun). The Batmobile weapon systems seem cool at first, but are fairly limited and make drone combat encounters frustratingly simple and boring. What makes it even worse is that the game forces you to use the Batmobile so much throughout the campaign that it overshadows the more refined gameplay aspects of Arkham Knight. The only aspect of the Batmobile I genuinely enjoyed was it's use for puzzles, though some might find these somewhat forced as well. In the end, your miliage with the Batmobile will vary, though I certainly didn't enjoy it as much as the game probably wanted me to.
Batman: Arkham Knight is the biggest and most badass entry into the Arkham saga to date. As highly antipcated as this game was for concluding the Batman story, it ends on a dissapointing note, despite some very clever moments throughout the story. Gotham City is packed with detail and filled with things to do, but neither of these eclipse the lifeless feeling of the city nor the meaningless nature of the side content. Combat, stealth, gliding, puzzles, and level design have all been excellently-refined, but lose the focus they deserve to the Batmobile, which unnecessarily forces more mediocre gameplay upon you. While Arkham Knight may be the Batman game we neither deserved nor needed, it's still filled with many moments of greatness and stands as a fairly decent open-world game.. assuming you're PC can run it.

Risk of Rain is a "Rouge Lite" platformer developed by two college students under the name Hopoo Games. In the game you control one of twelve total characters, marooned on a strange and unknown planet, each with their own abilities, stats and uses. You traverse the multiple levels attempting to get back to the ship you crashed on the planet with, facing enemies and bosses of increasing strength and gathering the lost cargo of the ship to make you more powerful along the way.
This is a 2D action platformer, where, as previously stated, you attempt to get to the final level and escape the planet you were marooned on. As you play, you unlock more characters and items in a similar way to The Binding of Isaac where as you play and make progress, you gain new items and characters. The characters are all different and have different abilities across the board. The default character, The Commando, have a high fire rate and deals moderate damage, but high knockback, making him a good crowd control character. On another end The Sniper has an ability that guarantees critical hits on stronger enemies, making him much better for bosses or singular targets.
The goal of each level is to reach a teleporter to, you guessed it, teleport to the next level after fighting a 90 second long wave of enemies and killing all the enemies before you can progress. There's a unique difficulty mechanic in this game, it becomes more difficult the longer you play, what I mean by that the seconds that you spend in each level increases the difficulty, adding a sort of risk reward system when you have to decide if you should farm the level more or check for items that you missed,
Overall, Risk of Rain is a high quality game that I'd recommend to people who are looking for a challenge or a good game to play with friends, did I mention this was Co-Op? Yeah, it is. Risk of Rain gets a 9/10 from me.

Not recommended in its current state. There's always hope this could become a great game, but let's consider the reality of that from experience of what has been and recent news:
As of May 2016 , the game has been in development for quite some time already. It seems like every time they release a patch, new problems arise. The updates are few and far between as well. Most recently, the updates have come a bit faster. Should be mentioned though, that was after a really long period where nothing happened. In other words, a lot of hasty "catch up" work has been done. With mixed results. The game is still largely incomplete, that has to be said.
It just can't hold a candle to what KF1 was, so old fans look elsewhere. You will be disappointed. It may be visually appealing, but lacks the soul of the original. KF2 could still be reviewed as a stand alone, online shooter. Which is the stance I have taken for most of this review.
With 200+ hours of game time, unsure if I will keep playing this. Once you progress in level, the idea is to move up to a higher difficulty for more of a challenge. Usually people play on Normal until level 5 or so, then Hard for level 10 or thereabouts, Suicidal is for a class level of about 15 and finally Hell on Earth (HoE) is for levels 20-25. Some will complain if you join HoE with anything less than the maximum, level 25. Beware. The same goes for the other difficulties, above Normal. People have a difference in opinion of what the minimum level to play a difficulty setting is, just as people differ in how well they can play. Note: This all may change, if they alter the game mechanics or tweak the balance. Just know that when you reach HoE as it sits now, there really aren't that many players out there. Filling up a team can be difficult then, so this game sort of has an "expiration date" when you have progressed. Heck, sometimes even finding 1-2 others to play with can be nearly impossible. Kinda like a story driven, puzzle game gets "done" in the way there is a conclusion to be reached, this one just stops dead in it's tracks after a while. Only KF2 is not supposed to be that... It's supposed to be an endlessly replayable shooter. No matter if you maxed out on levels. Well, they failed big time in that regard. You can play solo, but the fun is playing with others. This was designed as a cooperative experience, like KF1 which they based it on. Not sure who asked for PVP, but they added that recently. They should have finished up the other parts instead.
Fact of the matter is, there are too many arguments that arise. Not just about levels, but on how the game is supposed to be played. Quite a few of my friends who played this from the start, have now quit KF2 and moved on to other, better and more complete games. I am considering the same. Tripwire said they would have a more strict anti-troll and anti-harassment policy for KF2. I have not seen much of that. You pretty much have the option here of finding good people trough a lot of testing times with ragers, haters and just plain immature people. Some sore loser dies, they call a vote kick on some random person to blame. This easily means you, and especially the medic class gets a lot of undeserved hate. Even if the survivors really did all they could to help, lots of haters just refuse to accept failure. Some kids swear and are offensive. You just ask them to stop, they gang up on you and call a votekick. Someone's friend wants to join, you were in the game from the start but you're not on the "list". Guess what, votekick to ditch you so that some late joiner can take your place. After a lot of that and more variations of the same category, if you are lucky, you find enough of the good kind to make up a team. If you are all online simultaneously, and all of you can actually sit through one of these matches. That takes a lot of planning, which gets ever increasingly more difficult to do, seeing as so many players stop gaming KF2. If you don't have a full team of 6 players you know and trust, best get ready for vote kick battles between cliques of friend groups who want control of the server.
There are less problems on the lower difficulty settings. So if you are looking for a game to play just for a bit, then go for it. Consider the price, if you think it's worth it for a 1-200 hours of gaming. That's where most of the positive reviews are coming from, those who have played it just a bit. So many happy reviewers who have 50 hours. When everything is new and exciting, it's easy to rave about something then. See this review as one for how KF2 held up to the test of time. Yes, it's still in early development. After 1+ year. Just saying these days new, big games are being developed and released frequently. That in itself, may be an omnious sign of where KF2 is headed.
So, there we have it. Hoping for an improvement, really. But where this game is at the moment, stay clear. If possible, I will update this review or write a new one should the situation improve. *Fingers crossed*

This game takes the old X-com - one of the most interesting and well-loved turn-based tactical games of it's time - updates it with modern gaming technology, and manages to lose none of the core of what made X-com great. Some of the features I would have done differently, but ultimately, I cannot bring myself to complain.
The tactical genre has been dead for a long while - in fact, who am I kidding? It never took off. Everyone was always interested in FPSes and strategy games that had arbitrary mechanics like StarCraft. Not to bash on those, but the idea of a realistic game where you have to manage a war effort - finances, manpower, logistics, actual conduct of battles - has been a niche topic, and I don't know WHY. These games are interesting and addicting, and now, with the addition of this game, they are easy to pick up and play.
Buy it. Buy it full price and tell people that there is a market for this kind of game.

This feels like a long, interactive episode of South Park, complete with satirical jabs at gaming conventions (Audio logs and Nazi zombies, anyone?). The combat is also a very solid, familiar turn-based structure, but with the added flair of timed blocks and attacks, so it's not quite as set-and-forget as Final Fantasy and the like. Customization is quite varied, both cosmetic and strategic. You'll often find yourself poring over weapon and gear attachments, debating the merit of stacking certain debuffs or rigging up an anti-armor set instead. The main questline itself, yes, is about four hours long. However, this ignores the gigantic array of worthwhile side quests, which are absolutely worth noting. Replay value is also high, with four classes to choose from, each with a unique array of powers for different playstyles. Long-time fans of South Park will recognize a lot of recurring jokes both new and old, and newcomers will get a pretty strong feel for the show, in a good way. While it is absolutely worth your time, I do strongly suggest waiting for a sale. While it may be Trey and Matt's first real game, in a lot of ways it feels better planned out and executed than a lot of games released by veteran studios today. Absolutely recommended. 10/10

After finding all of those insanely boring Riddler trophies, I changed my mind, I was kinda 'mad' while writing the first one , I still am, but back to the review:
CONS: Game forces you at one point to get all 243 riddler trophies if you want to finish the game properly. And it wouldn't be so much of a Hell if some of these weren't broken. You will come across some insanely boring riddles that you need to go trough, going back to some locations you wanted to escape from while going trough story (at least I felt like that), and this is my biggest problem with the game. It's nice that you gave us opportunity to unlock all those character models that we can inspect at any time from menu, but forcing us to get all those unlockables is silly and really bad idea. Second thing I found annoying are challenges. Especially for people who purchased the Season Pass (as I did), they make huge part of the game, and you will come across a lot of problems. My biggest issue are enemies with shields that for some reason, won't be defeated the same way, to be exact, when I'm using default method to beat them, character will jump over enemy, and you will lose combo. Pretty irritating if you are aiming for 3 STARS on every challenge.
PROS: Oh, there are a lot of those. First, as I have skipped 2 games in the series, I do not have a lot to comprare to but Arkham Asylum, and I must say that I enjoyed it (Arkham Asylum), to see how many parts were inspired by first instalment is really beautiful. Graphics in this game are amazing. Seeing how each corner of the building falls down in dozen pieces while driving Batmobile trough alleys... To see how rain drops fall on Batman's cape while gliding... And to see that beauitful sea waves crushing into cliffs... Gameplay is satisfying, pretty much same as Arkham Asylum with way more animations and combo moves. There are a lot of new gadgets that I don't remember from Asylum as well as some that were in the game back then. Of course, Batmobile is really awesome, despite people saying how it's overused etc. I must disagree, it's welcome change, and it's really funny to use it, as well as race challenges that come with it. Story is amazing, very nice, and game is absolutely better than Arkham Asylum in every way, but it's 5 years between them, I must check Arkham City, maybe update this post once again.
Now, is it worth the price, as you know, launch for this game was a complete mess. And the dropped idea of supporting multiple GPU's make that pile of s*it bigger, but on my configuration (i7 920, GTX 680, 12GB Ram) it performs well, Hell, it performs nice if compared to launch edition. So, yeah, if you have good PC it definitely is worth the price... Season Pass on the other hand, not really. If you really want to enjoy those episodes and Season Of Infamy, sales may be your savior.

This is an amazingly designed game. If you like roguelikes and/or pixel shooters, stop reading and buy this game.
Risk of Rain is so, so well designed. The game feels organic, being completely foreign and impossibly difficult when you start playing, but becoming more familiar and easier as the game goes on; but not by virtue of leveling up or any kind of avatar strength. Instead, the player becomes more familiar with the level layouts, the monsters, the items, the bosses, and the characters themselves as they play, gaining a sense of skill along the way.
This is the way roguelikes should feel. Hostile, mysterious, and dangerous. But as you die and die and die, you learn and grow as a player, carving a much easier path for yourself through the game.
Not to mention that the art and music here are both top-notch and unique. If you're a fan of the pixel aesthetic, you'll love the look of the strange alien world.
It's a no-brainer. Highly recommended. You gotta play this.

After finding all of those insanely boring Riddler trophies, I changed my mind, I was kinda 'mad' while writing the first one , I still am, but back to the review:
CONS: Game forces you at one point to get all 243 riddler trophies if you want to finish the game properly. And it wouldn't be so much of a Hell if some of these weren't broken. You will come across some insanely boring riddles that you need to go trough, going back to some locations you wanted to escape from while going trough story (at least I felt like that), and this is my biggest problem with the game. It's nice that you gave us opportunity to unlock all those character models that we can inspect at any time from menu, but forcing us to get all those unlockables is silly and really bad idea. Second thing I found annoying are challenges. Especially for people who purchased the Season Pass (as I did), they make huge part of the game, and you will come across a lot of problems. My biggest issue are enemies with shields that for some reason, won't be defeated the same way, to be exact, when I'm using default method to beat them, character will jump over enemy, and you will lose combo. Pretty irritating if you are aiming for 3 STARS on every challenge.
PROS: Oh, there are a lot of those. First, as I have skipped 2 games in the series, I do not have a lot to comprare to but Arkham Asylum, and I must say that I enjoyed it (Arkham Asylum), to see how many parts were inspired by first instalment is really beautiful. Graphics in this game are amazing. Seeing how each corner of the building falls down in dozen pieces while driving Batmobile trough alleys... To see how rain drops fall on Batman's cape while gliding... And to see that beauitful sea waves crushing into cliffs... Gameplay is satisfying, pretty much same as Arkham Asylum with way more animations and combo moves. There are a lot of new gadgets that I don't remember from Asylum as well as some that were in the game back then. Of course, Batmobile is really awesome, despite people saying how it's overused etc. I must disagree, it's welcome change, and it's really funny to use it, as well as race challenges that come with it. Story is amazing, very nice, and game is absolutely better than Arkham Asylum in every way, but it's 5 years between them, I must check Arkham City, maybe update this post once again.
Now, is it worth the price, as you know, launch for this game was a complete mess. And the dropped idea of supporting multiple GPU's make that pile of s*it bigger, but on my configuration (i7 920, GTX 680, 12GB Ram) it performs well, Hell, it performs nice if compared to launch edition. So, yeah, if you have good PC it definitely is worth the price... Season Pass on the other hand, not really. If you really want to enjoy those episodes and Season Of Infamy, sales may be your savior.

I'd like to preface this 'review' with I love this game. But I can't, in good conscience let this slide. TWI has lost sight of their goal. They have their sights on sources of income. I am mostly fine with their cosmetic microtransactions (the prices could be tweaked a bit, and the different qualities such as battle scarred, field tested, mint, could be done away with), but they no longer have the original spirit as when they started. Whether this is because they are running out of money or any other reason is speculation at this point, but they are handling it completely wrong. I'd like to go over the primary reasons for my rant: things that they have promised and have done.
Censorship in the discussion board? Not cool, and completely undermines the United State's constitutional rights. Why are they doing this? well there could be various reasons: to promote their game in a more favorable light, or maybe since they have heard the criticism long enough they have built up tolerance for it and no longer deem them important. Maybe they hired some new guy who is going ham as a moderator. Regardless of what their intent is, censorship is
the answer. As people, we need positive
feedback to challenge ourselves and improve. Because of this, the only way to let others know about the issues in the game is to read reviews such as this one or find it elsewhere.
Attention to detail? Maybe, but I still see some slop in areas. I thought you guys had gun nuts on the dev team? The 9mm casings flying out of the Desert Eagle; double action trigger of a Beretta that is cocked is in the double action position instead of being in the single action position; hitting reload to mess with your scar or ak's ejection port and it stays closed.
Early Access done right? Again,
. When the game first launched, there were only 4 perks. Even then, switching between them caused some perks to carry over. Parry was pretty broken and inconsistent as well. Every update since then has had various bugs:
-Incinerate and Detonate? RPG and other shots do not go where you aim if you turn too fast and fire (I believe this is still an issue).
-Sharpshooter weapons release for feedback with a Prison map? Map crashes with the crossbow when picking up bolts.
-PVP? PVP had human players invulnerable to big zeds when a melee weapon was out. These just go to show how much testing they do before releasing these quality updates. Hell, we didn't even ask for PVP. It's a nice afterthought, but development time should have been spent on the core game. Afterall, we the consumers, and TWI wanted to retain that "core gameplay loop" that made the original so fun and successful.
They have stopped pushing originally planned content and are now focusing on other areas: PVP and Microtransactions when their main game is not even completed yet.
Now you may be wondering, "But Sam, why are you still playing? Why do you support these practices?" The answer is simple: I don't support these practices. As stated earlier, I love this game. Unfortunately it's the only one of its kind. Same goes with Aliens Colonial Marines. It may be underwhelming and not as promised, but its all I got, (either forever or until something better comes out). I am not buying anymore items from the market until TWI gets their crap together. From the looks of it, things are bleak and veering towards following the footsteps of Payday 2: Not listening to their customers/fanbase, and only focusing on greed. They may very well be hurting from lack of income but again, this isn't how it should be handled.
TL:DR - TWI is no longer great and went from Lawful Good to Chaotic Evil. Buyer cautiously beware

Killing Floor 2 was a game I had high hopes for. I joined in on KF1 only a few years ago, but it quickly became one of my favorite games, so of course I hopped right on the KF2 hype train. I didn't expect a perfect game upon release of early access, but I was at least confident that it would turn out all right. Boy was I wrong. I can excuse the slow progress for new content; they're a relatively small company. But there's a lot of things that they did that really don't make sense. They claimed they wanted to balance the game over time, yet they had no method of making small balance patches until a month or two ago, resulting in often terrible balance between major (quarterly) updates. They added a pvp mode that nobody wanted. Sure, they say the game mode development team made it, but what does having two modes imply? It implies they either need to balance guns with consideration for both modes, or create separate balance changes between modes. Both solutions result in requiring more work. Microtransactions wouldn't be so bad if they weren't pure randomness with crates and keys. As it is right now, your only options for getting that one accessory you want are either to spend lots of dosh hoping for what you want, or to buy the item from other players for more money than its probably worth. It doesn't help that in recent months, Tripwire has only added fuel to the fire. A majority of their recent patches have given the impression that they are prioritizing pvp, and forum moderators are becoming trigger happy with the bans for anyone critical of their game. I still get the impression that Tripwire intends to finish this game, and that slow development (at least recently) is partially due to the fact that they lost developers and are having a hard time replacing them. However, a long series of bad decisions and lack of communication has resulted in a snowball of (understandable) negativity in parts of the community. Now, they have resorted to hiding this negativity as much as possible, both on the steam discussion pages and on their own forums. There's so much more I'd like to list but for the sake of brevity, I hope anyone who reads this has already gotten the point.
Anyway, sorry for the long tangent. Back to the actual quality of the game itself: the visuals are great and everything looks amazing compared to killing floor 1.  Game balance is poor, but hopefully that gets fixed eventually. For me, KF2 lacks the replayability of KF1, in its current state. I don't know exactly why, so don't ask. Basically what you should take from this is that if you liked KF1, it doesn't mean you'll like KF2. And now for the bottom line: Is KF2 fun? It's fun when playing with friends (whether they're real life friends or ones you made over the net). But when those friends give up on the game and uninstall because they've lost faith in the developers, it stops being fun. In other words, don't get this game if you want to join public groups with randoms.

Opinionated Cons:

Awesome game.
Uh, details. So, it's sort of platformer action roguelike. Your goal on every level is to reach the teleporter, activate it, survive for a while and kill the remaining enemies on the level. Every enemy you kill gives you experience, which increases your character's damage, durability, speed, and so on (a bit depending on what class you play). You also get currency you can use to open chests, buy items, or gamble items. Anyway, currency = usually items in one form or another.
The thing is, the enemies get constantly stronger. The longer you take to finish a level, the stronger the enemies will be on the current level, and every following level. You need to find a good pace where your character is strong enough to progress, but not take too long and end up weak compared to the enemies.
The game doesn't take too long to finish, I think 20 minutes is doable ( in real time, in game time I think the record is somewhere like 12 minutes - there are items that stop time and such). The first playthrough can take a good while though, since the game isn't exactly easy. You'll likely unlock at least a few classes on the way.
Every class plays differently, like.. a lot differently. Although after a time the levels will start to repeat themselves, the classes and randomization of items will extend the gameplay value way beyond the initial playthrough.
Don't know what more to say... awesome game, buy it, love it :p

text:
When the original Half-Life was released in 1998, it took the gaming industry by storm. Hopes for a sequel were high, and Valve knew that they had to change the gaming industry again, but surely they couldn't make a sequel that's better than the original, right?
Well, after spending 6 years in development (and having the source code leaked by a hacker in late 2003), Half-Life 2 was released in 2004 to universal acclaim. It took everything we loved about the original Half-Life, and multiplied it ten times over.
As the game begins, you wake up after being put into stasis by that mysterious man in the suit from the first game. Getting off the train, you find out that a lot has changed since you were gone. Everything looks...Orwellian. It turns out that the Earth was taken over by a multi-universal alien force known as the Combine, and you gotta stop them! As you travel throughout the game, you meet underground resistance members who have the same goal in mind. Pretty soon, news spreads around that "The One Free Man" has returned, and you trigger a revolution.
Half-Life 2, in my opinion, is much better than the first game, and is one of the greatest sequels of all time. It may be 10 years old, but it's still an amazing game.

Sid Meier's Civilization V is a strategy game that allows you to play as a certain civilization as a notable leader in human history. This allows you to build your new civilization up from the ground as a small camp to a world superpower by researching technologies, inspiring other civilizations with culture, becoming the leader of the world, building up the strongest military, and/or ruling the world through your religion.
The game looks very appealing, veiwing the whole world like you are looking down on a game board because it goes by hexes (Spaces that allow a unit/resource/city to occupy). The world looks very colorful as it includes different types of terrain such as oceans, desserts, grasslands, and even arctic regions. The game also includes a choice between different generated fields or "Game Boards" such as different sized continents or a Pangea like continent. You can choose between many different civilizations in history from the United States, to England, to Germany, to Portugal, to the Zulu tribe and different Native American tribes. You can even customize the options even further by determining the number of civilizations and city-states and can determine which type of victories there are within the game. These include Domination, Science, Diplomatic, and Cultural. The Steam Workshop allows you to customize the game even more.
I think this game is very entertaining because you can build up many cities to your own customizations especially if you include your own mods. However this game can be very long and can be stretched out from hours to weeks for a single game, depending on how long you play. I still love this game regardless!

Risk of Rain is a solid game when it comes to being a challenge yet still interesting. The best comparison I can make is to The Binding of Isaac, where random number generation is a huge deciding factor, but if the player knows what he's doing and has experience, they can still manipulate their fate within whatever luck they get (that being said, if you enjoyed The Binding of Isaac, you'll definitely enjoy Risk of Rain).
That and the easy route to co-op play if you have the friends are the two top qualities of this game. It has a wide array of both passive and active items to use and a variety of monsters that upgrade in difficulty as time goes on, an interesting and pressing mechanic. Being a challenge game, it also has many unlockables that include new items and new characters, so you can feel rewarded when you set a new milestone as well.
As for graphics, aesthetics, sounds, and narrative, none of it sticks out in a good or bad way. They are pretty much at the point where they only influence the game on an individual basis.
If this game is available for cheap (and if you have friends willing to jump into it with you!), this is a definite buy.

XCOM is not the direct match to the much revered original, but an updated take on the turn based tactical series. The micro-management is replaced by a simple, but smoother, system which occasionally detracts but usually improves on the old tactical game. In doing the same to the geoscape part of the game XCOM loses some of its depth, and can feel detached where the original felt like a desperate race. However, this is a fine addition to the XCOM franchise, easily the best since Terror from the Deep. With mods (courtesy of Steam Workshop) this could be tweaked to taste to become the XCOM every fan was waiting for.

Risk of Rain's fairly simple pixel graphics bely its broad complexity and surprisingly impactful moments. Once you've become accustomed to its pace, unlocking each item becomes an interesting set of self-imposed challenges or goals that change how you play through the game.
By far the biggest mark against Risk of Rain is its initial roster of 1 character and its initially steep learning-curve. Figuring out how to properly engage enemies and pace yourself, as well as how to fully exploit the abilities of your character, as well as what each item does and if its worthwhile to pursue it, combine to create a starting wall that is off-putting. However, once you break through that wall the game opens up to a highly entertaining (and addictive) game that pushes you to improve your play on every run.
Recommended, but seriously consider reading starter guides for general tips and strategy after your first couple of runs.

Risk of Rain is a solid game when it comes to being a challenge yet still interesting. The best comparison I can make is to The Binding of Isaac, where random number generation is a huge deciding factor, but if the player knows what he's doing and has experience, they can still manipulate their fate within whatever luck they get (that being said, if you enjoyed The Binding of Isaac, you'll definitely enjoy Risk of Rain).
That and the easy route to co-op play if you have the friends are the two top qualities of this game. It has a wide array of both passive and active items to use and a variety of monsters that upgrade in difficulty as time goes on, an interesting and pressing mechanic. Being a challenge game, it also has many unlockables that include new items and new characters, so you can feel rewarded when you set a new milestone as well.
As for graphics, aesthetics, sounds, and narrative, none of it sticks out in a good or bad way. They are pretty much at the point where they only influence the game on an individual basis.
If this game is available for cheap (and if you have friends willing to jump into it with you!), this is a definite buy.

Risk of Rain's fairly simple pixel graphics bely its broad complexity and surprisingly impactful moments. Once you've become accustomed to its pace, unlocking each item becomes an interesting set of self-imposed challenges or goals that change how you play through the game.
By far the biggest mark against Risk of Rain is its initial roster of 1 character and its initially steep learning-curve. Figuring out how to properly engage enemies and pace yourself, as well as how to fully exploit the abilities of your character, as well as what each item does and if its worthwhile to pursue it, combine to create a starting wall that is off-putting. However, once you break through that wall the game opens up to a highly entertaining (and addictive) game that pushes you to improve your play on every run.
Recommended, but seriously consider reading starter guides for general tips and strategy after your first couple of runs.

Having played this game some 61h in I have to say I have had a lot of good times with this game. It is awesome and delivers a lot of content. Gameplay is very well done and fun. Graphics are "oldish" but that's the point sort of.
The randomness factor is there, but in fact it is not as well thought out as I would have hoped. In every playthrough you complete six levels the last of which is always the same. For the first four levels there are always two random terrains per level with two random layouts each, and the game just picks one of these. The fifth level is always the same terrain but there are two variations of it. This means that in total there are 4x2x2+2+1=19 possible levels +1 small optional bonus level if I recall this correctly, after some playthroughs you will pretty much remember them by memory. That is not so much and I would have hoped that there is more level content but unfortunately no, and I was a bit disappointed after a few playthroughs when I noticed that I'm actually prancing around the same levels all the time. You can replay the first five levels as many times you want in a playthrough but there is really no reason to do this because the game will get harder and harder. There are also 12 unlockable classes and a lot more unlockable items, some of which are more interesting and useful than the others.
The game is also very difficult, especially in the beginning where you only have one character and a few power-ups. Don't worry, you will get more of these the more you play, every playthrough makes the second one stronger. You WILL die, however. Many times. Sometimes it will infuriate you, because you were so close and it was just so unfair. :) Once you get the hang of it, however, it is probable that you will get pretty far during each playthrough. To me the progression seemed reasonable and fun, but it is also somewhat problematic. The more you play, the following things happen:
#1 you get better power-ups
#2 you get other characters
#3 you simply get better in playing the game
It's all very rewarding, but in the end it actually means that when you get further in the game it gets EASIER. I started playing Monsoon (hardest) difficulty very early, long before I beat the last level and finished the game, so after that there isn't much to do, except unlocking items and classes, trying them out and noticing that they are clearly not as good and interesting as you would have hoped so suddenly the replay value was gone. For this reason I recommend that you play on the normal difficulty at least until you have unlocked quite a few of the items and got the hang of the game.
Game is also great in co-op if you have friends who are into this, although I have mostly played solo. Playing solo is very difficult with some classes, and I would expect that you get the most out of them when trying different class combinations in co-op. All these things considered, the game is very good and having played it quite a bit I will give it a rating of 9,5/10.

Risk of Rain may well be my favourite game of all time.
Now, I love modern shooters and action games at least as much as the next gamer, but you can't go wrong with some good ol' retro-style modern-tech-improved action-platformers. Well, I call it a platformer, although it's really nothing of the sort.
The gameplay's simplistic and easy to learn, but the trick to using it effectively is difficult to learn - and changes with every class. You start with only one class, the Commando, unlocked. The lightest class in the game, he can still dish out some major pain. Other characters are unlocked by completing certain challenges or finding them during gameplay. One even requires you to find him AND defeat him before you can play as him, no small feat on higher difficulties.
Risk of Rain's unique feature is that the longer you play, the more difficult the game gets - and you can choose to play an eternal run if you feel, and eventually conquer the final boss.
Overall, though, the game's visual design is beautiful, gameplay extremely fun on its own but only improved upon when you add in the massive variety of enemies there are to fight. Boss monsters and small monsters generally only improve their health and damage when the difficulty rises, but elite monsters will spawn with increasing regularity when difficulty rises - even boss monsters can have an elite form, which bestows extra health, damage, and effects upon them. Some of these effects include explosive attacks, a passive electrical discharge, or a flaming trail.
I love this game, and love it to bits. Considering the game is only $10, if you're a fan of roguelikes or just love a grand old time, you will love this game.

=============================
This game WAS fun. It WAS great. But now it's just sort of... meh. Sadly, I have to say that Killing Floor 1 beats this.
The base game itself is fun and all, but it's what they did with it that bashed it down to what it used to be.  From an interview, Tripwire had said that when you buy the game, you get everything that comes with it. Maps, weapons, everything. But what do they do? Add a microtransaction 'tf2/csgo' kind of ordeal. Seriously guys?
Are microtransactions necessarily bad? No, not quite. If it's used the right way, that is. But in this game, they aren't.  It's one thing to put them off to the side and are optional. But here, they flash something like one of the 'crates.'  They say, "OOOO! LOOK AT ME! PAY US MONEY TO OPEN THIS AND POSSIBLY GET NOTHING OUT OF IT."
The PvP mode in the game is somewhat entertaining.  The major problem is the fact that the Zeds need to be toned down a little bit.  It added maybe 3 or so hours of playablility, but that's it.
Without trying to get that much into depth, Killing Floor 2 was an amazing game when it traditionally came out.  They promised and they delivered.  But after a while, it just seemed they're not listening to the community anymore. I will change my review stance once I find everything to be satisfactory in HOPEFULLY a few updates.

text:
When the original Half-Life was released in 1998, it took the gaming industry by storm. Hopes for a sequel were high, and Valve knew that they had to change the gaming industry again, but surely they couldn't make a sequel that's better than the original, right?
Well, after spending 6 years in development (and having the source code leaked by a hacker in late 2003), Half-Life 2 was released in 2004 to universal acclaim. It took everything we loved about the original Half-Life, and multiplied it ten times over.
As the game begins, you wake up after being put into stasis by that mysterious man in the suit from the first game. Getting off the train, you find out that a lot has changed since you were gone. Everything looks...Orwellian. It turns out that the Earth was taken over by a multi-universal alien force known as the Combine, and you gotta stop them! As you travel throughout the game, you meet underground resistance members who have the same goal in mind. Pretty soon, news spreads around that "The One Free Man" has returned, and you trigger a revolution.
Half-Life 2, in my opinion, is much better than the first game, and is one of the greatest sequels of all time. It may be 10 years old, but it's still an amazing game.
