Let me describe to you what playing this game is like.
You will start off weak. You will have some basic abilities. You'll find yourself on a planet where everything seems to be trying to kill you for some reason. Even human-like creatures are for some reason all hell-bent on your death. You will kill some weak enemies that appear. You will kill stronger ones as they appear and you get stronger. Your goal is to find the teleporter. Once you do, a boss will appear and more enemies will spawn for the next 90 seconds. You'll kill them all and move onto the next stage to do the same thing. While you're doing this, you'll find items to get stronger and time will tick on, increasing the difficulty.
You'll probably die after a little while though. No denying that. Eventually the enemies will overwhelm you in sheer power or numbers. Maybe you'll make a poor decision and go into a fight that you can't win. Probably you'll get hit with so many attacks all at once that your health will drop all at once. Sometimes it will feel cheap. Sometimes you'll feel like it was your own fault. (and it probably mostly was.) Maybe you'll play like I did and survive for over an hour- hard on its own with the aforementioned difficulty increasing- fight the final boss and then die finally.
And since it's a rouge-like, you'll have to start all over after that. You may unlock some items and characters, but you'll start at the begining.
But you know what? You'll probably start again. You'll have the hopes that you'll get just a little farther this time.
And that's the charm of a game like this. You make it farther each time because you've mastered the mechanics at play. There are unlocks as you go, but most of how far you get comes down to your own skill and the decisions that you make.
If you're looking for an easy game like many modern releases, look elsewhere. There are no checkpoints or respawns. When you die, that's it. And that's part of the apeal. It makes death meaningful and the stakes are always high.

690 hours into this game and from the first hour I could not stop researching conquering and brutally dominating my way to victory.
This may be the best turn based 4x Strategy game I have ever played. In my opinion, this is the best game I know that makes you feel like you are either an unstoppable tyrant or a wise and peaceful leader.
In Sid Meier's Civilization V, you are given the challenge of creating a civilization that will stand the test of time.
From the ancient era to the present and beyond, you must build an empire worthy of victory. Weather that be through diplomacy, science, culture or domination is truly up to you.
This game really has no main story to speak of. Instead, you make your own story. So, the game has almost unlimited replayability.
The single player is stable and the game will run on most computers. It ran on a pretty bad laptop I had on the lowest settings. Until I reached the later eras of the game.
Multiplayer at launch was unstable, but a lot of issues have been sorted out. Now, the multiplayer can be enjoyed without any disruptions, most of the time.
In the game there is a good list of starting civs to choose from but with DLC and expansions, the list of civs and maps is huge. Speaking of DLC and expansions, I reccomend this game to be played with all DLC. That is where you get the best time out of this game for sure so consider buying the complete edition which is a good price for all DLC including the game.
The maps are randomly generated but some maps like the Japanese mainland would be the same map every time but with resource locations randomized.  Maps like Continents, however, are randomized completely but usually form two or three continents or the map terra which is similar to earth in the shapes of the land.
Even with the new Civilization Beyond Earth being released, I still think in my opinion that this game is the best so far. Expansions are still to come out for Beyond Earth so we will see what the finished game will be like with all DLC but for now, this game is a must buy in my opinion if you are into turn based strategy or strategy games in general so I strongly reccomend you gives this a go. You wont regret it.

So, I'm going to start by saying I loved KF1 and had around 1000 hours across different accounts. So before the toxic community white knights start their ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t, I'll start with the positives of Killing Floor 2:
-The graphics looks somewhat better compared to the first game in some areas, for example, in Burning paris you actually see the buring Eiffel, and the map is destructible when it comes to lights.
-The characters look better, but on the same note, I feel that their lore is rather lacking compared to the funny bios we got in the first game
-Some of the zeds actually look better, and others, not so much.
And now for the part nobody wants to read, the negatives:
-Horribly balanced perks to the point that 2 of them are HOE meta since there's no need for the others. (Beserker, Medic)
-A completely pointless welder since they decided to add in perma breaking doors, where as in the first game, the welder had a purpose
-Maps are somewhat poorly designed in layout due to the fact that there's always one point to hole up in
-The AI is god awful when it comes to the ability to zerk wall as it targets the players behind the beserkers rather than the beserkers themselves which sets up for the 2 perk meta I mentioned above
-The gunplay in this game feels really weak, like super soaker weak when it comes to hitting the big guys
-The teleportation is incredibly annoying and game breaking when you need to run away and heal and then the thing you were running away from appears in front of you effectively ruining the point of kiting/evasion recovery tactics
-The scrake and fleshpound went from logical mechanics to bullet sponges, even with explosives
-The game feels really arcadey and overly casual compared to it's prequel
-The trader is now just a pod, rather than a person
-Some of the VA is really awful, even by Killing Floor standards
-The music isn't really fitting when it comes to song choice, it just feels cheesy
-Aside from the zerk wall meta mentioned previously, there isn't really any teamplay aside from spraying the bullet sponges with super soakers
-The MT system is pretty trash, where as the DLC system in the first game was perfect for what was delivered
-The update times are incredibly long and quite laughable for what's delivered on an update day
Overall I'd rate this a 4/10 for obvious reasons.

Firstly, of course I recommend this game, it's aged fairly well and is still one of the best FPS games out there.
Why the thumb's down, then? Well - three words: Orange. Box. Engine.
Yep, I appreciate the achievements and all, but Half-Life 2 from 2004, or so, on the old Source engine was a complete game, a cinematic experience, an adventure etc. etc.
I recently replayed the game and I wish I hadn't - physics are all messed up, ragdolls especially (g_ragdoll_collide doesn't work, which made the Citadel part with the Blue Gravity Gun less fun. Bodies clipping through each other give no real sense of power the blue GG gave in old Half-Life 2), but what really was tragic is the part with the crane. You made a major leap backwards in physics by porting the game on the TOB engine. What else? Scripts, characters feel the urge to walk backwards when talking to me, DOG gets stuck, Rebels get stuck, Alyx gets stuck which results in awkward pauses and immersion ruining teleportation of characters. I've spotted at least three dropships that froze mid-air.
Grigori's final speech simply didn't trigger, if I didn't know what happened from previous times I played this game, I'd say it's not a finished product, and we all know that's not true.
Last but not least, I really don't see the appeal of the updated blood effects. They look out of place, like they're straight out of TF2.
"If it ain't broke, don't fix it." - Especially goes to Counter-Strike: Source, which feels totally different on the new engine.

It saddens me to give this one the thumbs down guys but I've uninstalled the game today and don't forsee re-installing unless there are dramatic changes.
As many reviews have already mentioned, the developers have taken a path to completion that is meandering into territory that is unwanted. Traditionally Killing Floor has always been about a solid class based co-op experience (PvE) and now there is a focus on PvP (humans versus Zed) which in my opinion is problematic - especially at this stage of development - because it has the potential to impact PvE in terms of class/perk abilities i.e. balance decisions as well as taking away developer time that could be used to complete the core game instead (updates are slow).
It seems like at some point during development a decision was made to try incorporate features from other titles such as CS:GO and Left 4 dead which again, in my opinion have no place in the KF2 arena. These features are key/crate purchase systems and the Player verus Player aspect of L4D with humans versus special infected. Instead of focusing on what made Killing Floor 1 at least somewhat unique with systems like the door welding and the gritty atmosphere, Killing Floor 2 is trying to be everything to everyone and that's simply not going to work.
What they did try to take from Killing Floor 1 is currently broken. Door welding (a tactic to barricade yourself from the hordes for a while) is meaningless because of the Zed teleportation "feature" whereby Zeds too far from players will be teleported to a nearby location to the players where no-one is currently looking. Think that corner was safe a second ago? Well look away for a second and surprise - in your face pal - as a Zed suddenly occupies that space and wastes no time in hacking people - that thought they were safe -  to death. Not fun and so many people have complained about this it appears that Devs are not going to address it any time soon - if at all.
Weapon choices are very limited. The perk/class abilities are not all that interesting and really could use a complete overhaul to allow for more combo-play to encourage team-work and up the skill ceiling a bit. It would be much more interesting for perks from one class to directly link-up with perks from another class to deal more damage to enemies or create some other useful defensive effects.
As a PC gamer I am also not pleased to see obvious consolization creep into this title. Chat wheels instead of the key-bound menu drill down from Killing Floor 1, welders only appearing when you are near a door, auto-aim medic healing darts etc. These all impact the PC experience negatively.
So, I rather like the music and graphics in this game - at least those are good in my opinion but not enough to save it.
It is my opinion that you'd be much better off buying Killing Floor 1 at this point even though it is quite a bit older now - the gameplay is so much better.

Stick of Truth is a JRPG with a turn based combat system. The combat is fairly intuitive, with a Super Mario RPG active attack/defense system that allows you to up your dmg, or lower the enemy’s dmg each turn by pressing a button. I did have some issues with defending using the system, but nothing that was a game killer to me. There are elements (Ice, Poison, ect..) that vary the battle, and for the most part it was pretty straightforward. You can have 1 ally aid you in each fight, and for the most part, each ally is different enough to be noticeable. Character balance is the same with any JRPG, mages are OP and the other character builds are sort of fun ideas. I played as a thief and it didn’t affect the gameplay too much, and with each character build there is a few changes in dialog. Honestly, I wish there was more variation to each character (such as an epic sidequest only a thief or Jew gets) but that’s something that might be added later in DLC. Overall, there is a lot to the gameplay that I thoroughly enjoyed, talking to characters was fun, hunting down FB friends ingame was fun, and the general game layout was amazingly detailed while interesting to explore (the first time, still hate all the ♥♥♥♥ing walking I was forced to do). Overall, the game mechanics are easy to pick up, and only a few bumps stand in the way of making it perfect.
The gameplay itself I have mixed feelings about. Depending how you play the game, the difference in gameplay speed can be drastically different, with a few parts of the gameplay that only seem to be included to fabricate game length. For instance: there is ALOT of walking involved in game, and it leaves you begging to have a bike or horse to pick up the pace. There is a travel service, but it only somewhat shortens the length. The travel services also do not take you directly to some key locations that you have to visit several times, thus sort of teleporting you to the front of a place you will have to spend 10+ minutes hoofing it. And because there is a level cap in this game (one easily obtainable) there seems to be no reason why you would want to continue fighting enemies other than for money. I also want to point out that because enemy’s level with you, every place has enemies that you HAVE to fight. What wrong with that? Well I don't want to fight the rats in the damn sewer, because it’s ♥♥♥♥ing pointless, I’m only walking through the damn thing so I can get Mr. Hankey to summon again.
Side quests are fun, but occasionally tedious. I really wanted something more out of them, and there honestly was not enough of them. I feel that it was a great way to compliment the show and maybe give people a chance explore more of each SP character, something that they only occasionally took advantage of. So while I think that there was a lot of game time inflation going on, SOT also has a lot of fun throwbacks to the shows’ history. Also, a game this well thought out for a JRPG missed what I think is the quintessential throwback to the genre, New Game+. I loved playing as a thief, and at the end of the game the first thing I wanted to do, is replay as a Jew. It was frustrating to think that I would have to do a full restart when I have already beaten the game in the manner that let me experience it as a whole. Lufia 2 had an exp multiplyer, as well as a cave to stock up on epic items, Tales of Symphonia had a buff of your choice to apply to your character, and the Granddaddy of all NG+ games Chrono Trigger had a NG+ that allowed you to unlock 10 different endings as well at keep all of your exp and skills. I don’t know what form it should have taken, but I hated that there was no incentive to replay SOT, when it is a game that deserves to be played multiple times. Storyline itself in a humor based game only works the first time, and I know that I will replay the game again someday, but not while the jokes are still fresh in my memory.
The best parts of the game give you the feeling that Matt Stone and Trey Parker really poured everything they had into making a great product. If you like SP humor, then this game is for you. If you like JRPGs, I can say that there isn’t one that has been even close to as good as SOT in years (and I have played many of them). If you like a fast paced game that doesn’t slow down (for a JRPG I mean) than this is the game for you. I know I wrote a lot of negative in this review, but I want to stress that those are the things I noticed that DIDN’T allow me to say that SP:SOT is a perfect game; if these issues are addressed in some DLC down the road, I can honestly say SOT would go to the top 10 of most JRPG enthusiasts lists, it certainly would be in my top 3.

It saddens me to give this one the thumbs down guys but I've uninstalled the game today and don't forsee re-installing unless there are dramatic changes.
As many reviews have already mentioned, the developers have taken a path to completion that is meandering into territory that is unwanted. Traditionally Killing Floor has always been about a solid class based co-op experience (PvE) and now there is a focus on PvP (humans versus Zed) which in my opinion is problematic - especially at this stage of development - because it has the potential to impact PvE in terms of class/perk abilities i.e. balance decisions as well as taking away developer time that could be used to complete the core game instead (updates are slow).
It seems like at some point during development a decision was made to try incorporate features from other titles such as CS:GO and Left 4 dead which again, in my opinion have no place in the KF2 arena. These features are key/crate purchase systems and the Player verus Player aspect of L4D with humans versus special infected. Instead of focusing on what made Killing Floor 1 at least somewhat unique with systems like the door welding and the gritty atmosphere, Killing Floor 2 is trying to be everything to everyone and that's simply not going to work.
What they did try to take from Killing Floor 1 is currently broken. Door welding (a tactic to barricade yourself from the hordes for a while) is meaningless because of the Zed teleportation "feature" whereby Zeds too far from players will be teleported to a nearby location to the players where no-one is currently looking. Think that corner was safe a second ago? Well look away for a second and surprise - in your face pal - as a Zed suddenly occupies that space and wastes no time in hacking people - that thought they were safe -  to death. Not fun and so many people have complained about this it appears that Devs are not going to address it any time soon - if at all.
Weapon choices are very limited. The perk/class abilities are not all that interesting and really could use a complete overhaul to allow for more combo-play to encourage team-work and up the skill ceiling a bit. It would be much more interesting for perks from one class to directly link-up with perks from another class to deal more damage to enemies or create some other useful defensive effects.
As a PC gamer I am also not pleased to see obvious consolization creep into this title. Chat wheels instead of the key-bound menu drill down from Killing Floor 1, welders only appearing when you are near a door, auto-aim medic healing darts etc. These all impact the PC experience negatively.
So, I rather like the music and graphics in this game - at least those are good in my opinion but not enough to save it.
It is my opinion that you'd be much better off buying Killing Floor 1 at this point even though it is quite a bit older now - the gameplay is so much better.

Arkham Knight Experience:
The game has a nice story, the combat system is much better than the earlier games in the Arkham series, and it's just overall good fun. I've played this game a lot compared to other games I have, I just can't seem to get enough of it. The graphics of the game are pleasing even at the lowest quality there is, which is kind of what you have to run at when it comes to this games performance. The performance of the game is absolutely horrible, but it's not always like that. If you're in one area mostly and not moving aorund fast you seem to get great FPS, but when you start moving fast you'll see the entire world has yet to actually load and then it all of a sudden loads and you get a nice little spinning batman symbol in the bottom right corner. This leads me to believe that the game was poorly designed in the concept of rendering the large world, instead of having an overall lower FPS and a constantly rendering world they decided to make it have large FPS drops and even a full pause to load the new area you're in. Now I thought modern games were past that but I guess not. If you can deal with the bad performance design of the game and you want a batman game with a good story mode, I'll highly recommend Arkham Knight. But if you can't deal with the fidgity performance, I'll suggest looking at some of the older games in the Arkham series for a well running batman game.

Firstly, of course I recommend this game, it's aged fairly well and is still one of the best FPS games out there.
Why the thumb's down, then? Well - three words: Orange. Box. Engine.
Yep, I appreciate the achievements and all, but Half-Life 2 from 2004, or so, on the old Source engine was a complete game, a cinematic experience, an adventure etc. etc.
I recently replayed the game and I wish I hadn't - physics are all messed up, ragdolls especially (g_ragdoll_collide doesn't work, which made the Citadel part with the Blue Gravity Gun less fun. Bodies clipping through each other give no real sense of power the blue GG gave in old Half-Life 2), but what really was tragic is the part with the crane. You made a major leap backwards in physics by porting the game on the TOB engine. What else? Scripts, characters feel the urge to walk backwards when talking to me, DOG gets stuck, Rebels get stuck, Alyx gets stuck which results in awkward pauses and immersion ruining teleportation of characters. I've spotted at least three dropships that froze mid-air.
Grigori's final speech simply didn't trigger, if I didn't know what happened from previous times I played this game, I'd say it's not a finished product, and we all know that's not true.
Last but not least, I really don't see the appeal of the updated blood effects. They look out of place, like they're straight out of TF2.
"If it ain't broke, don't fix it." - Especially goes to Counter-Strike: Source, which feels totally different on the new engine.

All right folks, being serious for a second. Risk of Rain is the new red. Really, this game is one of the best (for this price) on the Steam. But I'll get into that in a second.
The story is really well made. Some entity called Providence tp's aboard the cargo ship USS Contact Light and manage to take it down into the alien planet. We, the "heroes" are stranded there, clinging to our lives by all means (which boils down into gulping down every single crap we will find while killing off local wildlife of the planet). The whole point is to, off course, survive and escape. But the story is more than meets the eye. We collect logs throuout our experience, gaining information on how and why we are in this cluster♥♥♥♥ of deadly monsters and stuff. But the authors never gives us definite information. We don't know who or what Providence is, how did he get on board, why did he destroy Contact Light, where are we, what are we fighting and why does everything want to kill us. When I first played the game, after final credits i thought, that with each ending the story will unfold bit by bit, right? Nope, it doesn't. We know jack, we will know jack and all we can think of are some wild theories. Hell there is a whole community theorycrafting as we speak. As if the story itself was some sort of Enigma, which was never meant for the players. Which is awesome! The lone definite thing about the story would be the ultimate question, who is actually the monster here. The Providence, destroying ship because his world is in danger? Wildlife for protecting their young(ever thou it's not implemented, its plausible)? Other entities, wanting to destroy this iddilic planet? Or the player him/herself clinging into his life so thightly, that he would do anything (literally) to preserve it? This moral question is quite strong, while being fun to think for a while.
Graphics are well made. It's a mix between Atari2600 and hand drawn images done right. I really enjoy this kind of pixelness, so for me it's great. If you don't like using imagination thou, you will find no eye candies here. Special effects are also present done well and while being a little too much here and there, they don't obscure our perception over the battlefield.
Music. Oh boy. I don't know who came up with those tunes, but he is the new Ceasar of in-game music. It's that awesome. 8bit chiptunes mixed with some chorals and electric guitars? Olny in RoR! I'm really disappointed that there is no OST to this piece. I want to rock out every time I hear some of those great loops. The olny downside would be sound effects, which are painfully generic, but the music is awesome!
Gameplay is as basic as it gets. We can jump, use skills, run and use usable items. That's it. It's like a mix between SMB and roguelike. We gain levels and collect crap to make our character stronger while jumping around and killing of hordes of monsters. Every now and then the boss will pop up to endanger our lives even more in the constant outslaugh of enemies. As I said, it's quite fun.

Review 2.0, post release.
Great Co-op game. Expanded and improved gameplay from the orignal game: more enemy types (elites) and attacks, 10 player classes with perk skills every 5 levels, some maps change during gameplay (ex. starting at dusk and getting darker as waves progress), leveling improved from Killing Floor 1, some weapons are dual class (where logical), and crate drops can be recycled to craft weapon skins or cosmetic items.
Weapon selection is currently smaller than the orignal but, since release, several weapons have been added or announced.

Risk of Rain is a 2D platformer rogue-like. Within a sci-fi setting you have to explore different planets using a champ of your choice. To leave a planet, you have to beat a boss. Afterwards, you can progress to the next planet. The levels have slightly random layouts to increase the replay value.
While being on a planet, enemies will spawn in different time intervals. The main rule of the game is: The more time passes, the harder it gets. To scale you can both level up your champ and more importantly, find/buy items along your way.
When first starting the game, you can only chose one champ. But the more you play and unlock, the more champs you will be able to select from. Each champ has 4 different spells to chose from (no mana, only CD-based). Additionally, you can carry one active item to activate if you need it. Most items give passive effects.
The game is hard as nails, but a lot of fun. The variaty of champs, items and enemies makes it a lot of fun. At times, it can be frustrating, but overall you will start a new round very soon just to get to the next stage, unlock a new achievement etc.
One issue is, that the performance of the game does not scale too well with increasing number of enemies, but this is something which the dev's already announced to be fixed in the near future. Another thing which could be better is the randomness of the levels. The main layout is often nearly the same.
Score: 4.5/5
TL;DR:
Hard rogue-like sci-fi platformer, which will keep you playing due to a variety of items, champs, enemies and more!

Apart from the hardware requirements (which are not so bad at the moment. GTX780ti: ~50 fps ultra settings, all nvidia toys enabled), AK is certainly the best of the Arkham series. If you loved the story of previous games as much as i did and have strong enough machine, this title is a must for you.

Welp; if you like the series and even remotely enjoy RPGs, then you'll love this game!
While a little short (my first playthrough clocked around 19 hours, according to Steam), this game has everything a Southpark fan could want; there's vulgarity, scenes that have been censored on consoles and on PC in certain countries (but not for the majority), remote mountain town idiocy, extreme faithfulness to the series, solid gameplay, excellent humor and Kenny dies. A lot. (Though that may be because of my lack of skill.)
From a visual point of view I can be simple: it looks just like the series. Which is great, since I would've been offended had it looked any other way. As another Steam user review of this game noted (paraphrasing from memory): 'Someone walked in on me playing the game and asked what episode of Southpark I was watching'. Yeah it's like that.
Sound's pretty awesome too; The voices are exactly the same as from the show, so voice acting is top-notch. The game's soundtrack seems inspired by other fantasy related titles, but mainly by Skyrim and the Lord of the Rings trilogy, but done in Southpark-style, which is excellent, since we even have Cartman as the background chorus.
The plot is excellent, actually, since, again, it's just like a Southpark episode (albeit a long one, which is good). It might not have the depth as some other plot-driven games, but if you're expecting Southpark, then you're getting everything you've wanted and then some. Apart from the actual plot, the humor in this game is Southpark, which means it's excellent if that's your thing. I've lost track of the amount of times I literally laughed out loud, and that's an awesome thing. Sure, explaining the various scenes from this game to other gaming / Southpark enthousiast colleagues
result in some sick and offended faces by non-Southpark colleagues listening in on the conversation, but perhaps that'll teach 'em from listening in. How very rude!
And then there's the gameplay: well, if you're buying this game mainly for the gameplay then I have got some bad news for you; the references and humor make up about a third of the game and another third is adventuring / questing / plot progression through Southpark. The last third is combat, which is turn-based RPG style combat. It's a strategic kind of combat as opposed to hack 'n slash, where planning your next move and keeping your party alive are more important than your skill with the mouse. The various attacks require you to press various buttons, so a lot of the (special) attacks could be considered quicktime events, though I wouldn't necessarily agree with this; yes, you need to press buttons at certain times, but you can usually decide between options, in order to do different attacks. The timing is also used to maximize damage. A last interesting note; why don't you fail some of the special attacks on purpose? Some of them have something funny happen when you misuse them. (Granted: most of them involve the party buddy Kenny.)
Overall; I paid €40 for this game and was very happy with what I got. Yes, I would've liked about 10 more hours of gameplay for this money, but the great fun I had playing as well as laughing more than compensated for the somewhat short content. This might not bother you that much if you're a younger gamer though, since for today's standards in singleplayer gaming, 15 to 20 hours is considered average to slightly long. (By comparison: in ye olde days your average shooter took you about 25 to 35 hours. Well, it took
, but maybe I'm just slow.)
In the end: a solid 9/10 for me, would definitely recommend this game, just make sure you like Southpark and/or its humor.

If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding pie recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.

UPDATED:
After seeing the video, screenshots, and hearing the hype I wanted to give this game a try,
In my first experience with the game I tried launching it and realized there was no audio. There was also a red error message crossing the top of my screen during the (muted) opening cinematic.
Thinking it was a user error I then did some searching and discovered the FAQ by the developer (as well as a few threads) in the discussion section of the game, each offering a way to "fix" the error.
The next two hours were spent following those steps, as well as a dozen more I uncovered through a thorough search of the internet: on forums, help sites, and youtube. This extensive search online proved that this issue is actually rather common.
Eager to play the game I tried all of the fixes I could find. But nothing enabled my audio for this game.
I gave up that evening and played a few games that weren't plagued by audio problems.
The next day I tried again, driven by my friends who were playing the game without audio issues on their computers. In frustration I did every step a half-dozen times, and each time the audio wasn't fixed. AND THEN, after one of the many restarts of my computer, it worked! The audio played.
This was incredibly odd, because I know with utmost certainty that I'd done nothing different from the other half-dozen attempts. But still, it worked, so I didn't complain. I played multiplayer with friends and had an amazing time. We closed down the game after we had our fill and moved on to something else.
And then I tried to open to game again at a later time. No audio. Same error as before.
What followed was an exact repeat of the previous attempt. Try everything, try different variations on the steps, combine a few, log off and on, restart. Did that and again, after about half a dozen times it worked again. It wasn't even the same steps as before. By all reasonable accounts It was entirely at the roll of a die. I got lucky. And because of that the audio played.
Despite what so many people are shouting out on the discussion boards, I am personally among the ranks of MANY others (just do a quick search and you'll see this) who are at the whims of fate. The "solutions" provided by the developer and general user alike are at best "work arounds" that will likely have to be repeated over and over again until you get lucky.
There are those who don't experience this problem at all.
I envy them.
But this is affecting too many people. And all of these uncertain efforts taken by users to overcome an obvious error in the game should never be held up as a "fix" or even as reasonable expectations. This is not a stable game. The developer needs to fix this bug. It's not something affecting a small area that people can't explore. It's the audio. All of the audio. And it's affecting a LOT of people who would otherwise love this game.
You might be one of the lucky ones. The game might work for you when you buy it. I don't know why you'd take that chance though. There are other games, just as good and in some cases less expensive, that don't demand that you roll the dice to see if a central component of the game will work every time you try to load it.
I recommend saving your money until the devs have provided a patch to actually reliably fix this.

Welp; if you like the series and even remotely enjoy RPGs, then you'll love this game!
While a little short (my first playthrough clocked around 19 hours, according to Steam), this game has everything a Southpark fan could want; there's vulgarity, scenes that have been censored on consoles and on PC in certain countries (but not for the majority), remote mountain town idiocy, extreme faithfulness to the series, solid gameplay, excellent humor and Kenny dies. A lot. (Though that may be because of my lack of skill.)
From a visual point of view I can be simple: it looks just like the series. Which is great, since I would've been offended had it looked any other way. As another Steam user review of this game noted (paraphrasing from memory): 'Someone walked in on me playing the game and asked what episode of Southpark I was watching'. Yeah it's like that.
Sound's pretty awesome too; The voices are exactly the same as from the show, so voice acting is top-notch. The game's soundtrack seems inspired by other fantasy related titles, but mainly by Skyrim and the Lord of the Rings trilogy, but done in Southpark-style, which is excellent, since we even have Cartman as the background chorus.
The plot is excellent, actually, since, again, it's just like a Southpark episode (albeit a long one, which is good). It might not have the depth as some other plot-driven games, but if you're expecting Southpark, then you're getting everything you've wanted and then some. Apart from the actual plot, the humor in this game is Southpark, which means it's excellent if that's your thing. I've lost track of the amount of times I literally laughed out loud, and that's an awesome thing. Sure, explaining the various scenes from this game to other gaming / Southpark enthousiast colleagues
result in some sick and offended faces by non-Southpark colleagues listening in on the conversation, but perhaps that'll teach 'em from listening in. How very rude!
And then there's the gameplay: well, if you're buying this game mainly for the gameplay then I have got some bad news for you; the references and humor make up about a third of the game and another third is adventuring / questing / plot progression through Southpark. The last third is combat, which is turn-based RPG style combat. It's a strategic kind of combat as opposed to hack 'n slash, where planning your next move and keeping your party alive are more important than your skill with the mouse. The various attacks require you to press various buttons, so a lot of the (special) attacks could be considered quicktime events, though I wouldn't necessarily agree with this; yes, you need to press buttons at certain times, but you can usually decide between options, in order to do different attacks. The timing is also used to maximize damage. A last interesting note; why don't you fail some of the special attacks on purpose? Some of them have something funny happen when you misuse them. (Granted: most of them involve the party buddy Kenny.)
Overall; I paid €40 for this game and was very happy with what I got. Yes, I would've liked about 10 more hours of gameplay for this money, but the great fun I had playing as well as laughing more than compensated for the somewhat short content. This might not bother you that much if you're a younger gamer though, since for today's standards in singleplayer gaming, 15 to 20 hours is considered average to slightly long. (By comparison: in ye olde days your average shooter took you about 25 to 35 hours. Well, it took
, but maybe I'm just slow.)
In the end: a solid 9/10 for me, would definitely recommend this game, just make sure you like Southpark and/or its humor.

Unlike the failed re-releases that take old ideas but repackage them in "something more suited demographic" (yes, I'm talking about you, Jagged Alliance 3), X-Com remains true to its tactical, turn-based, alien-fighting roots. This is what the game was missing originally, something to get you invested in the story at the first-contact tutorial mission, and keep you going all the way through to the no-doubt glorious victory.

This game truly ends the Arkham series on a great high note.
The graphics and mechanics were as great as I was expecting and even a little more with the seemingly ability to do anything you wanted as the batman.
I have heard of many reports of glitches and errors however the only ones I found were ones already present in the other games (e.g. bodies merging with walls). I also did not experience any crashes or frame drops using the batmobile.
The batmobile felt amazing to me to use and fluent to drive. The ability to switch from pursuit and attack mode so easily was great. I was expecting the batmobile to be a cheap gimmick to boost sales of the game however, I found my self driving more than actually flying as I was having so much fun with the car. The fight sequences in the car were also great and I felt I won off pure skill.
The combat system in this game was just amazing. Being able to just move so much more fluent was so amazing. What also made things great was the increase of special takedowns (Batmobile and enviromental). These made the game fell really fluent but as well make it look really cool. I believe its hard to deny the fighting in each game gets better with ever new release (including Origins), it just makes me sad this is the end of the series. Some of my favourite combat moments were with companions which to me made it feel even more fluent but as well made it look so cool. They truly did much better than expected with that mechanic.
Spoiler Warning:
The story for me was great in how it presented batman in the continuing struggle between himself and joker. I really enjoyed flying around the city to find the joker sitting and monologuing about something. The ending of the campaign where you run around as joker in a destroyed world that was great and was an absolute find screw at the same time. Ultimately, the story was great with nice little easter eggs from preivous games scattered around the place. My only negative part of the story was with how they dealt with deathstroke. That was soooooo dissapointing. It was so anti-climatic when all it took to take out deathstroke was to destroy the tank. Here was the game creator's chance to redeem themselves of deathstrokes poor portrayl in origins and they just made it into a crappy side quest. The fight sequence should have been the most over the top destruction fest where it truly felt like there was a lot at stake.
Ultimately I thought this game was epicly compelling, visually, mechanily and story-whise. The game compelled me to go back and play the older titles and to play it over and over again.

Where to start?
For what it's worth, the game has come a long way from the mess that it was on intial release. Gameplay is fantastic but be prepared to adjust if you're used to how Asylum and City played because of the Batmobile (I binged on both as a refresher before touching this).
Story is absolutely amazing. The best yet in my opinion and Rocksteady produced another knockout in that regard.
The gameplay is much of the same but the newest improvements definitely make for an awesome experience. The new "Fear Takedowns" are phenomenal as well as the Disruptor and new ways to hack with the hacking tool. The batmobile can be a bit repetitive but fits into the story very well.
Now for my experience - The game has run beautifully on my hardware (more on that at the end of the post). Steady 60fps throughout such a large world. The rain effects on the batman-suit are jaw dropping as well as much of the level of detail (I'm running max settings btw). The level of detail on the characters faces is astounding and puts a lot of other games to shame when it comes to the level of realism they have gone for.
As stated, for the most part the game has run pretty well. I have experienced several crashes while playing but never in the same spot. I haven't tested if it is the video drivers or just the game itself, though it most commonly occurs during fast-paced sequences associated with either flight or the batmobile in the open world("races" seem to run just fine). You can work around it if you don't mind the occasional stop in gameplay though it can be frustrating at times.
All in though, it's been a fantastic ride and I'm looking forward to finishing (just the Riddler trophies left now). Rocksteady AFAIK is continuing to resolve the last of the bugs within the game which will finish making this game shine. In its current state it's worth playing though try to find it discounted somewhere first.
Lastly, lots of comments mention having higher-end hardware so your mileage may vary. I don't consider my system "high-end" but here goes :
AMD-FX Vishera 8320 3.5GHz (8core proc)
8GB G.Skill Sniper series memory
Mushkin 500GB SSD
AMD Radeon R9 380 w/ 4GB GDDR5
Windows 10
No O.C. on anything

WARNING - SPOILERS AHEAD:
This was a hard thing to write about as there has already been so much said about this game. I have absolutely loved the Arkham series as a whole, but even still, Arkham Knight was ultimately a bit of a disappointment for me. I won't go into the whole bit about the dismal PC port - that's been talked about to death. I think it was simply a title where Rocksteady really strove for something - a certain game direction/goal - and yet didn't quite make it. Despite some absolutely brilliant pros, the cons simply couldn't be overcome, so let's do those first:
CONS:

1.  Rocksteady really doubled down on the Batmobile. Granted a lot of folks asked for the car but the problem is, I just didn't find it *fun* to drive.  In fact, it was very hard to control and I think my Batman not only killed 500 people, but ended up destroying hundreds of millions of dollars worth of property as I couldn't stay on the damn road half the time ! Add in the bit where you had to use it for the absolutely horrid Riddler missions and upgrade it to take down certain villains and you end up with a car that turned into an essential character. I HATED that I felt it necessary to use my first few dozen upgrade points on the damn car in the hope that it might be less painful to drive. It was a cool design, but was much too integrated into gameplay.
2.  Riddler. I've unlocked 100% of the Riddler trophies among all 4 games and I never EVER enjoyed them.  I have obsessive compulsive disorder though and feel the NEED to do them. Roleplaying as Batman also means I can't cheat or let Eddie go free so I have to do them ALL.  This game at least gave us much fewer trophies to hunt than before which was good, along with a few varieties (bomb guys, car races...grrrr), but I swear Eddie was more obnoxious than ever.  I mean, how could you not do 100% just to shut him up and enjoy the satisfaction of punching him in his stupid face?  The normal Most Wanted questline to save Catwoman was more than enough thanks, especially considering those *AWFUL, AWFUL* race tracks !
3.  Story.  I found the story very weak.  It was easy to guess who the AK was and I was disappointed that the Scarecrow was not actually in the game very much. But overall, there were some truly obnoxious areas to play through like the Batmobile vs the Excavator area, the Batmobile vs the AK super tank and the Batmobile vs Deathstroke in HIS Supertank.  The airships and underground areas were not very fun to play through either. I felt like the genreral story tempo was just "off" - after you face AK and learn who he is, it felt like that was coming to the end - yet then there was suddenly MORE tank fights ahead (I can't tell you how discouraged I was to finally clear all the tanks, bombs and checkpoints - only to have them all reset after DS takes over).  Soooo much recycled content.
4.  Robin, Nightwing, Azrael and Catwoman - the gang was all herre, looking great and ready to help Batman at a time of greatest need, yet they were all woefully underused.  And no, saying Bats wanted to protect them is just a cop out from not integrating them more into the story.  I mean, Nightwing is insanely popular - GET HIM IN THERE !  Rocksteady seemingly did the impossible and made Robin kick♥♥♥♥♥and cool yet they then decided to stick him in a cell and use him as Bat-bait!  The supporting cast deserved better.
5.  Performances. Whoever voiced Gordon, Deathstroke and Two-face were terrible and I hate to say it, but Kevin Conroy's performance was wooden at best.  No, I don't buy the whole "Batman was sick" thing - he was monotone through the whole game and frequently pronounced words weirdly "I have to get to Bris-Tol immediately !".
6.  No free roam.  Seriously - fans have been asking for this for how long now?  I know there are mods out there, but RS would win a lot of brownie points back from fans if they would simply let us roam around the beautiful city they created with the hero of our choice (and don't tell me it's not possible RS - there are mods out there that can do it easily enough - just give us something official please !
Pros:
1. It wasn't all bad.  Rocksteady deserves to take a bow on their interpretation of Gotham City.  I frankly loved Arkham Origins version as it was *really* dark and gothic with lots of room to roam around, but I have to give the edge to RS's version as the scope of it is brilliant and was the highlight of the game for me.  It's true - part of the Batman mythos for me is swooping around the large cityscape canyons between skyscrapers and gothic buildings. The structures here are higher, the addition to the newer, modern buildings on Founders Isle are great, the industrial areas and the entire lower level areas mixed well with Chinatown and more traditional gothic structures. It was a joy to nosedive off the top of Wayne Tower and glide through the city while swooping onto cars, etc.  The water and rain effects were wonderful too !
2.  Performances  - Mark Hamill and John Noble were both *outstanding*.  My only regret with John was that I wish we had more of him. I understand that this was his first voice acting gig; I hope it is not his last.  Mark really outdid himself though as Joker was a major, major highlight throughout the game.  The song and dance number was the most entertaining part of the whole game for me ; ) Oracle, Robin, Nightwing, AK, Riddler, Penguin were all top-notch as well.
3. Combat and predator moves - just when I think they couldn't refine their combat system anymore, they go and prove me wrong.  Additions such as medics and heavy weapons guys add to the challenge, as do gadgets such as the wonderful voice modulator.  Dual-mode fighting was a lot of fun too.  A shame the grapple gadget Batman stole from Deathstroke in Origins didn't make it into this game, that was the one thing I was missing.
4. Challenge modes are fun and varied.
In closing, this game was - for me at least - an admirable misfire. I applaud Rocksteady for having the ambition to put a lot of effort into building a massive city to explore and attempting to infuse a new style of gameplay into what is, granted, a very established franchise that is getting long in the tooth.  But at this point in the franchise, there is no exscuse for a weak story and AK suffers from that. The new Batmobile gameplay was a major addition, yet it was not very entertaining (it was actually outright tedious and obnoxious at times - lookin' at you Riddler and Drone army). The PC technical issues undermined the whole experience with frequent crashes and weird graphical glitches.  Sadly, I feel that will be the real legacy of this title, at least on PC; certainly not the story or gameplay and that's a real shame. All in all, not the worst game I ever played; if you decide to get it, I recommend making sure you're buying it on sale.

This is my VR review using Oculus Rift.
Cons
Playing Vr really shows the flaws of an older game. Akward jumping off of thin platforms is a bad design flaw. You do it mildly in the beginning, but then towards the end, it becomes a chore. Aside from that, the melee combat is too simplistic. For something that relies heavlily on close quarters combat, with creatures constantly jumping at your face, a slingle attack button does not cut it.
Pros
Aside from that, the engine still holds up. Mainly because of the art style and facial animation. The weapons are unique to the level, which helps mix up the gameplay challenges. Levels also have a personality of their own. I havn't really played other games with worlds like City 17. I think the haunting atmosphere is what sets HL2 apart from most shooters.
I played this game with several periferals over the years. The keyboard and mouse, Xbox 360 controller, ps3, ps4 dualshocks,  mini keyboards with gyro mise and now the Rift.
VR
There are a lot of wow moments. The ones that stand out most are the Alien scenes where you feel like their eyeballs are popping out of their heads when closing in on their personal space. Also when you kill a crab creature its fun to stare into it's mouth. There's a scene that reminds me of War of The Worlds where you are fighting tall stalky insect looking creatures. You get a sense like you are playing in a 50's scifi movie. Lastly, the mission where you get your last upgrade for the gravity gun had a cool 3d effect. The orbital balls that shoot out of your gun look amazing and ad to the immersion.
I also thought it was cool to look down cliffs. I sometimes would commit suicide just to scare myself. I made my mom try it and she pannict and tried to take the Rift off her face.
If you wanted to nitpick the VR, I guess you could run into problems with feeling sick at first, maybe the 720p is a bit blurry when zoomed into your face, screen door effect is there but never bothered me.
........
For improvements in Half Life 3 or reboot, I'd like to see fixes on the core gameplay. The melee system needs to be more robust. Put in a hp, lp, hk,lk system. For platforms, we need a parkour system where it's easy to pull yourself up ledges. The suit should also give you powers like rocket boosting/ jetpack. Maybe the suit should have gadgets that a secret agent would use. If you ever get lost, the suit could also act as a compass. Lastly I would like to see puzzles return. This is something that helped mixed up the shooting sections.

NOTE: Because I've only played 7 hours, my opinion is likely to change depending on new updates and more hours exploring the game.
I've really enjoyed this game so far, the maps are well made, small but with a lot of detail packed in, yet not small enough so they things get in the way, it's really well balanced honestly. Guns are pretty good, there are many classes to choose from each with different styles of guns and weights etc. One class called "Firebug" which has flamethrowers and various other guns to do with fire, this is a fun class. The classes are a good addition, it can completley change up your play style and make you go through different situations.
Although this game is in early access there is quite a lot of maps and guns to choose from with their own style and weights. You can only carry a certain ammount of weapons due to their weight, this gives the game a more fair balance and doesn't allow one player to be too OP.
Maps have different bosses (I think there are 3 different bosses) who have different weapons, speeds and melee weapons, this is great as it will also make you change your options for weapons and melee wepons. As well as this, in different levels there are different collectibles to find, finding this will earn you more XP and money and can give you achivements, finding these have been enjoyable for me and especially due to the extra XP and money.
I would also definatly reccomend this game to people who really enjoy CoD Zombies, it is the same idea, but with more weapons, characters, skins, enemies just to name a few.
Due to it's early access state the game has a few bugs which I have noticed through my time playing. One bug which is the most annoying to me is when you get trapped into an invisible wall or barrel which completley consumes you until you get hit out or die, this forces you to wait until the next round and can result into you and your friends losing the game, this happends more frequently when a ZeD hits you and you fall into these spots. In addition to this there are large lag spikes when a round has ended and you are allowed to buy ammo and new weapons, these aren't game breaking but are a nuisance and can get in the way of the fun.
This game however needs a quite high end system even though the requirments are not very high, I would say anything over a 950 will be fine to run on medium settings, my 970 chugs on Ultra but high/very high seems to be the good spot, during explosions there are minor frame drops but nothing to get in the way of a fun expierence.
Overall this is an amazing game which I would reccomend a lot and partly due to it's low price point.

It was all in that moment when I just sat back and laughed. I couldn’t believe it was quite this good. I chuckled in muddled disbelief, expectations utterly defied. My nervous fingers reloaded the level, knowing that I had to see that breathtaking sequence one more time. It was then that I knew for certain: Valve had surpassed not only themselves, but everyone else too. Half-Life 2 is an astounding accomplishment. It is the definitive statement of the last five years of first-person shooters. Everything else was just a stopgap.
Half-Life 2 is a near perfect sequel. It takes almost everything that worked from Half-Life and either improves on it, or keeps it much the same. But that simple summation undersells how the Valve team have approached this task. Half-Life 2 is a linear shooter with most of the refinements one would expect from years of work, but it is also a game of a higher order of magnitude than any of the previous pretenders to the throne. The polish and the stratospheric height of the production values mean that Half-Life 2 is a magnificent, dramatic experience that has few peers.
It would be madness for me to spoil this game by talking about the specific turn of events, so spoilers are going to be kept to a minimum. We’re going to talk about general processes and the elements of style and design that make Half-Life 2 such an energising experience. Key to this is the way in which Gordon’s tale is told. Once again we never leave his perspective. There are no cutscenes, no moment in which you are anything but utterly embedded in Gordon’s view of the world. Everything is told through his eyes. And what a story it is. Gordon arrives at the central station at City 17—a disruptive and chilling dystopia. And from there? Well, that would be telling. This is not the contemporary America that Gordon seemed to be living in during the original Half-Life. The events of Black Mesa have affected the whole world. The crossover with Xen has meant that things have altered radically, with hyper-technology existing alongside eastern bloc dereliction.
The world is infested with head-crab zombies and the aliens that were once your enemies now co‑exist amongst the oppressed masses. This very European city is populated by frightened and desperate American immigrants, and sits under the shadow of a vast, brutalist skyscraper that is consuming the urban sprawl with crawling walls of blue steel. It’s a powerful fiction. City 17 is one of the most inventive and evocative game worlds we’ve ever seen. The autocratic and vicious behaviour of the masked Overwatch soldiers immediately places you in a high-pressure environment. People look at you with desperate eyes, just waiting for the end to their pain, an end to the power of the mysterious Combine. Who are they? Why are you here? Who are the masterminds behind this tyranny? The questions pile up alongside the bodies.
Half-Life 2 isn’t big on exposition, but the clues are there. You’re thrust into this frightening near-future reality and just have to deal with it. Your allies are numerous, but they have their own problems. Your only way forward is to help them. And so you do, battling your way along in this relentless, compelling current of violence and action, gradually building up a picture of what has happened since Black Mesa. The Combine, the military government that controls the city in a boot-stamping-face kind of way, are a clear threat, but quite how they came to be and what their purposes are become aching problems. Once again Gordon remains silent, listening to what he is told so that you can find those answers for yourself.
But even with Gordon’s vaguely sinister silence (something that is transformed into a subtle joke by the game’s characters) there are reams of dialogue in Half-Life 2. It is spoken by bewilderingly talented actors and animated with almost magical precision. Alyx, Eli, Barney and Dr Kleiner are delightful to behold, but they only tell part of the story. There are dozens of other characters, each with their own role to play. And each one is a wondrous creature. They might be blemished, even scarred, with baggy eyes and greasy hair, but you can’t tear your eyes away. People, aliens and even crows, have never seemed quite so convincing in a videogame. Doom 3’s lavish monsters are more impressive, but Half-Life 2’s denizens are imbued with life. More importantly, they offer respite. Half-Life 2’s world is a high-bandwidth assault on the senses that seldom lets up. That moment when you see a friendly face is a palpable relief. A moment of safe harbour in a world of ultraviolence. As Gordon travels he is aided by the citizens of City 17 and the underground organisation that aims to fight the oppressors. Their hidden bases are, like the characters who inhabit them, hugely varied—an abandoned farm, a lighthouse, a canyon scrapyard and an underground laboratory—each superbly realised.

Consistency is a thing this game does not have.
Quality control is all over the place, there's a lot of weird "lazy" bugs, and difficulty is so arbitrary at times it's jarring.
That said, had a lot of fun.
The Notes:
Positive #1: 4 player local co-op is so rare, it's really nice to have something you can fire up and play with friends who are hanging out with you (honestly, devs over the world, are you convinced gamers don't have social lives any more and need the Internet to find gaming friends?). That said, this game really shines in co-op. 2 player was the most fun I had in this game (not 4? more on that later).
Positive #2: Character variation, item variation, and the ability to completely change your gameplay with "artifacts" made for TONS of replay value on these concepts alone. One easy to obtain artifact in particular gives you the option to change item drops to little boxes that let you decide which item in the tier (there are varying tiers of power in items) you wish to take. You can try to min/max or custom tailor up your perfect little Commando or whatever to utilize the strengths of your character to their maximum potential and see what works and what doesn't, etc. Or just try something really wacky like stacking Barbed Wire (Aura of damage around your character) with the item that makes an ever-growing aura of lightning (grows each kill) as powerful as possible so that everything around you (and eventually in the map) is constantly suffering and dying without you even firing a shot.
Positive #3: It is graphically pleasing. A lot of pixel games look awful. Devs often mistake "retro pixel art" with "license to look terrible" and throw things like proper color usage and animations out the window. If you threw in HD Crysis-like graphics in to this game but kept the designs and colors it would look amazing, not nightmarish like many other pixel graphics attempting to make the leap into 3D. To me that is a mark of a fantastic graphics design team.
Positive #4: If you play this game solo, it will destroy you. Beating it on anything above Easy becomes a growing nightmare of pain. To explain: This game plays like a Roguelike, or for those who are not familiar with that genre, a game where you start out as a tiny peasant of worthlessness who rapidly levels and grows and finds mystical items in a world that is different every time you play it (to varying degrees) and becomes a HERO... who then dies because the monsters are insanely difficult every time you go to the next "level." In Risk of Rain, every level produces harder monsters, as per expected in the genre, however there's a ticking timer going at the same time. The longer you play, the the more monsters spawn to kill you, and the harder class of monster goes up. Speed is really important if you wish to beat this game, as the timer never resets and instead will just cap out with the difficulty description set to "HAHAHAHAHAHA".
Negative #1: Previous point noted, it's virtually impossible to lose while playing co-op. When you total party wipe you start back at level 1 but you keep all your upgrades and money. You can hit your head against the game until you win on even the hardest difficulty, etc. There should be an option to lose at wipe, but there isn't.
Negative #2: This game, surprisingly, gets framerate issues even on my medium-grade gaming computer. Those if you with lower end computers may go "oh good, retro games run great on my toaster!" then be sorely disappointed that your game grinds to a halt when there are so many monsters / projectiles on screen that it's overloading your computer somewhere.
Negative #...Kind of 3: This is REALLY nitpicky, but there are only a couple (2) variations per level which, in Rogue style is still variations but there just aren't very many. This isn't a valid complaint, really, you just memorize the level setups really quickly playing this game. (Counter-point: the way unlocks work in this game, the "randomization" really is based around unlocks, so again with it not being a very legitimate complaint.)
TL;DR Lots of fun, has some minor issues but they are by no means worth not trying the game for.

Risk of Rain is an action-platformer with roguelike elements, with some interesting mechanics wich I'll try to explain the best I can.
Even if you start with only one playable character, there're ten of them total, and each one plays differently, thanks to his own four attacks.
As time passes, difficulty will increase and enemies will spawn endlessly until you find the teleport, wich makes you fight for one last endurance round; beaten that, you can advance to the next level. Like other games of this genre, you can find active/passive upgrades (like piercing shots, increased defense, missiles and so on), but you can level-up too by collecting experience. An interesting fact is that powerups do stack, so you can have increased effects by collecting more of the same.
Once you've completed enough levels, you can choose between replaying them to gain more loot, or going to the final one; you can easily grind more powerups if you want to, but the game can be beaten in less than a hour in a good run.
Bear in mind that this is the kind of game where things get bad pretty fast, and you have to start all over again.
Pixelated graphics are really good, but sometimes the action on screen become a little too chaotic. Chaos apart, gameplay is overall pretty much solid and fun.
The game's soundtrack is AWESOOOOOME, I love it.
Also, this game has coop, playing with other people works well and in my opinion some classes are not meant to be played alone.
Reccomended if these features caught your attention, and/or if you have friends to play with.
I don't think Risk of Rain is a masterpiece, but it's a really solid game.

In a general review I can say that Risk of Rain offers great fun and addictive gameplay, and it's a must have for retro style games and platformers enthusiastics.

Nearly all video-game review sites (namely, IGN and Metacritic) have this as the best video game of all time. I slightly disagree.
It's quite fun at first, when you have no weapons and have to use your wits to evade the soldiers. You find secret passageways, duck into them as the brilliant AI-powered soldiers rush past.
Then the game sags. It's just "Here's a handgun, shoot me some zombies". Or, in the first vehicle level, you're hitting 90mph in a boat with infinite ammo--then you crash into a barricade and spend half an hour trial-and-error-ing your way past it, usually accidentally exploiting bugs in the physics system.
This is why I don't call this game absolutely amazing.
But wait, it picks up. After a level taking place inside a certain high-security facility that I won't spoil, during which you get to control things that I also won't spoil, the story hurtles forward at a breakneck pace. The timing of AI bursting through a door, the placement of items to faintly hint at how to solve a puzzle (e.g. and infinite grenade box when you need to catapult something using a loose floorboard) and most importantly, the use of stealth over strife.
From here, the game is amazing. Best of all, those sneaky Valveians got it to end with an amazing feeling in your stomach. If you made it this far, you MUST purchase Episodes One and Two. One and Two have a similar feel to the endgame of HL2 (I honestly can't see why they can't just be called the same game), which is why I would confidently name this trilogy the best videogame series of all time.

This is an edited review for XCOM: Enemy Within, the new DLC expansion for XCOM.
Do take note, that Enemy Within requires Enemy Unknown to play. The campaign for EW is exactly the same as vanilla EU, just that the new Meld mechanics (Meld canisters, Gene Mods, MEC troopers) and new enemies (Seekers, EXALT, Mectoids) are added in. For newbies that have never played EU, I recommend that you wait for an EU+EW bundle offer on Steam and purchase all of them at once. There is no point going back to play vanilla EU since EW makes the game so much better.
For the people that have already purchased EU in the past and are unsure about EW, you will pretty much have to replay the same campaign again with the new content just to "experience" what EW has to offer. If the asking price (US$29.99) is too much for you just to replay the campaign with some bonus content, then I suggest waiting for a Steam sale offer.
Everyone else, the diehard XCOM/X-COM fanboys like me, purchasing EW should be a no brainer. It makes an already awesome game even better (and harder).
I highly recommend that experienced players play the campaign on Classic difficulty (Ironman or not is up to you). Easy and Normal difficulty are much easier in EW, while Classic and Impossible are now much tougher: the AI is more aggressive in their patrolling, and the new EXALT enemies in particular are incredibly tense opponents that will use the exact same tactics as the player. The strategical aspect of the Geoscape is also slightly harder: funding for all nations has been decreased, research times are increased, and some of the late game Plasma weapons cost a lot of money to produce.
To summarise:
Enemy Within is a great turn-based tactical game with an overarching strategical aspect. Beginners and veterans of the series will be able to enjoy it, although I highly recommend that everyone should eventually tackle the game on Classic/Ironman once they are ready, because that is where the game's truly terrifying experience will manifest itself.
The real Enemy Within is not the aliens or EXALT, but yourself, the player. Classic/Ironman will force you to completely change the way you play the game, and learn to live with your mistakes.

Ahhh Civilization V, you have no idea how much I love you. For a game that has been out for over 5 years, I still find myself coming back to this game, and often. Where to begin? It's tough to say, considering there aren't very many things in this game that I dislike and too many things that I enjoy to no end. Before we get into the nitty-gritty, let me say this: while $50USD is not cheap; the Complete Edition is the way to go if you are looking to pick this game up. You may ask yourself, "What is Civilization V?" Or "What should I expect from this title?", well reader if you'll bear with me I'll do my best to explain what the game is and what to expect when you hit that beautiful "Play Now" button.
Civilization V is simply put: a turn based strategy game that offers you different world powers and empires from history to pit against one another to see who can become the dominant people in the world. This can be acheived in quite a few ways: You can annihilate your opponents under the pressure of your military might, having many of history's famous and feared units at your disposal such as the famed Roman Legion, England's impeccable Ships of the Line and hell, you even have access to mankind's most destructive technology of all time: nuclear weapons. And if you aren't the type to wrestle with your neighbors, you have the ability to build space shuttles to net yourself a science victory, or maybe you prefer to build up a flawless culture and force everyone to listen to your people's pop music and wear your people's blue jeans. Even religion in this game is far more meaningful than in the past, giving you bonuses ranging from extra money per turn for the amount of people whom identify with your faith, or even the ability to buy great people with your collected faith.
Things I enjoyed:
-Game's charm: Call me weird, but the most important thing for me in any game is wether or not the game has a charm, and this title offers it in spades. There's something... charming, about meeting President Washington for the first time, or uniting with Ghandi against the Roman led coalition against China... only to have Ghandi turn traitor.... By nuking you... nonstop... Screw you Ghandi. But in all seriousness, it's tough for me to explain, but there's a feeling you get, a connection with foreign leaders from actual nations and empires than you get with pretend factions from Civilization: Beyond Earth, and that is very important.
-Streamlined: Normally this can be seen as a negative, but here: it is not. For those who are new to Civilizations or even turn based strategy games in general, this game is actually a simple game to pick up and play. The game offers a solid tutorial that assists the player as they progress in the game but bringing your attention directly to what the game is teaching you and offers you different solutions to the issues. And for me, coming from Civilization 4, I'm glad to say that city health is a thing of the past. And the removal of stackable units (aside from aerial units and trade routes) help enhance the strategy in the game and push war into a game in which unit placement matters, as opposed to who has the larger stack of units.
-Graphics and music: The visuals are very pleasant and vibrant. In my opinion, this game still looks amazing. From things such as the water, to the different types of tiles. Hell, even some of the units look quite nice. Some. But the bigger thing that helps immerse the player is the music. Each empire has their own distinct music style set to the era the empire is in and to what type of culture the empire possess, for example the United States will have more European influenced musics as the Japanese have more of a kickass Asian style music. And the sound effects are well done. You haven't lived until you've detonated you first atom bomb. Either in the ocean, or on Attila's Court.
MODS!!!: Need I say more? Realistic Earth maps. More empires and countries to choose from (Adolf Hitler, anyone?) and even things to tweak how the game is played, such as improving towns and redoing units to balance them and even adding entirely new technology types for you to discover.
And I can go on, but these seem to be the biggest positives in my eyes. Now in terms of negatives? The only glaring issues that come to mind for me is how long the game tends to take to load, especially in the later stages of a game. Another issue is the computer AI can be.... bad at times. And I mean, BAD. Bad as in easy to manipulate. Too easy to do so. But for a game that is 5 years old? That can be forgiven.
I can't really think of anything else to say at this point other than: get the game. Seriously, it is well worth the money.

I was fortunate enough to not have nearly the ammount of drama others have had with this game, and therefore was more able than those who suffered, to appreciate the better aspects of this incredible Batman experience.
While the voice acting of some characters, including Batman and Gordon, don't hit a satisfyingly believable threshold for me, the story, set pieces, mini games, DLC and gameplay (including the Batmobile) were incredibly enjoyable.
There is enough content to keep you interested for a very long time.
I personally got sick of the fighting as soon as i got to Arkham Origins, and didn't even finish the first couple of hours of it, but i feel like this entry nailed in in terms of variety and viscerally satisfying impact of player input. Each of the gameplay mechanics feels right, and feels tuned and refined. The problem is, there are arguably too many mechancal systems you have to remember on the spot sometimes. But when you're in the moment and you remember all of what you need to remember to get you out of a sticky situation... you feel like Batman.
Pre-Re-Release
The only hickups i had along the way were the video memory hitches and crashing on my 680 FTW+ 4GB and 980ti SC+ 6GB. This appeared to come from either running out of (!!! 4GB, 6GB !!!) video memory, or the video memory cleanup process removing something from video memory, then another process trying to access the address of that item after it had been taken out of memory. So this resulted in having to restart the game every hour or so... and i have to admit, it did bother me enough to give it a break until one of the final patches before it was re-released. Close to the re-release all was good again and i continued slowly (as other games had then taken my interest away).
Post Re-Release again
I made it to around 50-60 percent before the re-release and completed the game at around 86 percent completion of the main game (including side stuff, but not DLC yet) after the re-release.
Given that i didn't deal with most problems and my system was way beyond spec (980ti) to have a smooth experience (even my particular 680 was good enough for a good chunk of the game), i really enjoyed the setup of situations and it was very easy to suspend my disbelieve and let my imagination run wild in this world the developers created.
Glitches aside, there is a ton of Batman fan-service and you can tell that everything was lovingly and pain-stakingly crafted for those that love Batman. The DLC, while short and sometimes not always produced with the same quality of the main game, are a huge bonus. They feel like side missions that just didn't make the cut for various reasons for the main game, but i'm glad they didn't just cut it out entirely, but re-craft them for DLC.
If your system is decent enough, and you can get over the drama of publishers pushing it out before it was ready, i think its now a great time to play through it, especially since we might not get another for a really long time. This feels like the definitive Batman game, and had it not been the victim of publisher greed, and its reputation marred by the community for this, i think it could have been a contender for game of the year. I think i enjoyed it overall, a bit more than i'm enjoying The Witcher at the moment.
