This game is not worth buying at the moment. At least not if you're like me who expected to play it for hundreds of hours like Killing Floor 1.
While this game is pretty and some of the guns are well designed, the gameplay gets boring fast. There are no interesting combos to kill big zeds like there was in KF1. No nade chaining, no flinching, no siren cancelling, no precise and time-sensitive combos. Parrying seemed to have some promise at the beginning of EA (v1008), but it's useless now with the introduction of unparriable attacks. The meta is just shoot it til it dies.
Support was my favorite perk in KF1 and it is now sadly underpowered with little ammo, low-damage weapons and a VERY underwhelming double barrel shotgun. Demo is also garbage with the first 2 tier weapons, and the insane C4 stacked damage dropoff; plus instead of the amazing M32 we got an RPG. Firebug and zerk are OP and boring; they don't even require skill with their spam-M1-to-win weapons. Commando used to be very good and fun during v1008 but requires an ammo buff now. Medic and gunslinger are alright I guess.
Updates take months. They can't even bother to release frequent balance tweaks. You have to wait months for the big update to see if the sequel to your favorite game is interesting to play again (hint: I'm still waiting).
Now this is just nothing compared to the insult of purchasing this game on Early Access under the premise that TWI was going to "do it right", when goes months without being updated, and they hardly ever listen to feedback (unless thousands of people are complaining). Instead, they release a full-fledged microtransactions feature (instead of focusing on finishing the perks and balancing). To me, it's infuriating and completely disrespectful to need to extract the last bit of cash from your playerbase while the game is still not finished. If they ran out of money, maybe they should learn to allocate resources properly. An argument to defend the money-grabbing strategy of microtransactions is that it will allow TWI to have resources to continue working on the game and add awesome content, which brings me to my next point.
TWI spent four months working on a Player vs. Player game mode that nobody had showed much interest in. A PvP mode is the LAST thing I'm interest in Killing Floor. When I want PvP I play BF3. In KF I want to shoot cool guns and kill zeds, not run around slashing and swinging around in the air to be killed in seconds and wait to respawn. It's a pathetic waste of development resources which should have been allocated to the sharpshooter perk. Very few people asked for PvP; a lot of people have been asking for sharpshooter. One should be able to distinguish the priorities for development based on browsing forums, steam discussions or reddit, but I guess maybe the players know nothing about what's wrong with the game they spend hundreds of hours playing?

I was fortunate enough to not have nearly the ammount of drama others have had with this game, and therefore was more able than those who suffered, to appreciate the better aspects of this incredible Batman experience.
While the voice acting of some characters, including Batman and Gordon, don't hit a satisfyingly believable threshold for me, the story, set pieces, mini games, DLC and gameplay (including the Batmobile) were incredibly enjoyable.
There is enough content to keep you interested for a very long time.
I personally got sick of the fighting as soon as i got to Arkham Origins, and didn't even finish the first couple of hours of it, but i feel like this entry nailed in in terms of variety and viscerally satisfying impact of player input. Each of the gameplay mechanics feels right, and feels tuned and refined. The problem is, there are arguably too many mechancal systems you have to remember on the spot sometimes. But when you're in the moment and you remember all of what you need to remember to get you out of a sticky situation... you feel like Batman.
Pre-Re-Release
The only hickups i had along the way were the video memory hitches and crashing on my 680 FTW+ 4GB and 980ti SC+ 6GB. This appeared to come from either running out of (!!! 4GB, 6GB !!!) video memory, or the video memory cleanup process removing something from video memory, then another process trying to access the address of that item after it had been taken out of memory. So this resulted in having to restart the game every hour or so... and i have to admit, it did bother me enough to give it a break until one of the final patches before it was re-released. Close to the re-release all was good again and i continued slowly (as other games had then taken my interest away).
Post Re-Release again
I made it to around 50-60 percent before the re-release and completed the game at around 86 percent completion of the main game (including side stuff, but not DLC yet) after the re-release.
Given that i didn't deal with most problems and my system was way beyond spec (980ti) to have a smooth experience (even my particular 680 was good enough for a good chunk of the game), i really enjoyed the setup of situations and it was very easy to suspend my disbelieve and let my imagination run wild in this world the developers created.
Glitches aside, there is a ton of Batman fan-service and you can tell that everything was lovingly and pain-stakingly crafted for those that love Batman. The DLC, while short and sometimes not always produced with the same quality of the main game, are a huge bonus. They feel like side missions that just didn't make the cut for various reasons for the main game, but i'm glad they didn't just cut it out entirely, but re-craft them for DLC.
If your system is decent enough, and you can get over the drama of publishers pushing it out before it was ready, i think its now a great time to play through it, especially since we might not get another for a really long time. This feels like the definitive Batman game, and had it not been the victim of publisher greed, and its reputation marred by the community for this, i think it could have been a contender for game of the year. I think i enjoyed it overall, a bit more than i'm enjoying The Witcher at the moment.

Ahhh Civilization V, you have no idea how much I love you. For a game that has been out for over 5 years, I still find myself coming back to this game, and often. Where to begin? It's tough to say, considering there aren't very many things in this game that I dislike and too many things that I enjoy to no end. Before we get into the nitty-gritty, let me say this: while $50USD is not cheap; the Complete Edition is the way to go if you are looking to pick this game up. You may ask yourself, "What is Civilization V?" Or "What should I expect from this title?", well reader if you'll bear with me I'll do my best to explain what the game is and what to expect when you hit that beautiful "Play Now" button.
Civilization V is simply put: a turn based strategy game that offers you different world powers and empires from history to pit against one another to see who can become the dominant people in the world. This can be acheived in quite a few ways: You can annihilate your opponents under the pressure of your military might, having many of history's famous and feared units at your disposal such as the famed Roman Legion, England's impeccable Ships of the Line and hell, you even have access to mankind's most destructive technology of all time: nuclear weapons. And if you aren't the type to wrestle with your neighbors, you have the ability to build space shuttles to net yourself a science victory, or maybe you prefer to build up a flawless culture and force everyone to listen to your people's pop music and wear your people's blue jeans. Even religion in this game is far more meaningful than in the past, giving you bonuses ranging from extra money per turn for the amount of people whom identify with your faith, or even the ability to buy great people with your collected faith.
Things I enjoyed:
-Game's charm: Call me weird, but the most important thing for me in any game is wether or not the game has a charm, and this title offers it in spades. There's something... charming, about meeting President Washington for the first time, or uniting with Ghandi against the Roman led coalition against China... only to have Ghandi turn traitor.... By nuking you... nonstop... Screw you Ghandi. But in all seriousness, it's tough for me to explain, but there's a feeling you get, a connection with foreign leaders from actual nations and empires than you get with pretend factions from Civilization: Beyond Earth, and that is very important.
-Streamlined: Normally this can be seen as a negative, but here: it is not. For those who are new to Civilizations or even turn based strategy games in general, this game is actually a simple game to pick up and play. The game offers a solid tutorial that assists the player as they progress in the game but bringing your attention directly to what the game is teaching you and offers you different solutions to the issues. And for me, coming from Civilization 4, I'm glad to say that city health is a thing of the past. And the removal of stackable units (aside from aerial units and trade routes) help enhance the strategy in the game and push war into a game in which unit placement matters, as opposed to who has the larger stack of units.
-Graphics and music: The visuals are very pleasant and vibrant. In my opinion, this game still looks amazing. From things such as the water, to the different types of tiles. Hell, even some of the units look quite nice. Some. But the bigger thing that helps immerse the player is the music. Each empire has their own distinct music style set to the era the empire is in and to what type of culture the empire possess, for example the United States will have more European influenced musics as the Japanese have more of a kickass Asian style music. And the sound effects are well done. You haven't lived until you've detonated you first atom bomb. Either in the ocean, or on Attila's Court.
MODS!!!: Need I say more? Realistic Earth maps. More empires and countries to choose from (Adolf Hitler, anyone?) and even things to tweak how the game is played, such as improving towns and redoing units to balance them and even adding entirely new technology types for you to discover.
And I can go on, but these seem to be the biggest positives in my eyes. Now in terms of negatives? The only glaring issues that come to mind for me is how long the game tends to take to load, especially in the later stages of a game. Another issue is the computer AI can be.... bad at times. And I mean, BAD. Bad as in easy to manipulate. Too easy to do so. But for a game that is 5 years old? That can be forgiven.
I can't really think of anything else to say at this point other than: get the game. Seriously, it is well worth the money.

My god. This game has the potential to eat entire afternoons whole.
It's a side-scrolling procedural death labyrinth that controls a little like Terraria and its ilk. There's no building here though, it's pure combat and that works spectacularly well in this context.
The unique mechanic here is that as time passes, the challenge increases. This causes you be in a constant battle to balance obtaining loot and levelling up with progress. Wait too long and the difficulty becomes punishing, rush ahead too quickly and you'll be unprepared for later levels.
The collectables are worth a mention too. Working in a similar way to the pickups in Binding of Issac, these augment your abilities though unlike Binding they stack. They unlock as you discover them, and there's mini-challenges to complete to unlock further pickups. Last of all there are multiple chatacters to unlock, each with a different play style.
The music is also great!

In a world where both turn based strategy games as well as challenging ones are virtually non-existent, XCOM may come as a surprise to many, boasting both of these things in a AAA release. The game is a brutal TBS that sets you in the shoes of the Commander of XCOM, a clandestine organization charged with the elimination of extraterrestrial incursions on Earth, and funded by the many nations that make up the Council. There are two main phases to the game: the Geoscape and Missions. The Geoscape sees you managing the grand scheme of XCOM's operations: such as expanding the base, researching new tech, and managing national panic levels (consequently, funding). Secondly comes the Missions, where you command a squad of XCOM operatives in a variety of missions involving the elimination of alien invaders. You and the aliens take turns trying to kill one another, which requires both strategy and luck to win, and any soldiers who die aren't coming back. Brutal yet fun, and definitely worth it.

After the patches this game has become very playable. In fact, I rarely got any hitches at all(a couple of stutters while driving and one crash in, at the time of writing, 20 hours of gameplay). Granted, I had to turn off most of the nvidia fancyworks settings to maintain a constant 60 fps, but I didn't miss that stuff too much as the game was already gorgeous without it.
On to the game itself:
It's very very good, in my opinion. I'm thoroughly enjoying it. A lot. Honestly, putting it like that feels like an understatement.
The gameplay is smooth and satisfying; flying and combat are as good as they've always been(even better in some aspects). There are new gadgets and new ways to use old gadgets. I've caught myself saying "that's so cool" or "wow that's clever" multiple times. AND THE BATMOBILE IS A FANTASTIC ADDITION! At first I was really eeehhh about it because I just wanted to glide around and stuff like usual, but driving, shooting, and doing puzzles in it are all very fun activities. Honestly, it doesn't feel out of place at all. It's kind of hard to put into words. Just take my word for it.
The story is compelling and very interesting and I can't wait to play more of it(I haven't finished it yet so I can't give a verdict on the full story). You really care about characters(Even a couple of villains).
The voice work is phenomenal as always; the characters feel real. And Mark Hamill is a god.
Overall, I bought this game at full price and I'm actaully very satisfied. I know, I'm surprised too. It feels like it's exactly the game I've been waiting for since Arkham City. And more!

This game is not worth buying at the moment. At least not if you're like me who expected to play it for hundreds of hours like Killing Floor 1.
While this game is pretty and some of the guns are well designed, the gameplay gets boring fast. There are no interesting combos to kill big zeds like there was in KF1. No nade chaining, no flinching, no siren cancelling, no precise and time-sensitive combos. Parrying seemed to have some promise at the beginning of EA (v1008), but it's useless now with the introduction of unparriable attacks. The meta is just shoot it til it dies.
Support was my favorite perk in KF1 and it is now sadly underpowered with little ammo, low-damage weapons and a VERY underwhelming double barrel shotgun. Demo is also garbage with the first 2 tier weapons, and the insane C4 stacked damage dropoff; plus instead of the amazing M32 we got an RPG. Firebug and zerk are OP and boring; they don't even require skill with their spam-M1-to-win weapons. Commando used to be very good and fun during v1008 but requires an ammo buff now. Medic and gunslinger are alright I guess.
Updates take months. They can't even bother to release frequent balance tweaks. You have to wait months for the big update to see if the sequel to your favorite game is interesting to play again (hint: I'm still waiting).
Now this is just nothing compared to the insult of purchasing this game on Early Access under the premise that TWI was going to "do it right", when goes months without being updated, and they hardly ever listen to feedback (unless thousands of people are complaining). Instead, they release a full-fledged microtransactions feature (instead of focusing on finishing the perks and balancing). To me, it's infuriating and completely disrespectful to need to extract the last bit of cash from your playerbase while the game is still not finished. If they ran out of money, maybe they should learn to allocate resources properly. An argument to defend the money-grabbing strategy of microtransactions is that it will allow TWI to have resources to continue working on the game and add awesome content, which brings me to my next point.
TWI spent four months working on a Player vs. Player game mode that nobody had showed much interest in. A PvP mode is the LAST thing I'm interest in Killing Floor. When I want PvP I play BF3. In KF I want to shoot cool guns and kill zeds, not run around slashing and swinging around in the air to be killed in seconds and wait to respawn. It's a pathetic waste of development resources which should have been allocated to the sharpshooter perk. Very few people asked for PvP; a lot of people have been asking for sharpshooter. One should be able to distinguish the priorities for development based on browsing forums, steam discussions or reddit, but I guess maybe the players know nothing about what's wrong with the game they spend hundreds of hours playing?

This game has its faults, but they are outshone by how fun a challenge it is.
The game starts out fairly tame; it's very easy to pick up and get started with the commando class and you get a feel for AoE, single use abilities, dodging, etc. The game doesn't really begin until you unlock a few extra characters, and then you're able to have a bit more fun.
Unfortunately the characters are very distinctly tiered. Some are great, some are okay, some are mediocre. This is good if you want to give yourself another challenge! But if you want variety, you'll have to handicap yourself to get it.
The RNG doesn't effect too much in this game; you can definitely have "better" buff drops as the game goes on, but the game drops are set up in such a way that it is highly unlikely you'll get a 'useless' collection of drops.
The difficulty is fairly tame on the standard difficulty; I'd suggest doing the harder difficulty setting for a better experience... but only after playing lighter settings to unlock things.
The game gets harder the longer you play it (which is good), but it also caps out at a specific difficulty level. I found myself near invulnerable at the end boss when it came to fight him due to all the drops I had!
All in all the game is fun, but if you're the kind of guy who can't look back a few design flaws and just have to play a weak class because you like their feel... you might be frustrated. If you're the kind of guy that will get a drop that gives you +max health upon killing an enemy and then continually farm enemies that cannot hurt you until you have obscene amounts of health, this game may turn boring for you quick.
Otherwise, you'll have fun.

Getting the negatives out of the way: the PC port is bad. Everyone knows this, but it needs to be said. I myself have never had an issue with it (i7 4790k + GTX980 + 16GB RAM at the moment) but pretty much anyone with lesser specs than mine seems to run into problems. Also, the boss fights are underwhelming and Mr. Freeze is missing from the game, which is a tragedy.
But that's it for the negatives as far as I'm concerned. Aside from that, this is a very good installment in the series. The art direction is over the top awesome this time around — I wasn't a huge fan of the other games, one of the main reasons being their art direction. I much prefer this darker, grittier approach to Gotham and Batman. Visually it just looks incredible, and the audio and VA quality is right up there with it. As for the story, it is fine for what it is. Predictable, but perfectly fine. This is also one of my favorite renditions of The Joker I've seen; I love the role he plays in this game. It adds perfectly to the darker atmosphere that this game has.
The combat plays about the same as the previous games but there's nothing wrong with that; there's still some new moves to unlock, and now you have the Batmobile which is a whole different game. Many people complain that the Batmobile combat and platforming is no fun, but I thought it broke up the monotony that the hand-to-hand combat creates, which made it a good addition to me. And I just love burning through the crime-ridden streets of Gotham in it. There's a fun, healthy variety of mission types to play in this game so I rarely felt like the game was repetitive.
So yeah, if you have a good PC like I do and you think the art direction is superb, there should be no doubt in your mind. Get the ♥♥♥♥ing game.

In some ways, this is a very old-fashioned FPS.  You have a variety of weapons, but can only hold so much ammo.   When you pick up stuff (by touching it), it adds those bullets/health to your supplies if you have any missing, and any excess is lost.  Carrying around health packs/extra ammo is impossible.  You still progress through a bunch of areas, needing to press the right button or trigger the right event to proceed.
What sets it apart is the obvious polish, quality design, and good story.  The game uses only in-engine cinematics, and never takes over the player's camera.  It counts on you to observe the world around you, take an interest in the environment, and solve the various physics puzzles.
Instead of just a bunch of corridors and enemies (though it has those, too), it focuses on small engagements, then big set-piece battles.  You'll play for a while in one setting on foot, then switch to a more vehicle-oriented bit, then a new mechanic is introduced, then it kind of repeats those 3, etc.  This varies up the gameplay and keeps introducing fresh concepts through little in-game tutorials.
About the only complaint I had is that the game wants you to be immersed in its world, and use their impressive physics engine to solve puzzles.  It wants you to approach the obstacles as if you were actually there, making use of the objects around you to get past them.  This is great when it works, like making use of plastic barrels' buoyancy to get past one spot, but then you get to points where you try out a solution over and over, convinced it should be working, and it won't.  Oh, it
work, because it seems obvious, and because it totally
work in the real world, but in the game they want you to do something else pre-scripted, and until you figure out what that thing is, you're not going anywhere.  They make you stack boxes & crates in several spots to climb up/over things, but try it in the wrong place and you'll hit an invisible wall.  There's one area where you have to get past an electric fence and can see the power cable running above you.  Even though you've got a way to hurl nice big, sharp, wide saw blades with great speed and accuracy, you can't sever that cable.  No amount of shooting will help, either.  That cable's not a solid object, it's just there to let you know where to go to hit the switch that you need to find in order to turn off the fence.
Despite a few tired elements and some minor breaks in the immersion, this is one hell of a game.

This game has its faults, but they are outshone by how fun a challenge it is.
The game starts out fairly tame; it's very easy to pick up and get started with the commando class and you get a feel for AoE, single use abilities, dodging, etc. The game doesn't really begin until you unlock a few extra characters, and then you're able to have a bit more fun.
Unfortunately the characters are very distinctly tiered. Some are great, some are okay, some are mediocre. This is good if you want to give yourself another challenge! But if you want variety, you'll have to handicap yourself to get it.
The RNG doesn't effect too much in this game; you can definitely have "better" buff drops as the game goes on, but the game drops are set up in such a way that it is highly unlikely you'll get a 'useless' collection of drops.
The difficulty is fairly tame on the standard difficulty; I'd suggest doing the harder difficulty setting for a better experience... but only after playing lighter settings to unlock things.
The game gets harder the longer you play it (which is good), but it also caps out at a specific difficulty level. I found myself near invulnerable at the end boss when it came to fight him due to all the drops I had!
All in all the game is fun, but if you're the kind of guy who can't look back a few design flaws and just have to play a weak class because you like their feel... you might be frustrated. If you're the kind of guy that will get a drop that gives you +max health upon killing an enemy and then continually farm enemies that cannot hurt you until you have obscene amounts of health, this game may turn boring for you quick.
Otherwise, you'll have fun.

A rather great revamp of the original Killing Floor, but the unscrupulous behavior of the devs can cause some hesitation toward the future of this title.
With only the choice between "Thumbs Up" and "Thumbs Down", I must very reluctantly give this game a "No" IN ITS CURRENT STATE.
PROS:
+ The guns are among the best of any game out there. They feel great. They have excellent impact. Their models are spot-on. Their animations are very appealing. Their sounds are on point for the most part. Bullet velocity is unrealistically slow, but that's only apparent in ZED time.
+ The game looks absolutely gorgeous. The lighting and fine detail on the maps are top-notch.
+ Characters are not particularly memorable beyond the old favorites, but they all have many cosmetic options and excellently peformed voices. ZEDs as well are appropriately frightening and discusting with well-mixed grunts, screams, and voice lines.
+ The gore system is excellent. Even hard-to-kill ZEDs give nice visual feedback. Guns rip appart enemies in responsive ways. Low-cal bullets chip away at a ZED's face to reveal its skull and brain as it's still walking. Bladed weapons split a ZED down the middle to reveal its full anatomy. Gorey soup goes flying when a ZED is hit by an explosive, etc.
+ Soundtrack is not original, but well-compiled nonetheless. Hard and fast metal with a few electronic tracks that remain interesting for a while.
+ Action is faster and more intense than Killing Floor 1. Camping one spot and one doorway has been replaced with faster humans, faster ZEDs, different spawn patterns, and areas that become less viable (lights/doorways get destroyed) to hold out in over time.
+ Skills are much more well accounted for than in KF1. Progression takes a bit of investment but is not a never-ending grind like in the first game. Perk trees offer one of two interchangeable skills (that can be changed any round) for each 5 of the 25 levels in a tree. It's a simple-yet-complex system that gives most classes some good choice and variety, plus flat-out buffs each level increased.
+ Steam Workshop support. A good distribution of maps, cosmetics ideas, weapon propositions, and other neat game tweaks. There are many servers that run custom maps that can keep the gameloop fresh.
+ Well optimized. Lots of options to tweak for solid performance.
NEUTRAL:
+- While maps are much more gorgeous and more detailed, they are also noticeably smaller than anything you'll find in KF1. While this serves to keep the team together, it's a shame there don't seem to be many vast landscapes to explore, and some maps get very samey.
+- Microtransactions. I detest the principle of this move (I will explain that in the cons) more than the MTs themselves. It's very similar to the TF2 crate system with the Steam Market tie-in. The crates contain player cosmetics and weapon skins. While many of these skins are nothing short of cancerous, at least they are not game-affecting.
CONS:
- "ZED Time", this game's "Bullet Time". I didn't like this system in KF1 either. Semi-randomly, a few times a round for a few seconds, time is slowed down and the world goes to shades of only black, white, and red. While visually neat, it's mostly an aggravation. Bullets move stupidly slow, making you have to do a lot of unnnecessary leading of targets. Many classes do not benefit from the extra percision. While an auto-rifle-wielding Commando or a percision-based Sharpshooter might enjoy ZED time, the AOE Firebug/Demo, close range shotgunning Support Specialist, non-percision-based Bezerker, or the reload-intensive Gunslinger benefit very little from this frequent occurrence.
- The devs. "Early Access done right", they promised. The basic elements of the game have not arrived after over a year. Each class only has four weapons (1-3 of which you'll probably be using), there are only 7/10 classes in the game, and a small handful of maps. The devs claim they want player feedback, but instead of finishing the content the game was sold on, they allocate their resources towards a poorly balanced ZEDs vs Humans mode that no one asked for. Did I mention they're working on a PS3 version of an unfinished game?
In addition, microtransactions have been added midway through Early Access for a game that not only has a purchase price, but has future plans of paid DLC. Add the fact that they refer to updates as "free content packs", and you know Tripwire has been touched by the modern games industry in the wrong way.
This is not Overkill Studios level of abuse, so I will continue to the play the game, but very cautiously.
- Versus Survival. The game was not originally designed around this the way Left 4 Dead was. As an afterthought, it is currently very imbalanced and unfun. Playing as ZEDs often results in instant slaughter. Their moves largely consist of mindlessly spamming mouse 1 to smack players with futility. Players are treated to new ZED attacks that consist of biological landmines and kamikaze attacks that make only the real challenge trying to wipe a bunch of annoying decals from your screen.
The mode is still in its infancy, but considering it's good enough for Tripwire to ship out, it's good enough to be critqued.
- Class balance is quite out-of-whack. Classes like Demo have very few effective options low-to-mid level and can't hold their own too well. Classes like Medic seem blatantly overpowered in their seemingly infinite survivability and viability in all situations. One Medic seems good enough to wreck an entire game of Versus Survival for the ZEDs.
OVERALL:

For newcomers, the new XCOM offers excellent squad-based action and simple strategy puzzles; for veterans, many a fun afternoon. Both can play safe in the knowledge that this game is built around the player winning, not getting crushed if they don't know precisely what to do (the old X-COM games were pretty merciless). There is still a good amount of challenge in the new game on higher difficulties, and it can swiftly punish you even on low difficulty.
The Enemy Within DLC is essentially a big patch that fixes a lot of the clunkiness the base game experiences thanks to its less-than-optimal porting. The improvements are only available by buying the DLC. The DLC also adds complexity to the plot and new challenge to the missions, and I think it would be worth the price of a DLC on those merits alone.
The EW DLC falls quite short on item, map, and unit content, however. Considering the asking price of 30 €, this is unacceptable - you are essentially being charged for a patch that should have been applied in the first place, and given very little actual game material for your extra investment.
I definitely recommend trying your hand at XCOM:EU. The Enemy Within DLC you should also get, as it enhances the experience greatly, but only when it's properly priced as what it is - a little 10-20 € DLC. At that price the greedy, exploitative charge-for-a-patch logic can be overlooked, as the content can justify the cost.

Risk of Rain is quite the entertaining platformer rogue-like. What I particulary enjoyed, was;
-The characters. Even though I cannot play some of them, such as Sniper or Engineer, they were quite fun to unlock.
-The simple objectives. Although the game is so simple, of which all you need to do is find the teleporter and eradicate any remaining enemies, you know how to play Commando, itemwise and abilitywise.
-The replayability. No matter how many different characters you have unlocked, or how many times you've beaten the game, you always can play it much more than you thought. It isn't something where you have to mod it to be able to play it again (Yes, I'm talking about you, Minecraft.), instead, it teaches you more about the characters you play, and what items are best for  them.
-The soundtrack. This, made me so immersed into the game, from what I had seen in TotalBiscuit's review of RoR, really stood out. I turn my volume to 0%, and my Music to 100% in the game options. I just fight on, using every artifact or a few, listening to the soundtrack.
-The final fight. This can get annoying if you don't set up a strategy, much like the game Spiral Knights, when you are fighting the Royal Jelly on the 5-2 mission 'The Soverign Slime', you will get destroyed. I set up a tactic, as I had read about Providence after getting destroyed on my fight with him.
Overall, everything is well-made.

In some ways, this is a very old-fashioned FPS.  You have a variety of weapons, but can only hold so much ammo.   When you pick up stuff (by touching it), it adds those bullets/health to your supplies if you have any missing, and any excess is lost.  Carrying around health packs/extra ammo is impossible.  You still progress through a bunch of areas, needing to press the right button or trigger the right event to proceed.
What sets it apart is the obvious polish, quality design, and good story.  The game uses only in-engine cinematics, and never takes over the player's camera.  It counts on you to observe the world around you, take an interest in the environment, and solve the various physics puzzles.
Instead of just a bunch of corridors and enemies (though it has those, too), it focuses on small engagements, then big set-piece battles.  You'll play for a while in one setting on foot, then switch to a more vehicle-oriented bit, then a new mechanic is introduced, then it kind of repeats those 3, etc.  This varies up the gameplay and keeps introducing fresh concepts through little in-game tutorials.
About the only complaint I had is that the game wants you to be immersed in its world, and use their impressive physics engine to solve puzzles.  It wants you to approach the obstacles as if you were actually there, making use of the objects around you to get past them.  This is great when it works, like making use of plastic barrels' buoyancy to get past one spot, but then you get to points where you try out a solution over and over, convinced it should be working, and it won't.  Oh, it
work, because it seems obvious, and because it totally
work in the real world, but in the game they want you to do something else pre-scripted, and until you figure out what that thing is, you're not going anywhere.  They make you stack boxes & crates in several spots to climb up/over things, but try it in the wrong place and you'll hit an invisible wall.  There's one area where you have to get past an electric fence and can see the power cable running above you.  Even though you've got a way to hurl nice big, sharp, wide saw blades with great speed and accuracy, you can't sever that cable.  No amount of shooting will help, either.  That cable's not a solid object, it's just there to let you know where to go to hit the switch that you need to find in order to turn off the fence.
Despite a few tired elements and some minor breaks in the immersion, this is one hell of a game.

An incredibly well paced game with an excellent balance between exploration and action, and still, after 10 freakin' years, a leader in conveying an interactive narrative.
The people at valve are not only experts in gameplay and pacing, but also at facial animation and NPC player tracking which give the game an immersive step above the rest in terms of really selling the story to you.  Those features may not sound like much, but after all these years, in-game facial animation and player tracking are two things that countless "AAA" developers rarely hit or in many cases ignore completely and are substituted with cutscenes or scripted events and QTEs.
All those things that developers miss nowadays is what brings me back, not just to Half-Life 2, but to many of Valve's other amazing games. 2 out of 2 thumbs up, would synergize.

For newcomers, the new XCOM offers excellent squad-based action and simple strategy puzzles; for veterans, many a fun afternoon. Both can play safe in the knowledge that this game is built around the player winning, not getting crushed if they don't know precisely what to do (the old X-COM games were pretty merciless). There is still a good amount of challenge in the new game on higher difficulties, and it can swiftly punish you even on low difficulty.
The Enemy Within DLC is essentially a big patch that fixes a lot of the clunkiness the base game experiences thanks to its less-than-optimal porting. The improvements are only available by buying the DLC. The DLC also adds complexity to the plot and new challenge to the missions, and I think it would be worth the price of a DLC on those merits alone.
The EW DLC falls quite short on item, map, and unit content, however. Considering the asking price of 30 €, this is unacceptable - you are essentially being charged for a patch that should have been applied in the first place, and given very little actual game material for your extra investment.
I definitely recommend trying your hand at XCOM:EU. The Enemy Within DLC you should also get, as it enhances the experience greatly, but only when it's properly priced as what it is - a little 10-20 € DLC. At that price the greedy, exploitative charge-for-a-patch logic can be overlooked, as the content can justify the cost.

TL; Don't want to read... 9/10. Good for some good hours of fun, even better with friends. Good soundtrack, but a little loud. Good use of Pixel art.
At first I was a little skeptical of this game. I played Rogue Legacy, I had my game when I wanted the tar kicked out of me every second, but my friends swore up and down that this game was ridiculously fun and was challenging, so I picked it up to give it a try.
First forty minutes in and I was still alive and wondering what the heck my friends were talking about this game making you a glutton for punishment. Little worries, a couple heavy swamrs of enemies, but nothing to really get scared over. Then the bells kept tolling, to which my friends continued to tell me to not worry, it'll all be over soon. I had my guy all decked out, survived portal 3, tons of equipment, then my friends told me to look in the top right corner, to which a little gauge had filled up more than 3/4s full. They begun to chuckle, and I soon learned why. The waves of enemies just came pouring in. My commando couldn't keep his life-saving rolls going enough, my time-stopping item couldn't hold out... and I was dead. That night I played a good amount of time.
The graphics are well done. They have a Fez kind of feel to them for the scenery (minus the 3D rotating map aspect.) They did the pixel art very well in this, and it shows quite nicely in all aspects.
Gameplay is pretty solid. Of the ten classes, none of them play like the others. Each has their own flair and quirks. Some are good by themselves, others are better with company. The game gives you coins and xp per kill. You can use those coins to unlock chests, use item tanks (either random or a "shop" of 3), or save them for the end where they turn into XP. As I stated earlier, give the game enough time and you'll be swarmed with enemies, this happens more and more the higher game modes you get to. We had played for a good hour and reached a stage where all we saw were Boss monsters and little to no "trash," to which we were crying for the teleporter to be reached just so we could get a breath, that match had 6 Magma worms on the screen at once, and it was nuts. I couldn't tell you what this does to us frame wise as two friends have a Titan Black and I have a Nvidia 760 GTX, and our processors are pretty new, so we stayed at a solid 60 FPS.
Now the soundtrack is great. I love the music in this, but this is where my only problem comes in, the game is LOUD. I mean so loud that 10% on game and lowered values in the volume mixer barely made a dent in it.
Another thing that is nice is the achievement system. In this, it actually matters. If you kill a boss with the Bandit using his special ability, you unlock an item to drop for your games going forward. Survive x amount of time? Another achievement, another item. Beat the game? New character. Found a secret area? New character. Most of it is based on luck of the map, but some of them are skill-based.
Pros:
Great gameplay
Achievements mean something (unlocks more items to use and playable characters)
Good co-op
Great soundtrack and art style
A good challenge
Cons:
Too dang loud even at 10%

You can heal in terms of HP, Power Points (PP), take off or cause statues effects, and allows you to attack. You can attack by consuming PP or stamine-like points that can be very powerful in terms of raw damage or status effects. Another way to attack does not use up PP (power points). You can time hitting a button like A if using an Xbox 360 controller, or on the keyboard, to do additional damage (either an additional attack/hit or simply dealing greater amount of damage). I figured out that it'll work fine as long as it's in windowed mode with just a 1366x768 resolution.

So while I understand that a lot of folks faced issues, the game works very well now for me, and I've enjoyed it thoroughly.
You do need slightly higher than normal specs to get this going on PC, but if you do have it, then I highly recommend purchasing it.

Risk of Rain is an 'action rogue like platformer' where you explore a level to find an exit, fight some bosses, picking up powerups, while racing against a rising difficulty meter.
One reason it took me so long to buy the game is because I hate games with timers in them.  Timers generally just add stress and frustration to games without any additional fun, and are a misguided fallback to the arcade days.  If you also feel this way, fear not.  The difficulty timer in this game doesn't work like that, it's more of a real-time representation of the standard difficulty curve of a roguelike.  It is quite possibly the only game with a timer which seems to work ok.  You don't fail if you run out of time, it just appears the difficulty stays maxed.  The game might still be better without it (why can't levels just get harder as you get further through the game, like every other game?) but it's not the fatal flaw I feared it would be.
I also think the MMO inspired skill timers are not very intuitive to use, it would have been nicer like every other game where you just push buttons and things happen.
The music is also great and if you are a sucker for good music like I am (check their videos for samples) it is worth the price of admission alone.

Has to be one of the better Licensed titles I have seen in a while.  The game is basically set up as an actual episode of the show.  Side scrolling, same voices, everything you could want.  For the most part the writing is tight and in tune with the show but it goes down the toilet a lot more than the show.  Maybe thats due to a lack of censorship.  I loved it but I warn you it's not as intelligent as the show.  Lots of fart jokes.  LOTS of fart jokes.
The best part of the game is that its basically a classic RPG game set in the South Park universe.  The character building is actually a lot deeper than one might expect from a title of this nature.  You have lots of gear to choose from and even more enchantments to add.  Also 4 classes to play and several high profile buddies you can pair with.  Now granted its not nearly as deep as more tuned RPG's but I doubt it is needed.
The story is similar to the last 3 episodes of SP and it is quite absurd/hysterical.  Lots and lots of cameos to enjoy including side quests for them.  Collection quests also abound.
Having purchased at launch I have played through it twice now.  Its just fun.
Now the cons.
1.  For being delayed as much as this game was in development I was completely surprised by how unfinished it felt.  A part of me suspects that some of the menu mechanics and other unpolished elements have to do with the game being basically a port of the console release.  For instance the inventory screen is messy and you accumulate a boatload of "Junk".  Basically items that have no value other than little nostalgic pieces from past episodes that you sell for money.  You get tons of junk and its worthless to keep.  Unfortunately there is no "Sell all" button.  Just sell stack which makes it annoying everytime you go to unload your inventory.  Thankfully about halfway through the game you really dont need money all that much if at all.
2.  While the game is constantly throwing tutorials at you left and right you still will be completely lost as to what to do.  You are learning magic spells all through the game and they come in the form of cut scenes where certain characters teach you how to harness a specific fart.  Yes you heard that right.  Well, these scenes are annoying.  Despite them telling you what to do its all very vague and it requires a lot of attempts to figure it out, or you have to go into a Help Menu to read even more vague language.  This leads you to fail several times in practice and then you have to sit through an unskipable scene as they try to teach you yet again.  Just poorly tested IMO.
3.  Some visual or sound glitches.  Towards the end of the game I got some strange bugs where my character would flicker a lot or sometimes disappear entirely.  Also I lost animations in battle sometimes, forcing my toons to sit still and I had to launch my attacks merely by sound.  Hopefully thats patched out.
In the end I enjoyed the game and think die hards of the show will too.  Casual fans may find the humor to be a bit too low brow even for South Park.  Also, while I am mostly satisfied, I will say its a much better value at price drop.  It does have a lot of content but still not entirely worth $60 bucks.

With everyone bashing the game for the slow updates etc, I have been having lots of fun with this game. I was/am an avid fan on KF1 and even got all the micro transactions to support the devs. Still this sequel feels like a good work in progress, having played many tripwire games in the past it's always a bit choppy to start but they usually make it up. The game in its current state just doesn't feel as solid as KF1 yet, some good improvments but some parts feel a bit lacking compared to the orginal.
Pros:
- Meaty feeling guns
- Cool perk special skill specs
- The gore diversity is good
- The explosions feel very nice
- Better voice acting over the original
- Maps have good ambience
- Some interesting new weapons
- Sound track fits the game well
- The new zed knockdown system is good from first impressions
Cons:
- The game does feel a little unbalenced but that's to be expected at this stage, besdies I only play on Co-op so it's not like it's a game breaker
- Some maps feel a bit lacking their set up and currently feel a bit uncontrolable and chaotic compared to the first (with a good team that is)
- Welding seems to have become a bit useless, doors do not regenerate after a round like in KF1
- Voice acting dialog is a bit too serious (apart from the classic KF1 charecters using the old voices)
- The guns still lack some of the punch of KF1 guns, but only ever so slightly.
Overal liking the experience, lets hope that TWI do it justice.

Risk of Rain is one of the scariest fun Rogue-likes that I've played. The music is awesome, the amount of items, enemies, and general challenge keep you coming back for more, but that's pretty obvious and a lot of recommendations cover this already. I want to talk about why this game is "scary" and I can say that in three words: immersion and atmosphere.
From the start you are one of nine classes (the other eight you'll need to unlock just by playing), formally guarding a cargo ship for some reason that had been destroyed by some creature of incredible power. After that you have to kill the residents of the planet to get money to open chests containing the loot that used to be on the ship, many of which are incredibly harmful to your character's long term health (though darkly comedic) a la Binding of Isaac. As time passes, the difficulty increases, enemies get stronger and heartier and spawn ever more quickly. It even reaches a point where bosses will spawn in alongside enemies, sometimes IN PAIRS.
So how is this atmospheric or immersive? Well, let's start with the fact that as you read the monster logs it reveals that the residents of the planet are in fact VERY FRIENDLY and EVERY SINGLE ONE WANTS TO KILL YOU. There's no way to explain yourself, nothing, you have to kill normally sweet - though monstrous - creatures to survive. The creepy atmosphere in the game's embrace of mystery and self-illumination, item and monster logs, and the increasing difficulty fill half the quota. The other half is done through immersion.
How many times have you played a game and saw your hero in trouble? At his or her darkest hour? A damn many times I'm sure. It's a fight for your life in horror games, and sometimes you don't even really care if the hero survives because it's a formula and it can get predictable. Then you play a straight up survival game - like this one - and discover that there is no way to win, there are ways to progress but it's a matter of how far you can get without dying (and no, Slender kill screens don't count, again, it fulfills the obvious formula that horror games can follow). Risk of Rain advertises itself as a game that you will die a lot in and there's no way to win. Well, that's not entirely true. You can finish Risk of Rain, there is an ending, but never once is it mentioned in the game or in its advertising. And that immersion in the fact that you - the player - controlling this little powerhouse guy, may not actually survive, is terrifying. Don't lie and say it isn't.
In any case, Risk of Rain is a blast to play and is definately one of my favorite Rogue-likes next to Binding of Isaac. 10/10, buy it now, get reked nub, no re

How can I describe this game in two words? Kiting simulator. There's a huge variation of classes but with most of them you will be running around fleeing from your enemies while using a few skills here and there, the exception is the enforcer and the sniper which sort of don't fit into the games huge amount of tanky and damage absorbing mobs which deal more damage the more time you spend in the game.
Many people will tell you that the best tactic for going through levels is to spend as little time in the levels as possible but this is absurdly impossible because you will spend around 2-3 minutes looking for the teleporter and then you will have about a few minutes left until the next difficulty to deal with the boss, this is of course on the normal difficulty not hard so you can see just how unbalanced the game is. Unfortunatly the developer decided to add a 90 second timer and the mobs during these 90 seconds infinatly spawn so good luck with that... In my opinion this is a stupid design decision because if you do try to kill the boss with the mobs spawning around you there are more chances of you dying but you breeze through the level faster whereas if you try to kite for the 90 seconds and then kill the mobs after those 90 seconds are past you will spend more time in the level and ultimatly the difficulty gets harder, either way you're going to have to kill both the boss and the enemies that are left when the 90 second timer is over. This is where it fundamentally broken there isn't a middle ground it seems that all you do results in a harder difficulty for you and I understand that rogue like games do have a lot of risk behind them but players do need some sort of comprimise, you can't give the player multiple ways of tackling a problem when the end result is still the same because then the player will become fustrated and helpless.
The problems with the game does not just stop there. With the artifact Command which you will find by playing through the game you have the option to choose any item from a tier, this includes chests and random items (items that have a ? on them), it drops a little box and you can choose the item you want. The problem with this artifact lies within the shrines, as you throw your money at the shrine you get the random item with the help of the artifact, the key or button used to pay the shrines is the same as the key to choose an item from the box that just dropped, this means that you will end up accidently paying your money towards the shrine 2-3x more depending on how much money you have left and how many boxes drop. This is a major annoyance for me because at times I ran out of money because I ended up throwing paying the rest of my money to the shrines even though I did not want to. The developer really messed up with the artifact and I doubt he is going to read my review and patch it but if he does then that would be great.
Lastly... And this a problem that has caused me the loss of games when it wasn't my fault and rather the developer who failed to test this through properly or simply ignored the problem. When opening the boxes that you get with the artifact Command you have to select the item in REAL TIME, this means that when you're selecting an item from the box you will most likely end up getting chewed up if you do not select it quickly. There should be some sort of pause so that the player can choose the item without having to panick about getting killed, I cannot tell you how many times I have died due to this, you may say "just wait until you kill the mobs and then come back" if I activate the boxes during the boss timer then I face the threat of infinite spawning mobs and I'd have to leave the location and then return which would waste my time, didn't the developer even consider the fact that this would make the artifact annoying to players?
All that I said sums up how the game feels to me, it feels unabalanced and broken. Sure its a good timewaster and don't get me wrong I did enjoy the game but I felt far more fustrated and annoyed and I play my games to have fun and release stress not create stress. Thank you for taking the time to read this review, it was fairly short but I didn't want to spoil any of the classes by going too indepth.
One last note. I know that swarms of angry Risk of Rain fans are going to come swarming towards me since that is how Steam works, if a games mostly positive and you say anything negative about it you will get showered by hate and downvotes but before you do that please accept the fact that this is from my perspective, if you cannot accept it then you're too shallow. I won't be arguing with someone that is throwing around arguments with a primitive attitude.

There should be some sort of pause so that the player can choose the item without having to panick about getting killed, I cannot tell you how many times I have died due to this, you may say "just wait until you kill the mobs and then come back" if I activate the boxes during the boss timer then I face the threat of infinite spawning mobs and I'd have to leave the location and then return which would waste my time, didn't the developer even consider the fact that this would make the artifact annoying to players?
All that I said sums up how the game feels to me, it feels unabalanced and broken. Sure its a good timewaster and don't get me wrong I did enjoy the game but I felt far more fustrated and annoyed and I play my games to have fun and release stress not create stress. Thank you for taking the time to read this review, it was fairly short but I didn't want to spoil any of the classes by going too indepth.

I know that swarms of angry Risk of Rain fans are going to come swarming towards me since that is how Steam works, if a games mostly positive and you say anything negative about it you will get showered by hate and downvotes but before you do that please accept the fact that this is from my perspective, if you cannot accept it then you're too shallow. South Park: The Stick of Truth is an absolutely brilliant game, for many reasons. Trey Parker and Matt Stone have excellently translated South Park's style into video game format - this game is fun to play, yet at the same time hilarious in every possible way.
A large number of the characters that have ever appeared in the South Park TV show make an appearance in this game, even if some just appear in loading screens, and the dialogue has been carefully crafted to be absolutely hilarious every step of the way, not just for fans of the original series who might pick up on some of the references - even but for these references the dialogue is still hilarious enough on its own to be enjoyable for just about any player, be they a South park aficionado or someone who has never seen the show - Some of the references went right over my head, but it did not detract from the game's experience whatsoever.
This probably isn't the sort of game, however, for a hardcore gamer who looks for a deep and rich gaming experience - This may be an RPG, but it takes the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of its own genre more than it tries to emulate it, as such it's not the deepest experience gameplay-wise, however in spite of this it is still very much fun to play, because in all honesty it's clearly not supposed to be played as a serious RPG. It's meant to be played as a pisstake of the genre it belongs to, and in that sense it hits the nail right on the head.
Another thing that makes this game unique is the fact that, in making The Stick of Truth, Trey Parker and Matt Stone have essentially translated the South Park format directly into a video game, art style and all. It truly feels like you are playing out an episode of the series, which makes for a unique and interesting gameplay experience.
A word of warning however: In achieving the level of comedy that it does, the game is also very, very, VERY politically incorrect. Just like the original TV show, there is probably something in there that will offend everyone, from abortions to Nazis to sex - and if it doesn't offend you, it becomes absolutely hilarious.
To summarise, South Park: The Stick of Truth is an absolutely brilliant, game. The dialogue between characters will have you aching with laughter, the gameplay is easy but fun, and the fact that it looks almost exactly like an episode of South Park makes it all the better. True, it may not be the deepest RPG experience, or a very politically correct game, but that's because it isn't meant to be. What it is meant to be is a♥♥♥♥♥♥take of the genre it belongs to and an immensely offensive yet side-splittingly hilarious satire- and just like the series it is based off, it does that very, very well.
Final score: 10/10. Most definitely worth your time and money.

First, let's address the elephant in the room.
WB released this game before it was ready.
Twice.
Having now said that, let's forget it and review the game based on Merit.
My 16 gig ram PC running a GTX 680 ran this game just fine with the graphics dialed down.  About the same quality as Arkham Asylum, so I couldn't complain.  Every now and again during cutscenes I would have framerate hitches, but overall this happened only a handfull of times.
I found the gameplay and the evolution of Batman's gadgetry and abilities natural following on from Origins.  It was a little confusing to put a prequel in just before the end of the franchise however, and some of the references require you to jump back two games.  This non-sequential storytelling style led to less emotianal connection and a lower level of suspension of disbelief as I reminded myself "Oh yeah, from Arkham city..."
At first I wasn't too crazy about the Batmobile.  I especially didn't like being forced to use it to complete story crucial tasks.  I'm Batman after all, and I should have  a gadget in my toolbelt to solve that problem.  After a while the Batmobile grew on me, mostly once I got used to how it drove - but it took quite a bit of getting used to, especially after having just finished GTA V.  Now I use it just as much as gliding to get around Gotham.  And beat up bad-guys.

All up I was very satisfied with the game and found myself questioning the naysayers on various occasions.  There were certainly OMG moments during play, and only a few points left me wondering what the developers were thinking.
If you're a fan of Arkham and IF your computer can run the game, go for it.  When it's on sale.  It's still Batman as he was supposed to be, and you still get to kick butt all over the place.

A masterpiece of the FPS genre. There are good reasons why this got a metascore of 96/100. What propped the game to such a reputation is the immersion factor. It's been said before that playing through the eyes of  Gordon Freeman (in First person mode) enhanced the feeling of being part of the Half-Life universe and the cause being fought for in the game. That is quite true. But I must add that the surrounding characters also contribute to immersive feeling of the gamer. The characters are fleshed out; the facial animations, subtle expressive actions, running animations, and dialogue gave me the impression that I was engaging with "real" people.
If I had to describe the gameplay in two words they would be: fluidity and variety. Fluid because there are no cutscenes and very little breaks in the game. No framerate issues that make your mouse movements feel laggy (well, at least for me). Variety because you tread diverse landscapes in the game from the urban, daylight environment of City 17 to the creepy, dark, zombie-infested town of Ravenholm. There are also diverse obstacles in your way outside the Combine soldiers which include dangerous choppers, physics puzzles, sand traps, and much more.
Thanks to the variety, the game does not feel monotonous at any point; it often forces you to adapt your strategies in a given situation,which made it more interesting to me than just mindlessly shooting and plowing through enemies. Like the immersion factor, fluidity and variety helped this game achieve its masterpiece status.
Recommended for all FPS gamers. If you're still skepitcal about purchasing it for whatever reason, you can download the free demo to try it out.

You could do a lot worse for tenbux. This game rewards skillful play, and the mechanics may be frustrating if you are looking for a casual platformer.
You are one of several characters with a unique 4-set of powers. Look through the level for the teleporter, activate it, face a swarm of enemies, kill them all, and his the tele to get to the next level. There is a final level and boss fight, and then the game ends -- or you can choose to loop through the levels again with increased difficulty until you die or decide to go to the last level. Difficulty increases with time, so the longer you linger, the harder the enemies become. You get stronger by levelling up  by defeating enemies and by finding power-ups that allow you to do more damage per second (or let you move faster, jump higher, etc). You also get stronger by gaining skill with the character. Yes, your skill does factor into the balance of power.
The power-ups are easily the biggest hang-up about the gamer: they are mostly random. Some power-ups are more desirable than others. If you neglect to get good at the game, you will have a tough time and will likely be frustrated by random drops. If you want to get good, you will be able to make do with any set of random drops. There is an unlockable option that allows you to select what power-up you get from a randomly-dropped tier which alleviates this problem somewhat.
There are many unlockables; this is either good or bad, depending on your opinion about unlockables. The classes are different and each one offers a mostly unique gameplay. The levels are colorful and varied, but there are only so many of them, and depiste being pesudo-random, they do get a little repetitive. Some levels are easier (smaller) than others. The soundtrack is excellent. The game is poorly optimized: later levels will probably cause you to lag. Gameplay is tight and fast with only a little room to breathe. There is a multiplayer mode -- if you can get it to work -- if you're into that kind of thing. Some classes (sniper) depend on your skills more than others (huntress).

South Park: The Stick of Truth is an absolutely brilliant game, for many reasons. Trey Parker and Matt Stone have excellently translated South Park's style into video game format - this game is fun to play, yet at the same time hilarious in every possible way.
A large number of the characters that have ever appeared in the South Park TV show make an appearance in this game, even if some just appear in loading screens, and the dialogue has been carefully crafted to be absolutely hilarious every step of the way, not just for fans of the original series who might pick up on some of the references - even but for these references the dialogue is still hilarious enough on its own to be enjoyable for just about any player, be they a South park aficionado or someone who has never seen the show - Some of the references went right over my head, but it did not detract from the game's experience whatsoever.
This probably isn't the sort of game, however, for a hardcore gamer who looks for a deep and rich gaming experience - This may be an RPG, but it takes the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of its own genre more than it tries to emulate it, as such it's not the deepest experience gameplay-wise, however in spite of this it is still very much fun to play, because in all honesty it's clearly not supposed to be played as a serious RPG. It's meant to be played as a pisstake of the genre it belongs to, and in that sense it hits the nail right on the head.
Another thing that makes this game unique is the fact that, in making The Stick of Truth, Trey Parker and Matt Stone have essentially translated the South Park format directly into a video game, art style and all. It truly feels like you are playing out an episode of the series, which makes for a unique and interesting gameplay experience.
A word of warning however: In achieving the level of comedy that it does, the game is also very, very, VERY politically incorrect. Just like the original TV show, there is probably something in there that will offend everyone, from abortions to Nazis to sex - and if it doesn't offend you, it becomes absolutely hilarious.
To summarise, South Park: The Stick of Truth is an absolutely brilliant, game. The dialogue between characters will have you aching with laughter, the gameplay is easy but fun, and the fact that it looks almost exactly like an episode of South Park makes it all the better. True, it may not be the deepest RPG experience, or a very politically correct game, but that's because it isn't meant to be. What it is meant to be is a♥♥♥♥♥♥take of the genre it belongs to and an immensely offensive yet side-splittingly hilarious satire- and just like the series it is based off, it does that very, very well.
Final score: 10/10. Most definitely worth your time and money.

First, let's address the elephant in the room.
WB released this game before it was ready.
Twice.
Having now said that, let's forget it and review the game based on Merit.
My 16 gig ram PC running a GTX 680 ran this game just fine with the graphics dialed down.  About the same quality as Arkham Asylum, so I couldn't complain.  Every now and again during cutscenes I would have framerate hitches, but overall this happened only a handfull of times.
I found the gameplay and the evolution of Batman's gadgetry and abilities natural following on from Origins.  It was a little confusing to put a prequel in just before the end of the franchise however, and some of the references require you to jump back two games.  This non-sequential storytelling style led to less emotianal connection and a lower level of suspension of disbelief as I reminded myself "Oh yeah, from Arkham city..."
At first I wasn't too crazy about the Batmobile.  I especially didn't like being forced to use it to complete story crucial tasks.  I'm Batman after all, and I should have  a gadget in my toolbelt to solve that problem.  After a while the Batmobile grew on me, mostly once I got used to how it drove - but it took quite a bit of getting used to, especially after having just finished GTA V.  Now I use it just as much as gliding to get around Gotham.  And beat up bad-guys.

All up I was very satisfied with the game and found myself questioning the naysayers on various occasions.  There were certainly OMG moments during play, and only a few points left me wondering what the developers were thinking.
If you're a fan of Arkham and IF your computer can run the game, go for it.  When it's on sale.  It's still Batman as he was supposed to be, and you still get to kick butt all over the place.

Hello, I am here to tell you about Risk of rain, a sidescrolly, itemy roguelite that has a trailer so confusing and uninformative that I wouldn't have picked it up if I hadn't heard about it before.
-Important Sidenote! I am not critiquing the game, merely reviewing it.-
In Risk of Rain you are a traveler on a space courier ship that's attacked by a mysterious... thing. Causing you to fall to the ground of an unfamiliar alien planet, where you fight for your life. Picking up items dropped by the ship and ultimately finding your way back to the fallen ship to fight the menace and leave the planet.
When you first go into the game, you walk around the landscape and monsters will start to spawn, though slowly at first. You will then kill them, as they threaten your life, picking up their gold, which you then use to buy items out of the chests that have fallen down with you. When you first start playing, you will only have a small selection of items to find, but as you play more, you will unlock more, and these are persistant across lives. The difficulty increases over time, making monsters tougher and making them spawn more often, until you either die, or finish the game.
So, is it good?
Hell yes. It definitely is fun to play. It has a nice growth curve towards the start, both with unlocking items through "achievements" -eg, kill 20 golems in one life, or activate the third teleporter without taking damage- and through increases in player skill, both with the game and with it's myriad of classes. Classes that, are unlocked through slightly bigger and harder versions of the achievements for items. -eg, kill 3 bosses or activate 40 drones in total.-
It also has nice gameplay, that although slow towards the start of a game, gets progressively harder and faster paced as time goes on.
Expect to die in your first few runs.
The items are fun to use, with most of them providing unique effects that are not just simple stat bonuses. It's really refreshing. Having good items for your class is another challenge the game throws at you, as they all have different movesets with cooldowns as you use them, and different items will complement different classes much more than others. But of course, this all depends on what strategy you are using.
Though there are complaints to be had.
Risk of rain has a nasty thing called randomness, this can be good or bad, depending on your viewpoint. Some runs will be really easy, since you got good items from the -mostly- random chests, but others can be sabotaged by bad drops. Although I find that this can be overcome by player skill (and slightly balanced by the stat leveling system the game employs) this is a quirk of the genre that  can be good or bad. It makes the good runs stand out, certainly, but putting it the time to get there, at least initally, can be a slog. (I personally like it... now).
The game is also short, but very high quality. Being a completionist, I have put a disproportionate amount of hours in. -More if you count the fact that I did most of the early game offline. It's not a big immersive rpg. It's a short sharp game you will play for, a week maybe, and will have you utterly hooked. it provides a unique blend of elements that makes it stand out and provide an experience like no other. You can keep coming back to it, sure, but it's not going to change much, and you will get bored of it eventually.
UPDATE.
Recently, however, there was an update the added artifacts that can change the game significantly, this can make the round you are playing unique to you and anyone else playing with you. This adds a new level of replayability to the game, making it last for much longer.
I hope I've provided some insight.

My experience with this game pretty much consists of having loads of technical issues across multiple computers that are repeatedly reported on the forums, with no solution other than an occasional official acknowledgement of there being an issue.
Reflections are totally broken on quite a few AMD graphics cards (such as the 290/390 series), as well as most recent Intel desktop graphics chips (and have been since around August of 2015). You can fix this by downloading a config file tweaker and forcing realtime reflections to the highest fidelity levels, which will cripple most low-end cards (and, by extension, the intel cards).
There are some really weird stuttering/hitching problems across nearly all cards unless you tweak configuration files (such as turning off texture streaming). However, on some levels this may cause really weird bugs where textures just...stop working on certain surfaces.
On most Nvidia mobile cards the game will fail to correctly set resolution and won't let you change it (defaulting to some asinine resolution like 300x200)...that is, unless you enable the horrendously optimized PhysX modes, which will cause the game's resolution list to suddenly work just fine until it's turned off. Setting this manually in a config file frequently doesn't work, unless you force it to read only, as the game likes to reset the resolution on startup.
On many PCs, seemingly without any underlying cause, the game just won't start. I've not encountered this myself, but have continually run into complaints about it while troubleshooting other issues.
The developer has previously (and recently, as of the review) released updates that will break the game for days at a time on various configurations, usually Nvidia cards. This seems to be in an attempt to fix the broken/unoptimized PhysX implementation.
I've spent so much time trying to make the game function properly, that I've hardly even had time to experience the multitude of broken developer promises, genuinely terrible balance, extreme lack of content compared to the first game, glacially slow update cycles, the introduction of microtransactions, the missed deadlines (game was meant to be released 4 months ago as of this review, and it doesn't even have half the intended content nor half the content of the original), the crossovers, the decision to port the game to PS4 before it's finished despite running severely behind and being plagued with technical problems, the announcement of big features the community doesn't seem to want (PvP?), and general bugginess of the enemy AI at times.
Not to mention that, since the initial release of the game to Early Access, the devs have pretty much tanked the original neat idea of the destructible lights forcing you to change areas, have destroyed the utility of welding doors, have nerfed a chunk of the classes to weak as to be basically unusable, and show no desire to do anything about the lack of difficulty of bosses outside of a gargantuan health pool that just chips down the team in an endurance race rather than coordination or skill.
Really, it'd just be in your best interest to stay away. The first one is a FAR better game, go play that instead.

Highly recommended--- with some caveats. The game has some definite downsides:
1. The story has some clunky bits (how Gotham City conveniently ends up evacuated of citizens during the intro cinematic, telegraphing the identity of Arkham Knight way before the reveal, etc.) some of which I can accept for the sake of expediency.
2. The heavy integration of the Batmobile into the game is polarizing for many people. I liked the Batmobile bits for the most part though the Riddler's race track segments are a bit of a stretch thematically and annoying to have to endure to get the 'complete' game ending cinematic. The GTA meets Batman meets World of Tanks vibe may be off-putting to some people, but it really adds a lot of gameplay variety, the same of which cannot be said for...
3. The controls have gotten overly-complicated. When a game resorts to on-screen prompts for what should be intuitive actions you may want to rethink your interface choices. I know this is a problem of feature bloat over the course of 4 games, but it's no less annoying.
That's all a bit bleh, but the stuff Arkham Knight gets right it totally nails. The predator sections are as great as ever, fisticuffs are as satisfying and fun as ever, the side mission structure is a huge improvement over past installments, and the boss fights are all a good time. The game runs fine on my system at 4k resolution (with Windows 10 Pro x64, 16gb DDR4 RAM, overclocked Intel i7-6700k, overclocked Nvidia 980 ti, etc.), but I would expect it to. At least I haven't had the performance issues that have plagued so many customers. Graphically it's just to-die-for gorgeous. At 4k it uses almost all of my video card's 6gb memory but the payoff in texture detail is absolutely worth it. Animation and sound design are great, map layouts are well-thought out and some missions are downright inspired and original.
The bottom line for me is always to ask myself if I think I got my money's worth in a game. In this case, that's a definite yes, warts and all.
