You know the saying, "Easy to learn, but hard to master"?
This game is basically the opposite: "Hard to learn, but then easy to master".
Hard to learn, is because manymanymany newbies immediately dies at the first 10 seconds, then ragequits. This is because they don't know what to do (even though there is a short little preparation tutorial when first-time playing the first stage), panics at the weird walls creeping towards the center hexagon, and gets dizzy at the fast and changing spinning.
Easy to master (not really), is because once you figure out how to play the game (like recognizing the patterns), the game then becomes a meditation acid trip into awesome music.
So in short, it's a patience game. Very small (hence the price), but with high replay value. Trust me, you'll be wanting to try to beat the stage (60 seconds/stage, 3 normal and 3 "hyper" stages), beat your personal record, or compete with your Steam friends over and over and over again.
If you have a strong sense of direction, love 8-bit chiptune music (it's Chipzel, btw), good patience, and strong determination, then try this game out! It's worth the price!

It's on sale now for a pittance and in exchange you get 15-25 hours of game design of such brilliance that if you were to count all the games that are in the same stratosphere, you would not need more than one hand. A thoroughly essential part of the gaming canon. Unless you don't like shooters, puzzles, scary stuff, or games that lack cutscenes, dialogue trees or role-playing/character customisation. But I don't know. It's my favourite game, and if you give it a chance, it might be your favourite too. :-)

This game is very hard to review, I suppose that one of the key things to mention in any review of this game would be to state that not much of the base game has changed since it left early access sometime ago. For what this game is, it does it very well. It's a wave based shooter where waves of zed (basically zombies) are killed as you attempt to survive a set amount of waves of AI opponents. Their is a good variety of different zeds from the big and menacing, to the invisible and fast, to the mindless and slow. Difficulty spikes are significant and impactful, which is saying a lot because nowadays it not uncommon to have games that have difficulty settings that seem to be nothing more than cosmetic in nature. The mobs in this game are pretty threatening as well, the boys and girls over at Tripwire really outdone themselves in this regard. Even on the most tame of maps and difficulties it's not uncommon to be overrun by zeds. Many times you're given a “oh♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ feeling as you're chased around the map fighting tooth and nail to survive wave after wave of freaky creatures. Given the pace of  gameplay, and the nature of the maps and mobs, the game has qualities of both survival horror and an action packed first person shooter, which is not entirely unique, but KF2’s own formula in regards to this genre compares particularly well with that of it's own competitors.
So with all of this mentioned you might ask “What's wrong with this game?”, well it's complicated. The biggest boom to this game in my opinion is the player made maps. I mean it's shocking really to see the amount of detail and passion that comes from this relatively small and dedicated community. The only thing I could compare the modding community of this game to is that of left for dead. And i would argue that the only thing that's holding this game back from having as robust of a modding community as left for dead is merely the size of the average player base. KF2 is pushing 2000-3000 players max on average for online play and the latter of the player range is being very generous in general. This cripples the game in my opinion and is really the “achilles heel” of what is holding this game back, there's also a matter of the games development since leaving early access. It's not that Tripwire doesn't add content to the game, they do, and despite in game cosmetics most additions to the game have been through free updates. The issue is that these updates add classes and guns that “seems” to not be what the player base is interested in. I like the guns and classes added to the game, but on average players just don’t seem to be receptive to the direction that Tripwire has taken with this game. I always feel like this game is an update away from breaking out into something better but it just never seems to do so. Which is why the game seems to not have changes since it came out of early access. To be clear the game has changed since it's left early access, but for some reason it just doesn't feel like it has.

Killing Floor 2 is a dynamic, player-driven hybrid of RPG, RTS, and melee-oriented action. In Killing Floor 2, the player character is generated by choosing their character's history-who their father was, what they did when they were young, etc.. Then, they are placed right into the open world of Calradia, where several different kingdoms fight for control. From there, the player can do pretty much anything in the immersive medieval sandbox-from being a mercenary, a fearsome bandit, a strong warrior, or even a Noble or a King. The politics of Calradia are dynamic and can be influenced by the player, using intrigue and diplomacy. The party system is also dynamic, with the player able to collect soldiers from various villages across the map and use them to diversify their armies. All in all, Killing Floor 2 is a quality game with great strategy elements, a deep RPG basis, skill-based melee combat, and a diverse, dynamic open world sandbox. I would rate it a 9 if not a 10/10.

Alright so, the game is a blast, for about half-an-hour.
That is basically the story of this games product life-cycle for the time being. The gameplay is great, and it's very polished for an early-access game. But the sheer lack of content is killing... well, Killing Floor.
You'll wait a couple of months for an update, only find out that they fixed some minor bugs that you've never experienced, or made minor balance changes, it is beyond ridiculous. What makes the situation worse is that the implementation of microtransactions has not helped the situation, the cosmetic items available through the marketplace add nothing to the gamplay at all.
When new content is actually added to the game, it's fantastic. But given that we get so little and over such ludicrous periods of time; I've found myself playing the updated content to death, getting bored of it(because there isn't a great deal) and then repeating with the next update.
Now, to be perfectly clear and lacking of bias; this complaint is my only MAJOR reason to recommend against buying the game. Since I bought the game, some time last year, there have been three major content updates(using the word 'major' very loosely here).
- the first added one new map
- the second two maps, and two perks
- the third, two maps, one perk and a new boss
As the game so stands, we have eight official maps, seven perks/classes, and two bosses - each with a 50% chance of spawning at the last wave. The problem is that once you've familiarised yourself with the core content in the game now, the developers at TWI simply cannot keep up with the demand, and as a result additional features are being burned out faster than they can be produced. Which all in all, leaves me pretty bummed out.
I've played 70 hours, I'd say that its good for perhaps 20-40 in its current state. If you believe thats value for money, by all means purchase the game.

I cannot begin stating anything about Arkham Knight without discussing the (highly documented) technical and release aspect, due to which, this game is a cluster of things not to do.  The first strike against it was the changing ot the system requirements the day before the game was released.  I pre-ordered the game with the assumption that my system as it was could handle the requirements.  While I knew I wouldn't be opperating on the suggested requirements, I fully expected to be able to enjoy the final Arkham game.  When I tried to run it, I saw a frame rate that was akin to a (very beautiful) slide show.  I couldn't get beyond the inital cut scene before having to turn it off in disgust.
From there,the game went through being pulled temporarily from sale, a large number of updates and patches and a final re-release.  Oh yes, I must also mention a second change to the system requirements after the second release.  I had upgraded my computer and was able to play it while it was "removed" from purchase, but with the official patch that would make it playable, I lost access once more to the game.  And while there have been a multitude of promises to correct the isses with the game, the difficulties persist and will lessen the view of what is, in the end, a fairly good game.
All the technical difficulties aside, I did really like the game.  The story takes a different view of Batman as he tries to protect those around him from harm (all the while, seeming to put them in more danger).  And while the Scarecrow and Arkham Knight are the primary villains of the game, there is no lack of others in Batman's Rogue's Gallary, from Two Face to the ever present Riddler to Deacon Blackfire.  And while there are many more villains that could have been included, there is a distinct work to clean up all prior stories and set everything so this can be the final chapter.  One thing I did miss with the villains was the boss fights.  While in Arkham Origins and Arkham City you got to go Bat to enemy in a fist fight for the ages, there are no actual fights in this game except against large groups.  Against Two Face, who is robbing banks during all the chaos, he just acts like a regular henchman during it all.  I actually took him out first before bothering any of his crew.  And though satisfying to show that Batman is trully superior to most of his villains, it was disappointing for them not to include anyone who could give him an actual fight.
The predator enccounters are a great highlight for the game, with new gadgets and technics to take down enemies stealthily and nearly any speed you want to.  From using a gadget to command the minions in the voice of their leader to, one of my favorites, the Fear Takedown, which allows you to defeat multiple closely clustered enemies quickly.  And when you have taken down your share of enemies, the close-quaters combat feels more responsive then before.  It is greatly gratifying to pummel the endless ranks of foes as they charge at you one at a time, or sometimes in pairs or trios to be knocked out.  The addition of enviormental take downs to drop a light fixture on your enemy or slam their face into the wall just adds to the pleasure.
If the stealth and combat are the highlights of the new game, the Batmobile is one of the dull spots.  While the gameplay itself is not bad by any means, it becomes highly repetative and you end up wondering (as do the enemies opening sometimes) where the Arkham Knight got the money for all of these drones.  And they do make sure you know they are unmanned drones as the Arkham Knight even taunts you continuously about this during your first "boss fight" with him.  And by that, I mean a fight against a drone helicopter, because he knows you'll holdback if he was actually in it.  Which is states.  Multiple times.
All in all, the game is quite good, though if you are trying to complete all of it (except the Riddler trophies) it does become repetative.  The increased size of the world trully makes it feel like you are in the full Gotham City and makes traversing it even more fun.  If your system can handle the twice changed requirements then I do suggest getting the game.  It was fun and the story is satisfying and has even a few twists that I didn't see coming.  That being said, make sure to check if you can actually run it before shelling out the money.

Get this game off of steam for 60% off and then it's worth it.  The game by itself is entertaining.  It's just a shame that the PC port is still complete garbage.

I'm a longtime fan of the franchise, and I was very nervous to buy this game because of everything that's gone on with the PC release. With the refund policies in place, I figured I really didn't have anything to lose since the actual game itself is getting great reviews on consoles, it's just the PC port that has had issues.

So, I decided to wait until I got the Batgirl DLC content to give a review, even though the game always worked (near) perfectly for me. Quick note: I've played this game on two different machines - in both cases, I made sure they met at least the minimum system settings (and also recommended settings) before installing, and also, both machines use an intel processor. That being said, I've only occassionally had an issue, once when I didn't have an up to date nvidia driver - went super slow, and the others were random slow downs during play (which, interestingly only happened after the most recent patch (as of 11/1/15). Otherwise, the game has played beautifully - and it really is beautiful - and smoothly; I really like the lack of loading screens between areas in the game.
Since WB decided to pull the game from Steam and keep me from getting any of the DLC until the end of October, I was pretty frustrated, since I preordered the game with the season pass. But, in fairness, it wasn't that I didn't get what I paid for, but rather, a lot most of what I was hoping for was significantly delayed. And, in the end, they have re-releaseed it, and as promised, I got what I've paid for, along with their offer to give all the previous games (I already own city and origins on steam, and arkham w/o steam, But, I don't have lockdown so I do still get something of value. So, point is: While this situation frustrated me as I'm sure it did many other gamers, I won't knock any points of the game as a result.
So, onto the main game itself - I'm still not sure which one I like the best out of the series, but the Batman: Arkham series is easily one of my favorites. Probably my flat out favorite, including Final Fantasy, which I've also been a big fan of. The story in this game is a bit longer than the others, but not overly so. There's a great plot that makes good use of all it's major villains, and a definitely satisfying ending. I could pretty much say the same about each of the arkham games, apart from maybe Asylum (ending only), but in some ways, I think that's more impressive for the final entry of the series, since they've done so much already with the previous games. While the mystery of the Arkham Knight is not much of a mystery at all to anyone who knows the character, it still makes for a good story as you watch Batman try and figure it out. So, I give the game full marks for it's story. I'm close to knocking a couple points off for making all of it's prominent women damsels in distress, but in the end, I felt each character was treated pretty fairly and respectfully (Though, I might knock one point off for Oracle's watchtower defenses being non-existent).
The mechanics were pretty fun this time around, and ultimately, I think the batmobile is a positive addition to the franchise but it is kinda disappointing that several of the most significant boss battles use the batmobile. Since it's a Batman game, focusing more on stealth, or some combat-based boss battles would've been perferable. Actually, in general, it feels like the stealth element of the game has been toned down for this entry. But, that's relative to the previous games, and I still enjoyed every bit of it. The one awesome newly added piece though is the dual-combat fighting. I absolutely love that. Only wish it showed up more (but in fairness, there are many times during the story that you get to use it). The default controls are not at all great for the combat system, but since you can remap the keys, that's a minor gripe. Generally though, it feels nearly the same as the previous games, but with a slightly faster pace. With the free character select update, I'm pretty happy with the challenge maps. While I'd prefer a few more options for stealth, it's ultimately got some nice variety. So, I'd take a couple points off for having the game rely a little too much on the bat-tank, but otherwise, the basic gamplay is pretty great, as usual.
The sidequests in this game are the best in the series. Just the right balance of stealth & combat based missions, batmobile/battank missions, detective work and of course riddler problem solving. While there is a lot of it, when it's all said and done, that's only there for those who want to do it all, and as someone who enjoyed the game a lot, I was happy to do that stuff. There's a Deathstroke fight in there in the end, and that is disappointing, but really not that big a deal, since it's just a cap to one of the sidequests.
So, for the main game, I'd have to give it a 9.5/10. A couple of small complaints from me, but overall, a great experience that I will enjoy several more times. That includes the delaying of all the dlc that didn't come with the preorder. Speaking of, the Batman Beyond costume is awesome. Really looking forward to using the Nolan movie costume (TDK I hope, but I'll take the Begins one happily).
Now, before the game came out, I was hoping for one thing more than anythign else to be added to this final chapter: Batgirl. We had Robin and Nightwing playable in AC - which was great - and then Robin again in the Origins online game, alone with Deathstroke, Joker and catwoman in the previous titles. So as far as I was concerned, it was only missing one character. And now we got her. Note: This made the wait for the DLC particularly frustrating for me, because, honestly, I was more excited about the announced Batgirl DLC than I was for the main game.. slightly. Anyway, now that I've finally got the chance to play it: 10/10. Everything about it is solid. While I don't love pairing Barbara and Tim romantically, even that worked in the DLC. I will note that the hacking ability Batgirl has comes across as a little.., over-simplified. It's cool that she can hack things, but kinda weird how it's implemented. Still, probalby would've been a pain to create something more complicated, so I'll take it. Love using her, and even better using her and Robin together. Also, while I liked the costumes they redesigned for Harley, using her original outfit for this fight made it even better. The environment, gameplay, the story, everything in it was great. I can't speak for all the other arkham episodes (except for harley's, which I didn't like much), but this one basically made the season pass worthwhile by itself.

I will say that I have extremely mixed feelings about Arkham Knight. On one hand, the hand-to-hand combat is mind-blowing and the Batmobile controls like a dream (with Xbox One Controller). The graphics are amazing and the effects and destruction are almost revolutionary. The game is simply not fun in many sections though; the riddler sections can be repetetive, the side-missions can be extraordinarily dull and also repetetive (Firefly bursts out of the same window of a burning building each time you meet him, and you have to tackle a flying mutant the same way four times) and the tank battles, which were never exciting in the first place, started putting me to sleep after a while. The game does have its moments, however, and these moments sometimes make it the strongest Batman game ever. Its positives are just not enough to keep its flaws from making it a barely-better-than-average game, and so I recommend this game with extreme caution. You should not buy this game at full price. Buy it at $7.50 or something like that a year or two from now, and give the developers credit for making a half-brilliant game. Just do not reward them for their neglect of the PC port by buying this at full price like I did when I pre-purchased it!

So, I decided to wait until I got the Batgirl DLC content to give a review, even though the game always worked (near) perfectly for me. Quick note: I've played this game on two different machines - in both cases, I made sure they met at least the minimum system settings (and also recommended settings) before installing, and also, both machines use an intel processor. That being said, I've only occassionally had an issue, once when I didn't have an up to date nvidia driver - went super slow, and the others were random slow downs during play (which, interestingly only happened after the most recent patch (as of 11/1/15). Otherwise, the game has played beautifully - and it really is beautiful - and smoothly; I really like the lack of loading screens between areas in the game.
Since WB decided to pull the game from Steam and keep me from getting any of the DLC until the end of October, I was pretty frustrated, since I preordered the game with the season pass. But, in fairness, it wasn't that I didn't get what I paid for, but rather, a lot most of what I was hoping for was significantly delayed. And, in the end, they have re-releaseed it, and as promised, I got what I've paid for, along with their offer to give all the previous games (I already own city and origins on steam, and arkham w/o steam, But, I don't have lockdown so I do still get something of value. So, point is: While this situation frustrated me as I'm sure it did many other gamers, I won't knock any points of the game as a result.
So, onto the main game itself - I'm still not sure which one I like the best out of the series, but the Batman: Arkham series is easily one of my favorites. Probably my flat out favorite, including Final Fantasy, which I've also been a big fan of. The story in this game is a bit longer than the others, but not overly so. There's a great plot that makes good use of all it's major villains, and a definitely satisfying ending. I could pretty much say the same about each of the arkham games, apart from maybe Asylum (ending only), but in some ways, I think that's more impressive for the final entry of the series, since they've done so much already with the previous games. While the mystery of the Arkham Knight is not much of a mystery at all to anyone who knows the character, it still makes for a good story as you watch Batman try and figure it out. So, I give the game full marks for it's story. I'm close to knocking a couple points off for making all of it's prominent women damsels in distress, but in the end, I felt each character was treated pretty fairly and respectfully (Though, I might knock one point off for Oracle's watchtower defenses being non-existent).
The mechanics were pretty fun this time around, and ultimately, I think the batmobile is a positive addition to the franchise but it is kinda disappointing that several of the most significant boss battles use the batmobile. Since it's a Batman game, focusing more on stealth, or some combat-based boss battles would've been perferable. Actually, in general, it feels like the stealth element of the game has been toned down for this entry. But, that's relative to the previous games, and I still enjoyed every bit of it. The one awesome newly added piece though is the dual-combat fighting. I absolutely love that. Only wish it showed up more (but in fairness, there are many times during the story that you get to use it). The default controls are not at all great for the combat system, but since you can remap the keys, that's a minor gripe. Generally though, it feels nearly the same as the previous games, but with a slightly faster pace. With the free character select update, I'm pretty happy with the challenge maps. While I'd prefer a few more options for stealth, it's ultimately got some nice variety. So, I'd take a couple points off for having the game rely a little too much on the bat-tank, but otherwise, the basic gamplay is pretty great, as usual.
The sidequests in this game are the best in the series. Just the right balance of stealth & combat based missions, batmobile/battank missions, detective work and of course riddler problem solving. While there is a lot of it, when it's all said and done, that's only there for those who want to do it all, and as someone who enjoyed the game a lot, I was happy to do that stuff. There's a Deathstroke fight in there in the end, and that is disappointing, but really not that big a deal, since it's just a cap to one of the sidequests.
So, for the main game, I'd have to give it a 9.5/10. A couple of small complaints from me, but overall, a great experience that I will enjoy several more times. That includes the delaying of all the dlc that didn't come with the preorder. Speaking of, the Batman Beyond costume is awesome. Really looking forward to using the Nolan movie costume (TDK I hope, but I'll take the Begins one happily).
Now, before the game came out, I was hoping for one thing more than anythign else to be added to this final chapter: Batgirl. We had Robin and Nightwing playable in AC - which was great - and then Robin again in the Origins online game, alone with Deathstroke, Joker and catwoman in the previous titles. So as far as I was concerned, it was only missing one character. And now we got her. Note: This made the wait for the DLC particularly frustrating for me, because, honestly, I was more excited about the announced Batgirl DLC than I was for the main game.. slightly. Anyway, now that I've finally got the chance to play it: 10/10. Everything about it is solid. While I don't love pairing Barbara and Tim romantically, even that worked in the DLC. I will note that the hacking ability Batgirl has comes across as a little.., over-simplified. It's cool that she can hack things, but kinda weird how it's implemented. Still, probalby would've been a pain to create something more complicated, so I'll take it. Love using her, and even better using her and Robin together. Also, while I liked the costumes they redesigned for Harley, using her original outfit for this fight made it even better. The environment, gameplay, the story, everything in it was great. I can't speak for all the other arkham episodes (except for harley's, which I didn't like much), but this one basically made the season pass worthwhile by itself.

If you're debating on whether or not to pick this game up, I can assuage those doubts of yours. Before buying this I spent at least 30 hours in the game going through levels over and over again, trying to unlock those last few items (and this was before artifacts were added).
Risk of Rain is a skill based side-scrolling action game where your main objective is to find the teleporter in each level. Once the teleporter is found, however, a countdown starts where you must stay alive until it finishes, a task made all the more difficult due to the boss monster that spawns as soon as you activate the teleporter. The game falls into a good rhythm: find the teleporter, kill the boss/enemies, go to the next level. Of course there are mechanics that add a bit of complexity to it, such as the items that can be found for sale around the level, the ever increasing difficulty level, and the variety of levels. The game features permadeath, as no characters can keep their levels once dead. However, new items, characters, and artifacts can be unlocked for subsequent playthroughs through completing the game's challenges, which range from somewhat simple to, at times, ridiculous, and finding hidden items throughout the levels. It is in this way that Risk of Rain gives the player a feeling of progression even after the loss of all the avatar's levels after death.
The items found in the game can be purchased by money dropped by defeated monsters. These items increase your survivability in a myriad of ways, but the downside is that there is no explanation of what the item does when you purchase it. Players who come across one of the game's "Item Shops" (which are really just three items next to each other, two of which will disappear when one of them is bought) will only have the small picture of the item to give them some clue as to what it does. While some might find it frustrating at first, I liked the fact that there is no explanation, as it immerses the player into the situation of their avatar, stumbling across some strange object in a foreign planet where nothing is familiar and hoping it helps them survive the hordes of ever-looming alien creatures. All the pictures of the items are clearly discernable, however, and on subsequent playthroughs of the game the player will become intimately familiar with the items.
There are quite a few unlockable characters, and players will unlock some of them just by completing the levels in the game. A choice few, however, can be found in certain hidden spots throughout the levels. Each character has a different enough playstyle than the rest, and while some of the make the game a little too easy I believe that helps the new player learn the levels before going at another playthrough with a different character.
While the player can spend as much time as they need to on a level, there is a downside to spending too much time in one place. In the top right the player can see what looks like a thermometer, which represents the current difficulty level in the game. Every few minutes the difficulty level goes up, which means that more monsters will spawn, more elite (tougher) monsters will spawn, and every item will be more expensive with each new difficulty level. While I'm not a fan of timers, this does add a new time management dimension to the experience. By not penalizing the player with death for taking more time than needed and instead increasing the difficulty, the game opens up new strategies for players to interact with the game. For example, some players spend as little time as possible on the first level, as this means the later levels will be a bit easier and (more importantly) items will be cheaper. However, some spend up to five minutes on this level, as they want to get all of the items on the level so they can be better equipped for the next levels. More monsters also means more experience and money, so if the player's skill level is high enough they can intentionally spend more time than needed in order to force more monsters to spawn and level up even more.
The levels in the game are sprawling and visually attractive. Instead of forcing you to go to one level every playthrough, the game randomly picks from two levels. For example, for Level One there are two options (Worlds 1-1 and 1-2), for Level 2 there are also two options (2-1 and 2-2) and the same can be said for Level 3. Levels 4 and 5 are the same, however, but because of the variety in the first three levels it feels less grating on multiple playthroughs as the player does not know exactly what to expect.
There are also collectables to get in the levels that randomly drop. One such collectable is a monster log, which has a low chance of dropping when you kill a certain monster. This collectable unlocks some art and a description of the monster in the main title screen. The more interesting collectibles (gameplay-wise at least) are the artifacts, which will randomly appear throughout the levels. On getting these artifacts, you are able to activate them on subsequent playthoughs to make the game even harder.
Risk of Rain is an excellent game in all respects. The only flaws I can find in it are the soundtrack (which is good at times but not as great as others have told me it was) and the fact that getting online co-op to work is a chore (I mostly play single player though). The visual style is aesthetically pleasing (I especially liked the boss designs) and controls are tight and responsive. Definitely worth the money considering the time you can put into it.

I never was a big fan of the Half-Life series, I especially though this game was decent at least, but other people seem to call this "the best FPS ever" and "one of the best games ever". Personally, I just thought the game was mediocre.
The gameplay is nothing really that special, it's a first person shooter, and a very simple one at that. I do like the range of weapons, from pistols to rifles to shotguns, and you can carry them all at one, so there is a lot of variety, much like Bioshock. However, the puzzles are extermely straight forward and the vehicles are so finicky, I press the D key for a millisecond and the entire boat goes in a 90 degree angle, the gameplay was just simple and nothing special. It just got boring for me in the end.
The graphics weren't bad, for 2004 they look quite good, but to today's standards, they are a bit outdated to today's standard's like Infamous Second Son and the new Wolfenstein. Also I didn't care for the story or the character's for that matter, especially Gordon Freeman. He is possibly one of the boring video game protagonist. He is basically just there as a object of plot, he could be more intersting if we actually heard him speak, but he is just boring. People say that he is like Link from the Legend of Zelda, but the thing with Link is you can see his facial expreesions and see how he is feeling, making him more developed, Freeman is blank with no word of dialouge and no face in game. He is not a charactter, he is an object.
Personally, I don't like this game, because of the high critical acclaim it got, and it had a very sour payoff. If you like this game, that's fine, go ahead and play it, but for me, I'll pass when Half-Life 3 eventually comes out.

This game is a masterpiece. An enormous improvement on Arkham City both in storyline and in world design and truly lives up to the legacy of the original Arkham Asylum. There's not much else to say about the game itself, but I would like to give props for one specific thing.
As one of the apparently few people who was able to run this game, albeit with some frame-rate and audio syncronisation issues, from the original launch date in June I would like to congratulate the team for the multi-monitor support. I've been stunned by how many AAA titles are locked to 1920x1080 resolutions, even when having options for larger resolutions (Dead Rising 3, I'm looking at you). Arkham Knight worked right out of the box and had no issue reducing screen size down to 1980x1080 for the pre-rendered cutscenes.
It's truly tragic that this game will always have such a bad reputation on PC, even once it's been fully fixed, but I hope publishers learn from this and start doing QA properly. The PC gaming market hasn't been this stable in years, so piracy should no longer be a reason for companies to short-change us.

I should start this by saying that I am a fan of the series.  I still think the Arkham games are a must play for anyone who likes games, console of P.C.  I even went as far as playing through this game even when it first released just because I have a huge appreciation for what the Arkham games brought the table when it comes to world building, art and game design.  With that said, the release of this game was a sham.  The game was unplayable for a huge chunk of the P.C. fanbase and even those of us who could play it had to deal with countless issues.  The season pass was shady, as usual, and months later we've come to find that the DLC that we got was just... disappointing- barely adding anything worth experiencing.
Bugs and DLC aside, the game itself is a bit of a disappointment.  The story feels flat and unsatisfying, Riddler is extra annoying with his unnecessarily large amount of trophies and really out of place Riddler races.  The Batmobile was a thing you were forced with deal with rather than a fun addition to the game.  The cast seems interesting and promising but fails to deliver; I really wanted to see more of Robin and Catwoman, Batman's interaction with his constantly-falling-appart family, anything.  It's the last game in the series, give the fans closure... but no.  Instead there's a repetitive and predictable story filled with the same tropes and structure anyone who's read a Batman comic in the past 10 years has seen over and over again.
With that said, the gameplay is still good ol' Arkham.  Combat is still fun and snappy, beating up thug after brainless thug is still satisfying.  The game is gorgeous when it wants to be and the art design is still awesome.  I guess that's a plus.  Let's face it, if you're a fan of the series you're probably going to get the game anyway but, as much as it pains me to say it, I would hold on to that thought. Great game, it's quite the grind to reach lvl 25 in a perk but the game opens up once you hit that lvl 25. You can lvl other perks in the process of lvling one specific i.e. healing as a commando, or welding doors as a firebug. The mechanics are what make this game fun each ZED has a specific weak spot and a specific class they are weak against, this also makes co-op fun on harder levels it will require your team to be versatile and each class to know their specific ZED. The VS mode is fun but still requires work at times the ZEDS are OP then the Devs will make changes and the Survivors are the OP side, it's a work in progess and they are making steps to improve the game. They add things on a regular basis like new ZEDS, weapons, skins, modes, etc. so it makes the game fun to come back to. Community is one of the best out there it's very rare I run into a toxic player and if I do it's easy to just leave the game. Biggest problem with the game is match making the servers can be as if they were placed at the bottom of the ocean with 300+ ping it makes headshots pointless. But you can just browse servers to find one that works for you. All and all a very fun game.

This is deffinitly one of the better versions of Civ. I have played Civ since Civ 2 on the PS1 and this version introduces some ideas that don't totally destroy gameplay like Civ 4 did. The biggest addition is the City-States that you can win influence with to gain some extra resource however the game doesn't penalize you if you decide to ignore them. Pretty much all the usual Civ game play elements are here and streamlined for optimal performance while cutting down on repetitive needs.
The Civs you can choose from aren't really overpowered. The only thing the game really puts emphasize on is the policies you can adopt which can really make a huge difference outside of just fielding a massive army and attacking everyone.
I still like Civilizaton Revolution the best as that version simplifies everything into more of an arcade experiance rather than the traditional Civ games but Civ 5 is probably the best traditional Civ game next to Civ 3.
Get this game. That is all.

A very fun randomly generated rogue-like side-scroller. The ten different characters each have a different set of attacks allowing for different play styles, from long range single target damage to melee crowd control. Different items augment your character in a variety of way, from healing with each hit, firing missiles on hitting an enemy or raining meteorites down when you use it. Artifacts also alter the way the game plays once unlocked, allowing for extra challenge.
The goal of each level is simple, find the teleporter, activate it, hold out against the spawning enemies and boss/es and get to the next level until the finale. As time goes by the difficulty increases, meaning enemies get tougher and bosses will start spawning randomly, this forces you to balance between collecting items but risk increasing the difficulty or go as fast as you can while losing out on items and not being as powerful. Combat-wise the game is simple but is not easy, careful use and timing of your abilities is key to survivng against the alien hordes.
The game has solo play, local co-op or online co-op (The online lacks UPnP and so requires port forwarding). This is a great game, and is better if you can play co-op.

I love that the game is just like watching an episode of South Park in terms of visuals, voice acting, and humor.
That said, I have several criticisms:
1. The game is disappointingly short. Even taking my sweet♥♥♥♥♥time and exploring everywhere, I was able to reach the end of the game in under 18 hours.
2. The game is just too damn easy. I purposely set the difficulty to the hardest setting right from the start. Even so, I was never wiped out in combat. There are a few things to note here: The battle system uses timed hits and timed blocks, similar to Mario RPG. If you are already good at this type of thing, it's easy to succeed. It's virtually impossible to not have enough money to buy equipment and healing items. I bought almost everything in the game and still ended up with over $1,000 at the end. The out-of-battle "puzzles" are nifty, but offer nothing in terms of difficulty. Worse yet, the reward for successfully solving many of these puzzles is to skip certain battle encounters. Why would I want to skip battles?
3. I love South Park's over-the-top style of humor, and The Stick of Truth is no exception. However, the game presents a strange mix of self-referential humor and recycling of old jokes. If you haven't seen all of the episodes, you won't understand the self-referential humor. If you have, you will be bored by the recycled jokes. That said, this was not the game's weakest point. I actually laughed out loud at the Canada part (no spoilers).
All in all, I did enjoy the game, but I don't consider it a good buy at the current price tag ($60). The game offers little in the way of replayability, and like I said, is very, very short. It would be much more reasonable in the $20–$30 range.

Anyone who is wondering if they should by this game, I have but one question for you: Do you enjoy the show?
If you like the show then you will LOVE this game. It kept me laughing through the whole thing with its brilliant writing and raunchy scenarios. That being said: this game is certainly not for everybody, it sure earns its M rating and you will need to know how to just take a joke because the game can be very offensive and does not censor anything. and I mean ANYTHING (For the American version anyway).
Customization is deep and you can customize the look of your character as well the the effects of the weapons you use at any time when not in combat. The combat system reminds me a lot of Paper Mario, its a turn based RPG style with timed button presses to execute your attacks. The game is quite easy once you have mastered the timing for pulling off your attacks however, but this is a game that is more focused on giving you a great experience playing it rather than a challenge. For any fan of the show, I highly recommend this game. It captures the essence of the TV show perfectly and it honestly feels like you are playing an interactive season of South park.
However the game is not without faults. The game does suffer from the occasional graphical glitch but I have not encountered anything game breaking. The game is relatively short, the main story being about 4-5 hours long with another 4-5 in side quests. However there is replay value in the 4 different classes: Warrior, Mage, Theif, and Jew which all feel differently allowing for 4 worth while play-troughs.
Pros:
-Excellent humor
-Engaging combat system
-Deep character customization
-Excellent graphics
Cons:
-Short main story
-Occasional graphical glitches
-If you aren’t a fan of the show you probably won't like it

I never was a big fan of the Half-Life series, I especially though this game was decent at least, but other people seem to call this "the best FPS ever" and "one of the best games ever". Personally, I just thought the game was mediocre.
The gameplay is nothing really that special, it's a first person shooter, and a very simple one at that. I do like the range of weapons, from pistols to rifles to shotguns, and you can carry them all at one, so there is a lot of variety, much like Bioshock. However, the puzzles are extermely straight forward and the vehicles are so finicky, I press the D key for a millisecond and the entire boat goes in a 90 degree angle, the gameplay was just simple and nothing special. It just got boring for me in the end.
The graphics weren't bad, for 2004 they look quite good, but to today's standards, they are a bit outdated to today's standard's like Infamous Second Son and the new Wolfenstein. Also I didn't care for the story or the character's for that matter, especially Gordon Freeman. He is possibly one of the boring video game protagonist. He is basically just there as a object of plot, he could be more intersting if we actually heard him speak, but he is just boring. People say that he is like Link from the Legend of Zelda, but the thing with Link is you can see his facial expreesions and see how he is feeling, making him more developed, Freeman is blank with no word of dialouge and no face in game. He is not a charactter, he is an object.
Personally, I don't like this game, because of the high critical acclaim it got, and it had a very sour payoff. If you like this game, that's fine, go ahead and play it, but for me, I'll pass when Half-Life 3 eventually comes out.

It's a licensed game that really, at its core, is a parody of Skyrims and WoWs. The satirical comedy combined with the surprisingly fun gameplay makes for a great game with an interesting story.

First and foremost, this really is a South Park game. This means that if you do not like South Park or are offended by pretty much anything they could bring up, there is a very good chance you will not be able to enjoy this game.
I find this a bit tragic even personally enjoying South Park. I say that because there is a quite good Super Mario RPG-esque RPG that powers the game that I really enjoy, and I wish more people would enjoy that.
If you do like South Park, then there is a ton of fun to be had. There is all sorts of number crunching for the RPG parts and plenty of South Park flavor and story for the rest. The game is happy to suck you in and let you play in the sleepy mountain town for quite a while.
The game isn't particularly long even doing the side quests and doesn't exactly have replay value past trying other classes, but I definitely think that it being an about 12 hours of fun is much better than 20 boring hours. I admit to enjoying shorter games overall though.
The humor overall does well. At times, South Park enjoyers will actually laugh out loud. Even at its low point, I just found the jokes to be boring rather than really grating.
If you like South Park and RPGs, this is a must have. Otherwise, you should at least be prepared for what is here.

KF2 is an improved version of the original KF, but this game (even though still in Early Access) has a number of problems that need to be tweaked. First off is that when clots grab you in KF2, it forces your camera around so that you cannot continue to play the game until you kill or shove off the offending clot. This doesn't seem like a bad thing on paper, but the reality of it is that it's a cheap mechanic that fails to actually make the clot more relevant and it breaks the momentum of gameplay. Secondly, enemies can teleport around (this has actually been adjusted to be less frequent and less obvious) so that you can't kite enemies all day. This idea seemed kind of beneficial for shaking things up a bit...but when combined with the momentum-breaking clot grab, you can line up a shot against a fleshpound or scrake, just to be grabbed from behind by a clot that a few seconds ago wasn't even in the same room as you and the only way it could have gotten there was by somehow slipping through your sealed (welded) doors...it breaks immersion if enemies can illogically outrun you by teleporting ahead or by bypassing doors just because you didn't stand by the door to prevent teleportation into the room. Thirdly, (is moreso an Early Access gripe, but hey, it's MY review, so I'm including it) there's hardly any content...we have 4 weapons for each class (would love to see it go up to 6 or 7 per class), 7 classes (have 3 more slated for release but haven't seen jack of them yet), 2 bosses (1 of which is a rerelease and I would love to have 4 or 5 total by the end of EA), 8 maps (from what I'm reading another 2 in the queue for release, but I'd like to see maybe 24 total, maybe 12 by the end of EA), and only 1 game mode: Survival (I miss KFO, even if it wasn't the most popular mode...I would also like to see maybe 2 more modes introduced, 1 of which could be competitive in some way, either PvP oriented or 2 smaller teams competing for kills or another objective). Overall, the game looks like it could be great, but the first 2 problems in tandem kinda break the game for me at most times (except when I play firebug...NOTHING grabs me as firebug! MUWAHAHAHAHA!) so I'm kind of hard-pressed to give a thumbs-up to this game in EA until they change teleportation to be almost minimal (have to keep it in some way for those stuck zeds...) OR they remove the "needy clot" mechanic...they could replace it with any number of other shticks or gimmicks and the game would benefit from it. So overall, I recommend you save your money until Tripwire Interactive gets their act together and starts putting game development ahead of DLC and microtransactions.

(Summary: well executed and largely captures the spirit of the show, has some flaws, can only recommend to the most hardcore fans at this price, even casual fans should put it on their wishlist so they're notified when it gets a price break)
I've gone casual over the past few seasons but still enjoy watching the show from time to time.  I'd still call myself a big fan, and as a fan, I can tell you we've tolerated quite a few bad games themed after South Park (the boring FPS, the annoying pinball machine, a cash-grab tower defense game).  It's not lightly when I say that this is without a doubt the best use of the property in a game.  This shows that it is possible to build a game around a license and really nail the tone.  The characters here are fully voiced (except for the player character who is subjected to several running gags as a silent protagonist -- a great decision on behalf of the writers), and their interactions are exactly what you'd expect from the show.  Other times, the "edgy" gags can feel a bit forced, unnecessary and often cringe-worthy.  It reminded me how the creators of South Park talk highly about their self-enforced "censorship" because it prevents them from using the first and most obvious thought that comes to mind.  Overall, though, I think the game gets more right than wrong, so I won't belabour the point.
The game script suffers a few flaws.  At one point in the story, you free a captured character to advance the storyline, but because I couldn't figure out how to open an elevator (due to an interaction that wasn't explained very well), I thought I'd missed something.  I set off revisiting the areas I had just cleared where I could review monitors that showed animations of the character I'd just rescued, still trapped and pleading with me to free him.  Obviously, this is confusing to a player, and I thought I'd "broken the game".  No, it was just that the designers had forgotten to wall off that area or disable the monitors.  I was able to progress once I figured out how to trigger the elevator.  There's a few interaction problems like this in the game, but they are thankfully few.
You'll encounter some "side quests" you can't immediately complete because, unknown to you, they will become part of the storyline.  For example, I thought it'd be fun to befriend the goth kids; they're accessible from the opening moments of the game, and they even tell you exactly what you need in order to gain their approval.  But the items and events needed to progress here don't become available to you until much later.  And in retrospect, I see no reason why I couldn't have completed those tasks earlier.  This alone might be a minor concern, but this isn't the only time something like this happens.  If you choose to deviate from the storyline and go do some other tasks, prepare to have your time wasted because you never really know which quests you can actually accomplish at the moment.
These are pretty common complaints about these kinds of "open world" games, but knowing that the game was delayed several times, it would be expected that these issues would have been identified and worked out.  Still, we've tolerated far worse in the past.  Is it worth $60 to run around in this universe while putting up with some minor problems?  If you're not convinced, I'd implore you to at least put it on your wishlist and grab it when it's on sale.

PROS:
1.	The game is beautiful to look at. The amount of detail they put into the mountain town is quite amazing. I found myself sidetracking just to look at the scenery. Not to mention the animation is perfect. Every character move the way they are suppose to. Even characters and animals from older seasons (1-3) have the cheaper animation. It's just like watching an episode on tv.
2.	It's ♥♥♥♥ing hilarious. It's South Park. Do I need to say more?
3.	Nostalgia. Every second I was giving one reference after another, reminding me why I fell in love with this series 11 years ago.
4.	Simple/ user-friendly. Anyone who isn't familiar with RPG's will be happy to learn that this game is easy to pick up. Weapon attacks, special attacks, magic attacks, basic stuff you expect from out of traditional RPG's. Honestly it's the perfect gateway to a new genre of gaming.
5.	Good music. Fits every situation. They have original music but they also play a lot of songs from past seasons (though a few are missing like the songs from FAITH +1). Not only that but they also play the guitar music every-time you reload your file!
Okay, let me go over the cons:
1.	GAME IS TOO DAMN EASY! Don't get me wrong, the game is the perfect gateway for RPG's, but I found the difficulty setting underwhelming. I beat the game on the hardest difficulty and yet only died three or four times! If they had more settings for the difficulty the game would better.
2.	Lack of customization. Sure you can modify your character's weapons and wear different armor, but you can't customize your characters attributes. Like if I wanted to add more health or Mana I'm unable to; the game does it by itself. It gets worse though. You're unable to customize the attributes of your own party! Everyone has their own stats that you can't modify. Even JRPG's like Paper Mario allows you to do this to some degree.
3.	Game is pretty short for an RPG. I was able to beat the game within 11 hours on my first run, and during that time I was also doing side-quests! Now if you complete everything it might take you an additional 7 hours. Speaking of which...
4.	Easy to miss items. It is extremely easy to miss out on weapons and items on this game if you're careless. If you're the type of person who like to unlock achievements or trophies then I can tell you four of them that are going to♥♥♥♥♥♥you off.
That's about it. This game is fantastic as far as humor goes, as for the gameplay... is good for what it is, though I feel this game won't have enough replay value. Also 60 bucks is over price.
Final Verdict: 7/10.

It's one of those games that can be taken seriously and have a lot of thought put into it, but can also be played by a simpleton who just wants to have fun.
That's the thing - this game is FUN. That's what it tries to be. It's not trying to have RPG aspects deeper than your typical Skyrims and WoWs and all that. It's a licensed game that really, at its core, is a parody of Skyrims and WoWs. The satirical comedy combined with the surprisingly fun gameplay makes for a great game with an interesting story.

First and foremost, this really is a South Park game. This means that if you do not like South Park or are offended by pretty much anything they could bring up, there is a very good chance you will not be able to enjoy this game.
I find this a bit tragic even personally enjoying South Park. I say that because there is a quite good Super Mario RPG-esque RPG that powers the game that I really enjoy, and I wish more people would enjoy that.
If you do like South Park, then there is a ton of fun to be had. There is all sorts of number crunching for the RPG parts and plenty of South Park flavor and story for the rest. The game is happy to suck you in and let you play in the sleepy mountain town for quite a while.
The game isn't particularly long even doing the side quests and doesn't exactly have replay value past trying other classes, but I definitely think that it being an about 12 hours of fun is much better than 20 boring hours. I admit to enjoying shorter games overall though.
The humor overall does well. At times, South Park enjoyers will actually laugh out loud. Even at its low point, I just found the jokes to be boring rather than really grating.
If you like South Park and RPGs, this is a must have. Otherwise, you should at least be prepared for what is here.

(Summary: well executed and largely captures the spirit of the show, has some flaws, can only recommend to the most hardcore fans at this price, even casual fans should put it on their wishlist so they're notified when it gets a price break)
I've gone casual over the past few seasons but still enjoy watching the show from time to time.  I'd still call myself a big fan, and as a fan, I can tell you we've tolerated quite a few bad games themed after South Park (the boring FPS, the annoying pinball machine, a cash-grab tower defense game).  It's not lightly when I say that this is without a doubt the best use of the property in a game.  This shows that it is possible to build a game around a license and really nail the tone.  The characters here are fully voiced (except for the player character who is subjected to several running gags as a silent protagonist -- a great decision on behalf of the writers), and their interactions are exactly what you'd expect from the show.  Other times, the "edgy" gags can feel a bit forced, unnecessary and often cringe-worthy.  It reminded me how the creators of South Park talk highly about their self-enforced "censorship" because it prevents them from using the first and most obvious thought that comes to mind.  Overall, though, I think the game gets more right than wrong, so I won't belabour the point.
The game script suffers a few flaws.  At one point in the story, you free a captured character to advance the storyline, but because I couldn't figure out how to open an elevator (due to an interaction that wasn't explained very well), I thought I'd missed something.  I set off revisiting the areas I had just cleared where I could review monitors that showed animations of the character I'd just rescued, still trapped and pleading with me to free him.  Obviously, this is confusing to a player, and I thought I'd "broken the game".  No, it was just that the designers had forgotten to wall off that area or disable the monitors.  I was able to progress once I figured out how to trigger the elevator.  There's a few interaction problems like this in the game, but they are thankfully few.
You'll encounter some "side quests" you can't immediately complete because, unknown to you, they will become part of the storyline.  For example, I thought it'd be fun to befriend the goth kids; they're accessible from the opening moments of the game, and they even tell you exactly what you need in order to gain their approval.  But the items and events needed to progress here don't become available to you until much later.  And in retrospect, I see no reason why I couldn't have completed those tasks earlier.  This alone might be a minor concern, but this isn't the only time something like this happens.  If you choose to deviate from the storyline and go do some other tasks, prepare to have your time wasted because you never really know which quests you can actually accomplish at the moment.
These are pretty common complaints about these kinds of "open world" games, but knowing that the game was delayed several times, it would be expected that these issues would have been identified and worked out.  Still, we've tolerated far worse in the past.  Is it worth $60 to run around in this universe while putting up with some minor problems?  If you're not convinced, I'd implore you to at least put it on your wishlist and grab it when it's on sale.

The annoying part about video games is that we cannot just focus on the content of the game itself. Instead we also have to concern ourselves with the technical aspects as well. If we were reviewing Arkham Knight purely on the content of the game it'd be rated rather highly -- in fact it is on consoles where there are fewer technical problems. However in video games we cannot ignore the technical aspects of the game -- the performance, responsiveness and port quality are all extremely relevant to the enjoyment of a game.
To put it frankly and succinctly it's just not very good. I am running on a R9 280x with an old but still trustworthy Intel core i7 950 with 24gb of RAM on Windows 10. On foot I achieve around 60fps which on "normal" settings which is fine. However when it comes to driving around in the batmobile (which the game expects you to do several times) I can get dips as low as 35fps without any destruction or much happening. It's not just limited to me either which makes it all the more sad. When they announced that the September patch was just an interim I expected that a later patch would further address the performance issues. The interim patch was a good start to making this a
PC port. Instead with just that it's 4 months late and barely better than a crap port. Sure it has borderless options but that's pretty much it. Their SMAA implementation also has some weird things about it.
It's just not worth recommending in my opinion based on my performance. The "gift" they bestowed of the backlog of Batman Arkham games is worth very little to me as I was a fan of Batman Arkham series because of those games so I own them already (except blackgate which is crap). TF2 items don't interest me either bar selling them for Steambux.
Sigh I just want to play games.

Take Left for Dead and multiply it's diversity, bad-assery, graphics, and violence and you begin to get the picture of Killing Floor 2.
Killing Floor 2 has taken zombie horde survival to a new level and the game is awesome! For early access, this game is fantastic! I can't wait to see how the full release will be. Until then, this review stands and it will be ameliorated upon full release.
Pros:
Non-stop fast paced zombie killing action.
Impressive graphics.
Appropriately badass music.
7 engaging and fun perks of weapon classes to choose from.
Goal orientated waves ending in intense boss battles.
A plethora of immersive and large maps riddled with easter eggs and hidden items.
Team based, which means loads of fun with friends and other players
Cons:
Early access, so there are things to work on such as small glitches and only 2 mini-bosses and 2 bosses.
The perks are great, but they don't feel totally dedicated. For example, a Gunslinger can still fully operate the medic class weapons.
Leveling upon to access attributes takes a very very long time.

I've waited a long time for the sequel to release. It hasn't disappointed since.
Just when you think you were alone as nothing more than a scientist, everyone still recognizes you and considers you the hero. You have the plot laid down once you saw how miserable the people of the city walk around.
The new Source Engine's physics and graphics in the game show great fun and at times make you want to enjoy the scenery, if not for the Combine to keep your head back into the action. Valve didn't over-indulge on the eye candy, as Alyx Vance becomes more helpful than hot. The engine certainly motivated my friends to want their hands on the engine's tools to see what they can create, mods or movies.
The heroes in each chapter are handy to have around for the time being, and you know when you have to progress through the game further alone. Yet even though at times you are not with a companion, there is a special thing here and there that gets you places (dune buggy and airboat for example) and make you understand that there's more to the game franchise than merely running and gunning. This can be a negative if you're not into puzzle-solving.
It even has its own creep factor at times. No intentional jump scares, but as usual, headcrabs and zombies lurk around in hordes. The addendum being there are various types now, and they add to the challenge and scariness in their own way. The game has it's dark and grimdark areas, and with thoughtful ways to progress and combat through them.

This is a war game. Every geometric shape with 3-6 verticies is out to get you. You play as one triangle, against the never ending waves of edges coming at you. Now on to why this game is so fun:
This games takes 1.52 seconds to learn, and all of eternity to master. After you play it the first time, you will keep playing for one of two reasons:

2.You can't stand the fact that you still haven't beat your pathetic record

No crashes to desktop, fall through maps or any major glitches as reported by other users were experienced. The game ran somewhat smooth during the play-through as the fps fluctuations were noticeable. RAM usages stayed around 9.5gigs of my 16gigs. Twice the game loaded into a black screen which was fixed by restarting my pc and twice the game loaded and did not recognise inputs from both my xbox-360 pad and the keyboard, had to alt-tab out and close the game from task manager and then restart the game which loaded properly after. As for the game itself, the storyline was pretty good, if not, the best of the series. The gameplay was, as expected of all arkham games, awesome and easy to learn, including the driving mechanics of the batmobile, which was a task at first. Overall it was a pleasant experience…which, I noticed from other reviews, is a rare thing in this game.

How to NOT suck at this game (Single Player):
1. You can choose your civilization (Rome, Russia, or China I suggest)
2. Start your civilization and try to have as much peace as possible with the other civilizations
3. Make as many troops as possible over time
4. If a civilization wants you to team up and go at war with another civilizations, don't accept it since you'll lose many of your troops if you do
5. Don't just try to get as many troops, but try to have more than the other civilizations and spread them around to know what other civilizations lie out there.
6. If for whatever reason a civilization gets mad at you and steals one of your cities, then make more troops, surround your city, then make it into battle (be sure to have enough troops to drive your enemy out)
7. At the end, if you successfully get nukes before other civilizations and you are at peace with them, send in nukes and wipe them out.
8. Once you do this to one civilization, you know how to deal with the rest.
9. Good Luck!

Killing Floor is all grown up.
Sure, he's a lot less "cool" now that he's taking "things" slowly, but he's come to accept the fact that he isn't fully matured yet. He remembers the old days where he wasn't sure of his place in the world, or if he'd ever change - but now, he's more intelligent, more pleasant to interact with, and doesn't look half-bad either. You can tell he's been taking care of himself much more recently, and is a much more balanced individual.
His taste in music has improved slightly - he remembers the days where he'd only listen to two or three songs he really liked, tops. Now he listens to all matters of -core, his favorite song being Collapsing by Demon Hunter (and honestly, who could disagree?). With all the upgrading going on it seems he's temporarily lost his "Abandon All" MP3, however.
He never really shook that interest in "fashon economics", though, so he's pretty eager to sell you his "designs" like they're a mixtape. He's pretty subtle about it and it doesn't get in the way of him making or keeping freinds, but the concern is that he'll eventually scare everyone off by coming up with another scheme thats so money grubbing it'll make him seem like a scam artist.
We can only hope he continues his maturation, as too many other games like him find themselves abandoned with no place to go, or worse, dead in an ally somewhere.

Oh, hello. If you are a big fan of South Park, as I am, then surely you will enjoy The Stick of Truth and what is has to offer. If you don't care to involve yourself with games involving talking poo, becoming facebook friends with Al Gore to become united against ManBearPig, fighting a crossdressing princess under the supervision of a a nude elderly man, and becoming afflicted with Dire AIDS, then this game might not be up your alley. NOTE: this game is not for the easily offended.
The turn-based battle system is fun, there are just enough different moves to keep things interesting (though I would love to see more moves/variation). The story is great, it's like watching an episode of the show that goes on for 10 hours. The side missions, collectibles, and other various "extra" features of the game kept me busy during my second playthrough and kept me interested enough to finish that playthrough. Unfortunately there is not much variation between the 4 classes, so there is very little replay value - don't expect the game to "feel" any different when you play a different class, everyone can use all the same weapons and armor only the special moves are different (each class has 5 special moves, unlocked as you progress through the game).
My major complaint about The Stick of Truth: there is not enough content to justify the $60 price tag. One could beat this game to 100% completion in under 20 hours, which is actually a generously high estimate. I haven't heard any talk of expansions at this point in time, so while I do love this game I'm also upset with myself for dropping $60 on it.
FINAL VERDICT: This game is a must-have for any South Park fan, BUT you should wait for it to go on sale or come down in price. With any luck more content will come to those of us thirsty for more, but I'm not getting my hopes up.

I pre-purchased this game and started playing as soon as it came out. Although I highly recommend this game, I actually have one more gripe now than I did before that last patch.
It's really hard to knock this game. Despite the major hurdles that the team had to jump, the game just feels complete. This is the most open, detailed, and structured Batman game to date. It really feels like a culmination of what you expect from a Batman game.
The story is compelling and makes you want to keep driving on to complete it. As well, the side missions are well put together and add real gameplay that makes you want to complete them instead of skipping them entirely. My only complaint for side missions (A requirement for a separate ending) is the Riddler missions. I never minded doing Riddler puzzles in the past, but after 4 games, I just don't want to add an additional 30hrs of gameplay just to track down Riddler thugs and grab every trophy in the game. I feel like this could have been avoided by sticking to riddles as a requirement and not the collectables or destroyable items.
It's refreshing to see a villain besides the Joker taking on a major role to conquer Gotham. The Scarecrow really takes on his own, outplotting Batman alongside the Arkham Knight in an attempt to cover the city in his fear gas. The Arkham Knight is also a great villain, albeit probably ruined by previews, reviews, and DLCs by now if you haven't played the game already. The story creates a great drive to figure out the identity of the Arkham Knight and why he knows so much about Batman.
Most complaints about the game generally are about the graphics. Having said that, I played through the entire game with an R9 290 with very minimal issues. On first release, my biggest problems were frame drops from the Batmobile or while gliding or viewing the city. After the first major patch, all of that went away. I went on to buy a second 290, although arguably unnecessary to play the game at reasonable frames. I was also able to play the game well on my wife's 280x. My ONLY gripe so far with the final release was the crippling of Crossfire, as I've found no settings in-game or out to play without major flickering issues.
It's alright.

Oh, hello. If you are a big fan of South Park, as I am, then surely you will enjoy The Stick of Truth and what is has to offer. If you don't care to involve yourself with games involving talking poo, becoming facebook friends with Al Gore to become united against ManBearPig, fighting a crossdressing princess under the supervision of a a nude elderly man, and becoming afflicted with Dire AIDS, then this game might not be up your alley. NOTE: this game is not for the easily offended.
The turn-based battle system is fun, there are just enough different moves to keep things interesting (though I would love to see more moves/variation). The story is great, it's like watching an episode of the show that goes on for 10 hours. The side missions, collectibles, and other various "extra" features of the game kept me busy during my second playthrough and kept me interested enough to finish that playthrough. Unfortunately there is not much variation between the 4 classes, so there is very little replay value - don't expect the game to "feel" any different when you play a different class, everyone can use all the same weapons and armor only the special moves are different (each class has 5 special moves, unlocked as you progress through the game).
My major complaint about The Stick of Truth: there is not enough content to justify the $60 price tag. One could beat this game to 100% completion in under 20 hours, which is actually a generously high estimate. I haven't heard any talk of expansions at this point in time, so while I do love this game I'm also upset with myself for dropping $60 on it.
FINAL VERDICT: This game is a must-have for any South Park fan, BUT you should wait for it to go on sale or come down in price. With any luck more content will come to those of us thirsty for more, but I'm not getting my hopes up.

As a great fan of the Batman Arkham series, I thoroughly enjoyed this latest instalment. The most obvious issues on PC, which >90% of user reviews allude to, are those relating to PC specific performance. I therefore acknowledge that I'm in the minority of the user base who have found this game to be 'playable' since day one.  My experience is based on a GTX970 running alongside a i7-4770 (3.4GHz), 16Gb DDR3 RAM, no additional applications, and a 1920x1080 full screen resolution. My comments on performance are based on my experience of the patch released on the 03/09/15 (or 09/03/15 US). Settings put all post-processing effects on, texture resolution is on normal, shadow quality on high, level of detail on high, v sync is off; of the nVidia gameworks features, only enhanced rain and light shafts are on; and framerate is capped to 60 FPS (equal to monitor refresh rate). First off, the in-game benchmark is not a good indicator of in-game performance; result was average of 90 FPS. With an uncapped framerate, over a period of diverse gameplay, it ran in the range of 40 (batmobile and gliding) to 80 FPS, with an average of roughly 70. I would consider this playable; by no means perfect, but I've yet to encounter any major graphical bugs, stuttering or hitches (even with a mechanical hard drive).
Therefore, if you've enjoyed the other instalments in this franchise, I would recommend this game. I thought that, in particular, the gameplay (batmobile combat may be divisive), atmosphere and plot (although the 'Arkham Knight' feels like an unnecessary gimmick given his true identity) were fantastic and from a technical perspective the best in the franchise. I would go as far as to rate this as my second favourite in the series, behind Arkham Asylum - I definitely found it more enjoyable than Arkham City, which is noticeably shorter, felt more repetitive and life-less in comparison.
My only major criticisms are of the changes to the challenge mode. I felt it should have been built upon from the brilliant design in AC, yet has been made to be a WayneTech simulation - resulting in holographic enemies which appear as do characters who 'teleport' in Star Trek, the conspicuous blue borders which ruin the atmosphere and make every level feel the same, the inability to play as alternate characters, and the single round system which makes it noticeably less fun. As I understand (and to my great surprise and delight) RockSteady have been updating the game to minimise all these issues, but it's still not in a good enough state yet.
On a final note, if you think you'll enjoy it, buy it; and don't worry so much about performance.
And if it doesn't work on your system? Steam refunds!
