I waited patiently for four months for Rocksteady and Warner Bros. to put this game back on Steam and fix it properly. I bought it when it was first up for sale, and the game ran very poorly for me, yet I wanted to know where the story went so I struggled through all the lag and stuttering and horrible textures to play through it to the end of the main story. I only own a PC and not any consoles so that was the only choice available to me to play through the game. I was really excited to play the sequel to Arkham Asylum and City, two games that I really enjoyed, and I am a huge Batman fan. I read all the comic books, and I watch all the movies and cartoons, so I was always going to play through this game, awful port or not.
Now I will admit I don't have the best and most up to date computer in the world, but I find it more than adequate to play through pretty much any other game I might try to throw at it. I've enjoyed playing The Witcher 3, GTA V, MGS V and countless other great games on it this year with perfectly acceptable settings and stable performance. But somehow this game just won't quite run nicely for me, even after the update from a month or two ago, which did improve things for me and make the game run a fair bit better, it's still not quite right. The framerate jumps up and down like a yo-yo, from around 55fps to 25fps, constantly shifting. I'd prefer the game to run at a consistent 60fps but I honestly don't mind a framerate in the 30 range, but only if it's stable and consistent, but it is not in this game no matter what settings I put it on. It's kind of like watching a movie and somebody is constantly pressing the fast forward and pause button. The textures, which I have to play on 'low' as I have a 2gb VRAM card, have improved from the awful state of release, but I still see occasional objects that just look like a blurry mess. There's also still issues with dialogue going out of sync on cut scenes.
What annoys me here is that this is a game running on Unreal Engine 3, a game engine that has been around for over a decade and developers really have no excuse for not being able to develop stable and well optimised games on it at this stage. I understand that it is a 'heavily modified' version of Unreal Engine 3, but it really shouldn't matter. And it most certainly should not be an engine that requires amazing hardware to handle a game developed on it. I believe Bioshock Infinite runs on UE3 and I run that game at like a stable 80fps with everything on max settings, different type of game admittedly, but really there is no excuse.
Normally at this point I would say that graphics don't really matter, and it is gameplay, story and replayability that’s important. I would dearly like to say that about this game, but I just can't quite say that. I did enjoy many things about this game, it is basically the same as Asylum and City but with some cool new moves put in which work from the FEAR suit. I do love the design in this game. The way Batman's suit looks is seriously cool, and Gotham City is beautifully detailed and huge in scope. The new thing in this one is the Batmobile, I know a lot of people hate it, but I actually rather enjoyed it, but it is certainly overused. I particularly don't like it when you are literally driving the batmobile inside buildings to solve environmental puzzles. I get it, you've got this cool new thing, and you want to show it off, but there is no need to try and force it in to nearly every part of the game.
I did like the story of this game, I particularly like the references to The Killing Joke, and how they brought back a certain character. Many of the moments in the story were very emotionally charged in a way that the previous games lacked. What is a shame is that the game lacks the great boss battles that the previous games were so memorable for. Scarecrow as the main villain I found particularly disappointing. I've always found him interesting as a psychological manipulative villain, but all the stuff about him in this game just basically comes to nothing. There's also another villain in this game whose story is a bit odd, without wanting to spoil anything all I can really say is that it's just kind of lame the way they try to hide something which is very obvious to any Batman fan. They could have just done his story a lot better, and it could have been amazing, but as it is, it's just kind of a messed up opportunity.
I cannot give this game a thumbs up and I do not recommend it. It is not completely unplayable to me, and as described the game has a lot of commendable things. If you are a fan of the series and have to play it, then yeah get it, but do be aware that for a lot of people it is still unplayable. If you can get it on another system or are able to wait then don't get it now on Steam. Don't expect this game to ever be properly fixed. Warner Bros./Rocksteady have been saying for months about all the stuff they are going to do to fix it, but still haven't done all the stuff they said they would. They seem more concerned about getting the DLC up. Their idea of compensation is almost laughable, not that I ever wanted free stuff from them, I wanted a working game. But the way they treat their customers is disrespectful, and ultimately that is why I have to give this game a thumbs down.

So i got the game at launch. I am a huge fan of the Arkham series and i couldn't wait to play the last game in the series.
We all know that the PC launch was a huge disaster with all the game glitches, bugs and more. Some could play the game without any issues (Except maybe some lag or fuzzy texture) and some hade so much issues that the game was unplayable. I was lucky enough to play the game without any big issues and i completed the game in two days instead of waiting for Rocksteady to patch the game so it could be playable for everyone.
Batman: Arkham Knight is different than the previous Batman games. Arkham Knight is darker, more brutal and more non-child friendly than Arkham City. There are many more deaths in this game and a more darker story than the previous ones.
The story is great. Few stories from a video game has amazed me and Arkham Knight is one of them. I won't tell why and to understand what i mean, you should play the game. Arkham City had a better story but Arkham Knight isn't far behind.
If you played the last three Arkham games (Yes, including Arkham Origins), there isn't much to know about the gameplay here since it's the same. You go around, fly, beat some bad guys. Same controls but with some new combat moves. This time, you can also use the Batmobile who can be used as a tank. The batmobile can be extremely clumsy but also fun to use (Tho, it is faster to use the Grapnel Gun to get to your destination). I love the part where you use the Batmobile as a tank to shoot down Militia tanks. I love it.
Overall, Batman: Arkham Knight isn't the most perfect game out there and i think Arkham City is the better game. But Arkham Knight deliver something you barely see in other games who serves as a finale to a series.
I really think you should get Batman: Arkham Knight but play Arkham Asylum and Arkham City before you do (You don't need Arkham Origins or Arkham Origins: Blackgate but you can get them if you want).
Yes to Batman: Arkham Knight!

This really is a very well rounded roguelike. The game is unforgiving bu not unfair (as it might be the case with other RLs such as Binding of Isaac, or Faster than Light). When you die, it is always because you have done something wrong or you did not undertand well the mechanics of the upgrades-classes and how to make good use of them. Of coure certain combinations of items can make the game easier than others, but you will never feel like a game is doomed from the start. In all my hours of playng, i never quit a game because of the items i got, i always reached to the end or die knowing that i did by my own mistake. Time and money management is crucial, as is trying your luck with the shrines (you can decide either to do that and risk getting nothing, or spend more money for an assured item).
Summing it up, frustrating at first, but immensely rewarding and with endless longevity. The 10 classes play very different from each other and will make you go back to try and finish the game with each one of them.
By the way, the soundtrack is FANTASTIC. You'll be putting the game in pause just to listen to it.
If you enjoy roguelikes even if just a tiny bit, do get this game. And do get the soundtrack too :)

So i got the game at launch. I am a huge fan of the Arkham series and i couldn't wait to play the last game in the series.
We all know that the PC launch was a huge disaster with all the game glitches, bugs and more. Some could play the game without any issues (Except maybe some lag or fuzzy texture) and some hade so much issues that the game was unplayable. I was lucky enough to play the game without any big issues and i completed the game in two days instead of waiting for Rocksteady to patch the game so it could be playable for everyone.
Batman: Arkham Knight is different than the previous Batman games. Arkham Knight is darker, more brutal and more non-child friendly than Arkham City. There are many more deaths in this game and a more darker story than the previous ones.
The story is great. Few stories from a video game has amazed me and Arkham Knight is one of them. I won't tell why and to understand what i mean, you should play the game. Arkham City had a better story but Arkham Knight isn't far behind.
If you played the last three Arkham games (Yes, including Arkham Origins), there isn't much to know about the gameplay here since it's the same. You go around, fly, beat some bad guys. Same controls but with some new combat moves. This time, you can also use the Batmobile who can be used as a tank. The batmobile can be extremely clumsy but also fun to use (Tho, it is faster to use the Grapnel Gun to get to your destination). I love the part where you use the Batmobile as a tank to shoot down Militia tanks. I love it.
Overall, Batman: Arkham Knight isn't the most perfect game out there and i think Arkham City is the better game. But Arkham Knight deliver something you barely see in other games who serves as a finale to a series.
I really think you should get Batman: Arkham Knight but play Arkham Asylum and Arkham City before you do (You don't need Arkham Origins or Arkham Origins: Blackgate but you can get them if you want).

Still terrible. It seems the pc version of this game will never truly be fixed. If you're running a top-of-the-line system, you might find this playable (although that's not a guarantee) but otherwise you should stay away for performance reasons alone. Even if you get things running smoothly, it's still not a very good game.
The story is...fine. Incredibly predictable, but fine. If you've read even a few issues of Batman published within the last decade you're going to know exactly who the Arkham Knight is the moment you meet him. There's also just way too much going on. In addition to the core story missions, there is a glut of repeatable side missions that focus on different members of Batman's Rouges Gallery. The problem is that once you've played one kind of these missions, there's no reason to play any more of them except for completion's sake. All the penguin missions are identical, as are all the Two Face missions, as are all the ♥♥♥♥ing ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t Riddler Races, etc, etc.
Which brings me to the biggest problem in this game, one you doubtlessly know about, the batmobile. It sucks. It's completely antithetical to what the rest of the game tries to offer, and it's forced upon you again and again. Why would anyone who enjoys the satisfying, rhythm-based combat or the puzzle-like, predator sections want to play Missile Command with tanks? It's boring and feels like a tax you're obliged to pay to access any of the fun stuff. It's also weirdly tied to the Arkham Knight, so it makes me resent his inclusion in the game even more. Wanna go fight Scarecrow's goons? Too bad, you gotta make it through 5 waves of Arkham Knight tank-faff first.
What's more, by being so watered-down the fun stuff isn't even that fun any more. The combat is pretty much the same that it's always been (although the few sections you get to team up with another member of the bat family, wherein you may execute cool team takedowns, are pretty fun), and there are so few predator sections (which were my favorite part of the series) that the game doesn't feel like it has room to experiment much with them.
Don't even get me started on the Riddler garbage (too late!). In Asylum, the Riddler stuff was essentially a bunch of fun extras that led to a really cool secret. City was a bit more ambitious but it was all fairly do-able. In Arkham Knight there are over 240 of those ♥♥♥♥ers, not to mention awful races where you'll blow up the batmobile umpteen times trying to memorize patterns in a lethal (yet somehow hideously dull) car-based version of Simon Says. And they use this♥♥♥♥♥♥to gate the real ending of the game. That's right, if you want the conclusion to this pile of dross you're going to have to sift through a whole lot of it.
In summary, Arkham Knight is a mess. Even without the technical issues, it's still an overstuffed game where all the good bits are suffocated under the sagging, bloated flesh of bad mechanics and repetitive design. Please don't buy it.

South Park: The Stick of Truth - ShadowHatter Review
This is the South Park game fans have been waiting for.
The Good:
- The same South Park humor we've grown to love.
- Same exact animation style as the Television show, making you feel immersed in it's world and making you feel as if you're in an episode of South Park yourself.
- Create your own character and put yourself right into South Park with great friends like Butters, Cartman, Craig, and more!
- RPG Combat in the same vein as Mario RPG
- Tons of fan service for any South Park fan, with tons of video game and movie references to satiate your palette.
- lots of fun collectibles like Friends on Facebook, Chinpokomon, and awesome weapons like a Rod of Awesome Boobage.
- Randy Marsh plays a big role in this game, though not as big as the main characters but still enough that you get your daily Randy Marsh dosage of everyone's favorite cartoon dad.
- The setting of the game, where kids are LARPing and making playtime seem oh so real to the point where you'd want to start LARPing with friends.
The Bad:
- Missable collectables which can ruin any completionist's day.
- Some bug issues with few people, though I personally haven't experienced any myself.
- Copy/Paste environments with few changes. Lots of the houses and rooms are pretty much the same template copy/pasted with different changes here and there. Most of the kid's rooms don't even look like the originals from the show, though tbh I never really pay much attention to the rooms during the hilarity that ensues in the show.
The Neutral:
- Beating this game with a 100% completion will run you about 12-15hrs of gameplay. Some people see a problem with this considering this game is an RPG, but considering this is a South Park game, I give it a pass.
Honestly, like I said before, this is the South Park game we've all been waiting for, and the wait was definitely worth it. I can honestly say that, despite the AAA price this game has ($60) I got my money's worth considering the fantastic South Park humor it has and having the chance to be a part of it as the New Kid.
As a fan I truly loved this game and everything it has to offer, which is why I have to dish out the score I gave and the bad points I gave, because I want this game to improve and would love to have more sequels of this game. Matt and Trey in an interview mentioned how they wrote over 850 pages of content for the game, but severely cut most of it to prevent the game from releasing in 2023. With that said apparently we have a DLC section in the game so we can only hope for some DLC in the future and hopefully some sequels.

Half-Life 2 is an incredibly popular game, on par with it's predecessor, and many people elevate it as one of the best games in all time. So, I have to get out of this way: This game is very over-rated. And while doesn't actually say much about the quality of the game itself, I have to honestly say that I was somewhat dissapointed when I played it and prefer the first game over that one. That being said, it's still a very good game and, while I don't like it as much, it's a worthy successor for Half-Life.
Overall, it was not as compelling as the first game. In that one, you were a lowly scientist, trapped in a facility, overrun by aliens and the army, with few friendly people, fellow scientists and guards (who also don't have a high survival rate). In the second game, you are a practically mythological figure, who nearly single-handedly fights against an alien army, that conquered the earth. The basic situation is not much different, since Gordon doesn't have much of a choice and has nowhere to run, but it feels less like you are an ordinary person and more a great, powerful hero. And with "feels" I mean that it practically spells it out for you.
That's the thing I dislike the most about the game: It does a really bad job at pretending that the world is self-contained and not just made to make you feel like a hero. Every action game, rather blatantly, tries to make you feel like a badass, but in no game is it so unsubtle as in Half-Life 2. And it's very annoying to get praised by nearly every NPC for rather unclear reasons. It severly hurst suspension of disbelieve and immersion.
The world itself isn't all that compelling either. You'd think it would be more interesting to visit the outside and different places instead of being confined to a single facility, but somehow that isn't the case. Generally, there isn't so much a sense of being trapped like in the first game and so it often feels much less dangerous. Aside from Ravenholm, there aren't many memorable places either.
The selection of weapons is rather pathetic, especially when compared with the first game. It's like they devised the Gravity Gun and thought it would be awesome enough to have no need for other non-generic weapons.
The selection of enemies isn't much better. There isn't that much variance and many enemies return or are a varation from enemies of the first game. And aside from the Combine, few are really fun to fight.
However, none of this means that the game is bad. Quite the opposite, it's a very good game that can be recommended to any fan of shooters. While it elevates you to a great, quasi-mythological hero this time, it still gives you a real sense of danger. In some ways, even better than the first game. The best parts of the game are when you are all alone and the Combine is breathing down your neck. It's very immersive and gives a feel of danger and urgency, without feeling too gamy. Quite the opposite, the game doesn't even pressure you to kill every enemy in your path and often fleeing seems to be the better option (and may even improve the pacing of the scene). The game could have used more scenes like that (especially near the end, where the game gives you a massively overpowered weapon instead) and I would like to see it in more games. Alone for that, the game is worth playing.
Aside from big action scenes, there are also calmer moments, that work pretty well, especially when they come after a wild hunt. Those occasionally feature physics-based puzzles. I don't like them all that much, as they sometimes feel a bit artifical and can be a bit clunky, but they are pretty easy, short and uncommon, so they don't overstay their welcome and a nice diversion.
And while I bashed the selection of weapons, it has its advantages. No weapon really feels useless or unnecessary and all of them find good use throughout the game. Except for the Gravity Gun, there is no overly gimmick-y weapon that is only useful in few situations.
All in all, it's not one of the greatest games in existence. It is, however, a very good game that every fan of shooters should give a try.

TLDR; 7/10 game running at a 3/10 performance. Game runs poorly, actual story is okay but ruined in the last hour, extra collectables were a chore and not worth the time and effort. Buy GOTY edition for cheap but the game still isn't good enough on PC. I will update this review with future patches.
Please note, I have played Arkham Asylum and City both to 100% on PC/xbox 360. I have also played origins but did not 100% the main. This review will not contain any spoilers. I played at 1080 resolution at around 60/45fps with very occasional dips lower, with the lowest settings for everything. I have an i7 4770k, 16gb RAM and a GTX 770 and I played this on windows 8. I played the game on a SSD so loading times might be considerably better for me than the files on a HDD. When I played the game, I had the interim patch but from what I understand, the full release hasn't changed much. Also, I played the game with a wired xbox 360 controller on a 1080 TV on hard mode. Your experience may differ based on your hardware and software. Also I will not be including a full dlc review in this.
Performance/appearance:
Batman Arkham knight ran poorly on my machine. There was issues concerning large frame rate drops about (20-30 fps decrease), textures not loading for a few seconds, micro stuttering and large loading times. The performance is unacceptably bad for a game in 2015 with a major publisher backing the studio. The patches have improved the performance however, it is still not good enough for most gamers. You shouldn't be required to have a SSD, over 8 GB RAM and a 760+ for a performance this bad. I suspect more patches will be added in the future to improve the performance so if you want an update of the performance based on my parts in the future then send me a mail and I will see if things have improved.
Batmobile sections were the biggest offenders of reducing the frame rate however the frame rate dropped at random during other portions of the game.
I will say, the game was nice to look at with some cool destructions physics, lighting effects some excellent rain effects. If you are using an nvidia card the nvidia gameworks options look nice but they completely crippled my frame rate to around 22-18 fps. I'm not sure what the effect will be on an AMD card but I imagine it will probably make things even worse for your experience.
Gameplay:
Gameplay is broken up into a few different sections. These include combat, stealth, free roam, driving the batmobile and small detective section. These mechanics are used in part with the side missions and the main campaign. If you have played any of the Arkham games you know how the combat is and the free roaming however there has been minor changes which did make a difference to my experience with the game.
Combat was much less precise than in Asylum or City. I found myself hitting enemies who I was not aiming for more than a few times which lead to some unfair deaths. My partner and a friend played the PS4 version and we found the same issue with their experience too. Some of the new enemies aloud for healing and revival which combined with existing enemies, meant combat lasted far too long in some sections. However, as a Batman veteran, the game was a nice challenge with the combat and it was nice for hard mode to actually feel like it was hard at times.
Stealth is for the most part unchanged. You distract enemies, you knock them out, you pick them up one by one and you which if you have played any of the previous games you know the song and dance. There are some minor changes but they don't change too much bar getting the fear multi takedown ability which makes many of the stealth sections much easier. In response, enemies have new gadgets and tech but it is given at a nice difficulty curve.
Freeroaming was probably the least changed mechanic but the most improved. The grappling hook has received a much welcomed boost in strength and you can go much further and faster than in previous games. I did have some issues with the frame rate during some of the very fast flight sections however they were not too frequent. The only down side to freely roaming the city is some sections will require you to use the batmobile. Which leads me to my next point.
The batmobile was the worst bit of the game and unfortunately you have to spend a lot of time in it. As I mentioned in my performance paragraph, I found the frame rate was at its worst during these sections with the frame rate dropping significantly when driving very quickly. The batmobile is also used in stealth section in some ridiculous ways and many times during the game when i didn't know what to do, the solution as using the batmobile in some silly way. I get that this is a game and I should suspend my disbelief but I also didn't have much fun during these sections due to the dull tank controls, low frame rate and at the rate I had to use it.
Detective mode has probably been one of the smallest but most significant changes for Arkham Knight. The main detective vision has been seriously nerfed giving less detail on objects, being blocked more often in stealth sections, not available in the batmobile and having a lower viewer distance. For most of the game this isn't an issue, however I will explain why it is an issue with the side missions.
There are some decent side missions but some of the supervillains were pretty lame and their side missions were tedious with the same mission repeated several times. If you aren't going to try and get all the riddles then move onto my story section. If you have played any of the previous games then you will know about the riddler mission which involves collecting question mark tokens and taking pictures of question marks and small hints of characters from the batman universe. As I mentioned in detective mode, the vision mode has been hugely nerfed and now riddler clues are not highlighted at all. This means you are almost forced to go find all the riddler informants and constantly check you map which can be a chore at best and a miserable slog at worse.
Story:
As I mentioned, I won't be spoiling the game. I felt the Arkham Knight was a little underwhelming but it was to be expected. I would recommend avoiding IMDB pages and looking up voice actors if you don't want to know who the Arkham Knight. However, the identity was pretty obvious about 50% through the story. Parts of the best bits of the story are literally there to develop the reveal or the Arkham Knight and was some brilliant depictions of some of the iconic sections of the batman lore.
There was a complaint I had that one of the best bits of the game and some of the story arcs of one of the characters was made completely pointlessly in the last reveal. This was a disappointment to me as it was one of the best bits of the game and probably the single most shocking part in any of the Arkham games.
Overall, the story was the only thing keeping me going and I found once I was done with the story, the fun I had with the game was diminished and I was getting impatient with the side missions. If you are compelled to collect everything like I was then go for it but if I were to do it for a first time again, finish all the side missions except the riddler and then watch the true ending on YouTube.

I was pleasantly surprised to see that on the in-game benchmark my rig (i7 3770k and NVidia 970 OC) had an average of 55fps@1440p with GameWorks disabled and 58fps@1080p with GameWorks enabled. All other graphics settings were maxed out. The in-game fps does drop a bit whilst driving but I never got lower than 45fps so far, and even then only for a split-second. Killing Floor 2 is a sequel to the popular and successful Killing Floor 1. Keep in mind that Killing Floor 2 is in early access and has yet to receive a full release. Many players from the previous title may know that some of the new features of Killing Floor 2 included sprinting and crosshair, which may come as a disappointment. While I personally do not believe this should be an issue at all for both veteran and new players, it does remove the aspect of having your knife out to run quicker.
About the
- there is no doubt that there is a big improvement. The game has updated graphics and textures which look significantly better than they did before.
There are 10
and on the 11th wave you have to fight against a boss (either the Patriarch or Hans Volter for now). By the end of your tenth wave the map you’re surviving appears splattered in blood from each shot you make. It’s a good feature and definitely adds atmosphere to the chaos.
The first Killing Floor provided a selection of 7
. Killing Floor 2’s Early Access contains 9 perks for now - Berserker, Commando, Support, Field Medic, Demolitionist, Sharpshooter, Firebug, Gunslinger and the new perk Swat. Once the game reaches its full release it is rumoured that it will include 10 perks in total. Each perk has its own special skill which is unlocked at levels 5,10,15,20 and 25 and there are two options of which you can't choose your special skill.
in Killing Floor 2 are a bit modified compared to Killing Floor 1. There are not many combos you can use for the insta - kill of the big zeds. I have seen one for the medic with his nades and I can't even call it a combo, more like a simple strategy and one for the firebug. So it is not very easy to kill Fleshpounds and Scrakes. The one thing I don't like is that if someone enrages the Scrake or the Fleshpound, they can attack anyone they want. So I find it really annoying to have them charging against me, without being prepared to kill them. Headshots here are essential, so try your best not to miss them.
I have a mixed feeling when it comes to

When the waves get harder in some of the cases everybody just runs around trying to save theirselves and it would be pure luck if you end the wave with your teammates being around you, because in some situations it is impossible to stay together. So it is best to count on yourself to finish the wave, alive.
There are not many
added to this game, but hopefully new ones will be released soon.
More maps, weapons, game modes, removing classes imbalance, fixing teleporting zeds and concentrating on the game's development rather than adding cosmetics will definitely make more Killing Floor 2 players happy.
Overall I would not recommend  this game to other people for now, because Tripwire have turned it into  a casual game. You play 1-2 maps and everything is okay, but  after that it gets deadly boring ... If I have to compare it with KF1 - a BIG lack of content. Sure it is an early access, but there aren't any signs of progress.
In the end after playing around 400 hours I came to the following conslusion: Killing Floor 2 - a game where disscussing other player's performance it is more important than the game itself. Enjoy.

Great game for a sequel to one of the best co op shooters around. Killing Floor 2 picks where End of The Line update for Killing Floor left off a few months later. Now, Europe is filled with Zeds not zombies as some people say. You only have one objective: Survive. The weapons have been redesigned for some such as the flamethrower. Perks have been kept the same with the addition of the Gunslinger perk; originally from SCrN mod in Killing Floor.
One little change is that now you can customize your own choices as to how you want a perk to work. So let's say you have a level 10 Commando perk. There is an option to either choose extended mags or have your backup weapons to have 60% more damage. And this makes the game more fun!
A very important key aspect of this game is Teamwork. Do not absolutely go RAMBO and try and solo this game unless you're really good at it. There's a reason why this game's tag is labeled CO-OP. Oh and please call out in the team chat for Scrakes and Fleshpounds. They will screw your whole team over.
That's all folks. Happy killing Zeds

TL;DR - 6 player co-op FPS. Tons of great action, weapon/character variety and cosmetics! Very nice visuals and smooth animations, fantastic gore system. Give it a go.
+ Zed-slaying FPS which can be played either offline solo or with up to 5 other friends.
+ Your choice between using a matchmaker or server browser, and even direct connect. Very nice.
+ For an early access game, has a nice variety of content. A few different maps to choose from at the start, with a ton of player created maps to play as well. Weapon variety for each class is decent so far, but overall there are quite a few different weapons.
+ Very nice graphics on best settings, still pretty good when watered down to save fps.
+ Smooth animations, very nice.
+When played with a good team like a well-oiled machine, gameplay can be both intense and tactical... for a fast-paced game.
+ Large amounts of very gory and very fun action
+ Paint your favorite areas red (with blood)
+ Took between 100-120 hours to feel like I was running out of new things to do. Not even close to boring yet.
+ tf2-esque-conomy with hats/masks and weapon skins that can randomly be earned over time
- Spend real money on the steam market, NOT REQUIRED. May be seen as good or bad, purely subjective.

1 word. Amazing.
I was not sure I would like this game.  I'm certain that many of you, like me, frequently buy games they don't really know of because they are on sale.  While this is not a key to financial success, it definitely paid off when I finally got around to playing this.  I wasn't sure what this was when I loaded it up, the screenshots and description don't adequately describe what it is.
In the game, you pan left and right, contra style, looking for a randomly placed objective.  Along the way, random mobs drop and there are random things you can activate (shops, minigames, "chests").  The game gets very frantic as the difficulty level increases for every few minutes you spend in the game.
You being to acquire active and passive abilities from these drops and from certain bosses (similar to Terraria, in that they take up a huge part of the screen and "chase" you).  These trigger with a button or when something happens.  They are straight forward and you will know right away which ones you prefer.  They range from awesome to only slightly helpful.  You can have infinite passive abilities and only one activatable one (like a super-weapon dropped from a boss).
When you die (sorry, no respawn even in coop - you have to wait for the other guy to die), the game restarts from the beginning; however, you respawn with your weapons and abilities - in the original location but with the difficulty scale remaining where it was when you died.  I like this because when friends are playing, they don't have to start from zero to continue on.
There does not seem to be any overarching storyline that I could see (although I haven't progressed very far).  I've played probably 80 rounds of this game and I really just enjoy the ride.  Every playthrough feels different and classes begin to unlock that play so differently and open up brand new opportunities for cooperative play.
It has great local playability with brand new players.  They can get used to the controls and orient themselves.  I buy games like this to play as "filler" games and everyone that has played it has enjoyed it; however, people that don't like games like this won't be won over.
This was an excellent game that I cannot recommend enough.  If you like the genre, old-school sidescrolling shooters, where the game encourages you to explore and screw around, this is a perfect game for you (and a friend if you have one handy).  If you like the combat in games like Contra, Terraria, and games like them, you'll likely love this game too!

1 word. Amazing.
I was not sure I would like this game.  I'm certain that many of you, like me, frequently buy games they don't really know of because they are on sale.  While this is not a key to financial success, it definitely paid off when I finally got around to playing this.  I wasn't sure what this was when I loaded it up, the screenshots and description don't adequately describe what it is.
In the game, you pan left and right, contra style, looking for a randomly placed objective.  Along the way, random mobs drop and there are random things you can activate (shops, minigames, "chests").  The game gets very frantic as the difficulty level increases for every few minutes you spend in the game.
You being to acquire active and passive abilities from these drops and from certain bosses (similar to Terraria, in that they take up a huge part of the screen and "chase" you).  These trigger with a button or when something happens.  They are straight forward and you will know right away which ones you prefer.  They range from awesome to only slightly helpful.  You can have infinite passive abilities and only one activatable one (like a super-weapon dropped from a boss).
When you die (sorry, no respawn even in coop - you have to wait for the other guy to die), the game restarts from the beginning; however, you respawn with your weapons and abilities - in the original location but with the difficulty scale remaining where it was when you died.  I like this because when friends are playing, they don't have to start from zero to continue on.
There does not seem to be any overarching storyline that I could see (although I haven't progressed very far).  I've played probably 80 rounds of this game and I really just enjoy the ride.  Every playthrough feels different and classes begin to unlock that play so differently and open up brand new opportunities for cooperative play.
It has great local playability with brand new players.  They can get used to the controls and orient themselves.  I buy games like this to play as "filler" games and everyone that has played it has enjoyed it; however, people that don't like games like this won't be won over.
This was an excellent game that I cannot recommend enough.  If you like the genre, old-school sidescrolling shooters, where the game encourages you to explore and screw around, this is a perfect game for you (and a friend if you have one handy).  If you like the combat in games like Contra, Terraria, and games like them, you'll likely love this game too!

Note: in this review you will find partial reviews of different stages of the game's development before (as in Early Access) and after full release.
Initial thoughts: (~ 65 hours played)
So the game, as it is currently going through the Early Access stage, is very well playable and enjoyable up to a level.
Shortly put, the pros of the product as is right now are graphics, well-done gunplay and the excitement from killing a whole bunch of mutants (meaning not zombies).
However, the game is being dragged down by unbalanced gameplay and difficulty - as a fan of the first KF game, I think this title so far provides very few ways of actually effectively dealing with stronger opponents as opposed to those most often killed by one shot to the head. As a part of the 'balancing' process the devs most often just nerf the provided perks or leave the already-weak ones be, thus making the game progressively more difficult even on Normal difficulty settings. There's only a handful of weapons for each of the perk, rendering the gameplay repetitive after playing as one perk for a couple of (tens of) hours.
All in all, what else would you expect from an Early Access game than a product constantly evolving (not necessarily just in the right way). If you're into e.a. and coop FPS games, I'd recommend this one, I just can't tell you how will the final product look like though (for better or for worse).
EDIT 1: (80+ hours played)
Just 10 days before the full release on Nov 18, the game's development feels consistent throughout the whole Early Access stage. There are more perks, the game features an impromptu difficulty-changing system that is supposed to make slight changes during a gameplay session to adjust the difficulty more accordingly to the players' party's skill and ability. I can't tell if it really works properly just yet, I haven't noticed any particular changes myself.
The game got harder though, as different variations of enemies (forming 'squads') were added to the game within difficulties from Hard upward (from the 2nd to the highest difficulty), providing more challenges to overcome during the match playthrough.
The perks are a mixed bag. The role balance is there but while some perks feel essential to the team's structure, others give the impression of the idea pit gone dry for the developers (particularly the SWAT perk seems like a tank version of Commando). However, the new 'Specialist' perk is bound to bring an interesting addition to gameplay due to its ambiguity to other perks.
There's also aplenty of maps to play on, but the selection of weapons is still limited to 4 options per perk + single- & dual-wielded 9mm pistols. We shall see about the content to be added after the full release, but the game is bound to get better.

I was gifted this by a friend and I'm still trying to thank him enough for showing me this thing.
Super Hexagon is a fast-paced, psychadelic action game where you control a little triangle orbiting a central hexagon (or pentagon, or square) while dodging obstacles to stay alive as long as possible. I've never lasted even 2 minutes on one attempt; usually, I don't even make it to 45 seconds. But after losing, you can start again almost imediately without sitting through any kind of cutscene or long "game over". Because of the quick return to gameplay, it feels more like one continuous attempt instead of hundreds of little ones, which keeps you (or at least me) engaged for quite a while in one sitting. I've logged over 15 hours playing this game, and I've still got a long way to go to beat the game.
I could sing it's praises all day, but there are a few things you should know before you buy this game. The high-tempo music, flashing lights, and rapidly spinning screen can make you nauseated or disoriented. Some people who have issues with motion sickness or epilepsy should be cautious when trying this game out. Even on the lowest setting, this game is hard, a quality which it flaunts proudly. As you last longer in an attempt, the screen will spin faster, your triangle and the obstacles will speed up as well, and the colors will change more dramatically.
Overall, I think this game is definitely worth getting, and at $3, it's a bargain.

Gameplay, meh. It's fine. It works. The fact that mobs teleport when not in line-of-sight is stupid as♥♥♥♥♥♥ though. Oh, and the way mobs jump up objects, rather than path-find around them is also stupid. It makes shooting mobs from certain places vertually impossbile, unless you want to waste your precious ammo on body shots.
My biggest beef is with controls. For me, and everyone I played the game with, the default senitivity was way too high (no big deal), but the aim assist features are garbage.
The camera feels more like the game was meant to be played on a controller than a mouse and desktop. I don't think the developers ever play-tested their settings with a mouse and keyboard. The only game that feels worse is PayDay 2, and at least the game has more variety.
The fact that you stop running if you need to do anything (like healing or reloading) is stupid. Especially when the last alive out of six players, you have a skrake or fleshpound after you, and you have ten life.
Crosshairs in this game suck. especially when you dual wield pistols (The fact that they disappear is bunk). They need to be smaller and enabled by default. This is a game where every buller counts, and the difference between missing one, and not, is big. Starting the game without it means aiming is hard (unless you are already accustomed to a crosshairless aiming). In addition, aiming at long distances with this large, wide crosshair is difficult. (compound this with the poor camera mechanics and you can see why this game doesn't play well)
I'll update with more complaints if I remember them. In addition, when the game receives updates that fixes my complaints, I'll remove the complaints. If I feel like the gameplay has improved or has otherwise gotten past the slow, methodical, slaughter house mechanics, then I'll recommend the game, but at the moment, I cannot. This is supposed to be a "Polished Beta", not a "Polished Alpha". The fact that there are this many issues makes me feel it is the later, not the former.

I can not honestly recommend this game to anyone without first warning them about its "difficulty." While an interesting and fun game for a short while, after many, many attempts at puzzling out its psuedo-random nature, it is easy to see that most of its difficulty is fake.
Now, this isn't "This game is stupidly hard! It must be fake difficulty!" claims. The game's challenge is genuinely fake, involving random changing speeds and directions of rotations, (mostly) unpredictable, radical changes in the playing field, and an obscenely small margin of error. Altogether, this makes Super Hexagon more an excercise in tenacity and repitition than a challenging, rewarding puzzler.
Avoid the game, unless you enjoy constant interface screws and ball-busting unforgivability hidden under excellent music and a simplistic, but charming, interface.

As you're piloting your cargo ship, the UES Contact Light, everything is going fine. You, along with your crew, some stowaways, an exotic animal, and the robot janitor, are going about your days, delivering packages across the cosmos. Suddenly, you lose all power, but the alarm sirens buzz off, running off the spare power. You search around, hoping to fing the intruders, suddenly, a kingly figures appears before a crowd of the planet's inhabitants, you start to pull out your gun, but the man flings you into a pod, and sends you towards your certain demise. You survive the crash, but your suit is damaged, and your crew is lost, leaving you, armed with a gun, your wits, and whatever you can scavenge from your ships cargo containers, you are forced to jump around the planet, teleporter to teleporter, to face "Providence," as you've come to call the kingly figure, and reclaim your ship, honor, and crew.
Risk of Rain is easily worth $10 dollars, if you have spare free time, enjoy rogue-likes, or are looking for a unique experience. This game will very easily hold you over, with tons of unlocks, 11 interesting classes, both a single and multiplayer experience, and the newly added artifacts, Risk of Rain holds much more than can be explained. I have put hours into unlocking the unique items, and enjoying the pleasing art and music style. The combat is smooth, the items are interesting, and the game provides a good challenge, but it always feels fair.

I can not honestly recommend this game to anyone without first warning them about its "difficulty." While an interesting and fun game for a short while, after many, many attempts at puzzling out its psuedo-random nature, it is easy to see that most of its difficulty is fake.
Now, this isn't "This game is stupidly hard! It must be fake difficulty!" claims. The game's challenge is genuinely fake, involving random changing speeds and directions of rotations, (mostly) unpredictable, radical changes in the playing field, and an obscenely small margin of error. Altogether, this makes Super Hexagon more an excercise in tenacity and repitition than a challenging, rewarding puzzler.
Avoid the game, unless you enjoy constant interface screws and ball-busting unforgivability hidden under excellent music and a simplistic, but charming, interface.

As you're piloting your cargo ship, the UES Contact Light, everything is going fine. You, along with your crew, some stowaways, an exotic animal, and the robot janitor, are going about your days, delivering packages across the cosmos. You search around, hoping to fing the intruders, suddenly, a kingly figures appears before a crowd of the planet's inhabitants, you start to pull out your gun, but the man flings you into a pod, and sends you towards your certain demise. You survive the crash, but your suit is damaged, and your crew is lost, leaving you, armed with a gun, your wits, and whatever you can scavenge from your ships cargo containers, you are forced to jump around the planet, teleporter to teleporter, to face "Providence," as you've come to call the kingly figure, and reclaim your ship, honor, and crew.

You do not have the graphical capability to fully enjoy this game. Whatever you think, your graphics card is most likely not powerful enough to support this game. That's all there is to it.
Against all warnings from friends, I pre-ordered this game along with the season pass to play it on launch date, like I've done with all of the Arkham series games. This is the first time however that I decided to get the game on PC, the last times were always on PS3. But since this game is next generation, I could not justify buying a PS4 just to play it, I instead decided to use my PC, which, while a year old at this point, is still very powerful, I can play most new games with the highest settings (Mad Max and Metal Gear Solid 5: The Phantom Pain work smooth as butter with maxed out settings). This was not the case with Batman Arkham Knight on June 26.
While I was one of the lucky ones to be able to play the game at all, throughout my playthrough I had only 2 crashes which came at two unrelated random points. But otherwise, I could play the game and I was willing to overlook most problems, chalking it off as it'll get patched in the coming weeks, I mean it's not uncommon. My nVidia GeForce Experience optimal settings recommended that I minimalise all settings, which to me was shocking, how needy could the game be? So I ignored it and wanted to experience how bad it can get. And oh man, it got bad. The framerate could not handle anything and would often drop down to 1.
Throughout my gameplay I eventually had a system going where whenever I was out as Batman, I would set my texture quality to medium, shadow quality to low and level of detail on high, but whenever I was in the Batmobile and there was any kind of action, I had to drop the texture quality and level of detail back to low and back again whenever there were any kinds of cutscenes going on so I could enjoy the experience even slightly. But even then, I played the game and defended it, because in the end, when it all comes down to it, it's NOT a bad game.
I enjoyed the Batmobile sequences more the more I learned how to handle the controls and the innovations in combat when you're controlling Batman were definitely the best so far. The parts of Gotham you get the explore (and it's not the whole city, just 3 parts of it) are big, but not overwhelmingly so, because the Batmobile makes pretty fast to traverse around. The usual controls were a bit changed however which did confuse me throughout the game, but it's nothing too damaging to the overall experience. I had fun, enjoyed the story which I will not spoil, but I'm pretty sure everyone knows at this point, and managed to complete my normal playthrough to 100%. I decided to leave the New Game+ mode for whenever the game gets patched and I can play it with optimum settings.
So if I liked the game, why the negative review? Simple. This port is atrocious compared to the console ports. The PC port was a simple afterthought and was handled by another developer, not Rocksteady. So when push came to shove in releasing the game, all the innovations that Rocksteady made, were not translated properly and the game sufferred. As most of you know, it was so bad that WB had to take the game off Steam so that they could develop a patch. For 3 months. It is now October and the patch was released. Can people play this game now? Yes. Did they fix some major issues? According to them, they have. Have they really? No, the game still functions the same as it did before for me. I can still only play the game with minimum settings.
Honestly, I think the only way they could have fixed it would have been if they reworked the graphics engine for the game and I seriously doubt they want to do that at this point. WB PR solution to this is to give out all the previous Arkham games out for free to the buyers who've waited for 3 months and not returned the game back in the first week. I already have all the Arkham games. I think most fans do. They're the ones that made us want to buy this sequel. Plus, the games have been on every other sale for around 5 euros each, so I'm pretty sure everyone has them. I personally am not getting anything out of being patient and supportive from all this time. From my perspective, they've done nothing to improve my experience.
So no, don't buy this game. Not on PC. Wait a couple of years. Let it drop in price, naturally upgrade your computer with time, let them patch it over and over and only then you'll have a good enough reason to play it.
Or go play it on the consoles now, it works perfectly fine there.

The sheer variety of civilizations, units, and playstyles is staggering, especially with the Gods and Kings and/or Brave New World expansions.  Each civilization has different strengths and weaknesses, and no two civs play the same.  The combination of civs and different playstyles are nearly endless.  Some civs excel on ocean maps, like Polynesia, while others are nigh-unstoppable on pangea maps, such as the Shoshone.  The AI isn't the smartest sometimes, especially on naval maps, but it's more than sufficient for your average playthrough.  Graphics are something Civ 5 does very well, with maxxed settings, the game looks absolutely gorgeous, especially considering since it was released in 2011.  I've been a fan of the Civilization series since I played Civilization 3 for the first time about 10 years ago, and I have to say, the combat in Civ 5 is a dramatic improvement over the earlier installments.  Some Civ diehards may disagree with me, but I for one, don't miss the giant death-stacks of hundreds of units attacking on a single tile.

Graphics and visual effects are on a whole different level than the first game, cooler and more grotesque enemy design making them look more like the medically-modified specimens they are supposed to be rather than looking like slightly mutated zombies in the first game, better enemy animations improving upon the very stiff movements the enemies had in the first game, much more detailed environments, you get to play as a hot french metalhead named Ana Larive, leveling up is much more reasonable, healing yourself is a little quicker, there's an added sprint button, and a killer soundtrack with three and a half hours worth of tracks, plus the option to either keep the songs instrumental or with the vocals playing as well. It shows that they put a TON of work into this game already and it's in early access, and thus far it doesn't look like they will be those devs that abandon the game in mid early access. They have plans to add in more maps, a couple more classes (like sharpshooter which I really wish they release soon because that's my class, man), and more. There are some microtransactions that you can do, but it's all skins and other visual stuff so there's no pay to win mess, and I do hope they keep it that way. Some of the only things I can think of that need to be fixed are the trader compass while the wave is still present is a little hard and sometimes confusing to navigate, whereas the arrow that they had in the first game in the top corner was clear and easy. This game was total frustration from the beginning. First of all I bought demo-version with almost no content (little perks and weapons) and few maps. Then I waited half a year to have at least something interesting to play for. As a dedicated Linux-server owner I was surprised with absense of Linux server version of this game. So I had to set up a virtual Windows machine entirely dedicated to hosting Killing Floor 2. When I got newest version 1020 I installed a couple of handy mutators similiar to those I used in Killing Floor 1. Everything seemed to go fine until two days ago when server updated to a 1021 version because of clients automatic update and all *stuff* broke up. So now I have entirely vanilla server and all accumulated server-side statistics went to hell, mutators are not working, I have to wait for them to get fixed. And for what? To have them breaking up againg in a week or two with next micro update which is going to *break* my *stuff* up again? Why the hell did I pay for a couple of copies? This game in and on itself is more for playing with your friends and venturing off to the unknowns fighting off the many hostiles and grubbing over who gets the many treasures to help you beat the game. Single player is not suggested due to the fact that single player feels so lonely and desolate considering that you did just come from a crashed prison ship, it doesn't feel like it should be played amongst just you the player. Even though unlocking other characters is quite a chore and it usually takes an hour to get to the final boss at a reasonable rate, this game is meant to be played in one sitting amongst the friends you love, not by yourself considering there is a lack of interactions or story during the time you are mowing down enemies. I findi it a bit annoying that you need to either be in the same room with your friends, or use some kind of program to play multiplayer online, since they used steam I thought they could use their servers but they did not similar to terraria. I feel that you could not beat the game in your first game since this is a rogue like and the many tricks and helpful items can not be obtained on your first time. THe main goal I had in this game with my friends were to beat it, the attempts we tried to beat the game in total was about 4 or 5 and the last session being an hour long. I have since stopped playing it since the challenge was lost to me to try and beat the game due to the lack of extra content and little easter eggs since they are so rare and few apart.
All and all this game is very well done, but lacks the kind of draw to keep me playing over and over again like many others, the only thing that would draw me to this game would be my friends and they also are done with it. Single player is more like a chore and less fun without the interactions of your friends since the scenery, music, and enemies are kinda repeated with some bosses even being variants of them. One of the drawing points to me was mostly the items and their many different effects, appearances, and names like binding of isaac. Another would be the characters, but unlocking them seems a bit of a chore but its worth it due to the different game play mechanics to each one of them. Graphics wise I feel the 8-bit fits it but I wish they had done the backgrounds less 8-bit to give it a bit more appeal. Game play wise it is very fluent and on point, the only problem I had though was after a while there are way too many enemies on the screen and slows down most computers considerably if you don't kill them all, I wish they didn't have the ai keep spawning even though you have like 100 or so on the screen already, they should have put some kind of ai cap or something to limit that. All and all a good game, just not one that I would come to over and over again for entertainment or to play with your friends repeatedly.

As a huge fan of Killing Floor, I was super exicited to finally be able to play this game. If there is one thing I have a guilty pleasure for in games, it's the mindless fun of brutally killing waves upon waves of enemies, even for no reason. And I have to say, this game is flat out amazing. For an early access game, everything about it feels so right. The atmosphere is cool and extremely fitting for the ♥♥♥♥ed up nature of the game, the characters are still an absolute joy to play with, and of course, the violence is top notch compared the first game. The gore system was improved heavily, and it's jolly good fun to run around with your Zweihander, lopping of the heads of zeds, while fully clad in black and red armor. Also, the soundtrack is amazing aswell. In the first game, the soundtrack was good, but the songs were just kinda genric metal, and it was kinda forgetable in my point of view. In this game however, the music choice was way better, and I have to say that "Collasping" by Demon Hunter is my favorite track in the game. Also you get the option to have VOCALS IN THE MUSIC, which is something I love. The monster designs also are superb, making the zeds more creepy looking, and making the Scrake and Fleshpound imtimidating as ♥♥♥♥. The bosses, while a little cheap in my opinion, are still full of personality, and really intense to fight. I'm not gonna lie, when I first fought Hans Volter, I was terrified. The only thing I can really nitpick on is that, since the game is in early access, there isn't alot of stuff in it yet. Theres not as many maps or weapons, only one gamemode, and not that many things in the workshop, but everything that is in here is excellent. A definte buy for people who either are a fan of the first game, or people who want to engage in a little mindless carnage.

Great roguelite platformer. Think Binding of Isaac, but as a sidescrolling platformer/shooter rather than a top-down shooter. Unlike Isaac, however, this game is less about breaking the game and the luck of what items you get, and more about your skill with a character and its abilities. The game's difficulty increases automatically based on time spent rather than levels beaten, creating a sense of urgency that reminds me of Spelunky's ghost, although much more subtle.
The game has lots of replay value, with plenty of characters with very unique skillsets to learn, difficult achievements to unlock new items and characters, 3 difficulty levels, and the newly added artifacts, which, once unlocked, function much like the Skulls from Halo, modifying the game with extra bonuses and penalties on the player and enemies. The game also has local and online co-op, although when playing local you are confined to the same screen.
If I have any major issues with the game, it's that the frame rate frequently tanks on my computer, and even with frame skip enabled, the game ends up moving in slow motion most of the time. Then again, it makes the game a lot easier (especially stopping the roulette chambers on the right item), and I need all the help I can get.

After spending around seven thousand years playing Sid Meier's Civilization® V. I am finally ready, to write my review on the game. Have you ever played Age of Empires 2? No? then go play it you noob, it's one of the best Real Time Strategy game ever made. You get to choose one of many factions such as Japan. The whole game has you build your cities from scratch and the combats are very intense once war get started. The best Unit to use is the car unit which you can get by putting in the codes. Go find it in google you lazy couch potato. But if you answer Yes then I can say that Sid Meier's Civilization® V is almost nothing like Age of Empires 2. Unlike AOE2, Sid Meier's Civilization® V is pretty much a turn based board game. First, I would like to talk about what I really like about the game. Sid Meier's Civilization® V is purely strategic. You need to plan ahead on what to build in order to be able to beat your enemies. Think of it this way, if you build a catapult but I buy a horseman I'll be able to attack your city and die before you can even get your catapult out. I also like the fact that you can play as a historical figure. I like to play as Alexander the Great because he look hot and because of his faction abilities. See, each factions in Sid Meier's Civilization® V has a special trait and around two special unit with their own special trait to give them an advantage in different stages of the game. Playing as Alexander you'll be able to seduce all of them city states to do your bidding and become like a sith lord of some sort. But let's ignore the city states and talk about the things I hate about the game. 1. It's long as hell. 2. Quick mode is still long. 3. it take me more turn to train a hoplite unit than a building. 4. Good Luck finishing this game with more than 3 other players. I also hate the fact that in the "Brave new world" Expansion? DLC? pack faith can't do anything. But looking past all of the great things and the bad things about the game you have to remember that this is a background game. It is meant to be played while you socialize with your friend that will eventually betray you for one of those worker that you have. It's like monopoly but for the computer with some historical setting. I rate Sid Meier's Civilization® V a 10/10/10 it's a must buy for those who want to kill massive amount of time to have an unsatisfied ending with each factions trying to nuke each other.

Music is great, and actually completing to more advanced levels can be a pretty powerful driving hook.  One thing to be wary of though is going to be the 'input lag' of your monitor/screen.  Its not a metric that comes up often and isn't something alot of display makers spend much time advertising/promoting.  Its basically the amount of time between when your computer sends a frame to the screen, and when the screen actually shows it to you.  The very best/fastest gaming monitors can have it down to 2-3ms, while the very worst/oldest/slowest ones can be 50-60ms or more.
In a game like this, where literally every single millisecond against your reflexes counts, having the right or wrong screen can easily make the difference between making it to the next level and crashing and burning hard on a wall you barely had time to register coming.
So yeah, super ultra twitch/reflexes based.  Even still though, the music is catchy enough that its worth a look despite what could ultimately be a very frustrating/demotivating slew of 5 second deaths.
(7/10) (One alternative for those without ultra fast reflexes would be to just look up the soundtrack out there)

Single player is more like a chore and less fun without the interactions of your friends since the scenery, music, and enemies are kinda repeated with some bosses even being variants of them. A definte buy for people who either are a fan of the first game, or people who want to engage in a little mindless carnage.

Great roguelite platformer. Think Binding of Isaac, but as a sidescrolling platformer/shooter rather than a top-down shooter. Unlike Isaac, however, this game is less about breaking the game and the luck of what items you get, and more about your skill with a character and its abilities. The game's difficulty increases automatically based on time spent rather than levels beaten, creating a sense of urgency that reminds me of Spelunky's ghost, although much more subtle.
The game has lots of replay value, with plenty of characters with very unique skillsets to learn, difficult achievements to unlock new items and characters, 3 difficulty levels, and the newly added artifacts, which, once unlocked, function much like the Skulls from Halo, modifying the game with extra bonuses and penalties on the player and enemies. The game also has local and online co-op, although when playing local you are confined to the same screen.
If I have any major issues with the game, it's that the frame rate frequently tanks on my computer, and even with frame skip enabled, the game ends up moving in slow motion most of the time. Then again, it makes the game a lot easier (especially stopping the roulette chambers on the right item), and I need all the help I can get.

If you're into strategy games, Civilization V is highly addicting. I've put in over a thousand hours into this game and I'm still playing it long after purchasing it. In this review I'm going to list what I think are the pros and cons. Lastly, I will point out what I think the devs should do in order to make the game even better in its next incarnation.
The Pros:
1. Outstanding Replayability: I can't stress this part enough. You can easily get addicted to playing through the different eras to see how things turn out. Also, I greatly enjoy exploring and uncovering the map once the renaissance era begins.
2. Setup Control: Civ V does a great job at letting you pick and choose the limitations for the game. You can decide how many other civs will be competing with you and which ones. Difficulty, map size, and victory conditions are just a few of the variables that you can control.
3. Modable: If there is something you don't like about the game or if there is something different you would like to try, you can easily find a huge number of custom mods here on Steam.
4. Multiple Ways to Win: If conquest isn't your thing, you can acheive victory through diplomacy, culture, or science. However, this comes with a bit of a caveat. Whichever victory condition you are trying to acheive, it has to be tempered with a healthy level of science. So even if you are not going for a science victory, ignoring science in the tech tree will hurt and ultimately doom your civilization in the long run.
5. Great complexity: Civ V is highly complex. However, it isn't so complex that beginners will need to get a college degree in the game before being able to win. While the tutorial doesn't cover everything, it is sufficient in covering the basics. Of course there is a learning curve - and it will take time to reach some level of mastery. Therefore, if this is your first turn based strategy game, you can't go wrong with Civ V.
6. Play with Your Friends: Civ V has a multiplayer feature. And it works pretty well - usually (see below in cons). I and few friends of mine have greatly enjoyed playing Civ V together. Get on skype or some other voice chat program and shoot the breeze while you play. It's a great way to unwind and have some fun after work.
The Cons:
1. A Few Minor Bugs: From time to time, I have noticed that the game has some minor bugs. For example, every once in a while you might notice that one of your cities is invisible. The city is still there but for some reason the graphic just isn't being rendered correctly. I haven't really noticed many gameplay bugs. However. in my last game, I had a worker tear down an old citadel in order to build a farm in the same tile. But, for some reason the worker was unable to finish the job.
2. Stop Jerking Me Around!: Whenever I'm giving orders to units in the game, I usually am interested in that specific nearby region first (usually because that is where an important battle is taking place). However, after giving orders to a unit, the game will often pull me away from that area to give an order to a unit halfway around the world. At first it's a minor annoyance. However, after a while this will probably begin to push your buttons just like it does mine.
3. Multiplay AI Usurpation: If you're playing a multiplayer game and you get disconnected (for whatever reason), the game will automatically assign the civilization you were playing to an AI. The AI will then being screwing up whatever it is that you were doing. And before you can rejoin the game and resume control, you will lose that turn to the AI. Then after resuming control, you will have to manually reissue orders to all your units in order to get them to stop whatever idiotic assignments that the AI gave them. It would have been better if the devs had given the option to the players still connected to allow the AI to take over or to wait for the player to reconnect.
Finally, there are several things that I think need improving.
1. I Hate Bananas!: I'm sorry but you can't build successful civilizations on bananas. You can't put bananas in a granery and store them like you can wheat. And even if you could dehydrate the bananas, they are just not a good civilization building foodstuff. Maybe I'm a stickler for details but this really breaks my immersion. Instead of tiles with bananas, how about corn or rice instead? No more bananas please.
2. Diseases and Natural Disasters: I think previous incarnations of Civ had something like this. I really don't know why they were taken out. But, I think they should be put back in - especially disease. Disease has played a great role in shaping the world in which we live today. Instead of just having a simple general disease mechanic. I think diseases should vary in intensity. For example, a level one disease might wipe out 10% of a cities population; whereas, a level four disease could wipe out 75% of a given population. Certain tech buildings (such as a hospital) could greatly diminish the effects of a disease. Also, diseases should tend to occur near tiles with domesticated animals such as horses or sheep. I can see that this mechanic is currently soaked up in the game by such buildings as aqueducts. However, adding in such a random element as disease could greatly improve the immersion in my opinion. I don't know but I think a good plague or epidemic here and there (especially before the industrial era) could really spice things up. Otherwise, a feeling of blandness settles over me when I'm playing through early eras.
3. Vive La Barbarians: I think barbarians should be allowed to conquer cities and form a new civilization using traits from that conquered civ or citystate. For example, an ignored encampent of barbarians conquers Hongkong. Then suddenly a random civilization (such as Mongolia - if not already in the game) is added and gains a tech level slightly below that of the conquered city. I think this feature would add great flavor to the game especially when archaeology comes into play. It would be really interesting to excavate ruins belonging to a conquered city that was actually taken out in the ancient or classical era.

Best. Game. Ever.  Seriously - if you're even *slightly* a fan of the humor of the South Park series, every single second of this game will be an absolute joy to play.  The attention to detail in this title is simple astonishing and commendable.  I'm GLAD the developers and UbiSoft took their sweet time in releasing this game to make sure that it turned out to be the title that it ultimately became (despite changing hands over the years).  It has everything you pretty much expect from an RPG - leveling, character customization, 'ultimate' attacks, etc. - everything with a distinctive and relevant South Park flair.  Combat isn't "real time" or truly 100% "turn-based" either, as you need to perform QTE-based timed button-pushed during your selected action when it's your turn (if you want to perform combos/max damage, as well as defend against incoming attacks and perform counter-attacks)...almost making it a hybrid of the two systems.  You could probably just burn through the main story quest pretty quickly if you wanted to...but you'd be missing the point entirely.  The glory of this game is wandering aimlessly around the city of South Park itself, finally getting to see and experience the town and it's people for yourself, do all  of the random side-quests you could possible find, discover all of the secret/hidden areas and treasures, and just be "♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥" for a while.  Sure, maybe all the classes ultimately feel similar because they can equip the same gear and play largely the same way if they *really* want to...but that's really irrelevant (if not appropriate) in a game that's really just about a bunch of kids LARPing.  Here's hoping for DLC expansions or just another flat-out new title in this same vein, although I think it would be almost impossible to equal or top in terms of quality.

I was both looking forward to and dreading to play this. South Park as a show is uneven, with every other episode being either a hit or miss. As it turns out The Stick of Truth is South Park at its best, with only very little of the bad.
Central to the game is the premise. This is about children playing a fantasy RPG in their town. Everything that happens is interpreted through their eyes as part of the game and the lore they’ve made up. This creates brilliant scenes where the real world pokes through and reminds you it’s all just make believe, and everyone in the game knows it’s pretend, but they’re 100% committed to the game. Even when real♥♥♥♥♥♥goes down the kids never break character and just incorporate what’s happening into their game. Not at any point do they stop “playing”, and this clearly confuses many of the adults who can’t always tell if they’re playing or not.
The game itself is an old school jrpg style game with tweaks here and there to make it feel somewhat modern. You explore the town and talk to NPCs, fight in turn based combat and use tools that you discover over the course of the game to access new areas Metroid style. Cutscenes are generally brief, and it doesn’t feel like you’re watching an episode of the show, even though it looks exactly like it. You definitely “play” this game. If you’re expecting something like The Walking Dead where you can pretty much take your hands off the controls for minutes at a time, this isn’t it. I found all the mechanics to be fun to play around with, and the difficulty of combat to be balanced the way I like it. Almost every review I’ve seen complains that the balance is tilted too easy, but I don’t agree. I never died, but it was close a couple times. I didn’t feel like I could breeze through every fight without using items and abilities.
The world isn’t particularly big, but it makes up for it by being dense in detail. Given that you spend the majority of the time exploring the world by yourself it’s good that they gave it the time and care it needed. Going through every nook and cranny, discovering characters, quests and nods to past episodes of the show feels rewarding. At no point did I feel like the game was wasting my time or padding for length, even during the more mundane fetch quests. There’d always be something on the other end which would make it feel worth it. The length of the game felt just right.
I had more fun playing this than I was expecting. The way it manages to poke fun at games and stories feels fresh, and makes this more than merely a good license game. It’s an excellent game. Definitely worth playing, unless you can’t stand South Park obviously.

The biggest issue to me personally is the current lack of varied content. In Tripwire's defence, it does take a LOT of time and effort to create the content and get everything just right - kind of like Valve, they don't seem to launch anything half-baked: either it's in and it's fully animated and working, or it isn't launched at all. There are no placeholder animations, missing textures, screwed up sound effects, or map clipping issues that often plague other alpha/beta/early access launches. There is ONE camera issue as of this review that happens only during the boss intro phase, lasts for less than 10 seconds, and corrects itself once the intro is over.
$33 is a pretty high price point for me, but I've been let down harder by $60 AAA titles. Ubisoft, I'm looking at you. So, for what it is, I'd go for it. Just don't contribute to microtransactions and you'll have a fun and relatively cheap romp through waves of enemies.
