Just as Arkham City was a big jump from Arkham Asylum, so too is Arkham Knight another big leap forward compared to Arkham City. They’ve built upon the mechanics of what came before, so between that and the fact that the storyline is a conclusion to everything that’s transpired, I very strongly recommend that you play through Asylum, City & Origins before starting this. (You can skip Blackgate.)
In City & Origins you could just roam around the city, fighting mobs as you encounter them to get experience. Now, those criminals have all wised up such that almost all of them will just run away. Your reward for fighting them is personal satisfaction. The only way to gain XP is from quests or completing AR challenges, so there’s significantly less hand-to-hand combat in this game. That’s unfortunate because they’ve added new enemy types & attacks/counters to Batman’s arsenal. Indeed, Gotham City is now SUPLEX CITY. Predator stealth areas offer new methods to deal with enemies as well. My favorite one lets you instantly KO several (non-Brute) enemies at once!
Arkham Knight features a completely different map than the one in City/Origins, along with entirely new types of sidequests. That’s important to making sure this doesn’t feel like the same game you’ve been playing for years only in a new place. The key is much of the game mechanics now stress the use of the Batmobile, which you can call to you at any time much like the horse in Red Dead Redemption. It’s a challenge for sandbox design to work in both cars & flying. In Saints Row IV I found myself asking the same question I asked regarding OJ in the airport: “why would you take a car when you can FLY?” Batman could already fly—fine, it’s a glide—through Arkham Asylum & City, so use of the Batmobile is encouraged by way of the city layout, story mode, sidequests, and the fact that it’s quick & easy to switch between gliding & driving. Arkham Knight puts thought into the placement of sidequests & collectibles; to show you areas and details you would otherwise neglect to explore, or use abilities you may otherwise not bother with.
The Batmobile in this game fits the overall aesthetic of the Arkham series: it combines the 1990s Batman: The Animated Series (derived from Tim Burton’s films) with the Christopher Nolan movies. It has two modes: the familiar “car with rocket engine strapped to the back” along with a “Ghost in the Shell tank” one. You’re going to be in more fights that grant XP using the tank than anything else, so you may want to prioritize upgrading it. As a car, it handles like you’d expect: fast on straightaways but tricky to turn. The city layout is very forgiving though, since much of the environment near the streets will simply be destroyed if you drive through. A few areas require tighter precision which can be downright maddening, but most are optional challenges. In tank mode you go about as slow as you would on foot albeit with omnidirectional movement plus access to the Tim Burton-approved Bat-machinegun & the Bat-60mm cannon. Don’t worry: Batman doesn’t kill, so whenever you target humans they’re special NON-LETHAL ROUNDS (fired at over 1000 m/s). Just like the special NON-LETHAL running people over after colliding into them at 100s of MPH using a car that can smash through walls! There’s an electricity effect on the people you hit to suggest they’re being magnetically repelled but WHATEVER. DARK KNIGHT RETURNS.
But seriously, this is the softest ESRB “M” rated game I’ve ever seen. PG-13 movies go well beyond even the most violent images in this, and there’s no nudity or strong language. A lot of characters do get shot by guns, but they just fall down with no blood or gore. The main departure this game has over the previous Arkham games is that there are a few bodies with red blood on or near them, and you can hit/shoot people with the car. This game really should have been rated “T”.
Knight might have the least memorable soundtrack of the entire Arkham series. I can hum the Asylum & City main themes, but no instrumental tracks in Arkham Knight stick with me at all, especially compared to tracks like “You Should Have Listened to My Warning” from Arkham City. Arkham Knight does have the greatest VOCAL tracks of them all though! As far as voices, “true Batman” Kevin Conroy is back as is the true arch-nemesis of these games…Wally Wingert as The Riddler! Seriously, Riddler is the perfect videogame villain because he’s constantly in your face, mocking the player for being stupid. He’s this generation’s giggling Duck Hunt dog that you’d do anything to shoot. There’s no mistaking Riddler dialogue with anyone else, or the way that he intones “Dark Knight” & “Detective.” Punching the smug off his face is what we look forward to most! As for the rest? Don’t check any cast list until AFTER you’ve beaten it, since just knowing what characters are present will just spoil the entire game for you. I did learn that I can't tell Matt Mercer from Troy Baker though.
As you can see from all the reviews now flagged “pre-release,” Arkham Knight got pulled from Steam almost immediately on release to be patched as it was “an unplayable mess.” So, how well did the old version run? There was one noticeable bug I encountered: the 2D overlays for Detective Mode/the mini-map in one indoor area started glitching out after checking it a few times such that you had to restart. Everything else was fine; I had a few crashes but upon checking they were all caused by my sound setup & the fact that I was streaming on Twitch (username “suratd”). On my single GTX 970, it ran 1920 x 1080p with all effects set to highest, including the PC-only nVidia Gameworks effects. The one drawback? It was a solid 30 FPS. That was Arkham Knight’s “crime” pre-patch.
But I think of it this way: even in the old “broken mess” state, it still ran at a higher resolution with more effects than the PS4 or XB1. The re-released version has removed the lock & improved the performance to bring me to 60 FPS in-game with all settings at their new maximum. Using the same GTX 970 GPU, the only thing now that incurs a framerate hit is enabling nVidia’s “Interactive Smoke and Fog” which sometimes decreases performance by about 5-10 FPS in scenes where such smoke appears. Way I see it, the Steam PC version was the best version of Arkham Knight even before it got de-listed, and now it runs better than before.
Arkham Asylum was the most focused experience. Arkham City’s more open-ended layout best captured how hectic “one night being Batman” is while having the best music and villain dialogue that inspired you to stop what you were doing and beat them senseless. Origins had the best and most varied boss fights as well as the most “comic book” style cutscenes. Arkham Knight succeeds over its predecessors not just mechanically, but in the thematic sense. There are not one, but several obstacles for which Batman’s victory over them is not a foregone conclusion. Where maybe you can’t “win” so much as “not lose” even when it looks like you’ve definitely “lost” with no way to recover. Some of the key plot developments are obvious and you can see them coming a mile away. Others are intentional fakeouts. But much like how The Dark Knight Rises is definitely the last Christopher Nolan Batman movie, this is definitely the last Arkham game. My biggest gripe with some of the earlier Arkham stuff, particularly Asylum and Origins, was the game explicitly went out of its way to show the futility of your deeds or the hypocrisy of your actions. But if I’m going to spoil ONE thing about this game...Arkham Knight’s the opposite of that.

Best. Game. Ever.  Seriously - if you're even *slightly* a fan of the humor of the South Park series, every single second of this game will be an absolute joy to play.  The attention to detail in this title is simple astonishing and commendable.  I'm GLAD the developers and UbiSoft took their sweet time in releasing this game to make sure that it turned out to be the title that it ultimately became (despite changing hands over the years).  It has everything you pretty much expect from an RPG - leveling, character customization, 'ultimate' attacks, etc. - everything with a distinctive and relevant South Park flair.  Combat isn't "real time" or truly 100% "turn-based" either, as you need to perform QTE-based timed button-pushed during your selected action when it's your turn (if you want to perform combos/max damage, as well as defend against incoming attacks and perform counter-attacks)...almost making it a hybrid of the two systems.  You could probably just burn through the main story quest pretty quickly if you wanted to...but you'd be missing the point entirely.  The glory of this game is wandering aimlessly around the city of South Park itself, finally getting to see and experience the town and it's people for yourself, do all  of the random side-quests you could possible find, discover all of the secret/hidden areas and treasures, and just be "♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥" for a while.  Sure, maybe all the classes ultimately feel similar because they can equip the same gear and play largely the same way if they *really* want to...but that's really irrelevant (if not appropriate) in a game that's really just about a bunch of kids LARPing.  Here's hoping for DLC expansions or just another flat-out new title in this same vein, although I think it would be almost impossible to equal or top in terms of quality.

I was both looking forward to and dreading to play this. South Park as a show is uneven, with every other episode being either a hit or miss. As it turns out The Stick of Truth is South Park at its best, with only very little of the bad.
Central to the game is the premise. This is about children playing a fantasy RPG in their town. Everything that happens is interpreted through their eyes as part of the game and the lore they’ve made up. This creates brilliant scenes where the real world pokes through and reminds you it’s all just make believe, and everyone in the game knows it’s pretend, but they’re 100% committed to the game. Even when real♥♥♥♥♥♥goes down the kids never break character and just incorporate what’s happening into their game. Not at any point do they stop “playing”, and this clearly confuses many of the adults who can’t always tell if they’re playing or not.
The game itself is an old school jrpg style game with tweaks here and there to make it feel somewhat modern. You explore the town and talk to NPCs, fight in turn based combat and use tools that you discover over the course of the game to access new areas Metroid style. Cutscenes are generally brief, and it doesn’t feel like you’re watching an episode of the show, even though it looks exactly like it. You definitely “play” this game. If you’re expecting something like The Walking Dead where you can pretty much take your hands off the controls for minutes at a time, this isn’t it. I found all the mechanics to be fun to play around with, and the difficulty of combat to be balanced the way I like it. Almost every review I’ve seen complains that the balance is tilted too easy, but I don’t agree. I never died, but it was close a couple times. I didn’t feel like I could breeze through every fight without using items and abilities.
The world isn’t particularly big, but it makes up for it by being dense in detail. Given that you spend the majority of the time exploring the world by yourself it’s good that they gave it the time and care it needed. Going through every nook and cranny, discovering characters, quests and nods to past episodes of the show feels rewarding. At no point did I feel like the game was wasting my time or padding for length, even during the more mundane fetch quests. There’d always be something on the other end which would make it feel worth it. The length of the game felt just right.
I had more fun playing this than I was expecting. The way it manages to poke fun at games and stories feels fresh, and makes this more than merely a good license game. It’s an excellent game. Definitely worth playing, unless you can’t stand South Park obviously.

I can't really recommend this game... I'm disappointed by what it has to offer. It has a ton of the "rogue-like" elements that are so popular in current indie platformers, the graphics are appropriately low-fi, the music is kind of mesmerizing, and there seems to be a lot of stuff to unlock over time... but there just isn't any fun here.
Character powers are largely pointless (i.e. ineffective against at least 50% of enemies and useless against bosses), and interactions with enemies lack punch because there's minimal collision detection. Something barely hurting you? Something ripping you a new orifice? Your little pixel dude reacts the same way, and only a floating purple number gives any hint. The same largely goes for damage you do to enemies, except for a few basic monsters who do react to damage.
The low fi graphics and low fi enemy interaction combine to make playing the game feel like wading through sludge, and deaths don't make me want to try again with a new strategy... they make me switch to another game that's more satisfying. If you are looking for a challenging retro platformer, there are hundreds of games on Steam that will fit the bill better than this.

Just as Arkham City was a big jump from Arkham Asylum, so too is Arkham Knight another big leap forward compared to Arkham City. They’ve built upon the mechanics of what came before, so between that and the fact that the storyline is a conclusion to everything that’s transpired, I very strongly recommend that you play through Asylum, City & Origins before starting this. (You can skip Blackgate.)
In City & Origins you could just roam around the city, fighting mobs as you encounter them to get experience. Now, those criminals have all wised up such that almost all of them will just run away. Your reward for fighting them is personal satisfaction. The only way to gain XP is from quests or completing AR challenges, so there’s significantly less hand-to-hand combat in this game. That’s unfortunate because they’ve added new enemy types & attacks/counters to Batman’s arsenal. Indeed, Gotham City is now SUPLEX CITY. Predator stealth areas offer new methods to deal with enemies as well. My favorite one lets you instantly KO several (non-Brute) enemies at once!
Arkham Knight features a completely different map than the one in City/Origins, along with entirely new types of sidequests. That’s important to making sure this doesn’t feel like the same game you’ve been playing for years only in a new place. The key is much of the game mechanics now stress the use of the Batmobile, which you can call to you at any time much like the horse in Red Dead Redemption. It’s a challenge for sandbox design to work in both cars & flying. In Saints Row IV I found myself asking the same question I asked regarding OJ in the airport: “why would you take a car when you can FLY?” Batman could already fly—fine, it’s a glide—through Arkham Asylum & City, so use of the Batmobile is encouraged by way of the city layout, story mode, sidequests, and the fact that it’s quick & easy to switch between gliding & driving. Arkham Knight puts thought into the placement of sidequests & collectibles; to show you areas and details you would otherwise neglect to explore, or use abilities you may otherwise not bother with.
The Batmobile in this game fits the overall aesthetic of the Arkham series: it combines the 1990s Batman: The Animated Series (derived from Tim Burton’s films) with the Christopher Nolan movies. It has two modes: the familiar “car with rocket engine strapped to the back” along with a “Ghost in the Shell tank” one. You’re going to be in more fights that grant XP using the tank than anything else, so you may want to prioritize upgrading it. As a car, it handles like you’d expect: fast on straightaways but tricky to turn. The city layout is very forgiving though, since much of the environment near the streets will simply be destroyed if you drive through. A few areas require tighter precision which can be downright maddening, but most are optional challenges. In tank mode you go about as slow as you would on foot albeit with omnidirectional movement plus access to the Tim Burton-approved Bat-machinegun & the Bat-60mm cannon. Don’t worry: Batman doesn’t kill, so whenever you target humans they’re special NON-LETHAL ROUNDS (fired at over 1000 m/s). Just like the special NON-LETHAL running people over after colliding into them at 100s of MPH using a car that can smash through walls! There’s an electricity effect on the people you hit to suggest they’re being magnetically repelled but WHATEVER. DARK KNIGHT RETURNS.
But seriously, this is the softest ESRB “M” rated game I’ve ever seen. PG-13 movies go well beyond even the most violent images in this, and there’s no nudity or strong language. A lot of characters do get shot by guns, but they just fall down with no blood or gore. The main departure this game has over the previous Arkham games is that there are a few bodies with red blood on or near them, and you can hit/shoot people with the car. This game really should have been rated “T”.
Knight might have the least memorable soundtrack of the entire Arkham series. I can hum the Asylum & City main themes, but no instrumental tracks in Arkham Knight stick with me at all, especially compared to tracks like “You Should Have Listened to My Warning” from Arkham City. Arkham Knight does have the greatest VOCAL tracks of them all though! As far as voices, “true Batman” Kevin Conroy is back as is the true arch-nemesis of these games…Wally Wingert as The Riddler! Seriously, Riddler is the perfect videogame villain because he’s constantly in your face, mocking the player for being stupid. He’s this generation’s giggling Duck Hunt dog that you’d do anything to shoot. There’s no mistaking Riddler dialogue with anyone else, or the way that he intones “Dark Knight” & “Detective.” Punching the smug off his face is what we look forward to most! As for the rest? Don’t check any cast list until AFTER you’ve beaten it, since just knowing what characters are present will just spoil the entire game for you. I did learn that I can't tell Matt Mercer from Troy Baker though.
As you can see from all the reviews now flagged “pre-release,” Arkham Knight got pulled from Steam almost immediately on release to be patched as it was “an unplayable mess.” So, how well did the old version run? There was one noticeable bug I encountered: the 2D overlays for Detective Mode/the mini-map in one indoor area started glitching out after checking it a few times such that you had to restart. Everything else was fine; I had a few crashes but upon checking they were all caused by my sound setup & the fact that I was streaming on Twitch (username “suratd”). On my single GTX 970, it ran 1920 x 1080p with all effects set to highest, including the PC-only nVidia Gameworks effects. The one drawback? It was a solid 30 FPS. That was Arkham Knight’s “crime” pre-patch.
But I think of it this way: even in the old “broken mess” state, it still ran at a higher resolution with more effects than the PS4 or XB1. The re-released version has removed the lock & improved the performance to bring me to 60 FPS in-game with all settings at their new maximum. Using the same GTX 970 GPU, the only thing now that incurs a framerate hit is enabling nVidia’s “Interactive Smoke and Fog” which sometimes decreases performance by about 5-10 FPS in scenes where such smoke appears. Way I see it, the Steam PC version was the best version of Arkham Knight even before it got de-listed, and now it runs better than before.
Arkham Asylum was the most focused experience. Arkham City’s more open-ended layout best captured how hectic “one night being Batman” is while having the best music and villain dialogue that inspired you to stop what you were doing and beat them senseless. Origins had the best and most varied boss fights as well as the most “comic book” style cutscenes. Arkham Knight succeeds over its predecessors not just mechanically, but in the thematic sense. There are not one, but several obstacles for which Batman’s victory over them is not a foregone conclusion. Where maybe you can’t “win” so much as “not lose” even when it looks like you’ve definitely “lost” with no way to recover. Some of the key plot developments are obvious and you can see them coming a mile away. Others are intentional fakeouts. But much like how The Dark Knight Rises is definitely the last Christopher Nolan Batman movie, this is definitely the last Arkham game. My biggest gripe with some of the earlier Arkham stuff, particularly Asylum and Origins, was the game explicitly went out of its way to show the futility of your deeds or the hypocrisy of your actions. But if I’m going to spoil ONE thing about this game...Arkham Knight’s the opposite of that.

Perhaps one of the best 10$ games out there.
I sincerely recommend you to buy this game.
Now here's my reasoning on the games contents.
Music 10/10
Nicely orchestrated music, you can see that Chris Christofensenchris (sorry do not know the last name but it has a lot of Chris in it) actually worked to provide music to fit each level, and often moments too. Very relaxing while you're blasting away on the enemies that come.
Story 10/10
It provides discoverable items that the specific mobs drop, that give you more intell on them (Including a background story) not to mention that the games main story is simplistic yet fitting perfectly.
Gameplay 10/10
Now here's the fun, you collect coins by killing enemies, theres plenty of rewards in the form of chests, statues and more spread over each level, finding the chests, collecting the loot, getting more powerful as your enemies get more powerful each level, and each 5? minutes you spent in game.
This balances out perfectly the random odds of the items you gain. You can find "use" items that are very powerful, and go on cooldown after each use. Not to mention that all the power-up's (Besides use items) stack, so getting a bonus twice is nothing less than still a great reward (as the bonus will be enhanced.)
I've picked up many games for this amount of money, plenty even over. This is just pixelated greatness and 10$ is WAY below the actual worth in fun you'll have if this is your type of game.
You can play it Co-op to upto 4 players, there's plenty different characters with unique abilities, secret findables and more to keep you occupied and coming back for more.
Definitely near or even on top of my recommendations.
Check the videos, see if this game is to your liking. If you like what you see, you're definitely going to LOVE what you get.

Not worth $60 at all. It is a♥♥♥♥♥♥port. There is no option to rebind keys, no aspect ratios above 16/9, and using a controller in the game disables your keyboard- actually even having a controller plugged in to your computer disables your keyboard upon start up. I often find myself having to quickly close the game and restart with my Xbox controller unplugged.
Another thing I had an issue with is that this game also uses quick time events. In the infamous abduction scene the player is forced to push the S key repeatedly in a certain amount of time in order to progress. Many people can push the S key fast enough, but on my mechanical keyboard I cannot. I even tried the even with my controller and I still could not push the button fast enough. So the game ended there for me.
I later came back to the game with a few programs I downloaded. They were Rapid-fire key programs people use for strategy games to not break their keyboards and mice with the thousands of presses and clicks they have to do in their games- I had no idea these things existed. But, as there is something fundamentally wrong with this title as a PC port, the game would crash if I tried using them. I finally found a program that worked and got past the abduction scene, but I believe that being forced to download 3rd party software in order to progress in a game is unacceptable.
If you think that you can get past its technical faults, then that is fine. These were my issues with the game and reviewers never made a big deal out of them. The game still isn't worth $60. The combat is way too easy; after battles are over all HP and PP are restored and during battle players can heal and attack in the same turn which takes away any challenge this game could have offered (besides pushing the S key X amount of times). I'm a die hard South Park fan, but I'm also a game fan- and this isn't a great game. The only reason I would progress any further in this title is to see the rest of the funny story, not because I enjoy playing it.
The story is worth seeing though, wait till it's much cheaper.

I recommend this game with CAUTION. From what I've played this game supports only one playstyle. If you're not running around constantly dodging bullets and getting up in peoples' faces (aliens, whatever), you're DEAD. I appreciate the lack of regenerating health, though. Half-Life 2 features some of the most annoying enemies ever. They have no personality whatsoever (unlike Wheatley from Portal 2 or the enemies in Halo). Game options could have a "very low to ultra" option to save time. There is little variety in the 3 hours I've played.
The story is all right. I'm neither utterly bored by it or blown away. Aliens, resistance, the usual.
Puzzles are all right. Navigation, though, is another story. In the beginning of the game, there is a canal you have to walk through. The way to continue is on the SIDE of a box, and the game doesn't give a hint where you're supposed to go. Batman gave subtle hints to the player through his inner thoughts in the Arkham games. Gordon Freeman didn't have to speak, but seriously, the exploration system definitely detracted from the experience.
Gun variety is HORRIBLE. You have to play with the same gun until you reach a certain point in which you can pick up a new gun. Rinse and repeat. Now, I know the generic alien army Combines are supposed to carry the same weapons, but couldn't the resistance give/modify cool weapons like in any good resistance story?
Conclusion: If you are willing to run around like Duke Nukem most of the game guns blazing, then spend your money on this. If you are willing to do puzzles, spend your money on this. If you are willing to wait a couple of levels to get a new gun, spend your money on this. I can barely recommend this game, because the playstyle it forced me to use made me more alert and fast. I can't say that I had a lot of fun, though.

If you don't know about the series of Sid Meier's Civilization games by now, it is not because you have been living under a rock for the last 3 decades, because there is no rock on the planet large enough to excuse having missed them.  That having been said, the fifth installment of Civilization is a natural progression from its predecessors.  It is turn-based strategy at its best, allowing players to build their civilization and win the game in numerous ways (military conquest, cultural domination, economic supremacy, diplomatic manuvering, etc.)  The scale is massive, the detail is mind-boggling, and the options are endless.  Three of my favorite changes from previous versions are 1) happiness is now civilization-wide, rather than city-specific, and thus much easier to manage;  2) units can no longer "stack", so each military unit occupies its own hex on the map, introducing actual tactical deployment and maneuver rather than just rolling in with massive stacks of forces, which also makes it more important to have better troops rather than just hundreds of weak ones, which leads to 3) ranged units actually attack from range, hitting melee units before they can even retaliate.  Cities can likewise defend themselves with ranged attacks against trespassers (and are much more difficult to capture now).  In summation, if you don't already play Civ, shame on you.  Sid stepped it up with Civ V, and it's great.

In this day and age, the standard retail game costs around $60, and provides either 1-2 hours of gameplay, or a large amount of gameplay, with no replay value at all . South Park: The Stick of Truth is a funny, well made game that fits snuggly inbetween both examples above.  I finished the game after about 10 hours of playing, which is very respectable, and provides you with juuuust enough that, perhaps later on, you'll pick up a mouse and keyboard (Or controller) and try it again. The dialogue is hilarious, the gameplay is good, and Mr. Slave's... "storage" is scary. You can meet all your more known South Park characters, like Randy Marsh, Mr. Hankey, The Underpants Gnomes... Jesus... But its not necessary to do so, and you can just go along the story without giving a damn. I did not stray from the main quest, and to reach 10 hours with minimal sidequest completion is great. You don't have to go into places you don't want to, either. I know you can enter the sewers, but I decided not to unless the game forced me, after a long history of playing games with forced sewer gameplay. I was quite happy that I didn't have to go at all. As a result, I didn't meet The Christmas Poo, but I could live with that.
The idea of a silent protagonist was obviously going to be a difficult thing to pull off, and South Park Studios and Obsidian Entertainment have pulled it off successfully. So congratulations to them. One thing I was unhappy with was the abilities, and how the were performed. almost everything involved mashing buttons on the keyboard or mouse. Wanted to poop? Mash a button. Want to use Jimmys abilities? Mash a button. Want Cartman to fat? Mash a button. It was very tedious and something I never really wanted to do after a while - But in order to win against many opponents, you needed to either A: mash these buttons, or B: use the normal attack, which did absolutely pitiful amounts of damage lategame. If you resorted to option B, you STILL have to press buttons, only this time, instead of mashing, it was timed with little "Ding" sounds, and a little flashing light. After a while, you could play the game with your eyes closed. In fact, to test this, I beat the final boss with my eyes closed (Except for the finale, which isn't really a battle. But I won't spoil it).
Is the game good? I'd say so.
Is it replayable? Maybe after a while.
Do I recommend it? Well, if you don't mind mashing singular buttons, which are being timed against you, and are occaisionally difficult to pull off (such as creating♥♥♥♥♥♥Nuggets), then I guess its worth the money.

Risk of Rain is a 2D sidescrolling, platforming, shmup of sorts. It is a roguelight with a permadeath system and procedurally generated levels. Like most Roguelikes and Roguelights, it has a plethera of items to be found that will ultimately decide the overall fate of your run. And like most of it's genre, it is very luck based. Unlike some others though, it is also very skill oriented. The items are much less necessary than most upgrades in roguelikes. Most of the items in The Binding of Isaac will make a very evident and game changing effect. Most of the items in Risk of Rain are situationally useful and will vary in helpfullness depending on your class. For instance, health leeching is very helpful for Acrid, a melee and poison based character, as it lets him get close without a huge fear of death. For the sniper though, it is helpful but not necessary, as he usually aims to kill enemies in very few shots. Classes also play a key role. They are all very different and require very different playstyles to succeed. The commando, the basic class, has notable mobility and avoidance, but his weapon lacks huge damage. Acrid, a poison based character, can kill much faster but has significantly less speed and next to no avoidance.
The story is also interesting but not much happens with it. Your ship is shot down and you must get back to escape. Why it was shot down remains largely a mystery at the end. Bosses are also a mixed bag. Bosses like the final boss are wonderfully made and intense, while bosses like the toxic beast just run back and forth and spawn enemies. Enemies also all have collectible bios which have more detailed portraits and info about them from a journal's prospective. Each item also has shipping information, seeing as you were in a transport ship. It all helps make the world feel alive.
The music is also just freaking wonderful. I swear all the tracks are different and extremely pleasant to listen to. Fantastic work there.
In total, great roguelike but it lacks a bit of replayability and some of the bosses are meh. Still well worth the price. It also has online and offline co-op for all those that are interested in it.

I was really into buying this game before I played it.  I will admit - it was a great fun, but not as awesome as I wanted.
It played great, levels are fun, power ups are neat, and lots of bosses: however I felt like mobility of my charactor made it less fun.
The concept of the game is to play several areas looking for a way home - each time you die, you must start over: however depending on what you did in your last game... you might have unlocked new power ups to find and playable charactors.
You collect power ups and money to unlock items.  Then you fight a boss and teleport to the next area.  The longer you play - the harder it gets but the tougher you become.  Eventually you make your way to a final space ship to go home with a last boss battle.
I did find the game to be very hard... until I realized I just needed to grind out each level for as many random power ups as I could find.  Eventually stacking power ups made me nearly unbeatable.  I played the game about 10-15 times (7 hours) before I learned to beat it.   With prior knowledge - it could be much faster.
Totally cool game, but doesn't hold my attention longer than the 7 hours I played it.  However I might occasionally play another round on a slow Saturday.

So my review of Stick of Truth is going to be pretty much a carbon copy of every other reviewers'. Why? Because the truth is that the game is very fun, funny, and off the walls insane but it suffers from serious issues with quality assurance. The only time in the game I wasn't really having fun was during a section where the game plays the same 20 second loop of stock porn sounds while you explore the inner walls of your house. The major bugs I ran into were a crash to desktop error during a cutscene that forced me to skip it and the occasional sprite flicker of my character during cutscenes. There are a myriad of other reported bugs in the game that I didn't run into but I imagine they are still a pain. In spite of this, I found the game incredibly fun and funny, though I imagine you do have to be a South Park fan to truly enjoy it. I was very skeptical about the game seeing as it was made by Obsidian who are notorious for extremely buggy games and considering that it's a turn based JRPG and I'm typically not into JRPG's. But the game stayed fresh, fun, fast, and hilarious throughout and that speaks very heavily towards the source material. If you're a South Park fan, you'll most likely love this game. If not, then check out the show first before shelling out the cash for this game.

If you don't know about the series of Sid Meier's Civilization games by now, it is not because you have been living under a rock for the last 3 decades, because there is no rock on the planet large enough to excuse having missed them.  That having been said, the fifth installment of Civilization is a natural progression from its predecessors.  It is turn-based strategy at its best, allowing players to build their civilization and win the game in numerous ways (military conquest, cultural domination, economic supremacy, diplomatic manuvering, etc.)  The scale is massive, the detail is mind-boggling, and the options are endless.  Three of my favorite changes from previous versions are 1) happiness is now civilization-wide, rather than city-specific, and thus much easier to manage;  2) units can no longer "stack", so each military unit occupies its own hex on the map, introducing actual tactical deployment and maneuver rather than just rolling in with massive stacks of forces, which also makes it more important to have better troops rather than just hundreds of weak ones, which leads to 3) ranged units actually attack from range, hitting melee units before they can even retaliate.  Cities can likewise defend themselves with ranged attacks against trespassers (and are much more difficult to capture now).  In summation, if you don't already play Civ, shame on you.  Sid stepped it up with Civ V, and it's great.

Gameplay: 8/10
Simple yet fun. Super Hexagon offers an enjoyable yet simplistic classic experience. You probably look at the screenshots and trailers and think it's boring, but it's like tetris or bejeweled; once you start, you get addicted, only there's more, because each level is only a minute long, yet take a good while to complete on account of difficulty. Much more than say yawning your way through the early levels of tetris, or going from "this is easy" to "aaaaaah!".
Visuals: 4/10
The graphics to this game are simple, yet get the job done.  The lighting is somewhat psychodelic and trippy at first, but extended plays can result in headaches or migraines.
Sound: 9/10
Great classic synthetic music that makes me desperately want whatever synthesiser they used. The announcer lady doesn't get annoying, which is another plus, and the sound effects are functional. I'd give it a 10 if there was any ground breaking aspect to the sound, but there's not.
Learning Curve: 9/10
The easiest difficulty is hard. Yet the game doesn't require any explaining to play, beyond maybe a paragraph. It's quick to learn but not so to master. That is what a good learning curve is. The only reason it's not a 10 is because the easiest difficulty is 'hard', where maybe there should be a 'normal' as well.
Replayability: 8/10
This game isn't sandbox, so it won't keep bringing you back in a few years time to try something new. But the game is fun and score-based, so there's reason to play beyond completion. Plus the gameplay is just fun to just go on to simply play rather than to reach some sort of goal.
Interface: 9/10
The game is open to many kinds of inputs, and given its simplicity, these are never complicated. The controls are easy, but controlling the triangle can get frustrating at times when you overshoot or undershoot where you're trying to go. The UI is simple and easy to follow.
Story: N/A
The game has no story. It is an arcade-style game.
Support: N/A
The game has very very little room for bugs, works on simple OpenGL graphics, and is unlikely to get updates. Thus there's no real need for any support.
Optimisation: N/A
The game's simple design means it can run on practically anything, so optimised graphics etc isn't an issue.
Value for money: 10/10
I just bought the game for under 40p. It's cheap even when not on sale, too.

After a solid 30 hours of gameplay I have to say; I love this game. Risk of Rain is an interesting blend between platforming, action, roguelike and even some hints of (MO)BA. To avoid too much spoilers; it's a 2D game set in space, and you're a survivor trying to get off a planet. Ofcourse this planet can't be friendly, so there will be a large variety of monsters that you will have to kill to finally get off that planet. The planet and it's stages (remember; roguelike) are all randomly generated (and a joy to play!) Trust me; it won't be easy. Even on it's lowest difficulty Risk of Rain is a challenge as long as you play it alone or with someone equally inexperienced. But that's part of the fun. Risk of Rain will laugh at you, mock you (literally) and it will force you to think of a different plan every single playtrough. 30 hours and I completed this game 6 times on normal difficulty, just to give you an idea.
Another part I love to address is the co-op element of this game. It's chaos, sometimes a little panick-y, but that doesn't make it any less enjoyable. The challenges accompanied by playing Risk of Rain make for enough of a challenge for even the most experienced players (up to 4), although divide and conquer seems to make it just a tad easier (just throw up the difficulty!).
Lastly, the soundtrack. Risk of rain is an atmospheric game set in a 2D pixel art world, and it's the music that ties the game into an epic whole. If I wouldn't enjoy the gameplay I would still play Risk of Rain for the different soundtracks. They determine the mood of the game, and they do it with precision and style.
Summary/TLDR; If you like roguelikes, platformers, chaos, pixel art or just great video game music, Risk of Rain is a

TL,DR: A South Park fans must own. Everyone else, give it a play, most fun you'll probably have had since Blood Dragon.
I've never, ever been a big proponent of DLC - let it be items like clothing, weapons or skins - but this is the first game that's left me wanting more to play with other than rerolling a new class after the final boss battle. A game that actually makes you want to buy the next adventure/side-mission pack for the game is faaaaaar to rare to come by these days. Yet in honesty, the sticker price for the game isn't worth the 60$ but I still found myself fulfilled with a great, fun time that made me feel like I was playing a South Park game set in South Park, unlike pretty much every South Park up until the release of SoT.
The mechanic of mix-and-match flair with costumes is a great alternative to the often rigid armor and equipment set-ups for modern rpg/arpg's and the straight forward "Yes, x item is better then y item" interface that many modern RPG's have taken up is present and in place and keeps you playing the game then weighing stats.
On the Kenny side of the tracks; the classes feel a bit on the 'samey' side, with little to differentiate them aside from their class names and spell animation flair. I played a Thief and rerolled to a mage after the final boss battle and found that he pretty much had the exact same starting abilities as my Thief: A stun and a dot - although their advancements do seperate them marginally, I think greater attention to how the classes could have been different really should be priority if there will be any additional content or sequels to the game.
Old Mister Hat's to the RPG/ARPG genre should probably play it on the hardest difficulty if you're looking for a challange, otherwise the myriad of stuns you're afforded will make much of the game a cake walk. Upon retreving your first ranged weapon, you're able to stun a member of the enemies you'll be facing on the battle screen by shooting them from the overworld and hitting one of their buddies. They're stunned for a round or two, which buys you a lot of time to work with, in addition to the way speed is handled, you'll find it incredibly hard to die on the lowest difficulty.
Which kinda brings me to my one major point: The game doesn't focus so much on being an RPG set in South Park but more as a South Park episode you get to be part of with it's 'magic', stylized turn-based combat and Matt Stone and Trey Parker humor that'll probably keep me coming back for more.

OK, here we go. My first Steam review. Now, where to start....
I originally started playing Killing Floor many years back. I amassed over 600 hours of gameplay in total. The game was strangely fun and addicting. Then came Killing Floor 2. Obviously I was hyped, like most veteran KF players. Hoping for a closed beta key (which I got) and dying for a release. Then... something changed. I bought it, yet only managed to get 80 hours in KF2. Partially due to my poor PC performance (it's a disgrace of a machine)... but also due to the game content itself. KF2 isn't (at least yet) what I hoped it to be.
Now, I realize the game is fairly young, but some gross shortcomings are already obviously visible and present for quite some time now.
Stuff that bothers me currently in KF2, as of now, 4th of January, 2016:
Honestly... it's trash. The first game's music from Zynthetic was much more fitting. Not only is the soundtrack mediocre at best, the engine is evidently written to have the same set of songs played regardless of the map. This kills variety and will probably limit the possibilites for future map makers.
As I said before, I realize it's still early access, but the fact that TWI actually took time, to add some totally pointless achievements (Get Level X With Perk Y, etc...) is a real downer. Achievements in KF were fun. In KF2, it's a chore. Like laundry. They didn't even bother giving them original names.
Crates, keys and... really TWI, REALLY?! Doing a bit of copy cat from Valve and the CS:GO concept? I mean I get it, getting some extra dosh if you're a developer is always good news. But this is just shallow money milking at best.
-Welding is one of the things that can affect available tactics. In KF, welding was useful and could turn the tide of the wave, making a difference between progressing to the next wave, or being mercilessly slaughtered. In KF2, it's just a "fad". Welding can be too slow in many cases (even with a Lv 25 Support, which should excel at that, since that's one of his perk attributes) and the doors, when they fall, are useless till the end of the map.
-Perk bonuses are poor. Comparing max level bonuses of a particular perk in KF with those of KF2, will reveal that KF2 perks, even when maxed out, don't stand up to the good ol' KF perks.
-Commando perk is still useless. Veteran KF players will know what I'm talking about.
These are the biggest flaws that I noticed so far.
Now for the good part, because let's be honest, the game isn't a waste.
Guts, blood annnnnd more guts. Especially If you own a newer nVidia GPU. Although excluding ATI out of this is less than honorable by TWI, but that's a different story altogether.
Certain lights in the maps can be blown out by players or zeds, changing the combat environment (usually for the harder)
Built-in game voice chat to quickly alert other meatbags on your team of that FP, coming to pound some meat.
The rest is pretty much like KF.
Bottom line, KF2 is currently mediocre. It doesn't topple KF... yet. Hopefully it gets changed heavily.
Do I recommend it? Yes if you want a modern FPS co-op game where guts are the new floor decoration. No if you're looking for a game that exceedes in content compared to original KF.

I'd give this game an overall score of 8.5/10.
Instead of a long review, I'm going to focus on a few, specific things. The RNG in this game is a big plus...and a minus, as well. It's great that the game has so many different items with varying effects (which range from health regeneration, to standard attacks knocking enemies back, to on-kill effects, and much, much more) that can be purchased for varying costs each level. You get currency (obviously) by killing enemies, and opening containers, and other items. But the issue here, that is almost always present in rogue-like games is that they're heavily reliant on RNG; you could get a great loadout and have a super easy time, you could get a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ loadout and have a very, very difficult time. Speaking of items, while they're (mostly) differentiated, they're not that greatly balanced. I get the fact that some items are going to be better than others, but I wish that it wasn't so drastic. For example, within the same rarity, we have the "Leeching Seed" (you heal 2HP on every attack you perform that hits an enemy), and the "56 Leaf Clover" (Elite mobs have a 4% chance to drop an item upon death). Which would you rather have? An item that greatly increases your longevity, or an item that works upon a 4% chance, if a rare enemy spawns? The choice is obvious.
One of the biggest things I should mention is the time mechanic; the game has a very interesting dilemma at all times because of it. The way it works is that while you're playing, at all times, a timer is being run. After a set amount of time (usually every 5 minutes), the difficulty increases, which increases the strength of enemies, and increases the frequency in which they spawn. So, the dilemma you're faced with at all times is this: should I finish the level, or should I grind enemies and/or try to obtain more items to make killing enemies easier? For myself this was a difficult dilemma, and got me killed on many occassions, because I'm the type of person that wants to grind, grind, grind and obtain ALL the items! It's also worth noting that when you start the boss battle on each level (after beating said boss, you can advance to the next level), you must also endure 90 seconds of enemy spawns in addition to the boss, so even if you are rushing to the end of the level, you must survive that long, in additon to finding the boss (there's no minimap, etc., so you must explore).
The game has ten different classes, that are (mostly) all different, with varying abilities and niches. For example, the first character you will play as is the "Commando", one that excells in long-range combat. He has four abilities (as all classes do), which include a default attack, an attack that has a large "beam" attack that hits and knocks all enemies back with range, a defensive ability that makes you immune to damage and effects for one second (four second cooldown), and an ability that deals a large amount of damage plus stuns every enemy that it hits. In contrast, the next character you unlock will be a defensive melee character, called the "Enforcer". His abilities are a standard melee attack, a melee attack that deals moderate damage and knocks enemies back, a defensive stance that negates all damage and effects from the front (but makes you move very slow and unable to change directions), and an AoE attack that stuns enemies. Even when certain classes "overlap" (a "Hunter" and "Sniper"), the abilities and niches are different, making for the classes to play differently (Hunter is about kiting and AoE, while the Sniper deals incredible single-target damage). I'm not sure if I suck at all classes except the Huntress (the aforementioned "Hunter"), but I couldn't beat the game after 7+ hours of playing (I suck, heh...), but after I unlocked the Huntress, if I didn't beat the game, I ♥♥♥♥ed up. Some classes are very much better than others, which is a balancing issue that I wish would be more addressed.
Something small that I wanted to touch upon is the music. I really enjoyed the overall soundtrack, with a couple of songs making my way onto my iPod, for repeated listenings. Specifically, "Chanson d'Automne" and "Coalescence", among others. Of course, some songs are better than others, but I liked most of the music. Subjective, of course.
My main complaint about this game, other than the RNG of course, is the difficulty that lies within the trash. A lot of video games have this issue, and it's one I can understand, but it's a real problem when you have died 50 or so times on trash, and about 2 times or fewer on bosses themselves. When the issue arises, the problem is either than I'm completely overwhelmed with enemies and I have zero options and must face the inevitability of death, or comes out of nowhere with an absurd amount of damage I wasn't ready for (which happens suprisingly often). Really frustrating.
A minor complaint is the graphics. While I don't find graphics (particularly for an Indie game) to be a major influence, the graphics within the game aren't that great. For an example, here's an example screenshot from the unofficial wiki:
. Again, it's nothing major, but it might turn someone off.
It's also worth mentioning that online co-op is largely a bust; you must forward ports and some other complicated stuff. I, as well as many people on the internet, cannot get it to work. Since online multiplayer is the first listed feature on the page, you should be aware of this.
Before I close, it's worth mentioning that the game was made by two total people! I find it especially interesting that the programmer was also the artist, it's rare to see that.
In conclusion, this game was a lot of fun, and one I'd definitely recommend, around an 8.5/10. I've put around 15 hours into the game, and since I have a lot of fun playing the game, I'll be putting at least 10 more into the game. For a game I bought on sale at $3.39, this is a steal, and one I'd recommend at even full ($10) price.
TL;DR =
+ RNG
+ Fun, time-based mechanic
+ Music
+ Varied classes (ten classes) that (mostly) have different niches
- RNG
- Graphics could be a turn-off to some (not myself, but...)
- Trash is more difficult and deadly than bosses
- Certain items and classes need to be better balanced

TL,DR: A South Park fans must own. Everyone else, give it a play, most fun you'll probably have had since Blood Dragon.
I've never, ever been a big proponent of DLC - let it be items like clothing, weapons or skins - but this is the first game that's left me wanting more to play with other than rerolling a new class after the final boss battle. A game that actually makes you want to buy the next adventure/side-mission pack for the game is faaaaaar to rare to come by these days. Yet in honesty, the sticker price for the game isn't worth the 60$ but I still found myself fulfilled with a great, fun time that made me feel like I was playing a South Park game set in South Park, unlike pretty much every South Park up until the release of SoT.
The mechanic of mix-and-match flair with costumes is a great alternative to the often rigid armor and equipment set-ups for modern rpg/arpg's and the straight forward "Yes, x item is better then y item" interface that many modern RPG's have taken up is present and in place and keeps you playing the game then weighing stats.
On the Kenny side of the tracks; the classes feel a bit on the 'samey' side, with little to differentiate them aside from their class names and spell animation flair. I played a Thief and rerolled to a mage after the final boss battle and found that he pretty much had the exact same starting abilities as my Thief: A stun and a dot - although their advancements do seperate them marginally, I think greater attention to how the classes could have been different really should be priority if there will be any additional content or sequels to the game.
Old Mister Hat's to the RPG/ARPG genre should probably play it on the hardest difficulty if you're looking for a challange, otherwise the myriad of stuns you're afforded will make much of the game a cake walk. Upon retreving your first ranged weapon, you're able to stun a member of the enemies you'll be facing on the battle screen by shooting them from the overworld and hitting one of their buddies. They're stunned for a round or two, which buys you a lot of time to work with, in addition to the way speed is handled, you'll find it incredibly hard to die on the lowest difficulty.
Which kinda brings me to my one major point: The game doesn't focus so much on being an RPG set in South Park but more as a South Park episode you get to be part of with it's 'magic', stylized turn-based combat and Matt Stone and Trey Parker humor that'll probably keep me coming back for more.

Cannot recommend this game after the botched launch and failure to patch.
The game has now been 're-released', tagging all prior reviews as 'pre-release' in an attempt to invalidate negative reviews (The game was around ~40% positive at 're-release', which is almost unheard of), despite the fact that the game was very much released and only pulled after public outcry.
Many of the performance issues have NOT been fixed as promised. There is a fairly serious memory leak, and their 'fix' was to tell users 'we’ve found that having at least 12GB of system RAM on a PC allows the game to operate without paging and provides a smoother gameplay experience.' (Windows 10), or 'If you encounter this, simply re-launching the game will resolve the issue.' (Windows 7). Other FPS issues, such as severe rain/batmobile slowdown as well as very clear object pop-in, are still present.
WB has issued an 'apology' in the form of free past-Arkham games, but most of the people affected, who bought the game at original launch, or pre-purchased, already own these prior games, as they are fans of the series. It seems more of a simple promotional tool to pull in more new buyers (The 'apology' free pack is for anyone who buys the game for the next couple weeks, in addition to the past), rather than actually compensating those who were affected. New buyers actually get all the same content as pre-purchasers and original launch buyers, while also benefitting from a $10 reduced price.
Performance aside, if you're lucky and have the game run well on your machine (it seems to be left to chance whether the game works well or not on any system, high or low end) the game itself is actually very well done and fun. Most of the characters, with the exception of the main antagonist (whose identity is made painfully obvious WELL before the reveal), are written and voiced well, and the different side objectives are mostly fun. The combat is fluid, as you'd expect coming from any of the past games. However, it doesn't add too many new elements. The one big new 'feature' is the batmobile, which should be a fun addition, but is shoehorned into any situation the writers could think of, and turns out to be very boring to use.
EDIT: Oh, forgot to mention. One of the optional boss battles, with the Riddler, is locked behind obtaining ***every riddler trophy in the game***. Basically, you do his side questline, which was actually pretty enjoyable, win, and he says 'well, you haven't won until you do ALL my challenges, peace!' and runs away. As someone that likes doing side missions and completing side-arcs, this really bugs me. I'm not willing to run around for hours and hours doing boring little puzzles and 100% the game just to get to a new peice of content/arc closure. I gave up and just watched it on Youtube.
===================================================================
All in all, with the performance issues, horribly handled launch, poor community support and self-serving 'apology', I can't recommend this game at anywhere near $50. Even if you buy it with a good rig, it seems to be a 50-50 shot whether or not you'll have performance issues that hinder your play. The actual gameplay and story is fun though, so it may be worth taking a risk (or 'demoing' it to test performance, then buying) once it goes on sale for $10-$15.

Super Hexagon is the cumulative knowledge of 2000+ years of humankind converted to flashing colours and dance music that screams through your monitor and projects itself directly into the corneas of your eyes, where it is transformed into beautiful hexagonal shapes and geometric patterns that will haunt you in your sleep.
The story of a young triangle attempting to escape its geometric overlords as they rush at him is more compelling and heartbreaking than all of the Cormac McCarthy books followed by Futurama's Jurassic Bark episode and finished off with that one scene from The Notebook you know you teared up a little at but don't really want to admit to. Every time I have to close Super Hexagon I feel as though a little piece of me is torn away and tossed into the void, never to be seen again. But that's okay, because I know that piece of me is in a better, more hexagonal place.
Please, for your own good, purchase this game. It is a life-changing experience that will have you questioning your sanity, three-dimensional existance, and ability to properly formulate sentences in whatever language it is that you speak.

TL,DR: A South Park fans must own. Everyone else, give it a play, most fun you'll probably have had since Blood Dragon.
I've never, ever been a big proponent of DLC - let it be items like clothing, weapons or skins - but this is the first game that's left me wanting more to play with other than rerolling a new class after the final boss battle. A game that actually makes you want to buy the next adventure/side-mission pack for the game is faaaaaar to rare to come by these days. Yet in honesty, the sticker price for the game isn't worth the 60$ but I still found myself fulfilled with a great, fun time that made me feel like I was playing a South Park game set in South Park, unlike pretty much every South Park up until the release of SoT.
The mechanic of mix-and-match flair with costumes is a great alternative to the often rigid armor and equipment set-ups for modern rpg/arpg's and the straight forward "Yes, x item is better then y item" interface that many modern RPG's have taken up is present and in place and keeps you playing the game then weighing stats.
On the Kenny side of the tracks; the classes feel a bit on the 'samey' side, with little to differentiate them aside from their class names and spell animation flair. I played a Thief and rerolled to a mage after the final boss battle and found that he pretty much had the exact same starting abilities as my Thief: A stun and a dot - although their advancements do seperate them marginally, I think greater attention to how the classes could have been different really should be priority if there will be any additional content or sequels to the game.
Old Mister Hat's to the RPG/ARPG genre should probably play it on the hardest difficulty if you're looking for a challange, otherwise the myriad of stuns you're afforded will make much of the game a cake walk. Upon retreving your first ranged weapon, you're able to stun a member of the enemies you'll be facing on the battle screen by shooting them from the overworld and hitting one of their buddies. They're stunned for a round or two, which buys you a lot of time to work with, in addition to the way speed is handled, you'll find it incredibly hard to die on the lowest difficulty.
Which kinda brings me to my one major point: The game doesn't focus so much on being an RPG set in South Park but more as a South Park episode you get to be part of with it's 'magic', stylized turn-based combat and Matt Stone and Trey Parker humor that'll probably keep me coming back for more.

So how this review will play out: I will discuss the pros and cons, summarise what I said in points, give a final comment and rate out of 10.
Let's start with the pros. So this game truly captures the feel of the South Park, it is written just like the show, jammed packed with characters, popular and unknown, and looks so much like the show that one could mistake it for being an episode, even the music reminds me of some episodes. The writing in the game does not let down the reputation the the show holds, it is all still so disgusting and clever at the same time and even if you know that you shouldn't laugh, you do anyway. The gameplay is great, the combat system is turn-based and during this sequence you can control you and another of our favourite characters from the series, the fights can take time but never seem to bore you as you have a selection of attacks on can choose from for both characters. When not in a fight scene you can use the characters abilities to get through certain areas as well as cause the demise of enemies without having to actually fight them, which can save time. Customisation of the character is also very broad. Countless items of clothing, makeup, and hairstyles are at you disposal (that is when you find them on the map) which can be used to make your character unique. One can also find weapons and armours around the world map, which can be enchanted to add special effects to the item, which can be useful at later stages of the game. The world map really does show the town in a different light, in the show all they had to do was cut to another location but in the game they had to map out where everything was in the town which really must have brought insight to the fans and the creators.
Lets go onto the cons, there were not many but they all seemed to tick me off. Firstly, this game is way too short for an RPG. I finished the story, all the side missions, and interacted with almost all the characters scattered around the map in about 15 hours. Comparing that to Skyrim, where I have finished the story, done about half of the side missions and done only a little bit of exploring in about 70 hours. So there is really not much to do with it once you are done with everything unless you want to start a new game. The game also had some bugs, most were not an issue but one would make my character and my side character dissapear during a fight scene when I did one of Butters' super move, but they were still playable, making it impossible to know when to block an enemy's attacks. Another problem that I specifically found was that in the storyline there were too little main missions (probably about 7 or 8) but there were many other missions inisde it that would lead to the main objective being completed. At points it would get so out of hand with all the smaller objectives that I would begin to stop and think "What does this have to do with my goal again?". That personally bugged me but it may not for everyone.
So to summarise:
Pros:
-Just like the show in all aspects
-Writing keeps with the show's standards
-Exciting turn-based combat system
-Ability to manipulate the environment
-Great customisation of cloting and weapons
-Town of South Park brought to life
Cons:
-Short for an RPG
-Some bugs
-Some missions for the main story seemed to be unrelated to the main focus
Although I went into depth with the cons, the pros still outweigh them. Overall this is an amazing game and a must-have for South Park fans.

But those of us who haven't upgraded our PC in the last two weeks are kinda screwed. If you are reading this review in the year 2018, when the game is $10 on sale and everyone has nuclear reactors in their computers (I mean, I assume, anyways) then your sheer strength of hardware will probably overpower the shoddiness of this port, and you will get a wonderful video game for your troubles! For those of us in October 2015, though... Yeah. We're screwed.

You think at first, "oh, this looks really simple, I could probably beat it in one hour," but then you would be wrong, dead wrong. The entire goal (if you can't tell by the video) is to guide your little triangle through an ever shifting pattern of walls, and survive for sixty seconds. It took over three hours for me to beat the first level, and it's so addicting, that it only felt like half an hour. Think you can do better? Try it. Think you'll get tired of it? Think again! The feminine computer's voice of "game over" every time you die is like one big taunt, mocking you, but at the same time, telling you to go on. There's no tutorial, and the difficulty for the first level is "Hard". If you're looking for a challenging, and incredibly addicting game, think about adding this little gem to your collection. Trust me, you'll thank me later.

Risk of Rain is a very solid experience that doesn't hold back its punches. While the game seemed a bit harsh when I first started playing, I found that the merciless nature of the game was actually enjoyable once I got acclimated to the game. The high difficulty makes it so that any enemy encounter could be your last and whether you survive or not could come down to simply deciding to use the right ability at the right time or knowing when its time to hunker down or run for your life. Even when the game crushes you it only makes learning how to survive and making it through the game that much more rewarding. The game is also a great experience with friends, and while setting up co-op isn't the easiest thing to do in Risk of Rain, it's definitely worth the effort. The types of synergy you can pull off between characters is fantastic, as well as the variety of builds available with the many items in the game. There's always reasons to come back such as unlocking new items, hunting for artifacts, unlocking new characters, trying out every level, going for new builds, speed-running, beating the game with each character, or beating the game with friends trying out different characters. I would recommend Risk of Rain to any co-op or indie-game enthusiasts. Definitely one of my all-time favorite indie titles.

Let me start off by saying that this is a absolutely fantastic game. I’ve found myself to continue coming back to this game after breaks and then playing it hours at a time. It’s a blast with friends and a challenge alone.
The game is a ‘roguelite’. You don’t save inbetween levels and if you die that’s it. There are a number of different classes to choose from and three difficulty levels.  Each class needs to be unlocked (with the exception of the starting class of course) and they all have their own skills and thus change up the gameplay a bit. The game exists out of a number of stages and then the final level. For each stage there are two (if I’m not mistaking) levels, which the game chooses for you. To vary the gameplay there are 100 items that can drop, though most of them need to be unlocked. These items can do things ranging from getting health after kills, increasing your attack speed or creating ghosts of enemies when they die.  As time goes on the game gets more and more difficult so it isn’t a good idea to stay around a level and open every chest you find. There are also unlockable modifiers to change up the gameplay even more but you can find out what they do on your own.
The soundtrack is absolutely fantastic (you can buy it here:
) and the visuals do what they need to. The biggest con of the game is the performance. I’m running an I7 920 and 5870, yet my computer never seems to get 60fps, even with the graphics settings turned down.
Overall a great experience and you'll get your moneys worth if you like having a bit of a challenge.

Hi guys! I think I should tell you straight-up: Arkham Knight is a FANTASTIC video game. If you don't mind 30 FPS and have an Xbox One or Playstation 4, I highly recommend you get it on those platforms! Unfortunately, you're reading this review on the Steam digital distribution service for personal computers, which I assume means you're gathering info on what the game would be like if you bought it from Steam. The answer to that is: It's ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥!
During the long hiatus where it was unavailable for purchase, Arkham Knight received one patch that addressed bugs and performance towards the end of September, and that was it. While improvements were made, the game's performance is still quite poor, and many of the errors that plagued launch haven't been fully fixed! Rain effects still don't work the way they do on consoles! As those of us in "the biz" like to say: Man, what a crock!
The patch that accompanied the relaunch added support for the game's DLC, and that's it! No improvements to the base game whatsoever.
If you install this game on an SSD, and have 16 GB of RAM and a high-end i7 and like a 980 Ti, great news! You can actually enjoy this PC game! But those of us who haven't upgraded our PC in the last two weeks are kinda screwed. If you are reading this review in the year 2018, when the game is $10 on sale and everyone has nuclear reactors in their computers (I mean, I assume, anyways) then your sheer strength of hardware will probably overpower the shoddiness of this port, and you will get a wonderful video game for your troubles! For those of us in October 2015, though... Yeah. We're screwed.

I finally bought this game yesterday after testing it for a bit. I honestly say that, if you're a true South Park fan, you can't resist this one. The game is a fun little RPG, with a turn-based battle mode when engaging or being engaged by various foes, from other little kids in the neighborhood to hobos and so on. You will encounter various - if not all - characters from the show, and you will be able to interact with certain things in people's houses, including toilets, which... let you pick up your poop to use later as a weapon in combat...
The battle mode is made to look in such a way that you're seeing what the imagination of the South Park boys see, and unlike other turn-based games, it's interactive, so you're not completely helpless to the enemy's actions.
It's not for the faint of heart though, as, if the show disturbs, offends, or disgusts you in any way, the game certainly will as well. I completely recommend this game if you're a South Park fan and want to enter their world.

I haven't played many rogue-lites myself, but I really enjoy this game's approach and its well-defined classes. Each class (10 in total) has 4 unique skills, and they allow for some fairly creative gameplay. The first skill is either a basic ranged or melee attack, although, some classes have an extra snippet tagged on. The second and third skills vary but are usually some combination of attack, mobility, or utility. The fourth skill is a class's most powerful and fanciful, with the Sniper and Engineer being the only exceptions.
Similar to most rogue-lites, there is no shortage of difficulty or challenge, especially when you're 'doing it wrong'. Obtainment of items is essential, but with chests and icons (for item gambling) scattered randomly throughout maps, you must temper exploration and gold farming with efficiency, lest the game clock itself defeat you. You can also obtain hidden items called Artifacts, each possessing some sweeping gameplay change or addition when toggled. I personally won't play the game without the Glass Artifact because otherwise the items--rather than your personal ability--substantially dictate your performance.
Co-op can be a double-edged sword if one of your partners is unfamiliar with the game. They may bring more firepower, but items and gold will have to be shared. Die too much, without optimal farm, and your partner will leave you behind for the rest of the game. This is kind of what I was talking about concerning itemization.

South Park fans who have been disappointed with lackluster tower defence games or cheaply pushed mobile games can rejoice, for this is the game they have been waiting for.  An open world rpg which takes place in the town of South Park, and makes no effort to dumb down or control it's trademark comedy to appeal to wider audiences or age groups.  It's as true a South Park experience as you would expect from watching the actual show.
The story is typical of Matt and Trey, full of pop culture satire and meta references which poke fun at the cliche video game genres, and the ending has one helluva twist.  Even if it was a massive WTF moment, it was one that I heartily enjoyed.
The gameplay on the otherhand is very much similar to Costume Quest, in that it's very light on the RPG combat.  There is room for error without making things too easy, and while the mechanics are fundamentally a little repetative, the game still keeps things fresh by tossing in new set pieces and enemies to fight.  Honestly...  I cant tell you how hard it was to focus on thinking about tactics when I'm laughing my♥♥♥♥♥off at something the game unexpectedly throws at me..
However, the one problem I have with this game is the instruction on learning new "magic" or performing certain QTE sequences...  At certain points during the story progression you will learn a new move, or be given a certain task to do involving QTE's.  And honestly...  It needs to be explained a lot clearer...
You might be thinking "It's a QTE dumbass!  Just follow the on-screen prompts!".  But trust me... you'll see for yourself when you encounter them.
Asking online how to beat it is your best way forward, and you feel somewhat cheated that the game didnt explain what you actually HAD to do better to achieve the desired outcome.
But this is my only gripe with the game.  Besides that, its been a true respectful nod to loyal fans, a game which not only honours the genre but actually put out a tie in game with Decent gameplay.  Which is rare to see in tie in games...
If they put out additional story content for this game too, it would only sweeten the deal.
A solid purchase and highly recommended.

One of the best FPS games out there! It may be an exaggeration but Half Life 2 remains - even today - one of my favourite games. I believe this game aged well and it looks good even today which marks the 10-year anniversary of this game. Valve later on released some updates to the Source Engine so the game support widescreen and has some extra features to make it look and run better.
Story-wise it is an excellent follow-up to the first game as now we have an alien race called Combine who have already invaded and enslaved humanity. Freeman - our numb protagonist - is now tasked with aiding those people who rose up to defy these visitors from space. While some of the creatures we encountered in the first episode return in Half Life 2 you mainly fight against humanoid-like creatures. It's a nice touch and it also showcases the artificial intelligence which is also superb in the game.
There are varied environments in the game and there are two things that keep you interested throughout your progress: occasionally you can hop into a vehicle and drive to your next destination. Early on you cannot access this car but you can use a boat to go through a sewers-like stage. The second - and probably best - feature of the game is the Gravity Gun. A gun that does not have ammunition and requires objects - objects in your surroundings that you can pick up and launch at your enemies. There is a level specifically designed for this weapon; a level where ammo is a scarcity and you rely on the precision-aiming skill with the gravity gun.
Single-player campaign offers a long (10-15 hour) experience and the game has two expansion packs (the two provide you with roughly 8-9 hours gameplay time). While Episode 1 is a bit of a letdown Episode 2 is an excellent expansion pack.
I wish Valve concluded the story of Gordon Freeman with releasing a final episode (Episode 3) or a 3rd sequel. I believe this request - coming from not just me but from the community - is well justified.
