I played this game back when it was released. Replaying it after these years felt very good, actually more so now than back then.
I apologise if this review will have a slight meandering walk, I just wish to convey many different beautiful characteristics that are still fresh in my memory.
I gained a new appreciation to the "puzzle"-elements of HL2. Puzzle here needs to be understood broadly, because HL2 doesn't fall for the arbitrary sudoku or Rubic's cube variety of puzzles one sees at times in games.
Gordon Freeman is the scientist, with a keen eye, and the problem-solving attitude that goes with science, you observe your surroundings and use what you find to experiment and gain the upper hand. The realization that something you see and can manipulate can influence your environment, is a rewarding one, even after some inital struggling to put two and two together. The puzzles also do not punish you in a completely arbitrary fashion. They can feel truly natural at times. This is in contrast to some other forms of puzzles where you need to figure out some very specific combination that you need to input in some obstacle in a very careful order, sometimes with an added annoyance of a quick-time-event-like killjoy of immediately having to start all over again if even the mere timing fluctuates.
I feel like the good people over at Valve truly have a grip on how nature and problem-solving usually works in real life, and with some imagination, managed to create a game that exploits some of the fun parts of the principles of doing science.
The puzzles are also used to keep combat fresh. Seeing the zombies, CP's and soldiers over and over again didn't grow old, because the game doesn't just rely on a big arsenal to allow variety for the player, but puts the player and their "obstacles" the enemies, in new situations, where you can, again, use the environment to gain the upper hand, rewarding good observational skills and a willingness to experiment.
Okay, perhaps that is enough about puzzles, next I wish to remark on the superb atmosphere. Valve put together a rich setting here, right from the start they managed to convey the dystopian and rather interestingly quaint european town of city 17, where the crumbling old buildings are warped with an ikea-style ready-made occupational starter-kit of combine cold blue structures. The dark and dead place of Ravenholm has it's own personality with Father Gregory, the zombie setting twisted with how we imagine someone would live in an infested old town, setting traps - again which the player can manipulate - the decay and history visible all around you. The beautiful but haunting coast, peripheral to civilization, and so ruled by chaos and neglect, with antlions making do and combine forces always pushing a little further. To the battle-worn and gritty city torn by the conflicts of the resistance and combine assaults, to finally the citadel, an alien and mysterious, again cold, but hinting at the magnitude and power of the invaders of earth. Multitudes of beautiful settings slightly corrupted to completely annihilated by strife and struggle.
I loved it, immersive beyond measure.
The story, characters and gameplay also hold up to scrutiny, personality brought to life by using what has worked across the ages in storytelling with the care and loving touch of committed developers with a broad picture already in mind, painted on a highly malleable and able canvas - the engine - with precision and passion.
Now I feel satisfied. I have a feeling that there was more to add, but I have exhausted my creative abilites to do justice for this fun and rich experience.

The only cons I can find about this game is that you are limited to the amount of classes you can play and the amount of weapons availible for each class. In addition to this, one of the maps added to the game when the Patriarch returned (Farmhouse) there is a certain area you can sit on and the zeds will no recogize that you are there, so they will just run around you thinking they can not get to you, but I am sure this bug will be fixed in the upcoming patch, after all this is an early release game and still has a long way to go and more content to be added. I definetley recommend this game to any player who enjoys zombie survival games.

One of the best FPS games out there! It may be an exaggeration but Half Life 2 remains - even today - one of my favourite games. I believe this game aged well and it looks good even today which marks the 10-year anniversary of this game. Valve later on released some updates to the Source Engine so the game support widescreen and has some extra features to make it look and run better.
Story-wise it is an excellent follow-up to the first game as now we have an alien race called Combine who have already invaded and enslaved humanity. Freeman - our numb protagonist - is now tasked with aiding those people who rose up to defy these visitors from space. While some of the creatures we encountered in the first episode return in Half Life 2 you mainly fight against humanoid-like creatures. It's a nice touch and it also showcases the artificial intelligence which is also superb in the game.
There are varied environments in the game and there are two things that keep you interested throughout your progress: occasionally you can hop into a vehicle and drive to your next destination. Early on you cannot access this car but you can use a boat to go through a sewers-like stage. The second - and probably best - feature of the game is the Gravity Gun. A gun that does not have ammunition and requires objects - objects in your surroundings that you can pick up and launch at your enemies. There is a level specifically designed for this weapon; a level where ammo is a scarcity and you rely on the precision-aiming skill with the gravity gun.
Single-player campaign offers a long (10-15 hour) experience and the game has two expansion packs (the two provide you with roughly 8-9 hours gameplay time). While Episode 1 is a bit of a letdown Episode 2 is an excellent expansion pack.
I wish Valve concluded the story of Gordon Freeman with releasing a final episode (Episode 3) or a 3rd sequel. I believe this request - coming from not just me but from the community - is well justified.

I played this game back when it was released. Replaying it after these years felt very good, actually more so now than back then.
I apologise if this review will have a slight meandering walk, I just wish to convey many different beautiful characteristics that are still fresh in my memory.
I gained a new appreciation to the "puzzle"-elements of HL2. Puzzle here needs to be understood broadly, because HL2 doesn't fall for the arbitrary sudoku or Rubic's cube variety of puzzles one sees at times in games.
Gordon Freeman is the scientist, with a keen eye, and the problem-solving attitude that goes with science, you observe your surroundings and use what you find to experiment and gain the upper hand. The realization that something you see and can manipulate can influence your environment, is a rewarding one, even after some inital struggling to put two and two together. The puzzles also do not punish you in a completely arbitrary fashion. They can feel truly natural at times. This is in contrast to some other forms of puzzles where you need to figure out some very specific combination that you need to input in some obstacle in a very careful order, sometimes with an added annoyance of a quick-time-event-like killjoy of immediately having to start all over again if even the mere timing fluctuates.
I feel like the good people over at Valve truly have a grip on how nature and problem-solving usually works in real life, and with some imagination, managed to create a game that exploits some of the fun parts of the principles of doing science.
The puzzles are also used to keep combat fresh. Seeing the zombies, CP's and soldiers over and over again didn't grow old, because the game doesn't just rely on a big arsenal to allow variety for the player, but puts the player and their "obstacles" the enemies, in new situations, where you can, again, use the environment to gain the upper hand, rewarding good observational skills and a willingness to experiment.
Okay, perhaps that is enough about puzzles, next I wish to remark on the superb atmosphere. Valve put together a rich setting here, right from the start they managed to convey the dystopian and rather interestingly quaint european town of city 17, where the crumbling old buildings are warped with an ikea-style ready-made occupational starter-kit of combine cold blue structures. The dark and dead place of Ravenholm has it's own personality with Father Gregory, the zombie setting twisted with how we imagine someone would live in an infested old town, setting traps - again which the player can manipulate - the decay and history visible all around you. The beautiful but haunting coast, peripheral to civilization, and so ruled by chaos and neglect, with antlions making do and combine forces always pushing a little further. To the battle-worn and gritty city torn by the conflicts of the resistance and combine assaults, to finally the citadel, an alien and mysterious, again cold, but hinting at the magnitude and power of the invaders of earth. Multitudes of beautiful settings slightly corrupted to completely annihilated by strife and struggle.

Super Hexagon is an arcade type game where you try to keep your triangle from hitting the walls of spinning hexagons while they come at you very quickly.  This is a review by a disabled gamer (I only play with a mouse).
As soon as I opened the game I hit an immediate roadblock.  You begin full screen with your left and right mouse buttons only scrolling the menu.  To actually select anything on the menu, the game says to press space bar.   I later accidentally discovered you can press both mouse buttons simultaneously to act as a space bar. but the game itself never tells you this.  So the first 5 minutes of my experience was spent trying to find someone to come to my PC to press space so I could access options.  Once I had help and could access the options, I could change to windowed mode.  Windowed mode is borderless and worked well with onscreen keyboard.  You can play with your mouse or keyboard only.  There's also an option for joypad.
Gameplay itself can be completely mouse controlled.  Left click to spin board left, right click spin board right.  Clicking needs to be quick to help with precision.  While Fun and adictive, it can also be frustrating. I could only last a few seconds.  The game is difficult for everyone with game modes starting with hard and moving on to harder, hardest & several locked levels.  With that in mind, I also had someone without a disability play and noticed it was still difficult to get far but moves seemed to be more precise.
The game is playable with only a mouse or keyboard.  That is Assuming you can press both mouse buttons at once or have someone who can press space to get it out of full screen, it is mouse only playable.  That being said, if you can't make quick agile clicks, get easily frustrated, or have issues with flashing spinning graphics...  I would avoid this game.
Besides issues you might have with accessibility, the game IS addictive fun, even when you're losing.

Once I had help and could access the options, I could change to windowed mode.  Windowed mode is borderless and worked well with onscreen keyboard.  You can play with your mouse or keyboard only.  There's also an option for joypad.
Gameplay itself can be completely mouse controlled.  Left click to spin board left, right click spin board right.  Clicking needs to be quick to help with precision.  While Fun and adictive, it can also be frustrating. I could only last a few seconds.  The game is difficult for everyone with game modes starting with hard and moving on to harder, hardest & several locked levels.  With that in mind, I also had someone without a disability play and noticed it was still difficult to get far but moves seemed to be more precise.
The game is playable with only a mouse or keyboard.  That is Assuming you can press both mouse buttons at once or have someone who can press space to get it out of full screen, it is mouse only playable.  That being said, if you can't make quick agile clicks, get easily frustrated, or have issues with flashing spinning graphics...  I would avoid this game.
Besides issues you might have with accessibility, the game IS addictive fun, even when you're losing.

Anyway, the game is a sequel to the original Killing Floor game, it's more focusing on the Fast-Paced Action, Graphics are tremendously beautiful, Soundtracks are amazing, Animations is fantastic, More perks and better Gunplay. It's a first person shooter coop game where 1-6 players has to survive waves (Depends on the Host settings if it's 7 or 10 waves) against the Zeds (Specimens who are failed experimental clones created by Horzine Biotech) until the boss fight part.
Short explanation about the gameplay, there are different types of classes called Perks, these perks have different types of weapons and playstyle, here's my brief explanation about these perks and what suits your playstyle.
1.) Berserker - They're the Vanguard perk, techincally a Melee Fighter and Tank
2.) Field Medic - Self-explanatory perk, main role is to heal your teammates
3.) Demolition - Explosions! if you love doing chaotic blowing things off, you should go for this perk
4.) Gunslinger - Dual-Pistols badass stuff, finishing the zeds in a short work
5.) Firebug - If you like to burn some Zeds and incinerate them, this perk is for you
6.) Support - Excels at Crowd Control using shotguns, you can easily take out big zeds with the powerful shotgun blasts
7.) Commando - You have assault rifles to deal with the trash zeds, you also have the "Eye" to see the Stalkers invinsibility.
8.) Sharpshooter - Trading the rate, fire and mobility for increased damage and accuracy at long range (Snipe stuff)
9.) Swat - Clear out small or big zeds using the SMG, being abit of tanky like Berserker but with smg weapons
10.) Survivalist - If you prefer to be the jack of all trades, literally.
- The shooting mechanism is just fantastic, the detailed gun animations and solid sound effects is quite stunning.

- The game doesn't support operating system 32-bit.
- Major Issues about the game, once you've played the higher Difficulties (Suicidal and HoE), you'll notice the problems about the Hardcore/Veteran KF players are talking about such as the unbalanced perks, teleportation specimens, big zeds takes alot of hits and etc.

Unlike the original, KF2 is more team oriented. Soloing is not viable on more difficult settings, although many can solo in the normal settings with the right class. The team aspect may be frustrating with the wrong team, but once you get a great group together it's a blessing. Having multiples of the same class isn't necessarily detrimental, as long as the players work together.
The mechanics are fabulous, and there are very few glitches on standard maps. Some of the custom maps have toruble here and there. Most of the custom map glitches involve zeds getting stuck or trader pod guide arrows not showing up. The traders aren't hard to find with your waypoint, and the zeds will usually find a way out if you run to the correct part of the map to release them from their trapped areas.
I recommend switching classes a few times to see what you enjoy, because the playstyle actually varries greatly between classes and difficulties. Some classes work better with different sized teams. Like a Commando is pretty good with a berserker or medic to tank the big zeds for them. Support is good with almost any team. Firebug is great if you have someone to knock back the small zeds for you. Demolitionist is good for the hordes. And Gunslinger deals decent damage per shot end game, but it can be frustrating to use if you don't have a goood team to back you up.(I disliked the slow reloading speed. A gunslinger should be lightning fast at reloading and shooting, while remaining somewhat steady handed.) I recommend saving Gunslinger for last, unless you enjoy it for whatever reaosn.
With the right PC the graphics are beautiful. Heavily detailed, intense gore options, and you can even change your max body count with the help of community guides. If you get enough bodies on the screen without disabling shadows it'll slow down decent, and even great PCs. I recommend about 25-80 body count with shadows, if you have a solid PC build. But if your PC is on the older side don't fret. As long as you meet the requirememnts you should be able to run on lowest settings and manually turn down the body count. I know my girlfriend's laptop has a Nividia 2GB GT 660m GPU with somewhere near a 1.0ghz clock rate runs the game as smoothly on normal settings as my new PC does on the highest settings. But my previous PC with an ancient 4GB radeon card couldn't run anything because it had a horrid clock rate. So check your specs before buying to be sure your GPU doesn't suck balls like my previous PC. Remember that the GB alone doesn't mean you can run a game, because the clock rate and chipset also make a difference.
All in all the game is worth the price. I've enjoyed it for many hours, and I'm sure I'll enjoy it for many more. If you like horror, shooting, and gore... Get this game. It's harder on your PC than the original, but it's worth it if you can run it.

This game goes back to the very fundamentals of reaction and precision games. You control a small triangle shaped object and you can move either left or right around the hexagon in the center of the screen. The objective is not to get hit by the walls that are coming at you for at least 60 seconds.
Sounds simple right? Well not quite. Since the level is constantly rotating and shifting form it become quite a challenge navigating the gaps with precision. The speed of the game doesn't make it easier either.
The music in this game is pretty good. I've never gotten to the point where it would start feeling too repetitive, but I don't play this game in very long sittings (10-20 minutes at a time).
Final verdict: If you like a good challenge this game will give you a handful and for a bargain price too!

Well, I don't know. I have sort of "mixed feelings" concerning this game... It's not bad, not bad at all, but also... it should (and could) be much better. And easier by the way. To see all the maps etc., you are forced to be "a hardcore player", meaning you ought to spend maybe 50 or 100 hours, and to become - well, I'm not sure, Superman maybe? I know it's not a kind of game for so called casual players, but I am pretty good and willing, and it's really still too difficult for me to proceed. And while I cannot save... Well. On the other hand the game is quite unique and plays well. So I'll probably unisntall, instal and reintstall ;) a few times. But it is not the game for everyone.
PROS:
- Good pixel-art graphics
- Nice tune
- Intense action
- You get new levels for your character, as well as many new items quite qickly and easy
- Next good game 'bout crashing on a distant inhabited planet ;)
- Funny and entertaining for a first few hours
CONS:
- You cannot save your progress...
- ...Meaning: Once you get killed on (let's say) the third map, you'll have to start from the begenning (every time, always!) And this is so stupid! I wish I had an option to save my progress to the next maps. Meh!
- It's generally a little bit too difficult to proceed to the next maps
VERDICT: If you're OK with "no saves" option, if you like pixel-art graphics and if you can buy it on a sale, you might give it a try. But once again, it easily could (and should) be much better. Also it's just too difficult to play for a regular player who's not willing to spend dozens and doznens of hours for training etc. Simply speaking, it's not for everyone. If you think you'll like it, you'll probably love it (for let's say 3-6 hours, or so). If you're not sure, just forget about it.

Unlike the original, KF2 is more team oriented. Soloing is not viable on more difficult settings, although many can solo in the normal settings with the right class. The team aspect may be frustrating with the wrong team, but once you get a great group together it's a blessing. Having multiples of the same class isn't necessarily detrimental, as long as the players work together.
The mechanics are fabulous, and there are very few glitches on standard maps. Some of the custom maps have toruble here and there. Most of the custom map glitches involve zeds getting stuck or trader pod guide arrows not showing up. The traders aren't hard to find with your waypoint, and the zeds will usually find a way out if you run to the correct part of the map to release them from their trapped areas.
I recommend switching classes a few times to see what you enjoy, because the playstyle actually varries greatly between classes and difficulties. Some classes work better with different sized teams. Like a Commando is pretty good with a berserker or medic to tank the big zeds for them. Support is good with almost any team. Firebug is great if you have someone to knock back the small zeds for you. Demolitionist is good for the hordes. And Gunslinger deals decent damage per shot end game, but it can be frustrating to use if you don't have a goood team to back you up.(I disliked the slow reloading speed. A gunslinger should be lightning fast at reloading and shooting, while remaining somewhat steady handed.) I recommend saving Gunslinger for last, unless you enjoy it for whatever reaosn.
With the right PC the graphics are beautiful. Heavily detailed, intense gore options, and you can even change your max body count with the help of community guides. If you get enough bodies on the screen without disabling shadows it'll slow down decent, and even great PCs. I recommend about 25-80 body count with shadows, if you have a solid PC build. But if your PC is on the older side don't fret. As long as you meet the requirememnts you should be able to run on lowest settings and manually turn down the body count. I know my girlfriend's laptop has a Nividia 2GB GT 660m GPU with somewhere near a 1.0ghz clock rate runs the game as smoothly on normal settings as my new PC does on the highest settings. But my previous PC with an ancient 4GB radeon card couldn't run anything because it had a horrid clock rate. So check your specs before buying to be sure your GPU doesn't suck balls like my previous PC. Remember that the GB alone doesn't mean you can run a game, because the clock rate and chipset also make a difference.
All in all the game is worth the price. I've enjoyed it for many hours, and I'm sure I'll enjoy it for many more. If you like horror, shooting, and gore... Get this game. It's harder on your PC than the original, but it's worth it if you can run it.

It seems like such a simple game. Rotate your triangle around the hexagon and avoid the lines. Then, it quickly turns to hell when you get a maximun of eight seconds on "that god-dang stage". But then, you improve, beat the stage, (a 60 second run) and feel great about it. I have never felt so amazing over such a simple premise.
There's something about this game that keeps me playing even though I have completed it. I'll list them here.
Control-
The controls are simple. As I said above, you're rotating around a hexagon and avoiding the incoming lines. Granted you have vertical-sync off, your stops will feel perfect and precise, helping the cause of the "fight." It's the way the obstacles are laid out that makes the game difficult and entertaining in its sense. Each time you begin a stage, the obstacles are randomized, but the obstacles themselves are consistent. This keeps the levels difficult until you learn the patterns, and then it's about keeping your focus. This adds to the sense of reward that beating a stage gives you.
Sound-
There are few actual sound effects in the game, ex. one for dying, one for starting, one for choosing a level. My focuses are the music and Jenn Frank's voice. The soundtrack mixes a sort of 8-bit-"esque" style mixed in with general music sounds for "techno." (As you can tell, I suck at describing music, you have to listen it to believe it.) The small soundtrack (5 tracks if you count the ending, clocking in at ~11 minutes total) strangely resembles the levels in the game, with 2 party-style songs 4 of the levels, while 2 others have a certain song played in a minor key--the same song featured in the trailer. In short words, the music adds to the experience.
Jenn Frank's voice is, for a lack of better words, perfect. Basically, she tells you how far you've gotten, in a sense. She says "Line" for the 10 second mark, "Triangle" for the 20 second mark, and so on up to "Hexagon" at 60 seconds. By far her most famous lines are "begin" when you start a stage, and "game over" when you fail a stage. These lines have created the joke of "BeginGameoverBeginGameover," which only a true Super Hexagon player can experience.
Graphics-
The graphics are as simple as they need to be. Since the game is so minimalistic, having high-tier graphics would only reduce the playability for some. Terry successfully makes the graphics as low as they can without being low-tier.
Difficulty-

This game will make you swear every word you know and curse Terry Cavanagh, the developer under these names and make you curse Jenn Frank for having her perfect "game-over" voice and make you cry yourself to sleep and make you type run-on sentences like me. It will take you at least 20 hours if you get good fast to beat the sixth stage. Some have taken 30, 40 and even 50+ hours to beat it. (Very Advanced)
Price- $3.00

This is a seriously low price. Would you rather buy 3+ candy bars, or would you rather play a game that keeps you engaged for hours? (Hard choice, eh?)
How Addicting?-
You will have to chop your fingers off to stop playing. Seriously, though. Some people have over 250 hours of playing this game! (CAUTION)
Negatives-
Very few and don't impact the game too much. Let me list them.

1. Vertical-sync, or Vsync. This keeps the graphics to their highest point and prevents screen-tearing, but delays your movements. It's a minor difference, but most people recommend to turn this off at the start.
2. If you decide to use a mouse, clicking both M1 and M2 at the same time will cause you to stop moving until you release BOTH keys and choose another direction. This usually isnt a problem as the game teaches you the controls for using a keyboard.
3. There are a few miniscule bugs. One can actually help you if you're fast enough (it involves an obstacle).
Although Super Hexagon isn't perfect, it wins the title of "near-perfect" until Terry Cavanagh fixes the negatives with a simple patch. It's a deadly addictive game, and a mercilessly difficult one at that.  Its asking price is low, and it will keep you engaged for many hours, whether it be the great feeling of dodging obstacles or just hearing the music in the game.

This experience has been the last straw for me. I will no longer commit to pre-orders, and WB has lost a consumer today. I admired the content that they published for their games, even apologized flaws and shortcomings. But this is just completely unacceptable. Even understanding that you can't make everyone happy by gifting games, I can't help but feel penalized for being optimistic and hoping that everything would be made right at re-release. Why should I support paying the price for another full game through Season Pass, when its concept is disjointed and incomplete?
I'm not sorry for not recommending this game, or any of WB's games in the future. Biggest sour experience that has severely overshadowed a great franchise and killed my fondness.

Let me start by saying this review has nothing to do with the actual technical issues faced by somany PC players. Enough has been said about that. With that said:
So I buy Arkham Knight - I must admit fantastic game and i can run it ok by reducing the settings. I have a season pass too. Yay! Oh but theres issues with the PC version? So they pull it from the store. Fair enough. Months go by. I wait patiently for them to get going again so i can get some DLC and continue to enjoy the game. That time has come, except apparently my season pass only unlocks about 3 pieces of DLC, non of the new mini campaigns no new batmobiles, and not most of the skins. So can i get this straight WB, i assume my season pass covered the 'season' where you stopped releasing DLC and i am now expected to pay for it ON TOP of my season pass? I am furious!
I will never buy a WB game again (and to be fair, I've really enjoyed their recent ones, Arkham Knight included) due to these shoddy business practices, and cannot reccomend that anyone else does. Please people, dont encourage them.
edit - Thought I'd throw an edit to be fair to WB; They have fixed the season pass issue. Yay!! However I can't help but notice that although WB have now stated that for Windows 10 machines they recommend a minimum of 12GB RAM, they have not updated the min/recommended sys requirements on the store page. Despite the fact that, with Microsoft ramming Win10 down everyones throats, more and more people will be finding this issue out the hard way. I can only assume it's because if they were honest it would almost certainly stop a large percentage of steam users buying the game and if we know one thing, it's that WB loves that money.  So, unfortunately, one issue is fixed but many more remain. And shoddy business practice is still rampant. I still cannot reccomend this game and my views on future WB games remain unchanged.
edit 2: More shoddy business practices, just when i thought it couldnt get worse. The 'offer' they have made as COMPENSATION (although i imagine most affected already own most if not all of the Arkham games) is being used as a marketing technique to get more people to buy this broken game. They're advertising it on the store page as a Special Offer. Why not label it what it is. Poor compensation to the schmucks who bought the game. I must admit though, i was pleased to see that they are offering refunds. So one step forward, two steps back i guess.

It feels great making progress in this game because for the most part it is skill based and it's rare I've found that the game will really dupe you with bad luck. This game is worth every cent I paid for it so far and I plan to sink more hours into it.

It's a really addicting game, its got simple strategies to understand that seem complex and alien at first if you aren't used to games like this, but it soon becomes an interesting game that you understand the limitations of your civ, your units and buildings, and their strengths as well. Once you understand the basics, this game is a masterpiece with insane replayability, it has options that let you customise pretty much everything you'd like when starting a game, to detail it to your desires so the game you want to play becomes the game you can play.
That being said, the game is pretty much a textbook example of a great game being cut up into pieces of cut content that gets released as DLC. The base game is nothing to be excited about, it has very few win conditions, little late strategy involved beyond min-maxxing production to get wonders first etc. The base game supports very little viability for passive play types, and has very little instances you have to think about before declaring war in comparison to the full game (all DLC installed)
I'm talking about people who bought the base game when it came out and had to pay full retail price to fix the base game, if you are lucky enough to have bought the GOTY edition during a sale then I'm sure you don't understand where I'm coming from, but both DLCs cost about 40 pounds at launch, invluding the base game at 40 pounds, if you bought them at launch because you wanted to see the full game, you had to spend a whopping 120 pounds to play what should have been given to players at launch.
As time has passed and the critical aclaim of the series has done nothing but increase, I feel like as respected developers who can quite clearly release excellent content, I find it shameful that they would milk their game to such an extent as to release a dull, stale game and turn it into a best seller with DLCs.
I can only say good things about the full game, but I have nothing but spite for the developers who helped push the industry standard of releasing a game and cashing in on DLC that fixes the game.

When I first watched the trailer to Super Hexagon I was blown away by the skill of the player in the video. The lightning fast reflexes, perfect timing, and inhuman stamina felt more like watching a technical masterpiece than a video game. But I knew in the back of my head that this was most likely a professional, and the average player could never achieve such heights. In fact I may have been slightly offended, perhaps through jealousy, that they would tease us so. Surely the game could not expect that much from us.
Little did I know, in just few weeks, I would make the trailer look like a joke.
As others have noticed, Super Hexagon is a game that teaches you how to play Super Hexagon. It’s less an experience and more a lesson of man’s technical abilities. Guiding you through six levels of blazing madness, the player must survive for only one minute in each stage to continue. The first night I could not pass 10 seconds on level one. The second night I was nearing 55 seconds. A week later found me hypnotized by stage three, training my eyes and fingers to grasp instantaneous scenarios on the fly. Super Hexagon is a puzzle game insomuch as the patterns repeat, letting your brain learn from mistakes. But these puzzles are randomly thrown at you at light speed and must be solved in milliseconds. By the end of the game a single mistake or hesitant thought kills you.
Randomness does hurt the skill somewhat. Eventually it’s less about mastering a level than replaying it over and over until you get sixty seconds of sequential patterns that are humanly possible. Despite what others may tell you, some pattern combinations are simply too unfair to call this a complete skill based game. Driving 100 miles an hour is not without its risks. Another issue is psychological. On stage four I freaked out when I noticed the level colors could be seen inversely, and the patters could be different depending on your perspective. This messed with my head, and took a while to process. More serious was the strain on my eyes and wrists from the repetitive colors and movements I’d exposed them to. I’m not kidding when I say this game takes physical stamina.
Super Hexagon is akin to learning an instrument. The demands on your senses are just as intense as on your brain, and the result of your hard work is nothing less than spectacular. Of course you lose the payoff that instruments provide in creating music, but if you do manage to beat the game you can wow your friends for an evening. But the best reward is the opportunity to impress yourself. To extract enjoyment from that makes the game a worthy buy.

- Every game feels organic (close call death, your friends saved you by headshot the zed infront of you while in slow mo)
- The customization, weapon skins, updates, ohh and THE SEASONAL EVENTS is the best (they'll update new maps, weapons, outfits, introduce new zeds, bosses, depends on the event) they will keep feeding you with things.
- Each Weapon that you use needs time to get a hang of it, its not just some weapon like other games, they really took time on the feels of each weapon, the weight, recoil time and everything. (makes every class/perk different from each other) love it
- Its Wave based shooter game, some might not like it, but they pull me everytime, im hooked AF.
- Co-op + zombies + gore + lotsa lotsa lotsa fire power... what more can you ask?
- 10/10

It's a really addicting game, its got simple strategies to understand that seem complex and alien at first if you aren't used to games like this, but it soon becomes an interesting game that you understand the limitations of your civ, your units and buildings, and their strengths as well. Once you understand the basics, this game is a masterpiece with insane replayability, it has options that let you customise pretty much everything you'd like when starting a game, to detail it to your desires so the game you want to play becomes the game you can play.
That being said, the game is pretty much a textbook example of a great game being cut up into pieces of cut content that gets released as DLC. The base game is nothing to be excited about, it has very few win conditions, little late strategy involved beyond min-maxxing production to get wonders first etc. The base game supports very little viability for passive play types, and has very little instances you have to think about before declaring war in comparison to the full game (all DLC installed)
I'm talking about people who bought the base game when it came out and had to pay full retail price to fix the base game, if you are lucky enough to have bought the GOTY edition during a sale then I'm sure you don't understand where I'm coming from, but both DLCs cost about 40 pounds at launch, invluding the base game at 40 pounds, if you bought them at launch because you wanted to see the full game, you had to spend a whopping 120 pounds to play what should have been given to players at launch.
As time has passed and the critical aclaim of the series has done nothing but increase, I feel like as respected developers who can quite clearly release excellent content, I find it shameful that they would milk their game to such an extent as to release a dull, stale game and turn it into a best seller with DLCs.
I can only say good things about the full game, but I have nothing but spite for the developers who helped push the industry standard of releasing a game and cashing in on DLC that fixes the game.

I'm sure by now you all have experienced/seen/heard about all the technical bugs/glitches/performance issues. I'm not here to talk about that. The fact is Arkham Knight has to be one of the saddest games to grace my library. It's sad because you can see the developers writing themselves into a corner with the story, coming to feel over burdened to incorporate the batmobile into every thing you do, and trying to give you an experience that is far from what batman fans truly wanted. If they had focused on the story and characters more and not even bothered to put in the batmobile they could have focused their time and efforts on the story and performance.
SPOILER ALERT: Joker comes back and the experience with him has got to be the hands down THE GREATEST thing I've ever experienced in a batman game. From the world changing around you, to the joker popping up in places that made me fall out of my chair laughing, Mark Hamill delivers so much to this game. Honestly that's what we all want as batman fans. Nobody cares about the "plot", it's just white noise to expereince the amazing characters, so to speak its the characters that drive every story line and if the devolopers had just realized this we could have had a great game. Let me be clear here: the overall story isn't good in my opinion. It's long and confusing, had me wondering why they put certain things in, and only had a few, though amazing, memorable moments unlike the past games. The Joker sub-story is what I'm saying made this game for me.
SPOILER ALERT: I called the arkham knight being Jason Todd when he was announced. It was so obvious that the whole game I felt it was just a chore getting to the climax. It gets to a point where they beat it over your head that he is Jason. What I'm also trying to say is that Arkham Knight had the potential to be possibly the best batman villian. Imagine everything you have learned over the past 3 games being thwarted by an enemy that knows Batman to his core. They could have blended this psychological aspect with the Joker portion and just UH WHY DIDN'T THEY DO THIS. If they ever do a overhaul of the game completely rework the second half of the game. Instead of the Joker arch ending and the Scarecrow arch going on forever have batman stop the gas bomb,♥♥♥♥♥♥have the gas bomb go off first thing in the game, Batman and his crew are safe and they save the city but because of so much exposure ot the fear tocxin the Joker comes in DURING THE SECOND HALF AND THE ARKHAM KNIGHT PLAYS ON BATMANS FEAR OF BEING LIKE THE JOKER AND CMON HOW DID THEY NOT SEE THIS.
On the note of characters I have to say graphically I have never been more dissapointed. Honestly if they had just copy and pasted the models from Arkham City it would have been more enjoyable then playing as a gorilla batman, with his skinhead robin sidekick, and a preppy looking nightwing. Gameplay wise another aspect the developers should have focused on was the co-op sections of the game with catwoman, nightwing, and robin. That was all the inovation we needed.
In conclusion the little details really are what you should play this game for. They expanded to far and sacrificed the things that should have been given the most attention.  Again I cannot tell you how amazing the joker section of this game is. If you are a huge batman/joker fan PLAY THIS GAME. I would like to mention the level designers did an AMAZING job creating Gotham City. They take in the Tim Burton style over the toppness mixed in with Christopher Nolans run down and grimy of the Dark Knight movies hats off to guys. The Harley Quinn DLC is worth mentioning as an amazing take on the character as a batman lore fan, though short I enjoyed it. Not really a review more like my thoughts and critiques but I hope it helps you on deciding to purchase this game if it ever gets back up on steam.

Oh boy! Where to start ?
South Park: The Stick of Truth, is one of those games you keep playing just to see what's going to happen next.
It's ridiculous, funny, sexually graphic, over the top, violent, racist, blood gory, black humor filled and so much more, it's basically one of the most politically uncorrect games you will ever see!
And that's precisely why it's humor is so good. Because it runs a foot on every topic and everyone and does not discriminate between who get's laughed with or/and at. You have to take this game with a truck load of salt and don't take it seriously.
If you have watched the South Park series before and like it, you will like the humor here too. If you are new to South park and are not sure if you will like the humor, I advice you to go watch one of the episodes on the net for free, before purchasing this game. Because the humor makes or breakes this game.
The Graphical style of the game looks fantastic to me but The Style is very dependant from person to person, you might like it or you might not. It's clear that they wanted to keep it in the form of their Series and they fully achieved that, it feels like you are in one of the episodes of South park while playing the game. Overall the style does not interfere with The Gameplay in most instances, although sometimes it can be a bit confusing or irritating for little things, like when trying to loot corpses for items, it might not be clear which corps you are looting... but these are only minor annoyances...
The Sound of the game is fantastic, they make it sound like you are playing skyrim or in a lord of the rings movie, the sounds of South park we know and love so much are in the game aswell. They are well balanced and everything is clear when a conversation is held.
The Gameplay is very interesting, Before purchasing the game I was under the impression the combat would be a simple Turn based RPG style combat system, as in, choose your ability/attack, than choose your opponent to use it against and that's it...
Oh how wrong was I....In essence the first part of it is correct, you choose your ability or attack and you choose your opponent or opponents but when the ability happens you are also more often than not asked to perform a certain Quicktime action to make the ability work as intended. this can be a quicktime event like pressing the mouse button at the right time or this can be a deceivingly hard button mash or even dance style (left right, right , up, down , left) combinations.
This made the combat so much more fun than I anticipated, because it still relies on me to actually play at my best and not simply click on some buttons....
The game also features potions and items, gear and weapons and upgrades for those weapons and armour, also the ever present character customisation (which can be hilarious at times).
The main gameplay itself is a up down, left right, walking/running game, where in certain areas you will have to use some abilities, you gather throughout the game, to get to certain places. (think teleportation or blasting away a wall with something)
Sometimes you will have to use combinations to get to switches and so on.
Pre combat also makes a difference, for example attacking the enemy first (simply hitting an enemy) will activate combat, but will give you the first turn to attack, while if the enemy hits you first (pre combat), the enemy gets to go first...
also shooting the enemy or using certain abilities can make a difference before going into combat.
The game features side quests that encourage you to do them. they feel like part of the story and they often reward you with friends or abilities.
the more friends you have, the better, because more friends means more perks, and perks give you certain constant abilities that can improve your combat skills.
other side quests give you the ability to ask help from a certain strong character to help you in combat.
Overall I loved this game, it was worth every last penny in my oppinion, the gameplay could have been slightly longer though, I think an extra 3 to 4 hours would have made it slightly better.
Some abilities are a bit hard to figure out how to use correctly (it took me a while) to hit those perfect attacks. so they should have made that a bit clearer.
Personnaly I recommend this game to anyone who loves the southpark series and anyone who likes to play a casual, sometimes intensive but overall casual, game with major humoristic elements and a wacky story and for people who want to to play something different than the usual mainstream game.

Dustforce truly is a work of art. I don't mean that lightly. The way it's animated plus its music gives it that title in my book. I can find myself playing one level for an hour, maybe even hours at a time. The frustration of losing levels is filled with relaxation and calmness because of the ambient music. The way the levels are crafted is truly mindblowing. They had a system in which you had to perfect a level to earn a key, and you would use that key to earn more levels. In layman's terms, to earn more levels, you had to perfect current levels. They ditched that and added an XP system in which you gain more XP to earn a key the more levels you play and perfect. I'm very glad they added this system and was skeptical about buying it. But now that I did buy it, I do not regret it even for a second. One thing I really love about this game is how you don't have to unlock base levels. In a sense, this game is open world. That sense is that many levels are available to you, and you can choose whether you want to advance into more challenging levels, or stay where you're at. To get an S in completion, you have to sweep up EVERY leaf, and to get an S in Finesse, you have to maintain your combo throughout an entire level.
Another thing I absolutely enjoy about Dustforce is its expasive community. There are lots of Community Workshop maps for you to sharpen your skills on, and lots of people who can set a good example. I'm sure most of the people who get best times on all the levels have a Youtube channel, so you can probably catch them there. The community may or not be active, but it sure is good and friendly.
Overall, in terms of gameplay, music, artstyle, animation, and difficulty (it's not an easy game, but it's not that hard of a game either. It just depends on how much you want to play it), I rate this game:
10/10

Arkham Knight is dramatically improved with the post-release performance patches, but its awful original release destroyed a lot of the goodwill Warner Bros worked so hard to develop as a first-rate publisher.  They released a game that was so bad it had to be pulled from store shelves and haven't offered so much as a free Batmobile skin as recompense.  Meanwhile, the game is loaded with additional DRM above and beyond what Steam provides.  Once you get past all that, though, the game is pretty decent.
One thing the Batman series has always done well is to empower the player with powerful tools and abilities right off the bat.  Rather than beginning a sequel with a fresh start, Batman retains most of his key abilities and still manages to become stronger.  The addition of the Batmobile, arguably Batman's most powerful tool, plays a large part in facilitating this geometric growth.  Rocksteady also added a plentiful selection of new abilities to combat, managing to freshen it up without negatively changing what worked so well in the past.
Not everything is perfect, however.  There are a few baffling design decisions that, while not serious enough to ruin the game by any means, do manage to hinder the immersion and fluidity of gameplay.  As an example, there are plenty of actions that require mashing a button rapidly even when it doesn't really correspond with the action on-screen;  why must I rapidly mash a button to rip a grate from a wall?  Or if I cannot use the awesome new exploding gel launcher to destroy a breakable wall, why must I switch to the gel tool instead of simply pressing a button after walking up to the structure?  I mean, the game prompts me to do so... it's not as if it's a puzzle to be solved.  These are pretty minor details, though, and do not significantly color the gameplay.
The game's story is on par with the previous titles, which ranks it as far better than average.  Rocksteady was quite clever in its presentation, largely eschewing the slow-walk dream sequences in previous games with more immediate and interactive sequences.  The cast of characters is sufficiently large and complete to thrill any Batman fan.  The story content to collectible ratio is much better than in the last two games, although having to search the map for missions can be tiresome.  Fans of the comics and fans of the game series would be amiss to let this one slip by without giving it a chance, especially now that the atrocious performance issues have been well and truly solved.

For a game of the popular Civilization franchise, one would expect later installments to be better than the previous. This sadly isn't the case with Civilization V. I've enjoyed my time with Civilization since Civ II came out, and I played both it and III to the extent that I burnt the CDs out. Even now, having repurchased Civ III, I've easily logged over 1,700 hours on the game.
Now, Civ IV was a fun game, I didn't play it quite as much but the addition of religions and some new features did give Civilization a fresh sort've smell to the whole experience, though many features that I thoroughly enjoyed within III were gutted from IV.
Civilization V however, is an entirely different story. I feel the game is perhaps the worst installment of the franchise, and not worth the money. It feels almost insulting to seasoned players of the series, to be given V, promised so much, and yet see something that quite literally has some flashy paint, but smells like rubbish. It's quite disappointing.
Many of the features that were extremely, extensively enjoyed within Civilization III and IV, were gutted and removed in V. To make matters worse, rather useless, and often fruitless and irritating features -- far too complex than need be, were added to the game. Diplomacy and war for III and IV use to be a challenge, and it was well balanced, even for the easy difficulties. For Civilization V, it's utter and complete trash.
City-states, were quite an interesting addition to the game, and this was a mechanic that I did thoroughly find curious and slightly entertaining. As peculiar as they were however, I quickly ignored them. They weren't fleshed out, and lacked any real depth to them, and outside of constantly bombarding you with rapid-fire 'go kill this guy, we don't like them' messages, they didn't have any real worth. It's as if the developers decided suddenly, to take something that could've been quite a beneficial addition to the game, gave it the personality of a doorknob, covered it in feces and dumped it randomly in the game. It was very quickly learnt, that the awards of helping out these city-states was so negligble that it was cheaper just to destroy them, if only to remove the annoying messages.
The devs also removed unit-stacking, and this, I found, was very aggrivating with cities. You could 'station' a single unit in a city, that was all. The defenses and the stressful need to build the correct improvements, and keep a large enough and well trained garrison within the city, like one had to in the previous installments, was eviscerated for absolute♥♥♥♥♥♥ Not even a nicer way to put it, than that.
This also made the tactics, and the need for strategy utterly simple and boring. I.E. There wasn't a strategy. It use to be, that the player would find themselves quite distressed, especially during times of war -- by determining who to send, and who to defend. This made the game challenging, as stationing the wrong units within cities, or not enough, could quickly result in you watching the literal definition of 'blitzkrieg' through your terrtiory. This was removed in V.
One of the most loved features, and I congratulate IV for this -- Spying. Espionage, the lovely filled giggles as you watched a spy become a saboteur, and bomb the living hell out of whatever that voracious enemy of yours was working on. This was an amazing addition to the franchise, and a major improvement from IIIs Espionage, but in V, it was completely removed. No spies, No blowing stuff up and being all 007, all of it -- POOF.
Religion. Religion, religion, religion. When they introduced this feature within IV, I was somewhat sceptical of it. I approached this sudden addition with the cautionary tale, of quite literally poking it with a stick, and hoping it wouldn't blast my face off. However, this addition was perhaps one of the most beautiful ones I'd seen in the franchise. I loved the religion within Civ IV, as it added a whole new element to the game, and added so much revolving around it, that you could practically spend your entire time just buggering around with this feature and ignoring everything else. It was amazing, and it made Civilization IV a close runner-up to III. Yet, it wasn't to last.
For some reason, I can't tell why outside of utter and sheer stupidity on behalf of the creators of the game, this amazing new feature was removed. All the influences, all the elements of it that made IV such a warming experience for me, was torn away with the sheer idiocy of morons.
Graphics. Oh graphics, how nice you are, when you're actually useful. I am a big stickler on graphics. Good graphical games, are a major stimulant to my often coffee deprived mind. When used correctly, graphics can make a game flow smoothly, they add something remarkable to the game. Hell, they can even make a game beautiful. Skyrim's major graphic mods, with 1024x1024 HD textures or even higher, make the game nothing else but absolutely stunning.
This can't be said about Civilization V. Remember the comment about new paint? Yeah. All the new graphics, and colours implemented within Civilization V do add a new, never before seen Civilization. But for a game with such♥♥♥♥♥♥game mechanics, and moron developers, the graphics did nothing to surprise me. Much of them - I found, were useless. Sometimes Simplicity is best, and other times not. They made the game mechanics so stupidly simple, and then dressed it up in some super-flashy, look at my big money pants body paint, and dared call a Lada a Bugatti Veyron.
Beyond all this, I found Civilization V. It was utterly depressing to play in all honesty. I spent almost 30 hours on the game, uninstalled, and re-installed Civilization III instead. The developers gutted the game so much, that about the only thing the player was left to do, was constantly decline the irritating messages of city-states, or move the stupid units out of cities because there were too many there. Diplomacy, War, Trade, Culture, Religion -- everything that made, and gave the franchise depth, the very challenging experience of the games, was horrendously gutted in Civilization V.
I'm not too certain what the developers were thinking. Civilization III was perhaps by far, and still is the best game of the franchise. In fact, the very nostalgia makes the rather outdated graphics of the game such an experience that one just can't pass up. Civilization IV had a few slight improvements, but didn't live up to the glory of III. Civilization V however, well, it would be an utter tragedy to even consider it apart of the franchise. The game, people, is quite utterly♥♥♥♥♥♥
I would suggest to the developers, if they aren't still drooling on themselves, to take a look at III and IV, what made them such a frenzy to the fanbase, and find a way to combine their features and build on that. Civilization V? The only fate this game deserves, is a firey death in the abyss of♥♥♥♥♥♥games, made by utter morons who have the audacity to call themselves developers.
In short, don't waste your money on this game. If I could get a refund I would. Buy Civilization III, its graphics are a bit outdated, but the games replay value is exceptionally high. And buy Civilization IV, it may not be as great as III, but it is still a very fun game. Cheers.

EDIT (12/3/15): Since Rocksteady has released a number of patches and just put the Arkham games into my account I’ve decided to revamp this review to reflect this and to be more helpful in general.
Note: This review may contain minor spoilers.
Many people had a lot of trouble trying to play this but for me it ran fine
. The updates haven’t really done much to allow me to increase the settings without getting low frames. Also, it is disappointing that multi-GPU support won’t be added (as my computer has dual GTX 760s) and that Rocksteady has said that there are unfixable problems. However, even on low settings I think the game looks fine so I’m not complaining too much.
The batmobile drives like a dream. Basically, it goes moderately fast, takes really sharp turns, and smashes through just about anything. I prefered driving to gliding a lot of the time. I enjoyed the tank sequences but there was just so many of them that they became rather burdensome. I also would have liked more high-speed vehicle chases and more specifically, I would have liked to chase down Two-Face.
Batman, just like his enemies, have gotten more capable each game. Well, Batman has. In Arkham Knight, Batman feels like he’s at the top of his game. He’s got new moves such as a Ground Takedown throw and an environment takedown. He’s also got new gadgets such as a voice synthesizer, that lets you order enemies around, and an improved disruptor that lets you disable more things such as gun crates. Batman can also (at certain points) team up and do a dual takedown with his partner.
To be honest, the guys you fight in this game seem much easier than in the previous ones. Sure in Arkham Knight there are guys who can hide from your detective mode and guys with mini-guns but in previous games they started mining the highpoints or scanning them or otherwise doing something to make things more difficult than it could have been. In this game they don’t do that kind of thing as much; even with the Arkham Knight giving them tactical advice.
I though the story was good. Though there are some twists and turns along the way, the Arkham Knight’s identity is pretty obvious (even to some like me who doesn’t really read the comics) and the story practically shouts out his identity to you before you actually find out. Still, the story is satisfying and the ending was well done. Also, John Noble voicing Scarecrow is, needless to say, a very nice touch. All that said, while I enjoyed the main campaign, the side missions were, for the most part, repetitive and anti-climactic with really lame “boss fights”.  Two-Face and Penguin could have had a bigger part in the story, as well. The Riddler stuff was, on the other hand, exceptional. Although not every “riddle” he placed actually was one (certain in-game characters even comment on this) his content and boss fight was enjoyable. The best of it was the insane race tracks he designed.
Like I stated, the game ran fine for me so there’s not much room for me to complain this way. The main compensation was the previous Arkham games. I already had Asylum and City so apparently I didn’t get these ones again so someone with all of the Arkham games would have, apparently, got nothing here. Personally, I would have preferred to get the Shadow of Mordor game instead but the game did run for me so it’s not a big deal. Someone else whose game didn’t run at launch and already had the Arkham would have some reason to be upset.
Since the game ran for me I give it an 8/10. The gameplay is fun and what you would expect from the series however, the repetitive side missions were a drag.

The gameplay is pretty simple and it works very well. Easy to learn, maybe hard to master until you find your favorite character.
Of course, there are some complications: the online game is a little bit tricky, you must give your IP and select a port to work, but aside that you'll have a lot of fun with this game.
I strong recommend if you like platformer / action games.

Risk of Rain...
A beautifully simplistic game that appeals to a large audience.
There is a large array of items to pick up, and 10 characters to unlock. This increases the re-playabilty of the game hugely. I have played the game for around 8 hours and have still only unlocked 3 of the characters, with no clue how to unlock the rest. The maps are randomly generated every game, and while you can see similarities between some structures within each level, it doesn't retract from the gameplay in anyway. There are also a multitude of bosses to fight, with different abilities and drops.
In addition to this, Risk of Rain is hard. Very hard. I have only ever got to the final level once, and that was with the help of my friend. This difficulty may anger and frustrate some, but it makes me want to carry on playing -  I want to beat the game.
The co-op is good too, and you will need 3rd party software to host a server, (such as Hamachi) to play. But with 4 player co-op enabled, you can play and enjoy this game with your friends.
Overall, I highly reccomend this game. It has a high re-playability and the difficulty really does make me want to carry on playing; even if I am tinged with anger.

I'm not sure what people are talking about regarding issues with this game. My system is hardly top of the line and I'm getting better than 30 fps on this game, and need I remind everybody that Arkham Origins was released for PC with one sidequest and the final QTE being totally unbeatable due to bugs.
On to the game itself. I enjoyed it. The gameplay met the standards set by the previous games, the story was quite good (Not up to AC, but much better than AO). Scarecrow does an incredible job as a creepy villain who taunts Batman regularly, and Arkham Knight presents a new threat as someone who understands how Batman operates and truly hates him. Overall, not as good as Arkham City, but still a fine sendoff to the series.

Killing Floor 2 is an extremely well polished Early Access title, however the game also has it's fair share of flaws. Furthermore, the game recently added microtransactions in the form of cosmetics and while I'm fairly neutral on this part, it has very clearly divided the community.
The good:
+The weapons are extremely satisfying to use even the low tier weapons look, sound and feel great.
+The visuals are extremely polished and the gore is ridiculous.
+The core gameplay is addictive and will have you grind away for hours.
+Movement has been overhauled, meaning that you can now sprint.
+The perk system has been changed so you now get a new skill every 5th level.
+Enemies unlock new moves and tricks as difficulty increases.
+PvP is a neat idea, but it lacks polish.
The bad:
-Less content than the original and slow updates (usually 4 to 6 months).
-Some perks skills are clearly under-or overpowered meaning that certain builds are simply superior.
-The game currently contains 2 different bosses, however Hans Volter is simply overpowered compared to the Patriarch and will often guarantee a loss.
-Earning XP to level up is a complete grind, but it is necessary in order to play at the higher difficulties.
-Enemies don't seem to make much sound when you are facing away from them, leading to enemies sneaking up on you with little to no warning and it just feels cheap because the enemies tend to be quite audible when you're facing them even slightly.
-The new resistance system is utter garbage.
While I have a lot of bad points I can't say KF2 is all bad, in fact I've rather enjoyed my time with it, but if you can I think it would be best to buy the game after it makes its way out of early access as the game currently lacks content and will probably tire you out before a new patch lands.

Significant upgrade from Killing Floor in terms of AI, pathing, and general behaviour.  It's prettier, the behaviour changes are much appreciated (like head hitboxes not being so easy to hit due to "erratic" (but obviously pattern-oriented) behaviours).  From observations it appears that there's a bit more "random" in the zed behaviour routines, so it makes the game less "easy" from a direct perspective.  (Though pretty much any large/special zed is a total pain as they always were.)
Being early access there have been some bumps, and it's fairly grindy compared to the original -- but the "tree" (pick one of two per-tier) for upgrading more or less requires it.  Tiering up your classes can be done using their base pistols/weapons, and even though it's time consuming it's probably on the easier side of things -- particularly for classes like the medic.
There are some things I miss (I'm typically a sharpshooter/medic in the original), there are some irksome things (like the katana being neutral and not being useful for perking up), and some things that could be explained better at times, but yes, it's a worthwhile upgrade on the original.
Gunslingers are awesome, and the "instant swap" to other pairs of pistols is just god-tier brokenly great (though you'll run out of pistols and be totally screwed if you play recklessly); 10/10 for the gunslinger as a Matrix lobby simulator.

Ok played enough of it by now so here goes...
Graphics
---------
Well the graphics in this game are simple amazing. More so than in the original KF game. The detail to the world environments, charatcers you play, the weapons, animations for everything, even the ZEDS is top notch. Everything in the game is artistically well done overall, that plus it's all due to the UnReal engine of course. Overall I give the graphics a 10/10 and that is just my honest opinion.
PERKS
-------
Aight the perks well they need a lil tweaking here and there. Not on what you can do with the perks, just more perks in general. Like so far there's Demolishionist, Firebug, Medic, Support, Commando, Bezerker, and Gunslinger. Now with that being said they need to bring back in the Sharp Shooter. From what I'm guessing the GunSlinger is taking the place of the SHarp Shooter, but where as the GS is only profecient in the use of pistols onl the Sharpie is catered to both pistols and rifles. None the less the perks are pretty good. The levels of perks is a bonus as well. Instead of just reach Perk 6 in the original KF now you can gain one of 2 skills at level 5, and same goes for each 5th level you reach until you get to the maximum level of 25. So basically the perks are good the way they are and maybe other perks might be added onto the game as since it's just an early release atm.
GAMEPLAY
_______
Alot has changed since KF, now the ZEDS are more... versatile. And what I mean by that is that they come up with newer moves with each level of difficult you play. Like say normal they pretty much easy to deal with but if you go play on hard mode then they get more harder to deal with and more difficult to kill. Not only that but they alter there move per say. Now that makes for an interesting game because you don't know what to expect from them and just makes it more challenging.
MAPS
------
What can I say the maps are very well detailed, vibrant, and just fantastic to look at. Sure som people have complained that the maps have become smaller, but from what I've seen the maps seem to be the same size as in the previous KF.
CONTROLS
------------
The control scheme to KF2 is basically the same as in the 1st game albeit that now you have the ability to run either forwards or backwards and for once that's a nice change. And it doesn't matter what perk you're using depending on what you are carrying, the weight does affect on how fast you can run. So the less you have the faster you can run, the more you're carrying the slower you can run. So in a nutshell the control are exactly the same as in the 1st game with no major changes so it's perfect the way it is.
CONCLUSION
_________
Well all I have to say about Killing Floor 2 is that it's an absolutely wonderful game to play, either you're playing solo by yourself or with pubs or friends online it more fun than a barrel of monkeys. Everything about the game just oozes fun. So with this review I give KF2 a 10/10 for being better than the original and alot more fun to play.
SIDE NOTE
-----------

The game uses the UnReal engine and the UnReal engine has that habit of spawning things randomly anywhere, and running actually helps you survive a bit longer, and the maps are not smaller they seem to be the same size, and big deal if the game is more graphically enhanced, most games today are.

There are plenty of reviews up about the performance of Arkham Knight.
That being said, there are patches to address these issues, and while it's sad that a high-calibur game had enough issues to warrant pulling sales, I want to talk to people who may be thinking of getting the game after the sales hold is released. I've heard talks of a 'Game of the Year' edition may be made at some point. While this is hilarious given that the game can't be bought on the PC, this is sure to be confusing for people who don't have a console and are looking at picking up the game.
For context, I have a good system with the game installed on an SSD. An SSD seemed to eliminate almost all of the performance issues for me. So, I was able to play through at release and it was relatively smooth. That being said, I can see a difference in the game after the patches.
I have enjoyed all of the Batman Arkham series so far and was eagerly anticipating the finale. The graphics in Arkham Knight are amazing and there are moments of pure awesome Batman-ness in this game (for example, Fear Takedowns will make your jaw drop every time). All of the iconic Batman moments are in this game; but is that enough?
I feel this game doesn't play to it's strengths.
They've made predator mode very powerful, but only rarely do you get to unleash the full power on thugs. The story moments that are supposed to be strong aren't and the points that aren't supposed to be strong are. The Batmobile is a ton of fun to drive around, but they rarely make good use of it.
When I say that about the Batmobile, I want to be clear: there are 2 'different' vehicles; the Batmobile (drives around really fast), and the Tankmobile (manuver around and shoot stuff).
If you don't like the Tankmobile, you will not like this game. It is like 90% of the game, and while fun for the first few fights, every fight is essentially the same + more tanks than last fight. There are 2 major Batman villians known for their hand-to-hand prowesss... that you fight while they are in a tank! WHY?
A friend put it to me like this "I just want to play as Batman. Let me punch some people, sneak up on some guys and drive around. If I wanted to play a tank simulator game, that's what I would have gotten"
I can understand that Rocksteady really wanted to have the Batmobile in the game and they likely came up with the Tankmobile and all the enemy tanks as a way to justify it, but there is way too much tank fighting in the game.
When a mod is released (I'm certain it will be) that drastically cuts down the number of tanks and/or tank fights... I will seriously re-evaluate this game as if that was the way it was meant to be released.
I do highly recommend to make use of the optional Batmobile toggle button via the menu.
For me, Predator mode was awesome... I just wish there was more of it or it was longer. The Bank heists were awesome and I'd love for there to have been more.
The past games had some good 'detective-y' bits that were fun and different, This seems to have been thrown in as an after thought via 1 side mission. There's ways this could have helped the game: There's a side mission where you rescue firefighters from thugs. Only, they seem to be randomly distributed throughout the city and end up being very difficult to find after you've gotten a few. Some detective work to lead you there would have fit right in.
There's 2 mission types that use the real (non-tank) batmobile: commanders patrol the city in APCs, which you have to chase down and a mission that basically has you race/chase a villian. There really isn't that many of these missions and they certainly are fun. Would really like for there to have been more. Something along the lines of "Batman! we just found out things are going to explode... on the other side of the city! How can we get there in time?!" would have worked just fine. There's a challenge map that has you race to a location, battle a hand full of tanks, then race to a new location and repeat a few times... I quite like this, despite what I said about the tank fighting. You're not overwhelmed with tanks; you're more concerned with doing it efficiently.
Combat is kind of hard to breakdown. It's the same basic formula that has been so great over the years (with enough new things to keep it interesting). Getting into a fight with the average joes on the street corner really isn't fair at all. You just demolish them. However, there are prepared/armored/armed guys that hang out in very large groups. It kinda seems like just being awesome with the combat system isn't enough, you have to find a good opening into the fight to really make sure you survive; but the game goes out of it's way to make sure that you don't get to make those good openings.
I've also heard that it's quite daunting to have so many moves and enemies that you have to attack in particular ways. Then again, there are the team-ups with other heros that are a blast, but you aren't facing the tougher thugs, so it's not like you really need their help.
Summary:
If you're on the fence about this game, I'd recommend watching some videos of the tank battles and see if that appeals to you. There are a lot of good console reviews praising the tank fights as fun, so that may be something for you.
If you've played the other Arkham games and just want to 'complete the story', you'll end up playing at some point anyhow.
For everyone else, I'd just say get Arkham Origins or City instead. That is way more Batman-like than Arkham: World of Tanks. Maybe when the price drops
Oh, and don't even bother with the DLC. The 'Story DLC' is simply 3 or so rooms chained together. Can be done in 1/2 an hour... very much not worth the $.
