Purely a review of the game itself:
To fully understand the Batman: Arkham franchise, you must first understand that most of the Batman games prior to that were either terrible, in the case of Batman Forever, or completely off-the-wall insane, as in Batman: Return of the Joker's strange Contra-esque gameplay.
About the only game prior to Arkham Asylum to capture the essence of the series would have been Batman: The Animated Series game on the SNES, but even that only aped the visual style, and missed the boat on the crime-solving detective aspects.  Arkham Asylum was the first game that really let you feel like you were stepping into Batman's shoes.  From using the shadows and verticality as your allies to take enemies down stealthily, to using the environment, gadgets, and good old-fashioned brainpower, Arkham Asylum and Arkham City delivered both content and the Batman "feel" with verve and panache.
Full disclosure;  I never finished Arkham Origins because I felt like it took an interesting concept and threw it down the drain to cram the Joker in yet again as the prime villain.  I'm pleased to report that with Rocksteady's final Batman game, Arkham Knight, the style and quality of the story have returned in spades.
Many moons (and many dollars) during pre-production marketing were spent on building the mystery of the Arkham Knight, one of the game's major antagonists.  If you are versed with Batman lore, you'll probably figure it out a quarter of the way through the game, if it hasn't been spoiled for you already.  Even if you can see the twist from a mile away, some of the returning voice actors from The Animated Series, coupled with an above-average script handle the material beautifully and it's a joy to be a part of the story.
The game strikes a masterful balance between gameplay and story, capably delivering relevant material to you in sidequests, radio chatter, and Batman's dialogues with the various characters. Even if they do throw a lot of story material at you overall, it never feels truly overwhelming, and due to the game's impressive length, it doesn't feel cramped.
From a gameplay perspective, there's certainly a lot to do, and while most of it falls into a number of broad categories, the sidequest stories themselves and the situations keep the game's many missions feeling fresh.  You'll solve tons of the Riddler's puzzles, rescue firemen, discover an arsonist's plot, train Azrael, clear the skies and the roads of the Arkham Knight's automated army, all of which are only a portion of the things you'll do during your time with the game.
I will say that they are very proud of their Batmobile content, as it is utilized in almost every plotline in the game in some fashion or another.  Some like it, some hate it;  I found that it controls well enough that it never really felt like a chore to use, although soaring through the skies on Batman's space-age glidey wings never gets old and just feels RIGHT.
Another thing that feels right is the combat.  Arkham Origins' combat felt stilted, while Arkham Knight's is smooth, and makes you feel powerful.  As you progress through the game's skill and tech trees, unlocking various cool takedowns and methods of mayhem to unleash on unsuspecting (and suspecting) thugs, the game rolls out new enemy types and configurations to test your prowess.  There's never a dull moment.
Another thing that I feel deserves a mention is the quality of Gotham itself;  it feels much more alive than in either City or Origins.  While the city is locked down due to martial law and the invasion of the Arkham Knight's forces, there are riots occurring all over, and the rainy, grimy, neon feel of Gotham is in full effect.  From the aging facades of Chinatown to the hyper-modern glass monoliths on the upscale Founder's Island, this vision of Gotham is breathtaking no matter where you look.

Luckily I was able to beat the game before they broke it even further, and now we're looking at the end of October to potentially fix it.  Absolutely ridiculous, and shameful.

Ok played enough of it by now so here goes...
Graphics
---------
Well the graphics in this game are simple amazing. More so than in the original KF game. The detail to the world environments, charatcers you play, the weapons, animations for everything, even the ZEDS is top notch. Everything in the game is artistically well done overall, that plus it's all due to the UnReal engine of course. Overall I give the graphics a 10/10 and that is just my honest opinion.
PERKS
-------
Aight the perks well they need a lil tweaking here and there. Not on what you can do with the perks, just more perks in general. Like so far there's Demolishionist, Firebug, Medic, Support, Commando, Bezerker, and Gunslinger. Now with that being said they need to bring back in the Sharp Shooter. From what I'm guessing the GunSlinger is taking the place of the SHarp Shooter, but where as the GS is only profecient in the use of pistols onl the Sharpie is catered to both pistols and rifles. None the less the perks are pretty good. The levels of perks is a bonus as well. Instead of just reach Perk 6 in the original KF now you can gain one of 2 skills at level 5, and same goes for each 5th level you reach until you get to the maximum level of 25. So basically the perks are good the way they are and maybe other perks might be added onto the game as since it's just an early release atm.
GAMEPLAY
_______
Alot has changed since KF, now the ZEDS are more... versatile. And what I mean by that is that they come up with newer moves with each level of difficult you play. Like say normal they pretty much easy to deal with but if you go play on hard mode then they get more harder to deal with and more difficult to kill. Not only that but they alter there move per say. Now that makes for an interesting game because you don't know what to expect from them and just makes it more challenging.
MAPS
------
What can I say the maps are very well detailed, vibrant, and just fantastic to look at. Sure som people have complained that the maps have become smaller, but from what I've seen the maps seem to be the same size as in the previous KF.
CONTROLS
------------
The control scheme to KF2 is basically the same as in the 1st game albeit that now you have the ability to run either forwards or backwards and for once that's a nice change. And it doesn't matter what perk you're using depending on what you are carrying, the weight does affect on how fast you can run. So the less you have the faster you can run, the more you're carrying the slower you can run. So in a nutshell the control are exactly the same as in the 1st game with no major changes so it's perfect the way it is.
CONCLUSION
_________
Well all I have to say about Killing Floor 2 is that it's an absolutely wonderful game to play, either you're playing solo by yourself or with pubs or friends online it more fun than a barrel of monkeys. Everything about the game just oozes fun. So with this review I give KF2 a 10/10 for being better than the original and alot more fun to play.
SIDE NOTE
-----------

The game uses the UnReal engine and the UnReal engine has that habit of spawning things randomly anywhere, and running actually helps you survive a bit longer, and the maps are not smaller they seem to be the same size, and big deal if the game is more graphically enhanced, most games today are.

Purely a review of the game itself:
To fully understand the Batman: Arkham franchise, you must first understand that most of the Batman games prior to that were either terrible, in the case of Batman Forever, or completely off-the-wall insane, as in Batman: Return of the Joker's strange Contra-esque gameplay.
About the only game prior to Arkham Asylum to capture the essence of the series would have been Batman: The Animated Series game on the SNES, but even that only aped the visual style, and missed the boat on the crime-solving detective aspects.  Arkham Asylum was the first game that really let you feel like you were stepping into Batman's shoes.  From using the shadows and verticality as your allies to take enemies down stealthily, to using the environment, gadgets, and good old-fashioned brainpower, Arkham Asylum and Arkham City delivered both content and the Batman "feel" with verve and panache.
Full disclosure;  I never finished Arkham Origins because I felt like it took an interesting concept and threw it down the drain to cram the Joker in yet again as the prime villain.  I'm pleased to report that with Rocksteady's final Batman game, Arkham Knight, the style and quality of the story have returned in spades.
Many moons (and many dollars) during pre-production marketing were spent on building the mystery of the Arkham Knight, one of the game's major antagonists.  If you are versed with Batman lore, you'll probably figure it out a quarter of the way through the game, if it hasn't been spoiled for you already.  Even if you can see the twist from a mile away, some of the returning voice actors from The Animated Series, coupled with an above-average script handle the material beautifully and it's a joy to be a part of the story.
The game strikes a masterful balance between gameplay and story, capably delivering relevant material to you in sidequests, radio chatter, and Batman's dialogues with the various characters. Even if they do throw a lot of story material at you overall, it never feels truly overwhelming, and due to the game's impressive length, it doesn't feel cramped.
From a gameplay perspective, there's certainly a lot to do, and while most of it falls into a number of broad categories, the sidequest stories themselves and the situations keep the game's many missions feeling fresh.  You'll solve tons of the Riddler's puzzles, rescue firemen, discover an arsonist's plot, train Azrael, clear the skies and the roads of the Arkham Knight's automated army, all of which are only a portion of the things you'll do during your time with the game.
I will say that they are very proud of their Batmobile content, as it is utilized in almost every plotline in the game in some fashion or another.  Some like it, some hate it;  I found that it controls well enough that it never really felt like a chore to use, although soaring through the skies on Batman's space-age glidey wings never gets old and just feels RIGHT.
Another thing that feels right is the combat.  Arkham Origins' combat felt stilted, while Arkham Knight's is smooth, and makes you feel powerful.  As you progress through the game's skill and tech trees, unlocking various cool takedowns and methods of mayhem to unleash on unsuspecting (and suspecting) thugs, the game rolls out new enemy types and configurations to test your prowess.  There's never a dull moment.
Another thing that I feel deserves a mention is the quality of Gotham itself;  it feels much more alive than in either City or Origins.  While the city is locked down due to martial law and the invasion of the Arkham Knight's forces, there are riots occurring all over, and the rainy, grimy, neon feel of Gotham is in full effect.  From the aging facades of Chinatown to the hyper-modern glass monoliths on the upscale Founder's Island, this vision of Gotham is breathtaking no matter where you look.

I completely recommend this game. It is without a doubt the best indie title i have played since kerbal space program. Its a retro rogue-like dungeon crawler platform that throws you into a randomly generated world, with one of several level themes.It has many different types of enemies with their own attacks and abilities, keeping the game interesting. It has a ton of items, along with many different ways of obtaining them, making each run different. There are a lot of unlockable heroes with different attacks, abilities and roles, making sure that there is something for everyone. It has unlockable "artifacts" that change different game play factors, allowing for harder/ different gameplay. It also has a unique scaling difficulty system, meaning that the longer you spend in game, the higher the difficulty, this nidges you to play quicker, and adds a sense of urgency.
Overall i give the game a 9.5/10, the only reason for it not being a 10 is that the scaling difficulty system cab be annoying and stops you exploring in great detail. Considering its cheap price, and the fact that you could pick it up for a key or to through trading (it was recently on sale at the time of writing this) i recommend everyone gets it.

I'm going to go ahead and give my rating and then explain why I gave it such. South Park: The Stick of Truth, in my opinion, gets a 9/10.
Now, you start off the game by creating your character. The amount of different customization combinations is actually pretty impressive. There are plenty of hairstyles, makeup, facial features and much more when you actually get into the game so I felt like my character was unique. I'll go ahead and compare it to Skyrim's character creation. Now, I'm not talking about all of the different things you can tweak on your character. I'm talking about the way you can make a character that is yours and yours only. I've yet to actually see someone else that has any characters looking similar to mine.
Alright then, now let's get onto the rest of the game since talking about cool character creation woulnd't be much of a review. I enjoyed the story very much. It was exactly of the quality you would expect from an episode of South Park. In fact, the whole game made me feel as if I was in the show because of how immersed I was in it. It was funny, weird, disgusting, racist and the many other terms that South Park is famous for. They even reference some old episodes in the game, whether by dialogue or abilities or even some items you see while exploring the town. There's a very good variety of side quests that you can do if you don't want to just breeze through the main one.
The combat system is also well-done. They do their own take on a turn-based battle sytem that I thought was pretty refreshing since I haven't played one of those in a while since Pokemon Y. What is even better is that their are so many things that can happen in combat that it actually makes you strategize so that you can win the battle. Your character can Bleed, Slow, become Grossed Out, set on Fire, and Dazed. Not sure if that's all of them either. And then their are things that do that opposite and increase either Attack, Defense, give you Shields, or restore your PP so that you can use another ability.
There are also a TON of weapons that you can use for combat. You either buy them, find them, or are given them at any time during the game. Each weapon comes with their own unique stat boosts or perks that can help you dominate a battle. Then you can even add more boosts onto them via Stickers, each either increasing the different types of damage you decide to do, increasing your health, gives you armor so that you basically become a tank if you have enough stacked on you, or even heal you after landing a perfect attack or blocking one. Needless to say, you won't be short on the different types of weapons that you can have and kick all of the other kids asses, whether it be with a sword or a♥♥♥♥♥♥♥
Oh, and the same goes with the armor. Plenty of them to put on your character and they can also have Stickers be put on them as well.
I like to talk about graphics but I kind of don't really see the point since... it's South Park. Not exactly supposed to be graphically oriented. I was happy with getting to walk around the town by having my character haphazerdly hop with each step everywhere he went.
Another cool thing is that you get to have a companion with you, both in and out of fights. The first one you start off with is Butters. He goes around with you, talking about where you are or what you're supposed to be doing for the main mission in the game, plus all of his own unique dialogue. The rest of the companions do the same as well and none of them sound like each other. No one says the same sentence another companion would and I really liked that.
I'm going to go ahead and wrap this up by saying that you will completely enjoy the main storyline in the game. It's about 12 hours long but they're going to be a DAMN good 12 hours. I was laughing and enjoying myself during the entire game and the ending was satisfying to me. Sure, the humor is crude but I've always loved that about South Park so I didn't mind it at all.
The only reason I didn't give this game a perfect score was because I had some performance issues at one point in the game. Don't know if it was because of my system or not but it just bothered me a bit. Other than that, it's a great game and deserves the sixty bucks you'll not have if you buy it.

I did not experience any problems at launch that others reported (twin NVIDIA 770 cards).  In game graphic tweaks are detailed now with a VRAM usage indicator so you can bump up the graphics to what your rig can handle.  Note that one setting is "film grain" - turning off just looked better to me, but does not affect performance otherwise.  5.1 headphones add to the experience, but the sound is great either way.
Game is still classic: fear takedowns allows for managing larger groups and some strategy, and the use of environmental objects for takedowns brings a little more to combat from the original Arkham game.  The use of the Big Villians as side missions is a bit weak, but this story has enough twists that even if you know the big ones you will still have a nice time.  I thought the plot had a few oddities - like having to communicate with others via his wrist monitor and changing into a costume out in the open while three armed guards are nearby ("I have to go take a lea... hey, is that Bruce Wayne trying to pull bat boots on?!").  Visually impressive but a bit lazy for the story.  And I miss the old Scarecrow costume - new one and facial features were unnecessarily grotesque.
Voice acting is phenomenal as always, and the original gang is all here unlike Origin.  Dwight Schultz (Faceman! Lt. Broccoli!) nails a special and especially creepy character.  I can't imagine what the voice studio was like on those days.  You dread hearing the microphone squeal knowing John Noble's haunting voice is next (or Nigma's annoying one).
Repetative - yes; but you'll be gunning for 100% for the extra special ending, too.

More tedious than fun. I enjoy playing skill based perma-death games similar to this, but many aspects of this game feel quite un-fun. The variation among enemies is scarce, and most monsters just try to run into you en-mass. Like FTL, this game requires a good bit of luck finding the right upgrades for your particular character early enough to make full use of them. Unlike FTL, each class only has a limited field strategy. A given class will have four skills and even though simpler games, like Binding of Isaac, offer less options, the supplementary power-ups leave you wanting more. The monsters in general seem to have too much health, and can be quite tedious to kill at mid to higher levels unless all the appropriate power-ups are gained. In addition, some power-ups seems strictly better than others, regardless of class; which I feel is poor design. The size of the characters and monsters seems unnecessarily small, and becomes bothersome at times. The size of the sprites creates of lack of character when compared to games like Rogue Legacy and Binding of Isaac. Overall its just not as charming or addictive as the game seems to think it is.

Skip this if you guys want:
You crash in a distant planet alone, scared and powerless. It seems hopeless, but you find your weapons intact and functional. You search the skies for a chance to see another life pod. A chance for someone to be with you, A chance to survive, but you only see storage units falling you say' "Must of been from the ship".
Alas, hopelessness grips you again. You shout of sorrow, not because of not seeing another life pod from the ship, but because knowing your the only one that survived and with what you have seen, the ship must of been destroyed. You place your weapon on your head knowing there is no chance of survival and prepared to shoot, but wait?!?!? You see the ship landing 10 miles away. With new found hope you ready your weapons and journey through this God forsaken planet.
You start with the Commando. A very agile and powerful character if matched with the right items. With him you'll learn how to kite, how to dodge and how every damage to an enemy counts.
Gameplay is smooth and fun. Controls are quite simple. It's an addictive game and has great replay value.The music is fantastic. It has achivements that you need to unlock for new items or characters (Yes I'm looking at you achievement hunters). You can choose from 10 different characters (If you unlock them all that is) and not every run is the same.
But a few achievements based items are impossible to get and multiplayer is buggy. Most new player will completely lost on what to do and die in the 10 min mark.
I wouldn't recommend this too everyone, but If you love platform and shoot em' up games. I can easily recommend this to you.

I don't have a lot to say, they simply fixed the teleporting Zeds, which was by far my biggest complaint. The larger Zeds don't teleport at all and for the smaller Zeds it's more or less impossible to notice since they need to be very far away.
I still believe the Zeds should sometimes spawn a bit farther away (if you are in a bad spot they can spawn directly around a corner, maybe 5 metres away), but it's ok the way it is most of the time. The new classes are nice and they constantly add more content. If they add objective mode in the future (and from all I've heard that's pretty much a given) the game will a worthy successor to the original game.
I don't mind the microtranscactions either - if someone wants to spend a few dollars to get a silly looking weapon retexture any Photoshop amateur could do in 30 minutes that's not my problem. Killing Floor is not the most serious game so I don't mind silly clothing and weapons. And if the mircrotransactions allow the devs to add more free content that's the best thing that can happen to me.
OLD, OUTDATED REVIEW:
It's early access, so I'll just write a short review for people who have played the first Killing Floor previously. I would love to say that this is more of the same with most of the small problems fixed, better graphics and (later on after early access) more content.
Unfortunately it is not. They pretty much butchered all of the fun by letting Zeds teleport to any location and spawn at any location at any time. The levels are completely interchangeable due to that, there is no exploring needed as there are no 'sweet spots' anymore like in KF 1, where you stop to fight the cheating AI doesn't matter at all. Checking your surroundings is completely pointless since Zeds will just spawn or teleport directly behind you if you are looking in the other direction for a second. You run away from the last 10 Zeds on the map and suddenly some of them magically appear around the next corner even though they were behind you a few seconds ago. Why can I even run away if it doesn't serve a purpose? It's silly.
Like expected the game does have better graphics, animations etc. But the gameplay is simply far, far, far worse than Killing Floor 1 right now. It's yet another victim of the 'adjust to the (dumb) player' philosophy that many games have nowadays. Whether it's RPGs that scale enemies and loot to your level (so your character's level becomes just a meaningless number), racing games that make your opponents drive faster or slower depending on your own performance (so you can win a race even if you constantly crash during the first 4 of 5 rounds and lose a race even though you drove perfectly for the first 4 rounds, but made a small mistake in the last corner before the finish line) or this now. I have no idea how anyone could like this crap. But I guess the brainless idiots who love this don't even notice that enemies spawn right in front of their face. I really hope they don't have any success with this trash.

The Story- The story is an epic tale about a man who is thrown into a "trial" created by satan himself, where he is turned into a triangle and is forced to dodge walls while rotating around a hexagon for all of eternity. Extremely well thought out, and I enjoyed it immensely. It really added to the whole experience. 10/10
The Gameplay- As I said before, you play as a triangle rotating around a hexagon dodging walls. Your goal is to survive 60 seconds without being hit, then the level is completed. There are 6 levels- Hexagon, Hexagoner, Hexagonest, Hyper Hexagon, Hyper Hexagoner, and Hyper Hexagonest. Their difficulty levels in the game are Hard, Harder, Hardest, Hardester, Hardestest, and Hardes♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, respectively. As the difficulties suggest, each level makes it harder to make it beyond 60 seconds by speeding up how quickly the walls come at you. Overall, it's very original and surprisingly fun. 9.5/10
Replay Value- This game is built so that every time you play the same level, it is different. In reality, the only things that are the same are the background colors, music, and difficulty/name. Never will you play the same level twice, which means that you can play for hundreds of hours experimenting with new stuff. And with 6 levels, it will keep you for a while. 10/10
Addiction and Difficulty- This game has a strange power I have never seen any other game come close to having- well, maybe except for Solitaire... anyways, this game is addicting as all heck. I tell you, I played this game every single day for 3 months. I kept coming back for more. Even long after I had beaten the game, I had kept coming back. This game is extremely difficult. Most people don't stay long after starting because they give up. However, it is genuine difficulty. It's not because of poor controls or level design, it's because they haven't practiced enough. Super Hexagon is a game of practice makes perfect. You cannot expect to be good at it right away. And with that, I commend it. For making people need to try over and over. 10/10
Graphics/Music- This game's "graphics" Are pretty much just vectors set on a colorful spinning background. They're simple. They don't try to be amazing, since that's not what this game tries to do. They aren't the best, but what they lack, is makes up for in music. This game has an amazing soundtrack of a whole 3 songs. But these songs are amazing. In fact, "Focus", the theme of Hyper Hexagonest and Hexagonest, is in my top 10 video game themes of all time. 10/10

I'm going to go ahead and give my rating and then explain why I gave it such. South Park: The Stick of Truth, in my opinion, gets a 9/10.
Now, you start off the game by creating your character. The amount of different customization combinations is actually pretty impressive. There are plenty of hairstyles, makeup, facial features and much more when you actually get into the game so I felt like my character was unique. I'll go ahead and compare it to Skyrim's character creation. Now, I'm not talking about all of the different things you can tweak on your character. I'm talking about the way you can make a character that is yours and yours only. I've yet to actually see someone else that has any characters looking similar to mine.
Alright then, now let's get onto the rest of the game since talking about cool character creation woulnd't be much of a review. I enjoyed the story very much. It was exactly of the quality you would expect from an episode of South Park. In fact, the whole game made me feel as if I was in the show because of how immersed I was in it. It was funny, weird, disgusting, racist and the many other terms that South Park is famous for. They even reference some old episodes in the game, whether by dialogue or abilities or even some items you see while exploring the town. There's a very good variety of side quests that you can do if you don't want to just breeze through the main one.
The combat system is also well-done. They do their own take on a turn-based battle sytem that I thought was pretty refreshing since I haven't played one of those in a while since Pokemon Y. What is even better is that their are so many things that can happen in combat that it actually makes you strategize so that you can win the battle. Your character can Bleed, Slow, become Grossed Out, set on Fire, and Dazed. Not sure if that's all of them either. And then their are things that do that opposite and increase either Attack, Defense, give you Shields, or restore your PP so that you can use another ability.
There are also a TON of weapons that you can use for combat. You either buy them, find them, or are given them at any time during the game. Each weapon comes with their own unique stat boosts or perks that can help you dominate a battle. Then you can even add more boosts onto them via Stickers, each either increasing the different types of damage you decide to do, increasing your health, gives you armor so that you basically become a tank if you have enough stacked on you, or even heal you after landing a perfect attack or blocking one. Needless to say, you won't be short on the different types of weapons that you can have and kick all of the other kids asses, whether it be with a sword or a♥♥♥♥♥♥♥
Oh, and the same goes with the armor. Plenty of them to put on your character and they can also have Stickers be put on them as well.
I like to talk about graphics but I kind of don't really see the point since... it's South Park. Not exactly supposed to be graphically oriented. I was happy with getting to walk around the town by having my character haphazerdly hop with each step everywhere he went.
Another cool thing is that you get to have a companion with you, both in and out of fights. The first one you start off with is Butters. He goes around with you, talking about where you are or what you're supposed to be doing for the main mission in the game, plus all of his own unique dialogue. The rest of the companions do the same as well and none of them sound like each other. No one says the same sentence another companion would and I really liked that.
I'm going to go ahead and wrap this up by saying that you will completely enjoy the main storyline in the game. It's about 12 hours long but they're going to be a DAMN good 12 hours. I was laughing and enjoying myself during the entire game and the ending was satisfying to me. Sure, the humor is crude but I've always loved that about South Park so I didn't mind it at all.
The only reason I didn't give this game a perfect score was because I had some performance issues at one point in the game. Don't know if it was because of my system or not but it just bothered me a bit. Other than that, it's a great game and deserves the sixty bucks you'll not have if you buy it.

Wow. Originally when I first saw the release of this on steam, I was skeptical, but once I did end up getting it, I haven't regretted it since. There are tons of levels, tons of monsters, and tons of powerups (levels and items are randomly chosen each time to mix it up). A bunch of classes, AND there's co-op! This has an extremely low learning curve, so anyone can really pick it up and play decently within 5 minutes. The graphics combined with the amazing but fantastically themed music and smooth gameplay make this an all around great game.
Yes, this IS a one-life thing. If you aren't into this, then this really isn't for you. Get some friends together, and play through a few attempts (I love the fact that if one player dies in the co-op and another player progresses onto the next level, the dead player revives. OLD, OUTDATED REVIEW:
It's early access, so I'll just write a short review for people who have played the first Killing Floor previously. I would love to say that this is more of the same with most of the small problems fixed, better graphics and (later on after early access) more content.
Unfortunately it is not. They pretty much butchered all of the fun by letting Zeds teleport to any location and spawn at any location at any time. The levels are completely interchangeable due to that, there is no exploring needed as there are no 'sweet spots' anymore like in KF 1, where you stop to fight the cheating AI doesn't matter at all. Checking your surroundings is completely pointless since Zeds will just spawn or teleport directly behind you if you are looking in the other direction for a second. You run away from the last 10 Zeds on the map and suddenly some of them magically appear around the next corner even though they were behind you a few seconds ago. Why can I even run away if it doesn't serve a purpose? It's silly.
Like expected the game does have better graphics, animations etc. But the gameplay is simply far, far, far worse than Killing Floor 1 right now. It's yet another victim of the 'adjust to the (dumb) player' philosophy that many games have nowadays. Whether it's RPGs that scale enemies and loot to your level (so your character's level becomes just a meaningless number), racing games that make your opponents drive faster or slower depending on your own performance (so you can win a race even if you constantly crash during the first 4 of 5 rounds and lose a race even though you drove perfectly for the first 4 rounds, but made a small mistake in the last corner before the finish line) or this now. I have no idea how anyone could like this crap. But I guess the brainless idiots who love this don't even notice that enemies spawn right in front of their face. I really hope they don't have any success with this trash.

Arkham Knight fully embodies everythin that's made the Arkham games so great, but it doesn't expand beyond that. New combat moves, cool tricks, and the batmobile help keep things fresh but Arkham Knight loses the charm Arkham Asylum and to some extent Arkham City had.

Fear Takedowns and new guard perks are cool in the predator encounters, but it feels so much easier. These encounters took longer for me in Arkham City, but here they can take less then 5 minutes for me, since simply going up to them and whaming them works. The combat is the best in the series but the first few hours of the game are so easy because of how much more powerful Batman is. I feel like that what this game has really lost the most was it's metroidvania feel, which is what made Arkham City so great. Batman just gets gadgets whenever he wants it, he doesn't go through puzzles or bosses to attain a gadget, whenever he thinks he needs it, he'll just get it throughout the City either from Lucius or whatever other Bathideout he has with a million gadgets. Despite this, it's still a really solid game overall.
I haven't finished the story yet, so I can't really establish my thoughts on it, but it's exactly like the Arkham games: A ridiculous plot that makes no sense about a villain that takes a city/place hostage over for some reason.

Life Lessons From Super Hexagon
In no particular order:
◦ anticipating the end is counterproductive
◦ self-awareness critically endangers the ability to experience multiple perspectives
◦ inability to consistently and fluidly change perspective results in subsequent inability to adapt to new situations
◦ progress requires adaptability
◦ strong focus, even on the task at hand, compromises flexibility
◦ don't assume anything, but learn from past experiences and integrate those concepts henceforth
◦ there's no reason to expect the unexpected; just refuse to expect anything, and be okay with the fact that you don't and never will truly know anything

South Park: The Stick of Truth is quite literally a long episode of the show, encapsulating the formula that makes the show so successful and loved by so many all over the world. A feat that is just as impressive as the mechanics turned out to be 13.8hrs later. You feel like a cast member in one of those long running episodes where they are all LARPing and fighting in the various factions. It was just fun to explore and interact with people from the show. To go into peoples homes and take a dump in their toilets. All of which is well worth the asking price, it will be a game I will enjoy replaying as another class all over again.

Been playing this for 400 hours now and just love it, even though it's still in early access. It's an extremely fast paced, gory, hectic and frantic co-op shooter. It makes Left4Dead 2 feel like an old retirement home. The idea is simple, you are motley crew of survivors in a post-apocalyptic Europe, tasked to clean out the Zed (cybernetic zombies) infestation thats spread over the continent. Survive increasingly difficult waves of zeds, until you finally confront the end boss. Simple idea but perfectly executed. There are multiple perks (classes), all with unique weaponry and skills and a large variety of zeds to kill, from simple fodder to panic-inducing Fleshpounds and Scrakes. Survival, especially at higher difficulties takes teamwork and skill.
But where KF2 really shines is in the weapons and the physics engine. Each weapon is beautifully crafted, ranging from regular guns, to home-crafted flamethrowers and futuristic "mad scientist" beam weapons. All animated at a glorious 200 FPS so you can see every single shell fly out in slow motion. Few shooters have the same satisfying feel to it when mowing down the enemy. This tactile feedback is further enhanced by the physics engine. When shot, zeds are ripped to pieces in a giant cloud of blood, limbs flying everywhere. Explosions will send showers of mutilated bodies raining down all over the place. Blood, entrails, limbs, pus and gibs litter the map. After a few waves the map looks like a slaughterhouse. If your GPU supports Nvidia PhysX it becomes even more gory, with blood flowing down stairs and entrails spilling out. It's highly satisfying and suits the "zombie" theme perfectly.
In short: A beautiful, hectic, extremely gory, satisfying co-op shooter where you kill zombies to speed metal music. What could go wrong?

Killing Floor 2:
~~~~~~~~~~~
Are you ready to take your place in a small team of six soldiers? Be ready to look out for each other when the waves of “Zeds” are coming at you from each side of the hexagon? Oh dear…. The first wave is coming at us… Get ready to Zumble!
Killing Floor 2 is a co-op FPS game where you take control of one of six characters and try to eliminate wave after wave (between 7 to 10 waves, depending on which server you are playing) of Zeds until you face either the “Patriach” - this scary and rather large mutated zombie/robot/Hulk thingy who has a rather heavy arsenal and is very strong in melee combat , or “Hans Volter”- the Nazi evil doctor who is holding himself pretty well for his age (he is around 100 years old) and likes to throw Toxic and High Explosive grenades! But don’t give him a chance to cuddle you as he will squeeze the life out of you to regenerate his own!
But before you get to the bosses you will face eleven types of “Zeds”, some will be easy to eradicate and some will be rather tough. At the end of each wave, you will be directed to a specific pod (there are several pods per map) where you will be able to buy ammunition, weapons and armour. Every kill you get is more money to spend at the pod! You have 40 different weapons you can use in this game; each weapon will fall into one of 7 categories – Beserker – Commando – Support – Field Medic- Demolition – Gunslinger and Firebug weapons. Whatever you use, at the end of the game you will get points for it. For example, only use a hunting shotgun (I doubt you will do that) and you will level up your support category faster than the others.
10 original maps to play in, from Burning Paris to the Catacombs passing by the Farmhouse; they are all very good and well designed. Some are bigger than others but equally as fun and challenging.
From the difficulty point of view, it will depend on which server you will be playing but you will be able to choose between Normal, Hard and Suicidal.
Graphically, this game is fabulously detailed and it runs very well. I enjoy the slow motion effect too, it’s just great! If you like heavy metal, the soundtrack is really good and fits the game perfectly. It’s hectic!
Positives:
~~~~~~~
-	Great and fun co-op FPS game
-	10 maps to play in
-	40 weapons to use
-	Great re-playability
-	Great graphics & soundtrack
-	Achievements & Trading cards
Negatives:
~~~~~~~~
-	A bit repetitive I must say

Risk of Rain is a survival platformer centered around the "die and lose everything" perspective, and it does it pretty damn well. If you're a player of games like BroForce, or ones with Rogue-Like elements, this should be in you're Games Library. The mechanics are relatively basic with your starting class, Commando, and it does a good job teaching you the ropes, and as you unlock new characters, the fun really begins. Now every mechanic you previously used is out the window, and you have a whole new set of tactics to play with. This isn't one of those "play it this way or you're bad" it's more of a "don't f*ckin' die, in whatever way works best", and that's (I'd argue) the best way to play a game, your way.
The music is pretty classic and it'll be running in your head when you dream about evading Magma Worms, and getting butt-f*ck'd by the Imp Overlord. The sound-design is awesome and will leave you satisfied with every explosion and shot you take. And finally the pixel art is some of the best out there, combining minimalism with complexety in the best of ways. The variety of mobs gives you a familiarity and hatred of the level that you're playing in, as you encounted enemies that f*ck you, or be an easy grind (same goes with the bosses).
The only "down-side" to this game is that you have to port-forward for your multiplayer, but that's really not a big deal at all. Local Multiplayer is a blast, and Co-Op online is just as fun.
Grab your controller, snag your keyboard, pug in your keypad, you're going to have a good time!

South Park the stick of truth is a love letter to fans of the show. While playing the game you feel like you’re watching an entire season of South Park which stars you. The game’s presentation is outstanding from the voice acting, to the animation style, to the music. The game is laugh out loud funny. However, if you’re easily offended it’s best to stay clear. The humor is shocking, crude, and insulting the way it’s meant to be.
As far as gameplay goes it’s a turn based RPG like super Mario All-stars where you have to time your attacks and blocks with a button press. There are four classes to choose from expect the standard three classes (fighter, mage, thief) and the south park exclusive Jew class. The actual RPG elements are pretty simple but with the south park flair. For example, all the health potions and consumables are items from the show like cheesy poofs. There is also some small customization you can do with weapon and armor patches that give certain stats. While the RPG elements are light it’s simply a joy just to see the south park flair on certain attacks and summons. For example, you can summon Jesus to do your bidding, turn into professor Chaos to wreck your enemies, or watch how Cartman does a fire attack.
There are a ton of references and hidden Easter eggs in this game. Almost every major character from the show makes an appearance in some way. It was simply fun just exploring the town and seeing what people had in their houses.
The one downside is that the game is a little on the short side. It’s about 15 hours long if you do all the side quests as well. However, there is no grinding in this game to fill the time. Not once while I was playing did I get bored.
If you’re a fan of the show definitely pick this game up. It’s worth your time and your money. The creators of South Park and Obsidian Entertainment have possibly made the best licensed game besides the excellent Batman Arkham games.

Risk of Rain is an excellent little action-platformer with Rogue-like level generation, twitchy and fast-paced gameplay, and absolutely beautiful atmosphere.  You find yourself as one of ten survivors of a spacecraft wreck, wandering the surface of a world which (prior to your arrival, at least) is filled with peaceful inhabitants.  Unfortunately, now that you've turned up, they've become about as friendly as your average grizzly, and it's up to you to find the teleporters, get back to the wrecked remains of your ship, and get the hell off this rock.
Gameplay is incredibly quick and fluid, with each of the ten characters having his (or her, or for that matter, its) own unique approach to dishing out horrible violence.  You start out with the Commando, whose standard attack is an assault rifle and whose mobility and Combat Roll skills make avoiding damage relatively easy; he also packs a Full Metal Jacket attack which pierces all enemies in a straight line and a rapidfire chain that deals massive damage to single enemies.  Manage to take down a few bosses and you'll get the Enforcer, a slow, tanky sort of fellow whose riot shotgun has limited range and slow firing speed, but whose combat shield completely ignores damage from the front in defensive mode.  He's also packing stun grenades that harm all enemies in a small radius and a shield bash that lets people know if they're invading your personal space.  And then we've got folks like the Sniper, who can completely one-shot bosses if used correctly, and the Huntress, who can kite like an SC2 Mutalisk, firing all the way.
Your default abilities don't tell the whole story, either.  See, your crashed spacecraft was effectively the interstellar equivalent of the UPS Truck, and as you meander the alien countryside you'll find storage crates and vending devices that broke free of the ship on impact, granting you access to a wide variety of tools with effects both active and passive.  You'll find yourself wielding everything from a fungal shampoo hat that grants a regen bonus to a buzz saw salvaged from a factory accident to the absolutely horrific (and insanely powerful) Jar of Souls.  Full item descriptions (accessible from the main menu) grant flavor and a taste of dark comedy, as well as explaining the items' effects in more detail.  This, alongside a full bestiary, grants a subtle hint of story and a nifty bit of background about the various creatures you'll be introducing to the local equivalent of Death.
Add to this the fact that the game's minimalist pixel-art style and tiny-but-effective sprites create a visual atmosphere that cannot be mistaken for anything but an alien world, and to the often-tranquil, sometimes-strange, but never boring soundtrack, and you have a surprisingly vital world with a ton to explore and challenges that will keep you coming back for more for many hours to come.
The only negatives that I have encountered thus far are minor and seem to spring forth from the game's rogue-like nature: occasionally enemies will spawn in groups that render it nearly impossible to survive with your skillset unless you've reached a level of enlightenment far beyond my puny mortal self, and sometimes (though not frequently) item vendors will appear in an enclosed space, forcing them to overlap and making you roll the dice when you would otherwise be making a straightforward tactical decision.  The latter could be fixed with a minor patch, the former is probably just my lack of gaming skills.
Negatives aside, though, if you're a fan of action-platforming at its finest, of difficulty that is tough but fair, and of creative world and monster design, then give this one a shot.  You probably won't find it wanting.

Risk of Rain is a survival platformer centered around the "die and lose everything" perspective, and it does it pretty damn well. If you're a player of games like BroForce, or ones with Rogue-Like elements, this should be in you're Games Library. The mechanics are relatively basic with your starting class, Commando, and it does a good job teaching you the ropes, and as you unlock new characters, the fun really begins. Now every mechanic you previously used is out the window, and you have a whole new set of tactics to play with. This isn't one of those "play it this way or you're bad" it's more of a "don't f*ckin' die, in whatever way works best", and that's (I'd argue) the best way to play a game, your way.
The music is pretty classic and it'll be running in your head when you dream about evading Magma Worms, and getting butt-f*ck'd by the Imp Overlord. The sound-design is awesome and will leave you satisfied with every explosion and shot you take. And finally the pixel art is some of the best out there, combining minimalism with complexety in the best of ways. The variety of mobs gives you a familiarity and hatred of the level that you're playing in, as you encounted enemies that f*ck you, or be an easy grind (same goes with the bosses).
The only "down-side" to this game is that you have to port-forward for your multiplayer, but that's really not a big deal at all. Local Multiplayer is a blast, and Co-Op online is just as fun.
Grab your controller, snag your keyboard, pug in your keypad, you're going to have a good time!

South Park the stick of truth is a love letter to fans of the show. While playing the game you feel like you’re watching an entire season of South Park which stars you. The game’s presentation is outstanding from the voice acting, to the animation style, to the music. The game is laugh out loud funny. However, if you’re easily offended it’s best to stay clear. The humor is shocking, crude, and insulting the way it’s meant to be.
As far as gameplay goes it’s a turn based RPG like super Mario All-stars where you have to time your attacks and blocks with a button press. There are four classes to choose from expect the standard three classes (fighter, mage, thief) and the south park exclusive Jew class. The actual RPG elements are pretty simple but with the south park flair. For example, all the health potions and consumables are items from the show like cheesy poofs. There is also some small customization you can do with weapon and armor patches that give certain stats. While the RPG elements are light it’s simply a joy just to see the south park flair on certain attacks and summons. For example, you can summon Jesus to do your bidding, turn into professor Chaos to wreck your enemies, or watch how Cartman does a fire attack.
There are a ton of references and hidden Easter eggs in this game. Almost every major character from the show makes an appearance in some way. It was simply fun just exploring the town and seeing what people had in their houses.
The one downside is that the game is a little on the short side. It’s about 15 hours long if you do all the side quests as well. However, there is no grinding in this game to fill the time. Not once while I was playing did I get bored.
If you’re a fan of the show definitely pick this game up. It’s worth your time and your money. The creators of South Park and Obsidian Entertainment have possibly made the best licensed game besides the excellent Batman Arkham games.

Risk of Rain is an excellent little action-platformer with Rogue-like level generation, twitchy and fast-paced gameplay, and absolutely beautiful atmosphere.  You find yourself as one of ten survivors of a spacecraft wreck, wandering the surface of a world which (prior to your arrival, at least) is filled with peaceful inhabitants.  Unfortunately, now that you've turned up, they've become about as friendly as your average grizzly, and it's up to you to find the teleporters, get back to the wrecked remains of your ship, and get the hell off this rock.
Gameplay is incredibly quick and fluid, with each of the ten characters having his (or her, or for that matter, its) own unique approach to dishing out horrible violence.  You start out with the Commando, whose standard attack is an assault rifle and whose mobility and Combat Roll skills make avoiding damage relatively easy; he also packs a Full Metal Jacket attack which pierces all enemies in a straight line and a rapidfire chain that deals massive damage to single enemies.  Manage to take down a few bosses and you'll get the Enforcer, a slow, tanky sort of fellow whose riot shotgun has limited range and slow firing speed, but whose combat shield completely ignores damage from the front in defensive mode.  He's also packing stun grenades that harm all enemies in a small radius and a shield bash that lets people know if they're invading your personal space.  And then we've got folks like the Sniper, who can completely one-shot bosses if used correctly, and the Huntress, who can kite like an SC2 Mutalisk, firing all the way.
Your default abilities don't tell the whole story, either.  See, your crashed spacecraft was effectively the interstellar equivalent of the UPS Truck, and as you meander the alien countryside you'll find storage crates and vending devices that broke free of the ship on impact, granting you access to a wide variety of tools with effects both active and passive.  You'll find yourself wielding everything from a fungal shampoo hat that grants a regen bonus to a buzz saw salvaged from a factory accident to the absolutely horrific (and insanely powerful) Jar of Souls.  Full item descriptions (accessible from the main menu) grant flavor and a taste of dark comedy, as well as explaining the items' effects in more detail.  This, alongside a full bestiary, grants a subtle hint of story and a nifty bit of background about the various creatures you'll be introducing to the local equivalent of Death.
Add to this the fact that the game's minimalist pixel-art style and tiny-but-effective sprites create a visual atmosphere that cannot be mistaken for anything but an alien world, and to the often-tranquil, sometimes-strange, but never boring soundtrack, and you have a surprisingly vital world with a ton to explore and challenges that will keep you coming back for more for many hours to come.
The only negatives that I have encountered thus far are minor and seem to spring forth from the game's rogue-like nature: occasionally enemies will spawn in groups that render it nearly impossible to survive with your skillset unless you've reached a level of enlightenment far beyond my puny mortal self, and sometimes (though not frequently) item vendors will appear in an enclosed space, forcing them to overlap and making you roll the dice when you would otherwise be making a straightforward tactical decision.  The latter could be fixed with a minor patch, the former is probably just my lack of gaming skills.
Negatives aside, though, if you're a fan of action-platforming at its finest, of difficulty that is tough but fair, and of creative world and monster design, then give this one a shot.  You probably won't find it wanting.

Batman: Arkham Knight is the finale to the Arkham game series from Rocksteady Studios.
It has a sense of finality and builds on the revolutionary Freeflow fighting style with powerful new moves  and enemies. It expands on Arkham City’s open world with a larger, detailed Gotham City, introduces a new fully playable Bat-Tank and makes it an aggravating part of the action and puzzles.  The game brings all of Batman’s closest family of Gotham superheroes and rogues together for an amazing finale.
While the mystery of the identity of the Arkham Knight fails to surprise comic fans, there are other surprises to fall back on that kept the story engaging.
Several strong performances gave it personality: the monotone voice of John Noble makes the most eerie and yet emotionless version of the Scarecrow seen in video game form, Mark Hamill returns for some glorious, darkly hilarious posthumous Joker lines as well as reenactments of some of the most famous scenes in the history of the comics.
Of course the definitive Kevin Conroy stars as Batman yet again. Here and there, a few cheesy, awkward lines pop up, mostly in the side quests, but the same is true of nearly any game of this size.
The size of the map is significant. We’re now free to explore three islands of the dark and intermittently stormy Gotham City, which is given character and color by its many  landmarks like the Chinatown district, Wayne Tower, and Ace Chemicals. The areas are beautifully detailed recreations from the comics.
The city has been evacuated again, which conveniently takes the graphics card intensive inhabitants of Gotham to safety outside of the playable area. The streets are far from empty, however. They are livelier than ever thanks to vastly increased populations of criminals, both on foot and engaging in high-speed pursuits with the GCPD.
The animation you get from countering them when they try to run you down is hilarious.
The Batmobile can be remote-controlled, which makes it a semi decent addition to Batman’s environmental puzzle-solving toolbox. Need to be in two places at once to trigger two switches, or to sneak up on enemies who’ve got you cornered? No problem just blast them with supposed non lethal rounds...
The Batmobile can be summoned almost anywhere on the islands of Gotham, leading to a fantastic move where Batman dives in as it zooms to him.
The gimmick is that when you hold the left trigger, the Batmobile swiftly turns into a slower but highly maneuverable Battank that you use to blow up battle drones...
This is about as un-Batman an activity as I can imagine. He’s a hero known for using his fists, his non-lethal gadgets, and his wits to defeat his rogues gallery of villains since his parents were murdered by a gun, and yet here he is, a knight in futuristic BatRobocop armor, blasting away with guns galore.
Supposedly, the tank automatically switches to non-lethal ammo when targeting humans but what about running the humans over? Most people would die from being hit by a Tank at speed...
Rocksteady’s obviously aware of this, since more than one character comments on how it’s not his style.
Tank battles are far from fun.
I do like the idea of having hostile drones telegraph a visible line of fire where they’re about to launch a shell.
It allows for more awareness of enemies that are attacking from off camera and lets you avoid them.
It gets slightly aggravating when heavy and flying drones are introduced, but to balance it you’re given secondary weapons, such as EMPs and missile barrages, to counter them.
Tank battles are nowhere near as interesting as the improved brawling and predator-style fights.
Tank mode plays a big role in puzzles too, thanks to a grapnel winch that pulls things down for you.
Tank-based platforming puzzles are awful. While the Battank is maneuverable and can strafe, driving up a narrow ramp is still frustratingly clumsy.
Meanwhile, Batman’s signature strike-and-counter brawling and stealthy predator fights feel better and smoother than ever. They’ve been upgraded with dozens of powerful and interesting new mechanics and subtle tweaks that give us more to experiment with and master. Some of the new moves feel overpowered at first. In brawls you can pick up a dropped baseball bat or club, which gives you a few seconds worth of bashing through shielded or shock-baton-wielding enemies. In predator fights the surprise multi-takedown move knocks out up to five unsuspecting targets at once and the voice synthesizer gadget can lure thugs into traps in predator fights.
The increased number of enemies in play and new types, like the huge gatling-gun brutes and the medic (who can protect his allies with electric fields and revive anybody you’ve already knocked out) balance it out well. Also, being hunted by thugs who use denial tactics like firebombing ground vents, controlling hovering drones, deploying landmines, and detecting you if you use Detective Vision for too long made me change up my habits and targeting priorities.
A few flashy fight scenarios in the campaign and side missions let you team up with an AI-controlled Robin, Nightwing, or Catwoman, and use them to execute some awesome dual-takedown moves that knock out any enemy instantly and temporarily swap you to control of your partner (while maintaining your combo count). It doesn’t add much mechanically, but fighting side-by-side with a sidekick is a very Batman thing to do. These climactic showpiece fights let Arkham Knight get away with almost entirely dropping the gimmicky boss fights that ended up as low points of previous Arkham games. In a way it’s a let down that there’s no direct physical confrontation with most arch criminals, but nothing is sometimes better than something annoying.
The campaign is complemented by a ton of mostly excellent side quests built around stopping villains like Two Face, Penguin, Firefly, and of course The Riddler. Each mission series has its own gameplay style.
The Riddler, has a mix of his typical riddles and rage inducing Batmobile race courses which you have to race through while extending or retracting pieces of track or obstructions, moments before you plunge to your doom or crash and explode.
Two-Face’s crew robs banks, putting a timer and various rules on predator fights.
These twists can include Detective mode jammers, an alarm stopping the gang from hearing you.
Man-Bat requires listening for his echolocation screams and then performing aerial takedowns to make him take his
anti-mutant bat medicine.
The Arkham Knight’s Watchtowers and checkpoint mercenaries generally require either a good beating or a predator style of gameplay. For some, this may be enjoyable as its more of what makes Batman so awesome.
it's easily worth another dozen hours of variety-packed gameplay.
AR challenge fights also exist which include racing and tank battles and increase replayability.
If this is in fact the last Rocksteady-developed Batman game, the series will end on a bitter note for some.
The PC port upon release was broken, buggy, unfinished and badly optimised for some steam users.
While I was lucky and only encountered a few glitches, it was still enough to ruin my enjoyment of the game.
Like Two-Face, I am split as to what I really think about Arkham Knight as a whole.
The addition of tank combat clashes with everything Batman stands for.
However, having access to the Batmobile for the first time gives us a new world of possibilities for interacting with Gotham City. Arkham Knight is a mixed bag of disapointment and glory on almost every level.

Civ V. What can I say about this game that hasn't already been said? I don't know a single person who hasn't at least heard of the Civilization games, and there's a good reason for that.

There are some issues with the game. Not major ones, mind you, just something I find to be a bit of a pet peeve. As a matter of fact, it's something we all know about.
The AI cheats at higher levels of difficulty. I'm not joking, the AI gets huge buffs while the player gets huge debuffs, and the AI gets a boost to research so that by turn 100 they have medeval tech.
It's annoying, but it's not something that turns me off the game. Oddly though, that's my only issue.
In general, Civ V is a great game, and it's something I'd look into getting if I didn't already have it. Recommended? Definitely.

Let me preface by saying this; I bought and critique the game as a long time Batman fan and also as someone who has enjoyed all of the others games in the series immensly. I will try not to include spoilers in this review, but if you're really wanting to keep the game spoiler-free, I'd suggest not reading it.
This is a very broad game with not much depth, it offers plenty of distractions to go around that will keep you busy (and have a good time doing them), but it will probably not scratch that inner hardcore gamer in you, however, it is a tale of Batman and his final crusade as he goes on to save his city yet again. We see a return of many standard villains, but Scarecrow absolutely steals the show both with his voice acting, design and just overall impact on the story; while exploring Batman's psyche isn't anything new, it is done well in this game and provides for some really thrilling moments. Arkham Knight, ironically, falls a bit flat on his face, as his encounters often just exist to provide some hateful tension that doesn't really seem necessary. His reveal is a bit disappointing, but there's not many routes they could go here, so I can understand why they chose to go where they did. Ultimately, he is there just as another character with no real depth, but it compliments Scarecrow well because he is merely a sidekick villain.
On the flip side, I also really enjoyed my encounters with Riddler, they're really well done and utilize the batmobile in a very fun way, I don't like how some parts of the puzzles are locked until late in the game, but it sets for a nice change of pace after completing an epic story to just go toe to toe with Riddler's intellect. Most puzzles are well designed and while I wouldn't call them particulary difficult, I'd say they're interesing enough to provide that AH-HA moment, along with the snarky commentary you get from Enigma, they're an absolute joy to both participate in and beat.
What the game does extremely well is the tone and the setting, Gotham never looked grimmer and more atmospheric, I enjoyed how you can find side quests just cruising along the joy of the city and how it develops in both setting and tone as you start winning it back. I think most memorable and beautiful moments of the game lie in you feeling as the Batman and how you slowly overtake the city back, seeing enemy forces dwindle one by one, it really instills for some epic moments. Voice narrations are well done as well as the music, they provide for a very dynamic background that keeps you interested as you move through the quests and the quieter parts of the city. Detective mode is not utilized too much, but it does get some attention, mainly in the form of side quests, so it's still there for those "the best detective" feelings.
What the game lacks are boss fights, but I'll list this as a positive. So far, the other games had very generic boss fights in general and while they did provide for a nice closer to the end of a villain, what you get here is just raw gameplay, whatever you learn, you can use. There are some "bossish" like moments, but they never feel as grand as the final fight with Joker in Arkham Asylum or the brawl with Deathstroke in Arkham Origins; I think it gives the game a good sense of connectivity that didn't exist in the previous two open world games. This goes well with just how being the Batman really is, the animations are slick, the punches are great, riding the batmobile is a joy. One complaint I would have is how the gadgets feel meaningless, outside of the Riddler challenges, but in the end it didn't really matter, at least they didn't feel as forced as in the previous installments.
Many people complained about the prevalence of the batmobile, I think the previous games strictly fell into two "encounters", stealth and combat; I always felt like the stealth encounters took ages to complete and just wanted to go on to the next combat scenario or a grand cutscene or something more epic. This game blends it all, stealth doesn't feel so stealthy as you really have a lot more tools to dispose of armed enemies quickly, the combat scenarios are usually just brutal and awesome to execute and the batmobile is just full blown out explosive action. While there are a lot of batmobile scenarios, I reckon there's about the same amount of you being Batman on foot scenarios, so to me, it never felt overly used. I do agree that towards the end of the game, as you stop getting upgrades and enemies aren't being introduced, it feels like the same song and dance, but it didn't reach a point for me where I despised the batmobile. A good thing that it adds to the game is mobility! Traversing the city never felt so quick and smooth, without resorting to the silly batwing quick travel system, it really feels like you can get from point A to point B in no time in a good old Batman fashioned way.
Overall, I think this game is solid, I might even say it's my favourite game of all time. If you're a Batman fan or if you enjoyed the previous installments, I reckon it's a must buy; if you're on the fence, I hope this review helped you decide, but I'd recommend it if you enjoy open world epic grand adventures, I think you'll find a new love for everyone's favourite super hero.

I got into Half-Life 2 late like in 2007 when I got the Orange Box so odds are you already know how great it is but here are my two cents anyway.  I like solo campaigns and HL2 is as good as they come.  Great characters, gameplay, difficulty, adventure, it has it all.  Even the vehicel sections are some of my favorite parts and I don't say that often... or ever.  Usually a vehicle section in a FPS draws a groan out of me but not in HL2.  And have I mentioned the Gravity Gun?  Hurtling trashcans, cinder blocks, and circular sawblades at zombies?  Yes please.  You can do anything, there is a great sense of freedom and you control the pace of the action.  If you want to go exploring then go explore or if you want to stick to the mission at hand you can do that too.
The only thing I can think of that would have made it better is more choice of guns.  The gun selection is average: (1) melee, (2) pistols, (2) machine guns, (1) shotgun, (1) rocket launcher, (1) grenade, (1) exotic weapon you never have ammo for.  That's average for a game of it's type.  Did you hear me?  Average.  The only thing wrong with the game is something that's AVERAGE!
I would rather play Half-Life 2 than Call of Duty Modern Warfare 2, Black Ops, or Ghosts.  You may quote me on that and the real funny part is HL2 came out a decade earlier.

What makes this game pure is that you can train your brain to be able to parse the incoming visuals. You can train your fingers to precisely move the little triangle from one quadrant to another. You can learn to recognise each gauntlet and know exactly what you need to do to navigate through it.
For some people you can master this after a short time. For me? It took a lot longer. A LOT longer. But... I just desperately wanted to beat this game. And not just unlock all six achievements but keep going until I broke the 1000 second milestone.
Never in my life have I chased positions on a leaderboard, but Super Hexagon is different. It is so pure. The skills it tests are unique to Super Hexagon and so we all come to it as equals. There is no advantage to be gained with faster computers or fancy input devices. It's just you and your pure raw will to succeed.
That's why I love this game. For some it's probably just going to be a 'oh that's hard' and forget about it. But if you embrace the challenge this is a game that will reward you with the ability to pull of one of the most impressive gaming party tricks going: Being able to complete the Hyper Hexagonest level. You will blow minds.

I doubt anybody even realizes that people are mad at the microtransaction not because of any "childish reasons" as many of you reviewers say, but simply because of the professionalism Tripwire shows.
First of all, let's go with what everyone says; Why would you put microtransactions when the game is still Early Access?
There are probably a lot of reasons for that, good or bad would be an opinion. Some say it may be because they are running low on money, this game didn't sell out too well, so they decided to "Go CSGO", WAY too early.
Now, this "professionalism" I'm talking about might sound too fancy or too confusing for you ("Wow, this reviewer thinks we readers are dumb!"). What I mean by it, is for the simple fact that Tripwire could do, maybe not better, but something else. They could have spend their (actually, this would be more about making their significant others do it) time doing something else. That's all.
What in the name of Pirates, in the name of the Blood Eagle and in the name of the Christian God do I mean? Think about it or better yet don't, these developers (and the "others") could have been used for something else than cosmetics, something useful. Maybe they could have spared more time on balance changes, making more weapons...And well, sorry but I got no more examples. I'd put "making more characters" but I bet one of you would use that statement as an excuse to call me a hypocrite.
I know many of you, let me call you "Tripwire Ballsuckers", justify this microtransactions as something not to worry about because it's just cosmetic.
Well, let me tell you MY REASON I dislike this: I'm still using an old HDD that I didn't care to upgrade because I'm already tired of 4 months technology advances. Imagine me having only 100GB left, now KF2 is 10gb (probably not, just take it as an example and don't go too tight) at first release, then it's 15 because they added USEFUL, PRATICAL content. But then, 24 GB, why? Useless cosmetic content.
If I want cosmetics, I got one thing that I'm sure, or at least really hope so, everyone can agree with; Mods.
Modders exist for a reason, you know?
I don't want Killing Floor 2 to be riddled with useless cosmetic content, no way.
If people want cosmetics, like I said, we got modders for that.
We don't need to add it to the game.
We don't need it as a DLC which you must pay for just to enable these items because, go guess, the items ARE IN THE GAME but locked.
We don't need Tripwire to simulate CSGO, some say repetitive so for them it is the same.
As you may have noticed, this review doesn't mention the game much. This is simply because I saw a lot of these silly reviews about how "microtransaction is not evil, it's good". I don't care if it's evil or good, I only care about the real effects it actually does.
Even after beta release, this game still has quite the useless GBs you don't want at all.
There may be a trend with Tripwire; If you can ruin a game for money, do it.
Well, they did with KF1, it looks like they're doing it with KF2.
Want something that may be worth it to get this game? The Melee.
The "Berserker" class in here is the best melee I ever saw on a co-op game, you get a variety of choices for it too.
But the rest is just crap, especially the fact there's more crap than there's useful or cool stuff.
