This is the first full format review I've done since the site I used to write for died a slow death. Between the duties of getting older and a profession that relied on regular daily writing, putting up these kinds of reviews became more of a chore than fun. That said, it goes to show just how good this game is for me to say something more than a one liner on the quality of the end product I just experienced.
After putting a playthrough of this game, I can easily say that The Stick of Truth is a masterpiece. Being a licensed title, I was hesitant to place any serious thought into it. Licensed titles, almost as a rule, are terrible. Sure, there is the rare quality title out there - Magical Quest Starring Mickey Mouse way back in the SNES days and the old Ninja Turtles arcade game come to mind - but those are strong crap shoots. But between the pedigree of the developer, Obsidian, and finally getting the kind of time and resources needed to develop their vision of a good game (I still imagine what KOTOR2 could have been if it wasn't rushed for a Christmas release), it was worth the chance.
To sum it up here and now, I'll channel my inner Butters: boy howdy is this good.
The Stick of Truth does what video games have promised since the Playstation 2 released - produced an animation quality game. While that may not say much given the source material, copying the elegent low-rent crappiness of South Park is no easy task. If I hadn't failed to move the mouse cursor off the side of the screen, the game is almost indistinguishable from a full episode of the series. The only time it ever turns into game territory is opening menus, the occational notification of Facebook messages from other characters and the battle UI. Otherwise, it's a complete, flawless recreation of the South Park look and feel.
The feel goes well beyond the simple visual presentation. With the full contributions of Trey Parker and Matt Stone, the dialogue, story and voice acting also fit the bill to perfection. Sporting almost 100% original dialgue and fresh voice overs (one particular character aside which I won't spoil but you can figure out pretty easily), we get a complete South Park experience. The plot, starting with a simple play acting of a war between Elves and Humans, plays mostly in the imaginations of the kids, but seen as outside adult observers. Our main character, henceforth called ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ by Cartman no matter what you named him (I just named him that off the bat to save trouble), runs around the world in ridiculous cosplay weapons and armor and act out combat in a fantasy kingdom that suspiciously looks like the town of South Park. The story, as South Park is apt to do, quickly branches into multiple sub-plots with ever escalating insanity that no one but the main characters seem to recognize and all the various plot points seamlessly converging on each other in the climax. For a game built on fart jokes and crass humor, The Stick of Truth has suprisingly tight storytelling and an extremely advanced understanding of storytelling mechanics. This game could serve as an example of how to pace and deliver story content.
A particularly strong element are the gaming jokes interspersed throughout. For instance, TSOT gets the right amount of mileage out of the silent protaganist and lampoons it. Nothing ever overstays its welcome in this game and jokes are given the right amount of airtime without becoming stale. You'll love the insanity of your trip to Canada.
And that ending (or two if you found the other rather hilarious one right before the true one) is absolutely classic South Park.
That said, there were some troubles with the story elements themselves, mostly from the perspective of a person who was old enough to be able to watch Episode 1 when it was still new and not have to sneak it to avoid my parents objecting to staying up too late. The Stick of Truth is effectively a giant South Park museum. Nearly everything in its 17 year run was called back at some point or another during the story. Most of it was begnign, such as looking through backgrounds in the photo studio, each of the four main kids' closets and some other background areas, but there was a little too much callback in the plot for my taste. While the bulk of the story is original, there are too many elements from prior episodes, particularly in the main plot. Some callbacks were handled well, such as the side-quest involving Mr. Kim of City Wok which closed the story of the Mongorians (yes, it is spelled intentionally this way), but for the most part, the game could have used fewer of them and left them more in the background. 17 seasons and 247 episodes is just a bit too much to shove into the game.
The game itself plays relatively simply. You walk around the town, interact with the environment, mainly through farting on it and hitting it with whatever weapon you have handy, and enter battles. The battles are simple but I didn't find them monotonous as the interactivity of the moves kept me engaged. Combat is driven turn-base style reminiscent of classic JRPGs (with a lampshade hung squarely on this during the tutorial as to why it works this way) with the game giving you visual cues on when to press certain mouse or keyboard buttons to stick the perfect attack. While the skillset is relatively small - one melee, one ranged, four summons depending on your side quest progression and five abilities - the game throws enough variety in how each weapon operates and does enough interactivity to keep it fresh. Moving from warrior to thief changes the combat mechanics sufficiently to keep it interesting.
A few negative point on the gameplay come from knowing what you're supposed to do. In-combat is mostly self-explanatory and the tutorial does a good job of showing you the basics, but the outside activities can be troublesome. The most confusing element until I figured out the proper pattern was the abortion sequence, though I suspect this was made intentionally difficult to show off the rather humorous results of failure. Also, the difficulty curve is inconsistent, with enemies coming at you well above your level or certain points where enemies have an almost full immunity to negative effects and insane hitpoints, but a final boss that wasn't all that tough to deal with.
The game is sufficiently long, clocking in at a touch over 14 hours with side-quests compelted (not counting trying to find those elusive characters I haven't farted on or friended yet) and is quite satisfying without overstaying its welcome.
I also had a bit of a musing about this game. I would find it quite entertaining if Parker and Stone were given a feed on the most common character appearance, class, name, final equipment and story decisions and integrated it as part of South Park canon in a future episode. I would be interested to see "♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥" make an appearance in the show and integrate the commonplace decisions into the show itself.
Overall, I recommend South Park the Stick of Truth. It has the right balance of gameplay, storytelling and crass humor that I would expect out of a collaboration between Obsidian, Parker and Stone. The callbacks do get a touch overbearing, but if you're someone that hasn't consistently kept up with the show over a 17 year timespan, this shouldn't be too much of a bother. Otherwise, the flaws are relatively minor and the game shines practically everywhere else.
Overall, 9.4/10.

There's a reason why Half-Life 2 is tied for the highest rated game on Steam. Just let me explain why.
If you haven't played the first Half-Life or watched gameplay of it, here is the story so far. *SPOILERS*
You are Dr. Gordon Freeman, a 27-year-old theoretical physicist at Black Mesa Research Facility with a Ph.D from MIT. One day, an experiment you participate in goes horribly wrong. You are presented with the task of fighting through the invading aliens' army to reach the surface and close the portal that they are being teleported from. Soon enough, you discover the U.S Marines have taken control of the base, and are wiping out all life in the facility to cover the incident up. That includes innocent employees of Black Mesa. You must fight through the Marine forces to the surface, where the military have set up a sort of impromptu base. Once you reach the portal to the alien world, you must find the being holding the portal open and kill him. Once you do, a mysterious figure known as the G-Man puts you into a stasis in an alternate dimension. This is where Half-Life 2 begins.
G-Man drops you from stasis perfectly preserved as you were from 20 years earlier during HL1's events. You are now in Eastern Europe, which is on the brink of revolution against the Combine, the alien rulers who were the main antagonists in Half-Life. They now convert humans into their soldiers, the Combine Overwatch. Gordon Freeman is renowned the world over for saving humanity and is referred to as The One Free Man along various other titles, and is worshipped by the Vortigaunts, an alien enemy race from HL1 that he freed from their master. Gordon must lead the Revolution by the people of City 17 and the surrounding areas.
The gameplay is smooth as butter. The graphics also have aged very well, and still look very good ten years later (Actually, HL2 Steam version runs on the Half-Life 2: Episode 2 version of Source, released in 2007, so it's really six and a half, but still.). Half-Life 2 has the traditional FPS backpack, with a variety of different weapons for all combat situations. I don't really want to spoil anything, so I'll just leave it here.
Proves that stellar gameplay and replay value trumps graphical horsepower. Fantastic game!

This review is totally spoiler free.
Having only played the game post September patch, my experience with Arkham Knight has been a smooth one. Many of the bugs reported by initial playthroughs were not present in my experience. A few minor hitches exist, namely minor FPS drops (~8 fps) while driving the Batmobile in parts of the city. Running on a 3gb GTX 780, I am getting a steady 55 fps at 1440p with settings on normal or high, including Nvidia's physx-based paper and rain (smoke and fog disabled as they tanked my fps when present).
Having said that, Arkham Knight is the superb Bat-gameplay experience you've come to expect from Rocksteady's Arkham franchise.
The story continues after the bold climax of Arkham City, showing us a Gotham free of her insidious super-villian tormentors. This quickly changes, as a darker, more forboding Scarecrow upends the city in chaos. What insues is a masterfully crafted Arkham tale, worthy of its predecessors. Rocksteady introduces us to their take on a new character, the Arkam Knight. The Knight is great foil to Batman, knowing much about the Bat, conspicuously so. Unfortunately, as equally matched as they are, the Knight is nowhere near as compelling a character as Scarecrow. To add insult to injury, the player spends most of the time fending off the Knight's advances, and much less with Scarecrow himself.
That is not to say Arkham Knight does not provide ample opportunity to show Batman under the effects of Scarecrow's fear toxin, which many gamers (myself included) come to expect from the trippy, dazzling Scarecrow levels of Arkam Asylum. Prepare for the bittersweet, as no such levels occur in this game. Instead, Rocksteady has taken a more "subtle" approach, and in doing so makes for some of the most entertaining, oddly endearing parts of the Arkham Knight narrative.
The gameplay is what you've come to expect from an Arkham Title. All the gadgets from previous games are in place, along with the same combat takedowns. This is by no means a bad thing. This is the Arkham combat formula, perfected. Moves are faster, Bat reaction is tighter, and enemies are all the more varied. There are a few new special moves sprinkled in to keep combat fresh.
Preditor mode is still a blast as well. New enemy capabilities increase the difficulty of stalking from the shadows. Special enemy types now can track your position while you are in Detective Mode. Some operate long-range combat drones that attack on sight. Still others have camoflage that masks their detection in Detective Mode. With these added obstacles, Batman comes equipped to circumvent or outright booby trap enemy technology, using these to the players' advantage.
Side-missions are fun and varied. The commitment of cinematic resources to most of the side villians is really impressive. Each story feels very fleshed out provides extra opportunity to stalk and bash without coming off as game filler.
Despite the divisive nature of Arkham Origins, there is clear integration of that story into the Arkham mythos within Arkham Knight. Familiar faces show up, as does some the novel Detective Mode gameplay. For fans of Origins, you'll be pleasantly surprised. For those who weren't (or didn't play it), you'll hardly notice.
To the dismay of some Arkham fans, this game has very few boss battles. Nothing like the fights with Poison Ivy or Ras Al  Goul in previous titles. In my experience, this doesn't hurt the gameplay experience and, in fact removes an elment of tedium from the game. Taking on classic super-villains is more integrated into the combat and predator experiences the player is familiar with from all Arkham titles.
The Batmobile is great addition to the game, and a lot of fun to operate. The Mobile drives fast and slick, it takes so getting used to as it drifts with ease quickly climbs to a break-neck speed. Luckily the environment is extremely forgiving, as smashing through building corners or large obstacles is but fluff to this bat-tank. It is well integrated into the puzzle gameplay found in some of the main missions and I found the Riddler tracks to be a blast to navigate. Battling the Knight's drone forces is simple, but satisfying. Unfortunately, Batmobile combat is forced on the player way too often in the main campaign, deluding the experience and making these sections feel repetitive.
For completionists, you are in for a fun and satisfying confrontation with the Riddler. Collecting every Riddler trophy is an arduous (there are 243 of them), but rewarding experience in the end.
Achieving 100% in the game gains the player an alternate, much expanded ending to Arkham Knight. While it is questionable to put such an in-depth epilogue behind a Riddler-Collecting, Side-Mission-Completing barrier, it is a nice reward for those who have worked to get 100% completion. If you aren't up to the task, make sure to Youtube it after finishing the main campaign. It is definitely worth your time.
In all, I highly reccomend this game to Arkham fans. It is great capstone to the Arkham story. Make sure your hardware meets specifications, as this game is as gorgeous as it is technically demanding.

I've been a fan of South Park's unique brand of humor for quite some time, so I was able to appreciate all the innuendo pulled from the wide lore of the South Park world. Though the game's mechanics are simple, I feel this best compliments the gameplay because the emphasis is put on inside humor that fans of the series will recognize quickly. From the ever-kind Butters patting you on the back and giving you words of encouragement as a "Heal" spell, to Jimmy Vaughmer rocking the mic with a dirty lyric that he stutters through and ends by defiantly dropping the mic on stage as a Buff ability, the game is chock-full of South Park's idiosyncracies that made me laugh and chuckle more times than I can remember.
On the other hand, there are more than a couple instances where the game's UI frustratingly does not properly convey what you need to do, and instead, you are left to try and fail of your own accord repeatedly, or hedge your bets and find out through the Internet just what the hell they wanted you to see/do. Noteably, the game's "Mash buttons" Quick-Time-like events are a large failure due to the fact that if you do mash buttons too quickly, the game fails to register the presses and acts as if you aren't pressing at all. You have to try many times until you can find the sweet spot where it considers someone is pushing the buttons at the rate needed. As you can guess, this was a trial and error process that easily resulted in over 50+ failures throughout the game.
Ultimately, I completed every mission and sidequest on the first playthrough, coming in just at 25 hours of play. Despite the game's frustrating interface issues, Matt and Trey's unique bent on satire comes through this game in spades, and I give it a 84/100.

Not even sure how to start writing a review for Half-Life 2. I'd almost be tempted to just say this: If you are in any way the slightest bit interested in FPS games you owe it to yourself to play this game.
Even if you are not interested in FPS as a genre you owe it to yourself to complete this masterpiece at least once. Does it have the concepts of modern shooters? No. There's no grand cinematic scenes to rival a Hollywood blockbuster; no aim down sight; no realistically modelled weapons with upgrades; no xp, unlocking or levelling up system.
What it does have is almost genre defining. It boasts a well crafted world, a story that grips and propels you through its magnificent atmosphere and a protagonist you can't help but like and admire - a pretty strong feat considering that the man whose shoes you fill never utters a single word.
It's one of those classics that will stand the test of time. Even if you never play it again after your first playthrough it will have been worth it. Trust me - I've completed it at least once a year since it was released and I still have no reason not to.

South Park: The Stick of Truth turned out to be everything I'd expect from a game based on the South Park show: intentionally primitive in some visual and gameplay aspects but obscene and entertaining. I felt like I was part of the show, making the calls and mashing faces. It's one of those games you frequently remember at work and look forward to playing when you get home. I haven't beaten the game yet, so I can't yet say if there is much replay value. Chances are that there is.

A heads up, there is only one life per playthrough.  You die = you start over.
As far as I can tell, the levels themselves are built semi-randomish, but it's usually not that hard to find your way around after a little practice.  The first and second levels are always the same area (not same map), with the 3rd level (assuming you get there) apparently having a chance to be one of two, and so on.
There are 3 difficulties.  Drizzle, Rainstorm, and Monsoon.  You cannot unlock item and monster logs on drizzle, but everything else can be done there.  All this basically does is decide how fast the game ramps up.  It starts at about the same place, but on higher difficulties it gets more difficult faster.  The game's in-game difficulty starts at very easy with the words "Very Easy" next to a timer and an experience bar.  As the timer ticks away, the bar gets more experience and eventually the difficulty levels up.  It caps out at "AHAHAHAHAHA" (approximately spelled right).  The higher the difficulty in-game, the more health and damage and sheer numbers enemies have, and the stronger the enemy types that show up.  Realistically though?  It gets ridiculous as soon as the first difficulty level up occurs.
The whole point of the game is to get to the teleporter in each level, activate it, wait for 99 seconds, and then kill all enemies in the level.  99 seconds is basically how long it will take before enemies stop respawning.  When you activate a teleporter, a boss enemy is guaranteed to show up, but whatever happens at any other point in time varies by difficulty and time elapsed.  As far as I can tell, the level one boss is a colossus and the level 2 boss is a magma wurm.  I am not sure if this is set or not, but the 4 times I've beaten level one and the 2 times I've gotten to the level 2 teleporter it's been true.  The colossus is just a giant @#$# regular minion that does 4 times the damage, while the magma wurm is the hard to keep track of looping through the environment kind of boss.  I've also seen an ancient wisp as a random spawn, which basically summoned columns of fire to mess with me.  :)   Once you've killed all enemies after the 99 seconds has passed, you can reactivate the teleporter to go to the next level.  The game has a fixed number of levels, although the order apparently varies randomly (I haven't gotten far enough to truly verify this), with a fixed final level and final boss.
As difficulty goes, I have one problem with the game.  And that is that it really is a ton of luck.  Enemy damage and health amounts increase at a rate significantly faster than your health and damage amounts.  The difference has to be made up by in game items, which you have to get by killing enemies and spending the coins they drop (they also drop experience to level you up a little) to open chests / use shrines.  Chests cost a fixed amount, and some of them have items on display with your one time choice of one of three, but shrines are truly random.  Shrines have a chance of giving you absolutely nothing for your hard earned money, or worse.  The flipside of that is that chests are single use while shrines are multi-use, albeit at a higher price each attempt.  There are also some shrines where you can pay health, which is..... kind of severely risky but has higher rewards possible.
Never the less, a good thing about items, assuming you get enough to keep up, is that every single one of them is stackable and has a practical use.  None of them are bs items you hate to receive.  And there are dozens of different kinds, all of them unique.  A successful run will usually see you getting hundreds of items.
The enemy variety is also fantastic.  There are about 2 - dozen kinds of basic enemy, and more than a quarter of them have a boss version.  In addition, there are some bosses like the magma worm without a basic enemy :).  And almost every enemy is deadly.  There are also "elite" versions of enemies with elemental auras and such that cause you quite a bit of mischief.  Especially the overloading versions of bosses, which I have seen one of on Monsoon difficulty.
The controls are basic.  You have 4 abilities assigned to 4 buttons, you have the 4 directional movements, you have a jump button, you have a button to activate stuff, and you have a button to use your "use" item.  One problem with the controls is that you have to hold "up" down continuously to grab onto a ladder, and this is finicky enough to cause some serious issues at certain points in time.  Jumping also has to be done very exactly in certain areas or you miss very easily.
Multiplayer wise, the game has up to 4 player co-op.  The game becomes significantly easier in co-op.  I know this because I personally controlled two characters simultaneously (Jack can do that because he plays too much Guitar Hero), and one of them got to level 8 and the other got to level 12 before they both died.  This was one of the two runs where I almost beat the second level, and it was the significantly easier of the two.
The only real problem with multiplayer is that they did not include any kind of matchmaking.  Or lobbies.  AT ALL.  You have to either play locally, with the 2nd and up person(s) using other control devices, or have someone host a server themselves.  And heads up.  There are noticeable possible security risks to hosting a server if you don't trust the other persons.  Which basically means.......... it's very hard to get in an actual co-op game here.  Which means that even though the game feels built for co-op difficulty scaling wise, the lack of any matchmaking whatsoever makes it very very hard for you to get into a game and requires extraordinary planning ahead of time honestly to do it safely.  So ...... the multiplayer kind of sucks.
Overall, the only real problem other than no matchmaking I have had is that all of the unlocks, including the character unlocks that are supposed to be the replayability factor, come from doing things like beating the game 5 times, or beating a really hard enemy or something on level 4, etc.  I think the easiest is to beat level 3?  And some of the better items, the ones that make your playthroughs a lot easier, have hard unlock conditions in themselves.
Overall, I would recommend the game at it's current sale price.  It's 3.39 right now, which I believe is totally worth it if you like "rogue-like platformers".  That being said, I would not believe it to be worth $10.
Overall , I say 6/10 at the sale price.

South Park: The Stick of Truth: It’s a very rare thing to see licenses from television shows or movies be made into a videogame and actually turn out to be a great game. South Park: The Stick of Truth is one of those rare occasions. A great role-playing game made by Obsidian Entertainment (creators of Fallout: New Vegas) along with the creators of South Park (who also do a lot of the voice acting) to create a funny and simple game in which to celebrate the world of South Park and also to give fans something to enjoy for years to come. While relatively short by most role-playing game standards, lasting between 15-18 hours, The Stick of Truth gives enough variety and plenty of humor to make it an easily enjoyable experience and worth the asking price. Everything in the game is wholly belonging to South Park, it has songs from episodes dotted throughout the game, voice actors make a return to voice their respective characters and everything feels like South Park. Visuals also feel directly translated from the show, the game feels like a very long episode of the show. Controls are simple and easy to learn, the game overall is pretty easy with only a few enemies posing a decent challenge so you won’t feel very much pressure from the combat portion of the game. The only real detriment to South Park: The Stick of Truth is the fact that it is everything South Park. While I personally find the game to be funny and enjoy the jokes, it is easy to see how this game can turn away those who aren’t huge fans or hate the humor that South Park has and there isn’t an amazing enough role-playing game here to win those on the fence about South Park over. The other minor gripe with the game is the controls when using the mouse and keyboards. Some of the abilities didn’t feel like they responded as well when using their respective keys versus a controller. I also experience a few glitches such as Jimmy not getting out of his stuttering loop and some minor glitches of my character flickering in and out of a scene during a cinematic.
Overall I enjoyed my time with South Park: The Stick of Truth, there is a fun role-playing game here along with the great humor of South Park. Those who won’t enjoy this game are those who are going to be offended by what is displayed in the game or just don’t enjoy the humor of South Park. If you are middle of the ground and don’t mind the humor the role-playing game beneath may not be enough to warrant a full $60.00 USD price tag.
-Thumbs Up from Royial

A heads up, there is only one life per playthrough.  You die = you start over.
As far as I can tell, the levels themselves are built semi-randomish, but it's usually not that hard to find your way around after a little practice.  The first and second levels are always the same area (not same map), with the 3rd level (assuming you get there) apparently having a chance to be one of two, and so on.
There are 3 difficulties.  Drizzle, Rainstorm, and Monsoon.  You cannot unlock item and monster logs on drizzle, but everything else can be done there.  All this basically does is decide how fast the game ramps up.  It starts at about the same place, but on higher difficulties it gets more difficult faster.  The game's in-game difficulty starts at very easy with the words "Very Easy" next to a timer and an experience bar.  As the timer ticks away, the bar gets more experience and eventually the difficulty levels up.  It caps out at "AHAHAHAHAHA" (approximately spelled right).  The higher the difficulty in-game, the more health and damage and sheer numbers enemies have, and the stronger the enemy types that show up.  Realistically though?  It gets ridiculous as soon as the first difficulty level up occurs.
The whole point of the game is to get to the teleporter in each level, activate it, wait for 99 seconds, and then kill all enemies in the level.  99 seconds is basically how long it will take before enemies stop respawning.  When you activate a teleporter, a boss enemy is guaranteed to show up, but whatever happens at any other point in time varies by difficulty and time elapsed.  As far as I can tell, the level one boss is a colossus and the level 2 boss is a magma wurm.  I am not sure if this is set or not, but the 4 times I've beaten level one and the 2 times I've gotten to the level 2 teleporter it's been true.  The colossus is just a giant @#$# regular minion that does 4 times the damage, while the magma wurm is the hard to keep track of looping through the environment kind of boss.  I've also seen an ancient wisp as a random spawn, which basically summoned columns of fire to mess with me.  :)   Once you've killed all enemies after the 99 seconds has passed, you can reactivate the teleporter to go to the next level.  The game has a fixed number of levels, although the order apparently varies randomly (I haven't gotten far enough to truly verify this), with a fixed final level and final boss.
As difficulty goes, I have one problem with the game.  And that is that it really is a ton of luck.  Enemy damage and health amounts increase at a rate significantly faster than your health and damage amounts.  The difference has to be made up by in game items, which you have to get by killing enemies and spending the coins they drop (they also drop experience to level you up a little) to open chests / use shrines.  Chests cost a fixed amount, and some of them have items on display with your one time choice of one of three, but shrines are truly random.  Shrines have a chance of giving you absolutely nothing for your hard earned money, or worse.  The flipside of that is that chests are single use while shrines are multi-use, albeit at a higher price each attempt.  There are also some shrines where you can pay health, which is..... kind of severely risky but has higher rewards possible.
Never the less, a good thing about items, assuming you get enough to keep up, is that every single one of them is stackable and has a practical use.  None of them are bs items you hate to receive.  And there are dozens of different kinds, all of them unique.  A successful run will usually see you getting hundreds of items.
The enemy variety is also fantastic.  There are about 2 - dozen kinds of basic enemy, and more than a quarter of them have a boss version.  In addition, there are some bosses like the magma worm without a basic enemy :).  And almost every enemy is deadly.  There are also "elite" versions of enemies with elemental auras and such that cause you quite a bit of mischief.  Especially the overloading versions of bosses, which I have seen one of on Monsoon difficulty.
The controls are basic.  You have 4 abilities assigned to 4 buttons, you have the 4 directional movements, you have a jump button, you have a button to activate stuff, and you have a button to use your "use" item.  One problem with the controls is that you have to hold "up" down continuously to grab onto a ladder, and this is finicky enough to cause some serious issues at certain points in time.  Jumping also has to be done very exactly in certain areas or you miss very easily.
Multiplayer wise, the game has up to 4 player co-op.  The game becomes significantly easier in co-op.  I know this because I personally controlled two characters simultaneously (Jack can do that because he plays too much Guitar Hero), and one of them got to level 8 and the other got to level 12 before they both died.  This was one of the two runs where I almost beat the second level, and it was the significantly easier of the two.
The only real problem with multiplayer is that they did not include any kind of matchmaking.  Or lobbies.  AT ALL.  You have to either play locally, with the 2nd and up person(s) using other control devices, or have someone host a server themselves.  And heads up.  There are noticeable possible security risks to hosting a server if you don't trust the other persons.  Which basically means.......... it's very hard to get in an actual co-op game here.  Which means that even though the game feels built for co-op difficulty scaling wise, the lack of any matchmaking whatsoever makes it very very hard for you to get into a game and requires extraordinary planning ahead of time honestly to do it safely.  So ...... the multiplayer kind of sucks.
Overall, the only real problem other than no matchmaking I have had is that all of the unlocks, including the character unlocks that are supposed to be the replayability factor, come from doing things like beating the game 5 times, or beating a really hard enemy or something on level 4, etc.  I think the easiest is to beat level 3?  And some of the better items, the ones that make your playthroughs a lot easier, have hard unlock conditions in themselves.
Overall, I would recommend the game at it's current sale price.  It's 3.39 right now, which I believe is totally worth it if you like "rogue-like platformers".  That being said, I would not believe it to be worth $10.
Overall , I say 6/10 at the sale price.

You buy a video game to play it, not to stare at it and nitpick the ♥♥♥♥ing video quality. It's choppy, but no more than any of my other games are, get the hell over yourselves.

Killing Floor 1 was one of my favorite games of all time. I had strong doubts that Tripwire would be able to take the expansive, challenging, mod-based gameplay and bring it into a console-friendly sequel.
Those doubts are dead. KF2 somehow even better. The action is much closer and frenetic, but success still feels primarily dependent on teamwork. Experience and perks have been skillfully overhauled. The music and graphics are still unapologetically brutal (though I could do without the incessant little song title popups). The bosses are WAY more fun to fight, scaling up gradually rather than suddenly one-shotting people for slip-ups.
All KF2 needs now is more maps and weapons, which I'm sure Tripwire will be quintupling for free over the next year. Otherwise there's no reason not to buy this, for any price, right now.

My roomate tried starting a new game and it does let you have multiple save files but even though i never saved over his file it will magically dissapear, so I think there is some issues technically with the saving system. I will say this is more of an issue if you are sharing the game with a friend or you wanted to create another character but keep your old game.
The fighting system has some minor snags. The time the "block" icon comes up and when you push the buttons on a hooked up controller, has delay so pretty much just block when something makes contact don't pay attention to the block icon. You just have the time things yourself which is fine but it's irritatiing to have the icon even in the game if you'll never pay attention to it.
I beat the game on normal difficulty but I highly suggest lowering the difficulty to casual for your first playthrough so you can just enjoy the story and have fun. It gets quite difficult at the very end and instead of laughing with the game I was kind of just glad it was over because of how frustrating the final boss is.

I will be honest and say the ending is not as good as it could have been in a sense that I felt very little pay off for beating the final boss at the end of the main story. It wasn't awful, it was even decent but I think it could have been (should have been) way more over the top like the rest of the game was. A boss fight in the middle of the game is way more of a shocking and interesting moment then the last boss is. I think that's a flaw.
Anyways I'm glad I played the game and I don't want to come off the wrong way but I did have some issues with it that brought me out of the game. Again lower the difficulty on the first play. Overall I'd give technical parts of the game a 7 and the story an 8 so overall a 7.5  is fair I think. I'd also wait to buy it until it goes on sale unless you just have 60 dollars to drop like I did. Just saying :)

Killing Floor 1 was one of my favorite games of all time. I had strong doubts that Tripwire would be able to take the expansive, challenging, mod-based gameplay and bring it into a console-friendly sequel.
Those doubts are dead. KF2 somehow even better. The action is much closer and frenetic, but success still feels primarily dependent on teamwork. Experience and perks have been skillfully overhauled. The music and graphics are still unapologetically brutal (though I could do without the incessant little song title popups). The bosses are WAY more fun to fight, scaling up gradually rather than suddenly one-shotting people for slip-ups.
All KF2 needs now is more maps and weapons, which I'm sure Tripwire will be quintupling for free over the next year. Otherwise there's no reason not to buy this, for any price, right now.

It's nice that the game is finally in a good enough condition to play at least mostly properly. The game doesn't surprise and it definitely doesn't like feel like the grand finale to the Arkham series I was hoping for. It's good, even great sometimes, just not great enough.

While I did enjoy this game and I do recommend it...it does have some obvious flaws.
Mainly my biggest gripe is the saving. I willl save my spot in the game and it refuses to save right where I am at. I am pretty sure this has nothing to do with my computer, and I hope this is patched soon. If you try to save in an exact spot it will only let you save where you were at your last checkpoint. My roomate tried starting a new game and it does let you have multiple save files but even though i never saved over his file it will magically dissapear, so I think there is some issues technically with the saving system. I will say this is more of an issue if you are sharing the game with a friend or you wanted to create another character but keep your old game.
The fighting system has some minor snags. The time the "block" icon comes up and when you push the buttons on a hooked up controller, has delay so pretty much just block when something makes contact don't pay attention to the block icon. You just have the time things yourself which is fine but it's irritatiing to have the icon even in the game if you'll never pay attention to it.
I beat the game on normal difficulty but I highly suggest lowering the difficulty to casual for your first playthrough so you can just enjoy the story and have fun. It gets quite difficult at the very end and instead of laughing with the game I was kind of just glad it was over because of how frustrating the final boss is.
The story is the glowing part of this game. You will see many characters some you may have not thought about in a long time. I don't want to go too into it, but I will say it's an overall good story. I will be honest and say the ending is not as good as it could have been in a sense that I felt very little pay off for beating the final boss at the end of the main story. It wasn't awful, it was even decent but I think it could have been (should have been) way more over the top like the rest of the game was. A boss fight in the middle of the game is way more of a shocking and interesting moment then the last boss is. I think that's a flaw.
Anyways I'm glad I played the game and I don't want to come off the wrong way but I did have some issues with it that brought me out of the game. Again lower the difficulty on the first play. Overall I'd give technical parts of the game a 7 and the story an 8 so overall a 7.5  is fair I think. I'd also wait to buy it until it goes on sale unless you just have 60 dollars to drop like I did. Just saying :)

Early Access Review: I have been playing Killing Floor 2 since Early Access launched back in April. When the game released it was a breath of fresh air coming from Killing Floor but the content was very limited. At the time I believe there were 3 maps and four perks all of which got boring rather quickly. Fast forward to today and the game has certainly made a large leap in the somewhat right direction.
Not much has changed from the original Killing Floor when it comes to KF2. The basis is still the same. Kill zeds, survive the wave, obtain dosh, purchase weapons rinse and repeat until you down the boss in the final wave. Difficulties seem to be in a good spot as well with Hard increasing the difficulty from normal at the right amount and so on until you reach Hell on Earth.
The weapon diversity is slowly raising from when the game first released and each perk has a decent amount of perk and side perk weapons to choose from for you Zed killing needs.
The zeds themselves are well designed and each of their mechanics require you to think quickly if swarmed so that you dont get grabbed, puked on, stabbed, smacked across the room or have your ear drums explode.
The cash shop as of right now is the only downfall I see to the game, I feel it was implimented to early and alot of players from what I see feel the same. That being said I would be lying if I said I havent used it.
All and all the game is worth every penny I have spent on it and can only get better with each update.

While I did enjoy this game and I do recommend it...it does have some obvious flaws.
Mainly my biggest gripe is the saving. I willl save my spot in the game and it refuses to save right where I am at. I am pretty sure this has nothing to do with my computer, and I hope this is patched soon. If you try to save in an exact spot it will only let you save where you were at your last checkpoint. My roomate tried starting a new game and it does let you have multiple save files but even though i never saved over his file it will magically dissapear, so I think there is some issues technically with the saving system. I will say this is more of an issue if you are sharing the game with a friend or you wanted to create another character but keep your old game.
The fighting system has some minor snags. The time the "block" icon comes up and when you push the buttons on a hooked up controller, has delay so pretty much just block when something makes contact don't pay attention to the block icon. You just have the time things yourself which is fine but it's irritatiing to have the icon even in the game if you'll never pay attention to it.
I beat the game on normal difficulty but I highly suggest lowering the difficulty to casual for your first playthrough so you can just enjoy the story and have fun. It gets quite difficult at the very end and instead of laughing with the game I was kind of just glad it was over because of how frustrating the final boss is.
The story is the glowing part of this game. You will see many characters some you may have not thought about in a long time. I don't want to go too into it, but I will say it's an overall good story. I will be honest and say the ending is not as good as it could have been in a sense that I felt very little pay off for beating the final boss at the end of the main story. It wasn't awful, it was even decent but I think it could have been (should have been) way more over the top like the rest of the game was. A boss fight in the middle of the game is way more of a shocking and interesting moment then the last boss is. I think that's a flaw.
Anyways I'm glad I played the game and I don't want to come off the wrong way but I did have some issues with it that brought me out of the game. Again lower the difficulty on the first play. Overall I'd give technical parts of the game a 7 and the story an 8 so overall a 7.5  is fair I think. I'd also wait to buy it until it goes on sale unless you just have 60 dollars to drop like I did. Just saying :)

"EARLY ACCESS" While this game is in so called early access it is more of a early release than anything else. The game is polished and perfectly functional with few if any bugs. There were however too few classes available on release but that has been remedied since.
WARNING: this is more of a revew for veterans of KF1 as I will go into comparisons with the Original.
Let's make it simple:
Pros:
-Graphics: The game is beautiful and the gore is exeptional.
-Graphics: Blood is persistent (you will paint the town red)
-Immersion: The gore engine enables breaking up of zeds into multiple pieces, it's very satisfying.
-Immersion: Sc/Fp will sound a recognisable "scream" when they spawn building up your anticipation/dread.
-Immersion: The music is exellent, as usual.
-Gameplay: Perk progress is much better than in kf1, no more grinding stalkers and so on...
-Gameplay: Weapons are well priced and their damage scales well with each upgrade, no truly op guns.
-Gameplay: More than 1 boss now, you never know who you're going to fight at the end which keeps things interesting.
Cons:
-Gameplay: Scrakes and Fleshpounds are a little too powerfull in lower game difficulties and most pubs can't even handle them in Hard leading to 2-3 deaths every last few waves bringing the game to a halt. Scrakes espetially seem to have far more health than they did in kf1 but maybe it's just because everyone is low perked atm.
-Gameplay: While the two above seem a little op the boss on the other hand feels a little underwhelming, more of a health sack than an actual danger, I would find it more engaging if bosses didn't have this humongous health pool but dealt a little more damage, after all they do heal up... twice.
-Gameplay: Perks do not have enough weapon choice.
As far as the overall game is concerned that about raps it up, however there are issues with individual perks.
Berserker:
- I hate the new melee system, while it offers greater potential I just find something really off with it. I used to love berserker, I just can't stand it anymore.
- The Katana is the best feeling weapon but also not a perk weapon and therefor useless because of it's low damage.
Medic:
- Nothing much to say, it works well, you can level by dealing damage and you have a good range of weapon types.
Commando:
- Not overly powerfull but you are good at cleaning up those small zeds, just don't hope to be usefull against the big guys untill you have your Scar... not as much fun as in kf1.
Support:
-Probably the best class atm, very powerfull against anything and great fun to play. not enough weapons though and you need to be high level to use both of your top tier weapons at the same time. My favorit perk by far.
Firebug:
- Same as the support, a really fun perk to play, very powerfull against small zeds in groups but less so agains the big ones, a very powerfull cleanup class and not as anoying as in kf1. Nothing bad to say about it, just don't role with more than 1/team.
Demo:
- Bad perk atm, just so bad. The starting weapon is garbage, sell it and get dual 9mm asap to be usefull then hoard cash for the RPG. Then spend the rest of the match waiting for clumps of zeds to 1shot and then waist you ammo on scrakes because I just can't tell if it's actually hurting them. Strange class, used to be very op in kf1 I guess they nerfed it to the ground. You don't have enough ammo and you can't carry more than you RPG so you're going to spend most of your time spamming double 9mm all over the place... they need to fix this, don't get me wrong it kinda works it's just not fun.
Gunslinger:
- Best perk in the game for usefullness, it's also great fun to play. You are the one who will deal with the Big zeds by going right into their faces and unloading 6 weapons worth of ammo into their face. Nothing bad to say about it.
CONCLUSION:
If you were a hardcore fan of KF1 you might not like this one. I loved kf and while I feel at home with kf2 it's not quite the same home. I do go back to kf1 when I want a challenge, but a fair one with my favorit classes and weapons. KF2 just doesn't have that for me yet. The game is fun to play of course but I never play more than 2 games in a row. I can stay on kf1 for a whole day, even now. Give this game a little more time and I'm sure it will polish of what needs to be and we'll have a great experience with kf yet again.

PC Porting and performance issues aside, this is an amazing game. I have played every game in this series to completion, some to 100% and I consider this a worthy addition to the franchise. The main story is fantastic, the side plots are well developed and varied, and everything has a feeling of diversity. Taking the checkpoints and towers could have been repetitive but they did a great job of making each feel unique.
As with every prior game (save, perhaps for Arkham Origins) the developers worked hard to add new mechanics and tweak gameplay to make it feel like more than just a new story. There are new combat enemies, new aspects of the predator system, a new upgrade tree, and new gadget abilities. Even the grappling and gliding system was updated to be much faster to compensate for the tremendous open world.
And what a world it is. The devs did a great job at packing in tons of background activity that services no other purpose than to make the world feel real. The sum total of the environment is that the game, more than ever before, feels like a real batman simulator and less like a game. Whether you are flying over the buildings to driving around the streets, Gotham feels real, and I love that!
Speak of driving, it took me a while to warm up to the car. Right off the bat (no pun intended), the handling is incredibly bad. Even after hours of practice and a better understanding of the boost and drift mechanics, I often feel barely in control of the Batmobile. This slightly inhibits the “I am Batman” feeling that otherwise engulfs the game because Batman should be able to leave the GCPD without running over half the concrete barriers in the deck. I also feel like the environment destruction is almost overdone. I find it very enjoyable but being able to drive straight through a meter thick concrete pillar at 3 MPH seems ridiculous. I also find it interesting that Batman, who never kills, can drive head on into a car causing an instant explosion. Pretty sure they guys in there wouldn’t come out alive. However, in the end, now that I have obtained some semblance of control I consider the car to be a great addition to the game. The drone fights are enjoyable, the Riddler puzzles are interesting, and it adds a new way to traverse and experience the beautiful world. (Although, grappling and gliding will always be a method of choice)
A quick note on performance, I have a GTX 970 and i5 4590. Very early on, I found a guide to tweaking performance that worked quite well. Now that updates have come out, I am able to play on reasonably high stock settings. I still consider the porting fiasco to be inexcusable but I can’t really complain. I was able to buy a new game for $20. I also received a free copy with my GTX 970 (Newegg) which I sold for $20. Then I hit up Newegg and told them that the game didn’t work well so they gave me a copy of MGS V, which I sold for $35. I know, however, that a lot of people who bought the game through Steam pretty much got screwed and you have every right to be upset about that. I just want to make sure that people know that the game itself is fantastic. Once the game is patched well enough to work with your system, it is well worth playing.

Wow..... wow, what to say? As an established South Park fan I guess I was always going to go into this game with an apologist mindset trying my hardest to love the game; hoping that maybe after a poor track record, like every other licencesed property in the games industry, that the game would be even half to South Park what Arkham Asylum was to Batman. I did not expect this.
I ******* loved this game, and was overwhelmed with a sense of dread and sadness as I neared its conclusion, very few games have triggered that reaction. The characters, humour, graphics, animations, plot, soundtrack and general feel of the game were all absolutely nailed and I can't think of a single major flaw with the game. The closest I can get to a flaw is the length, people blasting through the main story as fast as possible might finish the game in just 8-9 hours, those who stretch it out with exploration, side quests and farting on as many people as possible can push above 25 hours in a single playthrough but when you compare that with the 100+ hours of a lot of other open world RPGs it DOES leave you wanting more. However, I'm left wondering whether that's better when compared to how Skyrim and Fallout 3/New Vegas, three of my favourite games ever, simply petered out for me, eventually withering away into boredom and eventual uninstallment whereas I'm being dragged away from South Park kicking and screaming. Die young and all that.
This isn't a game for only the most die-hard of fans, in fact the only people I wouldn't recommend the game to are the fuddy duddies who despise South Park and its humour, either getting offended by it or simply not finding it funny in the least. This is not the game for such fuddy duddies. For everyone else though, this game is amazing and completely worth the £40/$60 in my opinion, they could have retroactively charged double and I would still have paid it.

Early Access Review: I have been playing Killing Floor 2 since Early Access launched back in April. When the game released it was a breath of fresh air coming from Killing Floor but the content was very limited. At the time I believe there were 3 maps and four perks all of which got boring rather quickly. Fast forward to today and the game has certainly made a large leap in the somewhat right direction.
Not much has changed from the original Killing Floor when it comes to KF2. The basis is still the same. Kill zeds, survive the wave, obtain dosh, purchase weapons rinse and repeat until you down the boss in the final wave. Difficulties seem to be in a good spot as well with Hard increasing the difficulty from normal at the right amount and so on until you reach Hell on Earth.
The weapon diversity is slowly raising from when the game first released and each perk has a decent amount of perk and side perk weapons to choose from for you Zed killing needs.
The zeds themselves are well designed and each of their mechanics require you to think quickly if swarmed so that you dont get grabbed, puked on, stabbed, smacked across the room or have your ear drums explode.
The cash shop as of right now is the only downfall I see to the game, I feel it was implimented to early and alot of players from what I see feel the same. That being said I would be lying if I said I havent used it.
All and all the game is worth every penny I have spent on it and can only get better with each update.

It's been over 3 months since launch, I have the season pass and all I have to show for it is a skin, and we have no estimated release date on a fixed version.  To top it all off, I'm stuck on a roof in new game plus due to a logic error in the design and no one seems to be addressing that issue (Google "Arkham Knight stuck on roof Founder's Island"; I'm not alone).
The good: I beat the game and 100%'ed it, then started NG+ and would have beaten that were it not for the game-ending bug.  The story was good and they added new gameplay mechanics to stop us from falling into auto-pilot from previous installments.  For as much hate as they got, I really liked the "tank" sequences (except for one... "boss fight" that was ruined by the tank experience).  The team-ups with various Bat-family allies was pretty cool and there were a lot of really neat moments alluding to (or recreating) classic moments in Batman lore.  I genuinely enjoyed it.
The bad: The game's broken.  I have a GTX980 and 24GB ram and blah blah blah who cares.  It's a bumpin' system over here, you get the picture.  The framerate was wanting even considering these factors, and it plummetted during somewhat common occurrences such as powersliding the Batmobile.  When I was playing it, there was a weird bug where the lowest resolution textures would load.  They tried to fix this in late August--you know, two months after launch--but this patch, while a good first step, introduced some other issues.  I have this weird one where some building textures fail to render at all and appear as this weird, out-of-place, bright, confetti pattern.  I joked to my girlfriend that maybe this was some kind of surprise Crazy Quilt DLC, but I was stuck on a roof, so I couldn't investigate.
There are no challenge maps.  Sure, there  are AR challenges, but you don't have the choice of characters you did in Arkham City (or even Arkham Origins) and there aren't nearly enough.  This severely limits the game's value.  There is no DLC for the PC version currently, meaning if you paid for the season pass (like I did), you paid $40 (or in my case, $30 -- thanks, Steam sales!) for a Batman Beyond skin or something.
They said that they'd fix the game in the coming weeks.  Well, it's 3 months later and we have nothing.  The last status update was 26 days ago.  Even if they release a miracle patch that fixes everything, is this the kind of developer/publisher you want to support?
Avoid.

PC Porting and performance issues aside, this is an amazing game. I have played every game in this series to completion, some to 100% and I consider this a worthy addition to the franchise. The main story is fantastic, the side plots are well developed and varied, and everything has a feeling of diversity. Taking the checkpoints and towers could have been repetitive but they did a great job of making each feel unique.
As with every prior game (save, perhaps for Arkham Origins) the developers worked hard to add new mechanics and tweak gameplay to make it feel like more than just a new story. There are new combat enemies, new aspects of the predator system, a new upgrade tree, and new gadget abilities. Even the grappling and gliding system was updated to be much faster to compensate for the tremendous open world.
And what a world it is. The devs did a great job at packing in tons of background activity that services no other purpose than to make the world feel real. The sum total of the environment is that the game, more than ever before, feels like a real batman simulator and less like a game. Whether you are flying over the buildings to driving around the streets, Gotham feels real, and I love that!
Speak of driving, it took me a while to warm up to the car. Right off the bat (no pun intended), the handling is incredibly bad. Even after hours of practice and a better understanding of the boost and drift mechanics, I often feel barely in control of the Batmobile. This slightly inhibits the “I am Batman” feeling that otherwise engulfs the game because Batman should be able to leave the GCPD without running over half the concrete barriers in the deck. I also feel like the environment destruction is almost overdone. I find it very enjoyable but being able to drive straight through a meter thick concrete pillar at 3 MPH seems ridiculous. I also find it interesting that Batman, who never kills, can drive head on into a car causing an instant explosion. Pretty sure they guys in there wouldn’t come out alive. However, in the end, now that I have obtained some semblance of control I consider the car to be a great addition to the game. The drone fights are enjoyable, the Riddler puzzles are interesting, and it adds a new way to traverse and experience the beautiful world. (Although, grappling and gliding will always be a method of choice)
A quick note on performance, I have a GTX 970 and i5 4590. Very early on, I found a guide to tweaking performance that worked quite well. Now that updates have come out, I am able to play on reasonably high stock settings. I still consider the porting fiasco to be inexcusable but I can’t really complain. I was able to buy a new game for $20. I also received a free copy with my GTX 970 (Newegg) which I sold for $20. Then I hit up Newegg and told them that the game didn’t work well so they gave me a copy of MGS V, which I sold for $35. I know, however, that a lot of people who bought the game through Steam pretty much got screwed and you have every right to be upset about that. I just want to make sure that people know that the game itself is fantastic. Once the game is patched well enough to work with your system, it is well worth playing.

Strap yourself in for some platformed controller supported mayhem (I highly recommend the controller but that's a personal opinion based thing)! Risk of Rain is a lot like that Adventure Time episode "Dungeon Train", you venture through a fixed amount of stages where the objective in the first few are the same. Defeat enemies or loot treasure chests to gain XP to level up and acquire gold for locked gear chests. Why I compare it to the episode is because Finn found several unique items that had their own special abilities and he just stacked them which you do here, find gear with attributes and combine them to make you better in combat (damage heals you, dead enemies kill other ones, etc)!
You must find a teleporter in each of these stages to start an onslaught of monsters, including a boss fight or two and you must survive for 90 intense seconds then finish off the remaining mobs. That is your mission until harder levels (then the scenario changes to a larger onslaught :O), but you better do this fast! The longer time you take to finish your gameplay the higher goes the difficulty, and you better be geared up if it gets too high or it's back to the start for you.
Let's hit those pros and cons!
- The game is a rogue-like arcade game. If you die you must go back and try the whole thing again at the start and as Yatzee quoted in his review of Dark Souls 2 when talking about Dark Souls 1, he describes the feeling as stepping on a rake and having it slam in your face.
- Unless you have area wide attacks you better watch out for stacked enemies. They can grow to a troublesome bunch if they have too many kinds of bad guys and that CAN earn you a VERY cheap death if you're not careful.
+ It is a multiplayer game that also enables LAN (when done right, when all the rituals are prepared and the stars align)!
- It is a multiplayer game that also enables LAN but that a bit of a trickster to get right. The connecting in LAN is always troubling and hard to even establish contact with your friend or such. Be sure to have a Hamachi expert at hand before trying.
+ The game has a flawless soundtrack, very ambient and atmospheric that creates this mood to just keep going, all fitting with their co-responding stages!
+ You can fight two bosses at once!
- You can fight two bosses at once.
+ One gameplay is always unique and never like another because of the looting system! You recieve different gear everytime you venture through and that can give you the info of what powerups to choose and which one to (if necessary) leave behind to get that perfect stratagem!
+ As you play for the first time you are limited to one character, the Commando, and only a handful of findable powerups but just you wait. If you pull off a wicked gameplay, murdering away like you've never done before then you WILL unlock more powerups and also a new character or two! And not to forget, they ALL have special move sets and attacks which only makes even more possible combinations of powerups and characters!
Ok what's left? Uh, the game has a nice pixelated texture and animations? Uhh... it's fairly cheap? What else... oh that's right!

Batman Arkham Knight was poorly optimized at launch and still has some issues. The September 3rd patch fixes most of the graphical issues, but still has the slight stalling when using the Batmobile (which you use a lot). The game uses a lot of ram at max settings so be warned if you want a pretty experience. Gameplay is fluid and responsive when using a controller.
I recommend playing this, but waiting for the price to go down and some more patches to come for people on the lower spectrum of  PCs to have a pretty experience. Unless you really enjoy the series, then by all means pick it up if it interest you.
***There are spoilers  below**
The story is the same as previous games, with the villains flaunting in your face. You must save Gotham blah blah blah. A mysterious villain known as the Arkham Knight helps Scarecrow take over Gotham with the help of an army with unmanned tanks and aircrafts. However Arkham Knight knows Batmans strategies. If  you know the comics or any Batman lore you can figure out who it is right away when he starts his speeches.
As for the game.. It doesn't really feel like the previous Batman games. The stealth mechanics from Asylum, City and Origins are still there, but are far and few between. For example if you loved the predator mission in previous games, you only have a select few campaign missions that allow you to experience it. Otherwise you'll have to do Two-face's side missions which is about three extra missions. Don't get me wrong you can still stealth, but there are a lot less opportunties. Brawling and the Batmobile are the main ways to progress through the game.
Arkham Knight heavily focuses on the Batmobile. While the Batmobile is an awesome concept, I did not find this fun. You use it to travel, destroy tanks, mines, air ships, collect riddler trophies, do the riddler missions, fireflies missions and almost everything inbetween. You hardly play as Batman. It's like playing Battlefield's Conquest mode but with dumb A.I while being stuck in a tank. Be prepared to shoot a lot of enemy tanks and get no rewards for it other than skill points and a false sense of accomplishment, because you'll have to do it A LOT if you want to max out.
I haven't collected all the Riddler trophies yet, but like usual they unlock concept art and extra backstory in the game. There are about 250+ of them to collect if you enjoy that.

I'm going to write this review from three different perspectives, ranging from the perspective from which I was the most satisfied, and then the least at the end.
As a Batman fan:  This game is absolutely fantastic.  For the first time ever, you can be Batman in his entire city, not just enclosed areas of it.  As usual, Rocksteady weaves an intricate and intriguing story that provides both entertainment value, and fan service.  The plot ranges from sequences that gave me goosebumps, to parts that mad me feel sad to see this impactful series end.  Additionally, it also feels like they've tied up all the loose ends they began in Askylum and City.  And, as per usual, there are hundreds of little Batman references thrown across the lively map.  Also, because I love Batman, I thought the Batmobile was badass.  All-in-all it feels like the most bang-for-your-buck Batman experience, and I thoroughly appreciate the painstaking effort the developers put into making it that way.
As a videogame player:  Once again, everyhting here is really solid.  Rocksteady has expanded upon series staples, like the freeflow combat system and predator modes, to make the whole thing feel like a natural progression from previous titles in the series.  Speaking of progression, there are no parts of the game where these different gameplay sequences feel monotonous or repetitive, as the developers are always giving you interesting situations to utilize your arsenal of skills.  A very controversial addition to the game is the Batmobile, which I personally didn't mind from a gameplay perspective.  It did seem like something added on to the side, but that's expected when adding a new feature to a series with other adhered features.  Unlike some reviewers, I didn't think the Batmobile was repetitive, and I actually thought some of the puzzling with it was very interesting.  However, I can't say I liked how side missions ended.  Each main villain in the game has a "most wanted" story line to it, and once you complete it, you are able to capture them and put in them in jail.  The problem is, none of these have actual boss fights, and it can feel anti-climactic.  Other than that, Rocksteady has once again done very, very well in the gameplay department.
As a PC owner:  It's pretty obvious what I'm going to say here.  Everything about this port was unstable and cheap from the get-go, but I appreciate the newest patch that fixed all of the main issues.  And yet, despite this much-appreciated fix, the game still looks sub-par to console versions.  Again, completely playable (on high-end systems), but dissapointing.  It really could have been a homerun.
Overall, this game will be remembered.  It will become a classic for Batman fans and for lovers of videogames, and it will become a bittersweet reminder of what could have been for PC owners.

Strap yourself in for some platformed controller supported mayhem (I highly recommend the controller but that's a personal opinion based thing)! Risk of Rain is a lot like that Adventure Time episode "Dungeon Train", you venture through a fixed amount of stages where the objective in the first few are the same. Defeat enemies or loot treasure chests to gain XP to level up and acquire gold for locked gear chests. Why I compare it to the episode is because Finn found several unique items that had their own special abilities and he just stacked them which you do here, find gear with attributes and combine them to make you better in combat (damage heals you, dead enemies kill other ones, etc)!
You must find a teleporter in each of these stages to start an onslaught of monsters, including a boss fight or two and you must survive for 90 intense seconds then finish off the remaining mobs. That is your mission until harder levels (then the scenario changes to a larger onslaught :O), but you better do this fast! The longer time you take to finish your gameplay the higher goes the difficulty, and you better be geared up if it gets too high or it's back to the start for you.
Let's hit those pros and cons!
- The game is a rogue-like arcade game. If you die you must go back and try the whole thing again at the start and as Yatzee quoted in his review of Dark Souls 2 when talking about Dark Souls 1, he describes the feeling as stepping on a rake and having it slam in your face.
- Unless you have area wide attacks you better watch out for stacked enemies. They can grow to a troublesome bunch if they have too many kinds of bad guys and that CAN earn you a VERY cheap death if you're not careful.
+ It is a multiplayer game that also enables LAN (when done right, when all the rituals are prepared and the stars align)!
- It is a multiplayer game that also enables LAN but that a bit of a trickster to get right. The connecting in LAN is always troubling and hard to even establish contact with your friend or such. Be sure to have a Hamachi expert at hand before trying.
+ The game has a flawless soundtrack, very ambient and atmospheric that creates this mood to just keep going, all fitting with their co-responding stages!
+ You can fight two bosses at once!
- You can fight two bosses at once.
+ One gameplay is always unique and never like another because of the looting system! You recieve different gear everytime you venture through and that can give you the info of what powerups to choose and which one to (if necessary) leave behind to get that perfect stratagem!
+ As you play for the first time you are limited to one character, the Commando, and only a handful of findable powerups but just you wait. If you pull off a wicked gameplay, murdering away like you've never done before then you WILL unlock more powerups and also a new character or two! And not to forget, they ALL have special move sets and attacks which only makes even more possible combinations of powerups and characters!
Ok what's left? Uh, the game has a nice pixelated texture and animations? Uhh... it's fairly cheap? What else... oh that's right!

Welcome to A**♥♥♥♥♥♥Planet. Population: Every concievable thing in the universe that wants you dead.
A FANTASTIC action-platformer combined with a roguelike experience, this game will PUNISH you. It's primary feature is it's timer, which counts up from the moment the game begins. As the timer reaches certain points, the game's overall difficulty increases. This means more (and stronger) enemies will spawn to challenge you, so this is literally a race against time!
Start with the simple but effective Commando, unlock up to 9 more characters including (but not limited to), a Sniper, an Alien, and a Robot!
Run across brilliantly designed and semi-randomized stages and map layouts! Jump and dodge through waves and hordes and swarms of brutal enemies! Fight! Power through foes with your innate skills, and become more powerful via the various artifacts, some of which have incredible powers! Collect gold from fallen enemies to purchase MORE artifacts, but don't linger in the same stage too long... time is laughing at you!!!
You may hear some people nag about the multiplayer. It's actually much easier to beat the game with 2 or even just ONE friend. Despite having to share loot, having an extra hand is always a bonus. I highly recommend ONLY playing with good friends you can coordinate with, though. Public groups can be unreliable, trolling, or just plain not sync well with your style.

Batman Arkham Knight was poorly optimized at launch and still has some issues. The September 3rd patch fixes most of the graphical issues, but still has the slight stalling when using the Batmobile (which you use a lot). The game uses a lot of ram at max settings so be warned if you want a pretty experience. Gameplay is fluid and responsive when using a controller.
I recommend playing this, but waiting for the price to go down and some more patches to come for people on the lower spectrum of  PCs to have a pretty experience. Unless you really enjoy the series, then by all means pick it up if it interest you.
***There are spoilers  below**
The story is the same as previous games, with the villains flaunting in your face. You must save Gotham blah blah blah. A mysterious villain known as the Arkham Knight helps Scarecrow take over Gotham with the help of an army with unmanned tanks and aircrafts. However Arkham Knight knows Batmans strategies. If  you know the comics or any Batman lore you can figure out who it is right away when he starts his speeches.
As for the game.. It doesn't really feel like the previous Batman games. The stealth mechanics from Asylum, City and Origins are still there, but are far and few between. For example if you loved the predator mission in previous games, you only have a select few campaign missions that allow you to experience it. Otherwise you'll have to do Two-face's side missions which is about three extra missions. Don't get me wrong you can still stealth, but there are a lot less opportunties. Brawling and the Batmobile are the main ways to progress through the game.
Arkham Knight heavily focuses on the Batmobile. While the Batmobile is an awesome concept, I did not find this fun. You use it to travel, destroy tanks, mines, air ships, collect riddler trophies, do the riddler missions, fireflies missions and almost everything inbetween. You hardly play as Batman. It's like playing Battlefield's Conquest mode but with dumb A.I while being stuck in a tank. Be prepared to shoot a lot of enemy tanks and get no rewards for it other than skill points and a false sense of accomplishment, because you'll have to do it A LOT if you want to max out.
I haven't collected all the Riddler trophies yet, but like usual they unlock concept art and extra backstory in the game. There are about 250+ of them to collect if you enjoy that.
Boss fights from previous games are almost non existant(with the exception of a few).  All you do is either chase them down with your Batmobile, capture them with a counter or take them out with stealth. Then you use the Batmobile to transfer them to the Gotham Police Department and put them in jail. Literally nothing happens when you're doing this. No one tries to break them out or anything. Just a casual stroll to the police department with a little flavor text during the ride.
I shouldn't even have to say anything about this game.
The amount of time I have spent playing this when I could have been doing productive things is terrifiying.

Half Life 2. Called by many "The Greatest Game of All Time", the Half Life series has been known to deliver gameplay you don't see in any other series. ANY. Instead of treating you like a child with a hearing disorder by repeating dialogue to help you through the game and flashing button signs on your monitor at you when it's time to push a button, Half Life tells you to put your big boy pants, thinking cap, and awesome filter on, and to enjoy the ride. Half Life was stunning enough, but Half Life 2 really brought a new standard to the table.
You play as Gordon Freeman, the same badass scientist you played as in Half Life - but wait, what is this? You're 37 now? Insane, really, bloody insane! And who are these weirdos with respiratory issues that wear gasmasks, but are strangely awesome? Well, all these problems will be answered soon enough.
Valve didn't fail to deliver this game. They easily toppled the way we see games with one game: Half Life 2.
What you just read was a review I wrote for Half Life 2 back when it first came out. I still play it today, just to get a breath of fresh air. Do I reccommend this game? No. I treasure it for it's rich storytelling, exciting atmosphere, living, breathing characters.. The list goes on and on.
Truly a journey worth going on.
